The learned Attorney General submitted that as per Article 116 of the Constitution the control and discipline of the members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial function really vest in the president and the same shall be exercised by him in consultation with the Supreme Court. Thus he submits that as per Article 116 of the Constitution in case of posting, promotion and grant of leave and all disciplinary matters in respect of the persons enumerated in article 116 are to be exercised by the president in consultation with the Supreme Court. Under Article 116 of the Constitution the power though vests in the president but the constitutional mandate of consultation on makes it imperative that the opinion of the Supreme Court shall take precedence over the decision of the president. The learned Attorney General rightly pointed out that Article 116 speaks of vesting of control and discipline in the president of persons in the judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions that too in consultation with the Supreme Court to safeguard independence of judiciary. This provision of the constitution clearly reflects the independence of the judiciary. It will be necessary here to consider Articles 115. Article 115 reads as follows:

"Appointments of persons to the office in the judicial service or as magistrates exercising judicial functions shall be made by the president in accordance with the rules made by him in that behalf'.

As a matter of fact, no rule or law has been framed by the President till today in respect of the appointment of persons in the office of the judicial service or as magistrates exercising judicial function. On the president of the Republic a solemn duty is cast to make Rule regarding the appointments of persons in the judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions. The power given under Article 115 is built in power of the president under the Constitution to frame rules. This is the plenary power of the president to frame rules and this take immediate effect on the rules being made by the president. This legislative field has been exclusively given to the president by the Constitution. This rule making power of the president contemplates the manner, method, qualifications and other ancillary matters required to be covered by the rules before appointment of members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions. The President will also make separate rules regarding suspension and dismissal and other disciplinary procedures under Article 115. It is for the rule making authority, namely, the president to decide the manner and method of appointment of members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial function. In this regard the President is the supreme legislative authority to decide the qualifications, manner and method of such appointments. The president by the Rule-making authority can make Rules for appointments of persons to the offices in the judicial service or as magistrates exercising judicial functions with separate service conditions. In that view of the matter, I hold that the High Court Division correctly held that under Article 115 of the Constitution separate Rules may be framed by the president. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Attorney-General very candidly submitted that Rules should be made by the president under Article 115 of the Constitution for the members of the judicial service and for magistrates exercising judicial function.

<u>85. The learned Judges of the High Court Division also held that part IX of the Constitution which deals with services of Bangladesh will not be applicable in the case of subordinate judiciary, namely, members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions. It may be stated here that part VI contemplates judiciary as a whole as an organ of the State and part IX speaks of Services of Bangladesh. It cannot be denied that the members of the judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions are broadly in the service of Bangladesh. Chapter I of part IV speaks of "The Services of Bangladesh", Members of Judicial service and Magistrates exercising judicial functions of the state are in the service of Bangladesh and as such their terms and conditions of service can be separately made under Article 133 of the Constitution. It is to be borne in mind that the essential safeguard of independence of judiciary as contained in part II of Chapter VI of the Constitution should be maintained by the law making authority as contemplated within the scheme of our Constitution. Article 135 of the Constitution speaks of Constitution protection of all persons holding civil posts in the service of the Republic. The members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions are in the service of the Republic holding civil posts and as such they cannot be deprived of this constitutional protection. Article 135 of the Constitution deals with dismissal removal or reduction in rank of a person who holds a civil post. The Members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions are no doubt holding civil posts and public officers as they get emolument and render service to the Republic. Learned Attorney General candidly submitted that harmonious interpretation must be given to all relevant provisions of the constitution and in elaborating his argument be submitted that for framing of Rules of recruitment of judicial officers and magistrates exercising Judicial functions the president is to make rule under Article 115 which is distinctly separate in character from Article 133. We also find that procedure as enumerated in Article 135 of part IX is in no way in conflict with Articles 115 and 116 and as such the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in holding that Chapter IX shall not apply in case of members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial service. Further, I also find that members of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions of the State cannot be deprived of the benefit of Fundamental Rights as contemplated in articles 27, 29 and 135 of the Constitution which speaks of a procedural safeguard and the benefit of a second show cause notice. In that view of the matter, I hold that the judicial officers and magistrates exercising judicial functions are amenable to the benefits as provided in Article 135 and they are subject to the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal, As a matter of fact, members of the judicial service and judicial magistrates are amenable to the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal which is a creation of the Constitution.</u>

<u>86. Article 136 of part IX speaks of reorganization of service of the Republic by creation, amalgamation or unification of services and such Jaw may vary or revoke any condition of derive of a person employed in the service of the Republic. This concept of reorganization of service is available all other civil posts including executive service f Republic other than members of the judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial function as they have been treated separately under Articles 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution Article 36 refer to all general  services of Civil post. “Judicial Service” has been separately treated in the relevant constitutional provisions and as such conditions of service is to be separately framed under Article 133 and it cannot be tagged as Bangladesh Civil Service (Judicial) under paragraph 2(x) of Act XXII of 1975.</u>

87. In view of the nature of work that the judicial officers are performing the benefit that has been given by Annexure-E dated 8-1-94 should continue in-respect of judicial officers till new rules are made under Article 115 of the Constitution by the president.

88. The learned Judges of the High Court Division were absolutely wrong in holding that in order to give effect, carry out and implement fully the separation of the judiciary from the executive organs of the state no constitutional amendment is necessary is wholly wrong and untenable. Article 22 contemplates separation of judiciary from the other organs of the State and it is for the legislature to decide on this issue. Further, if we say that no constitutional amendment' is necessary then the existence of Article 22 will be nugatory which cannot be the intentions of the framers of the Constitution. Further, if the legislature in its wisdom think of granting meaningful and effective separation of judiciary from the executive organs of the state, the Constitutional Court cannot shut out the legislature. Hence this observation of the High Court Division was uncalled for within the scope of the writ petition.

89. The written Constitution of Bangladesh has placed the Supreme Court in the place of the guardian of the Constitution itself. It will not countenance to any inroad upon the Constitution. A reference to Articles 94, 95, 96 and 147 of the Constitution clearly reveal the independent character of the Supreme Court. Chapter-II of part- VI of the Constitution allots a separate and distinct existence of judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial function. Under Article 109 the High Court Division of the Supreme Court has been vested with the powers of superintendence and control over all courts tribunals subordinate to it. That being of it cannot be questioned that the Supreme Court has been envisaged in the Constitution as an independent institution. For its institutional independence I, therefore agree that the Supreme Court ought to get financial independence for effective and meaningful discharge of its constitutional functions.

For the above reasons, I concur with the judgment.

End.

full_judgment: Mohammad Ismaluddin Sarker J: These (3) three Writ Petitions were referred to this Special Bench because "in these three Writ Petitions the vires of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981, the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 and various Notifications of the Government constituting the Special Promotion Committee, the Superior Selection Board and the Council Committee on Promotion relating to promotion of Superior Government Officers have been challenged as being unconstitutional. " 2. In Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 the petitioner, Shafiuddin Ahamed challenged the vires of Rule 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 providing for the Council Committee on promotion, Superior Selection Board and the Special Promotion Committee with power to hold examination for appointment by promotion in the Service of the Republic, the vires of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979, the Notification dated 19.8.91 creating Superior Selection Board, the Notification dated 9.10.91 forming a Council Committee constituting of Ministers and State Ministers and the appointments made by the Notification dated 8.2.92. 3. It is stated in the application that the petitioner obtained MSc Degree in Geography securing Second Class from the University of Dhaka in the year, 1965, that he appeared at the erstwhile East Pakistan Civil Service (EPCS) Examination in 1968 and stood first in order of merit in the said examination; that on the basis of recommendation of the then East Pakistan Public Service Commission the petitioner was appointed to the East Pakistan Civil Service (Executive) Class-l and posted as Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector to which post he joined on 22.11.69; that the petitioner was promoted to the Senior Scale and was appointed as Senior Scale Section Officer vide Notification dated 12.12.79; that subsequently he was promoted to the rank of Deputy Secretary by the Government vide Notification dated 3.1.85; that the 12 persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (f) of paragraph 7 of the application also appeared in the erstwhile EPCS examination in 1968 along with the petitioner and were selected to the EPCS (Executive) Class-1 post and they also joined as Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector on 22.11.69 as the petitioner, that 11 out of the 12 above mentioned persons were promoted to Senior Scale on 12.12.79 along with the petitioner and the 12th one was promoted to the Senior Scale on 15.8.81; but subsequently, all the aforesaid 11 persons were promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary on 3.1.85 along with the petitioner and the rest one was promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary on 16.4.90; that 19 persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (g) of paragraph 7 belonged to 1970 batch of erstwhile East Pakistan Civil Service and they joined as Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector in October, 1970; that they were promoted to the Senior Scale on 15.8.81; that three persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (h) of paragraph 7 of the application were appointed as Assistant Commissioner in 1977 on the basis of their result of the erstwhile Central Superior Service Examination of Pakistan held in 1970 and they were promoted to the Senior Scale on 2.8.90 and subsequently those persons were promoted to the rank of Deputy Secretary on 3.1.85 along with the petitioner; that the persons mentioned in sub-paragraph(f) of paragraph 7 are junior to the petitioner as per the Bangladesh Civil Service Seniority Rules, 1983 and as per those Seniority Rules and the General Principles of Seniority published in 1970 the petitioner is senior to all the persons mentioned in sub-paragraphs (f)(g) and (h) of paragraph 7; that during 22 years of service the petitioner has been holding various responsible positions of the Government and discharging his duties and responsibilities with utmost honesty, efficiency and devotion; that he was never served with any adverse remark in his entire service career and he got promotion to the Senior Scale and to the post of Deputy Secretary in usual manner on the basis of seniority and merit; that as per Cabinet decision dated 16.9.89 for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary, one has to serve 5(five) years in the Modified National Scale IV or V and in total he\N must serve 15 years in Class-I service including 5 (five) years in Modified National Scale; but one person of sub- paragraph (g) did not serve in the Modified National Scale for five years and the persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (h) of Paragraph 7 did not serve 15 years in Class-I post; that the Constitution of the Republic of Bangladesh has framed a scheme for the Republic to have a public service Cadre and necessary laws regulating the said Cadre and at the same time provide for the principles and yardsticks and methods for determining the inter se seniority amongst the employees of the Republic; that the Public Service Commission has been created under the Constitution for the purpose of conducting tests and examination for the selection of suitable persons in the service of Republic as well as to advise the President in framing Rules relating to service conditions; that it has been made mandatory for the President to consult the Public Service Commission on the matters relating to qualification for recruitment as well as regarding the principles to be followed in making appointment, promotion, transfer and the suitability of candidates for such appointment, promotion and transfer and also matters affecting the terms and conditions of service; that though the Public Service Commission has been exclusively empowered to conduct tests and examination for selection of suitable persons for appointment in the service of the Republic but the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules provided for appointment by promotion to be made on the recommendation of the Council Committee on Promotion, Superior Selection Board or by the Special Promotion Committee by-passing the constitutional institution namely, the Public Service Commission by the Gazette Notification dated 10.10.91 that the Council Committee on Promotion in violation of the terms of reference, Rules and Regulations and also in violation of the provision of Article 140(2) of the Constitution introduced the interview and examination system for promotion for the post of Joint Secretary and illegally introduced marking system alloting 40% for viva voce, 10% for penpicture and 50% for ten years Annual Confidential Reports; that the petitioner along with 384 other officers have been recommended for promotion for the post of Joint Secretary but he was directed to appear before the Council Committee on 14.12.91 for interview for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and he appeared before the Council Committee on the appointed date and replied to all the questions put to him to the best of his knowledge; that thereafter the order of promotion was issued on 8.2.92 in' which the name of the petitioner was not included. It is further stated that the Council Committee did not conduct any interview for promotion to the post of Additional Secretaries and thereby committed discrimination by not applying the same law even-handedly in violation of the provision of Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution; that the introduction of interview and the marking system is violative of Articles 140(2) of the Constitution and the so-called examination and test has created scope for arbitrary selection; that the petitioner belonging to 1969 batch of erstwhile EPCS was interviewed with the erstwhile EPCS batch of 1970 and 1977 batch of the Civil Service Officers and thereby included his juniors for consideration for promotion along with him in violation of the provision of Article 29 of the Constitution; that the Respondents by the impugned Notification dated 8.2.92 promoted all the officers mentioned in sub-paragraphs (f)(g) and (h) of paragraph 7 to the post of Joint Secretary superseding the petitioner who is senior to the aforesaid persons. It is further stated that the so-called interview system for promotion for the post of Joint Secretary has been introduced with the malafide intention for perpetuating nepotism and favouritism as well as for the purpose of introducing partisanship in the service cadre purporting to politicise the Civil Service Cadre. 4. By filing a supplementary affidavit it is further stated that the provisions of the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 are ultra vires to the Constitution inasmuch as no law has been passed by the Parliament which is the pre-condition for making Regulation; that although the petitioner has been personally aggrieved as being not treated in accordance with law and Constitution in the matter of promotion to the post of Joint Secretary but he does not seek any remedy in personam and the remedy sought for by him is for restoration of the constitutional and legal frame within which the promotion of those performing their function in the services of the Republic ought to be considered; that the petitioner was promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary by the order dated 3.1.85 under the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 and the Notifications Annexure-J dated 10.8.91 and Annexure-K dated 10.10.91- have their origin purportedly to paragraph 6 of the Notification dated 17.7.89; that the power under section 4 of the Service (Re-Organizations and Conditions) Act, 1975 do not empower the Government to make provision for Superior Selection Board and Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure, and that the Notification dated 17.7.89 abolishing the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 is also ultra vires of the Constitution as well as section 4 of the Services (Recorganisation and Conditions) Act, 1975. 5. The respondent No. 1 namely, Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia that the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 is applicable for appointment either by direct recruitment or by promotion to the post of service specified in schedule I of the Rules; that Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 applies to the post of various BCS Cadre; that schedule II of the said Rules contains provision to be followed for appointment to a service; that ex Senior Services Pool posts including posts of Joint Secretaries are not mentioned in schedule II of the Rules as those posts do not belong to any BCS Cadre and those posts of Joint Secretaries do not come under the provisions of BCS Recruitment Rules 1981; that these Rules have been made by the President in exercise of powers conferred by Article 133 of the Constitution after consultation with the Bangladesh Public Service Commission as required under Article 140 of the Constitution; that the Constitution of the Council Committee on Promotion, the Superior Selection Board and Special Promotion Committee is neither arbitrary nor have these Committees been given unguided powers to hold examination for appointment by promotion to the service of the Republic and the powers to hold test and examination were given to enable them to determine merit and Suitability of the officers for promotion; that Regulation 4 of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation, 1979 provides that it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission for appointment to a Class I service or post of any officer who is already a member of Class I service and as such the matter concerning the promotion of Deputy Secretary and above who are already in Class-I service does not come within the domain of the Public Service Commission; that the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 have been made by the President in accordance with powers conferred by Article 140(2) of the Constitution after due consultation with the Bangladesh Public Service Commission; that there has been no arbitrary exercise of powers as all eligible candidates were given equal opportunity and there was no discrimination amongst the candidates; that the promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary is given on the basis of merit and seniority and not on seniority alone and persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (f)(g) and (h) or paragraph 7 of the Writ Petition have not been considered in violation of the practices or Constitutional provisions; that with the repeal of the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 and abolition of Senior Service Pool Officers (Seniority) Rules, 1982 which were applicable in the case of promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and above the same practices were followed in the case of the promotion referred to by the petitioner on the basis of merit and seniority; that the petitioner was given equal opportunity along with other eligible candidates and was treated equally and he availed the promotion process without raising any objection; but the petitioner was not found fit and, as such, he could not be promoted; that the promotion to the post of Joint Secretary was considered on the basis of merit and seniority and no discrimination was made in this respect; that the petitioner as well as officers mentioned in sub-paragraphs (f)(g) and (h) of paragraph 7 of the Writ Petition were promoted to the rank of Deputy Secretary on the same date by the same Notification and they were all considered along with the petitioner for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary; that as per guide lines given by the Government and prevailing practices seniority was not only the yardstick for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary but in order to select competent and most suitable officers merits of the officers were considered along with seniority; that for the purpose of consultation with the Public Service Commission the Constitution has provided for making Regulations and such Regulations have been duly made by the President in consultation with the Public Service Commission namely, the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation, 1979; according to Regulation 4 of the said Regulations consultation with the Commission in the matter of promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary is not necessary; and the Council Committee took interviews to determine merit and suitability of the Officers for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary on the basis of the guidelines given by the Government and prevailing practices in this regard; that there has been no by-passing of the Public Service Commission; that the Cabinet formed Council Committee on senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure to deal with the specific function of the Government and, as such, the Council Committee is an authority duly constituted and it is neither illegal nor unlawful nor it assumed the power and function of the Public Service Commission; that the Council Committee itself introduced interview and examination system for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary; and introduced system of allocating 40% mark for viva-voce, 10% for pen picture and 50% for 10 years ACR as per Government guidelines in this respect; that the Superior Selection Board did not recommend the petitioner for promotion; that the Council Committee was constituted with the authority to recommend the case of promotion; that the function of the Superior Selection Board was restricted to submission of eligible cases before the Council Committee only; that different system and criteria have been followed for promotion of officers to different level of posts for promotion of the cadre posts the provision of the Rule 5 of BCS Recruitment Rules is folic-wed, for the promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary, Joint Secretary interviews are taken as per Government decision, for promotion to higher post i.e. to the post of Additional Secretary and Secretary the candidates are selected by the Council Committee considering their merit on the basis of their ACR and performance; as such, there is no discrimination nor any violation of the Constitutional guarantees as provided under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution; that there was no violation of Article 140(2) of the Constitution; that all eligible officers were duly considered; that there has been no violation of the petitioner's fundamental right as the case of all eligible candidates including the petitioner and his seniors as well as juniors were considered and the petitioner was treated equally and subjected to the same yardstick along with other officers; that interview system was followed with a bonafide purpose to assess the suitability and competence of the officers; that it is not necessary to consult the Public Service Commission in matters of promotion to the post of Joint Secretary and such other posts, vide Regulation 4(a) and 8 of the Regulations; that the petitioner himself availed the process of the interview and as he was not found fit he was not promoted; that the Council Committee took interviews many times previously also as per guideline of such promotions and prevailing practices; that it is denied that the Superior Selection Board and the Council Committee have been formed to be used as a vehicle to promote sycophants and henchmen of the ruling party; that the petitioner cannot claim any remedy under the Writ jurisdiction as he has a remedy before the Administrative Tribunal created under Act VII of 1981. By a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1 it was further stated that the Council Committee took interviews on the basis of guideline given by the Govt.; that interview and marking system was followed by the Council Committee in accordance with the guidelines and prevailing practices in order to assess the suitability of officer for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary; that the Ministry of Establishment prepared a summary dated 3.11.91 containing the guidelines for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary which were approved by the Cabinet as well as by the Prime Minister as the head of the Cabinet. 6. The petitioner filed an affidavit-In-reply to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 1 and reiterated the statements made in the application and it is further stated therein that the subject matter of the case is very much under the Constitutional jurisdiction of this Court and does not relate to the Administrative Tribunal created under Act VII of 1981; that in terms of Regulations 4(a) of the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations 1979 consultation with the commission is necessary in matters of promotion to the post of Joint Secretary; that the Council Committee took interview for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary but nowhere in paragraph 1 (C)(2) of the Senior Service Pool Order, 1979 or Rule 5 of BCS Recruitment Rules, 1981 the terms of reference of the Council Committee constituted on 9.10.91 was to conduct test, interview or examinations awarding marking system, rather the Notifications dated 2.4.91, 12.3.91 and 19.8.91 clearly state that promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and above is to be made on the basis of ACR and Service record and that no test or examination would be taken; that the Council Committee acted beyond the terms of reference and interview system was introduced with malafide motive for perpetuating nepotism and favouritism and for introducing partisanship in the Civil Service; that there has been gross violation of the petitioner's fundamental right as guaranteed under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution. It is further stated that the Government usurped the powers and functions of the Public Service Commission violating the mandatory provisions of the Constitution in making promotions to the posts of Joint Secretaries. By a Supplementary affidavit-in-reply the petitioner further stated that Regulation 4 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 is ultra vires of the Constitution as no law has been passed by the Parliament which, is precondition for making Regulation; that by making Regulation the Executive Authority has pre-empted the law and exceeded the jurisdiction which is not available under the Constitution. 7. In Writ Petition No. 3193 the Petitioner Sk. Mozaharuddin challenged Rule 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 and the vires of the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 and creation of the promotion committee for the post of Deputy Secretary under notification dated 4.12.91 and the appointments made by the notification dated 8.2.92 in pursuance of the notification dated 4.12.91. 8. It is stated in the application that the petitioner obtained M.Com Decree from the University of Rajshahi in the year 1972 and he appeared at the Special Superior Service competitive examination in 1972; that having qualified in the said examination the petitioner was appointed in the service of the Republic as a Class I Officer and was placed in the Industrial Management Cadre service on probation by the Memo dated 22.10.73; that after abolition of the Industrial Management Service Cadre the petitioner was absorbed in the BCS (Administration) Cadre as Asstt. Commissioner under notification dated 4.12.82; that the petitioner was promoted to the Senior Scale on 28.12.85; that the petitioner completed various job training programmes and also training abroad and passed departmental examination; that during his service the petitioner held responsible posts in three Jute Mills and also served as Administrative Officer in the department of Industry; that he also worked as Assistant Commissioner and Upazila Nirbahi Officer and also as Additional Deputy Commissioner; that an official gradation list was prepared by the respondent No.1 on the basis of inter se seniority in which the petitioner's name appeared at serial No. 354 and 127 officers mentioned in sub-paragraph (I) of paragraph 7 who are junior to the petitioner had been promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary on the recommendation of the Committee headed by the Minister of State, Ministry of Establishment vide notification dated 8.2.92; that in the name of the holding of examinations and interviews there were wide-spread abuse of the said tests or examinations giving rise to nepotism and corruption and a committee was set up which suggested review and revision Of the system of maintenance of service record of the Civil Officers; that the said Committee submitted a report in July, 1982 suggesting reformulation of Annual Confidential Report which could help evaluate the merit of the Gazetted Officers; that this new system brought important changes for finding fitness and eligibility for promotions exclusively on the basis of ACR; that accordingly the Bangladesh Civil Service Rules, 1981 was amended in 1985 and the provision for conducting tests and examinations was removed vide notification dated 23.3.85; that although the provision for holding and conducting tests and examination were made and a new scientific system of evaluation was introduced but the Government in power in order to get their own party influence and their henchmen promoted, they introduced not only the illegal committee but also reintroduced the process of conducting examination; that in the system of examination, the respondents introduced an illegal system of allocating 60% marks for written examination and 40% marks for oral examination; that there had been serious allegation about this new system of promotion through tests and examinations by ignoring the recommendation of the Superior Selection Board; that due to the introduction of test and examination the petitioner has been highly aggrieved inasmuch as he has been superseded by officers junior to him; that the petitioner has been discriminated as having been dubbed as 1973 batch of Civil Service being supporters of the Awami League; that it has been possible only to promote 32% of the 1973 batch whereas 95% of 1979 batch who have been attributed as the supporters of BNP, were promoted; that the petitioner being senior to the persons mentioned above he has been superseded by the impugned order on the basis of unauthorized interview and marks system. It is further stated that the Public Service Commission has been created by the Constitution with the spirit of keeping all appointments, promotions and examinations of the services of the Republic above any bias, prejudice and discrimination and with this end in view the gentlemen who constituted in the said Commission have to subscribe oath under Article 148 of the Constitution; that the respondents usurping the powers and functions of the Public Service Commission with the malafide motive have formed the Superior Selection Board and Council Committee with a view to promoting sycophants of the ruling party to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and to create a cadre of political loyalists in the service of the Republic. 9. The respondent No. 1 filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein it has been stated that the notification dated 4.12.91 constituting a Committee for the purpose of making appointment by promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries was issued with due approval of the competent authority as per the existing rules and regulations; that these rules have been made by the President in exercise of the powers confered under Article 133 of the Constitution after due consultation with the Public Service Commission as required under Article 140 of the Constitution; that the constitution of the Council Committee on Promotion, the Superior Selection Board and Special Promotion Committee is neither arbitrary nor have those committees been given unguided powers to hold tests and examination nor appointment by promotions to the service of the Republic; that the powers to hold interview were given to enable them to determine the merit and suitability of the officers for promotion; that Regulation 4 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultations) Regulations, 1979 provides that it shall not be necessary for consultation with the Commission for appointment to a Class-I Service or post of any officer who is already a member of Class I, or holding a Class I post and, as such, the promotion to the Deputy Secretaries who were already in Class I Service does not come within the domain of the Commission; That Rule 5 of the BCS Recruitment Rules is not ultra vires of the Constitution; that the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultations) Regulations, 1979 have been made by the President in accordance with the powers conferred by Articles 133 of the Constitution after due consultation with the Public Service Commission and, as such, those Regulations have been lawfully made; that the Committee constituted for the purpose of promotions is to determine the merit and suitability of the officers for promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary on the basis of guideline given by the Government and prevailing practices in this regard; that there has been no arbitrary exercise of powers as all eligible candidates were given equal opportunity; that the petitioner availed himself of the promotion process and did not raise any objection on it at that time; but as he was not found fit he could not be promoted; that it is not correct that the petitioner has no alternative effective and equally efficacious remedy other than Writ Petition inasmuch as he has remedy in the Administrative Tribunal created under Act VII of 1981; that the fixation of seniority of officers of different Ministries had been done after consultation with the Ministry of Establishment and the Public Service Commission; that as the promotions were considered on the basis of merit, the petitioner and all other eligible officers including his juniors mentioned in the application and his seniors were considered for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary; that there was no examination held for the purpose of promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary and, in fact, the Superior Selection Board made an evaluation of the candidates on the basis of their Annual Confidential Reports and other service recommendations and thereafter the Committee for Promotion held an interview to determine the overall suitability of the candidates for promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary and in such due process of selection all candidates were given equal treatment and there was no scope for nepotism and corruption; that in the process of selection 60% marks were allocated for ACR and 40% marks for interview and since this was a case of promoting Class-I Officers to higher level of Class I posts consultation with the Public Service Commission was not necessary; that it is provided at serial No. 23 and 74(D) of the Schedule III of the Rules of Business, 1975, that specific Orders of the President are necessary for appointment to the post of Deputy Secretary and above and Regulation 3(b) of the Public Service Commission (Consultations) Regulations, 1979 provides that for appointment to the post requiring the specific order of the President, consultation with the Bangladesh Public Service Commission is not necessary and, as such, the Commission was not consulted; that it is not correct that the Superior Selection Board recommended the case of the petitioner for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary but the said Board submitted the eligible cases before the Promotion Committee for consideration of promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary and the Promotion Committee recommended the cases for promotion; that the allegations and complaints against this system was baseless and newspaper reports on the matter are not based on actual facts nor the deliberations in the Parliamentary Standing Committee indicated any irregularity or illegality in this regard; that the Superior Selection Board did not recommend the petitioner or any other officer for promotion but the said Board simply submitted the cases of eligible candidates to the Committee for promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary; that there has been no discrimination of the petitioner as an officer of 1973 batch of Civil Service nor the party in power treated the officers of 1973 batch as supporters of the Awami League nor the officers of 1977 batch are supporters of BNP; that the promotions of the officers to the rank of Deputy Secretary was not a political one but, an administrative decision for promotion on the basis of merit and suitability. 10. The petitioner filed an affidavit-in-reply to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 1 wherein he reiterated his statements made in the application and further stated that the Committee constituted under the notification dated 4.12.91 for the purpose or making appointment by promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary is not permissible as per Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitments Rules, 1981 that Superior Selection Board is the competent authority to recommend the person for appointment by promotion to the Post of Deputy Secretary in accordance with the Recruitment Rules and accordingly, the petitioner along with 373 superseded of his batch were recommended by the Superior Selection Board for appointment by promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary; that the Public Service Commission has been empowered under Article 140 of the Constitution to conduct test and examination for selection of the suitable persons for appointment in the service of the Republic and for making appointment by promotion to the higher post and to scrutinize the eligibility of the candidates; that Parliament may by law regulated conditions of service of the Republic as per, Article 133 of the Constitution and the President can also make Rule until provision in this behalf is made by any law; that Rule 5 of Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 providing for Council Committee for Promotion, Superior Selection Board and Special Promotion Committee is not consistent with Article 140 of the Constitution and, as such, the said Rule is void according to Article 7(2) of the Constitution; that the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation 1979 have curtailed the Constitutional power conferred upon the Commission providing in Regulation No. 8, that it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission in cases of promotion within the same class of service; that this Regulation is in contravention of Constitutional provision of Article 140(2)(b) and, as such, void as per Article 7(2) of the Constitution; that the Committee formed under Annexure-A for holding test or interview for promotion for the post of Deputy Secretary has no power to do so since those powers have been vested with the Superior Selection Board as per BCS Recruitment Rules, 1981 and those powers were not given to any Committee by any Rules and the impugned Committee had no power to scrutinize the eligibility of the petitioner for the purpose of promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary when the Superior Selection Board found the petitioner fit for promotion; that since Administrative Tribunal cannot strike down any law or Rule on the ground of its constitutionality the petitioner is competent to seek remedy under Article 102(1) of the Constitution for enforcement of his fundamental right and for challenging vires of law; that Rules of Business, 1975 are not above the Constitution and provision made in serial No. 23 and 74(d) of Schedule III of the Rules of Business about the cases to be referred) to the President but the President should consult the Commission with respect to the principle to be followed in making appointment to the service of the Republic and promotion and transfer to service and suitability of the candidates for such promotion and transfer as per Article 140(2) (b) of the Constitution. By a supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1 it has been stated that the Council Committee took interview on the basis of guideline given by the Government; that interview and marking system was followed by the Council Committee in accordance with the guidelines and prevailing practices in order to assess the suitability of the officers to the rank of Deputy Secretary; that the Ministry of Establishment prepared a summary and submitted the same by Memo dated 3.11.91 containing the guidelines for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary which were approved by the Cabinet as well as by the Prime Minister as the head of the Cabinet. 11.
