In Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1972 Division Bench of this Court issued a Rule Nisi on 2.8.92 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why section 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 providing for Council Committee on Promotion, Superior Selection Board, and the Special Promotion Committee allowing them power to hold test and examination for appointment by promotion shall not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the Notification constituting the Superior Selection Board and the notification forming Council Committee shall not be declared to be had or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 13. In Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 the same Division Bench issued a Rule Nisi on 18.10.92 on similar terms as in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 with a direction for hearing both the Rules together. All the three matters were taken up for hearing by the Division Bench which by an order dated 18.11.93 referred the matter for hearing by a larger Bench as stated earlier. 14. The respondents raised a preliminary objection as to the maintainability of the Writ applications on the ground that the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 and the Writ Petition No. 813 of 1993 are Deputy Secretaries to the Government of Bangladesh and the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1993 is serving as the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Mymensingh, all being in the service of the Republic have their remedies before the Administrative Tribunal created under Act VII of 1981 in accordance with Article 117 of the Constitution and that under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act the Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to determine applications in respect of terms and conditions of service of any person in the service of the Republic and as such Writ applications are not maintainable. The learned Attorney-General submitted that the applications relate to the terms and conditions of service in the garb of challenging vires of the law. On the other hand, Mr. M Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, referred to the case of Mojibur Rahman vs. Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 and submitted that a person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of law can seek remedy under Article 102(1) of the Constitution. Further, the learned Advocate for the petitioners has submitted that the petitioners are also invoking Article 44 of the Constitution for enforcement of their fundamental right since all the applications have been filed under clause (i) of the Article 102 of the Constitution. Mr. Islam has submitted that their Lordships of the Appellate Division did not take into consideration Article 44 of the Constitution in the case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111. In view of the prayer in the applications and the order referring the matter before a larger Bench on the ground that in the three Writ Petitions the vires of Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 and the Bangladesh Public Service. Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 along with the notification of the Government constituting Special Promotion Committee, Superior Selection Board and the Council Committee on Promotion were challenged, it cannot be said that these applications are not maintainable in Writ jurisdiction. 15. As stated earlier the Rules were issued challenging the vires of Rule 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981. The Rule is in the following terms: "5. Appointment by promotion—Subject to the provisions of Schedule II, appointment by promotion to specified post of a Service shall be made on the recommendation of the Council Committee on Promotion, Superior Selection Board or the Special Promotion Committee, as the case may be, constituted by the Government in this behalf; Provided that— (a) appointment by promotion to the New National Scale of Taka 750-1470 from a post of lower Class shall be made on the recommendation of the Commission; (b) No person shall be promoted to the New National Scale of Taka 1400-2225 unless he is found fit in a test or examination conducted by the Special Promotion Committee; (c) no person shall be promoted to the New National scale conducted by the Superior Selection Board; (d) no person shall be promoted to the New National Scale of Take 2350-2750 and above unless he is found fit by, the Council Committee on Promotion. Conducted by the Superior Selection Board; no person shall be promoted to the New National Scale of Taka 2350-2750 and above unless he is found fit by the Council Committee on Promotion. Service Commission(Consultation) Regulations, 1979 to be ultra vires, being inconsistent with the provision of Article 140 (2) of the Constitution. Article 140 of the Constitution runs as follows: "140. (1) The functions of a public service commission shall be- (a) to conduct tests and examinations for the selection of suitable persons for appointment to the service of the Republic; (b) to advise the President on any matter on which the Commission is consulted under clause (2) or on any matter connected with its functions which is referred to the commission by the President; and (c) such other functions as may be prescribed by law. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, and any regulation (not inconsistent with such law) which may be made by the President after consultation with a commission, the President shall consult a commission with respect to- (a) matters relating to qualifications for, and methods of recruitment to, the service of the Republic; (b) the principles to be followed in making appointment to that service and promotions and transfers from one branch of the service to another and the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions and transfers; (c) matters affecting the terms and conditions (including pension rights) of that service; and (d) the discipline of the service." 16. It is contended on behalf of the respondents that the provisions of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations have been made by the President in accordance with the powers conferred under Article 133 of the Constitution after due consultation with the Bangladesh Public Service Commission and, as such, these Regulations have been made by the President lawfully and they are not ultra vires of the Constitution. The respondents relied upon Regulation 4(a) which provides that it shall not be necessary to consult with the Public Service Commission with regard to the selection for appointment to a Class I service or post of any officer who is already a member of Class I service or holding a Class I post and the respondents also relied upon Regulation 8 which provides that it shall not be necessary to consult with the Commission in cases of promotion within the same class of service. According to the learned Attorney-General the promotion of the petitioner from Class I to Class 1 service and this being the case of promotion within the same class of service consultation .with the Public Service Commission is not necessary. On the other hand, Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate challenged Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 as ultra vires of the Constitution firstly, because no law was made by the Parliament, secondly because in the absence of any law made by the Parliament the President cannot make any Regulation and thirdly neither any law made by the Parliament nor any Regulation made by the President after consultation with the Commission can dispense with the Constitutional requirement of consultation with the Commission. According to Mr. Islam, in case of appointment and promotion consultation with the Commission is mandatory requirement which cannot be dispensed with by any law made by the Parliament or any Regulation made by the President. According to Mr. Islam, the law made by the Parliament and Regulations made by 'the President should only regulate the manner of consultation with the Commission but, cannot dispense with the consultation of the Commission. The learned Advocate contended that Part IX of our Constitution relates to service of Bangladesh which includes Articles 133 to 136 in Chapter I and Articles 137 to 141 in Chapter II. Article 137 provides for establishing one or more public service commission. Article 138 provides for appointment of members of the Commission. Article 139 provides for tenure of the office of the Chairman of the Public Service Commission; Article 140 provides for the function Of the Public Service Commission and Article 141 provides, for submission of the annual report by the Commission. According to Mr. Islam, the function of the Public Service Commission is to conduct any test or examination for selection of the suitable persons for appointment to the service of the Republic and no other person or authority is authorized by the Constitution to conduct any test or examination for selection' of persons for appointment to the service of the Republic; further the commission is to advise the President on any matter on which the commission is consulted under clause (2) of Article 140 or on any matter referred to the Commission by the President and such other functions as may be prescribed by law Clause(2) of Article 140, according to the learned Advocate, provides for consultation with the Commission by the President subject to any law and Regulation in respect of matters relating to qualifications for and methods of recruitment to; the service of the Republic and the principle to be followed in making appointment to that service and promotion and transfer from one branch of service to another and the suitability of the candidates for such appointment and promotion, apart from the matters affecting the terms and conditions of the service and discipline of the service. In other words, according to Mr. Islam consultation with the Commission is a "must" and any law of the Parliament or any Regulation made by the President may only regulate the manner in which the consultation should be made. 17. The learned Attorney-General, however, on the other hand, has contended that the President need not consult the Public Service Commission on every matter and there are fields which are excluded from the purview of consultation. He has referred to Section 266 of the Government of India Act, 1935 wherein similar provisions were made for consultation with the Federal or Provincial Public Service Commission subject to the Regulations made by the Governor-General. In exercise of power given by the Government of India Act, 1935, the then Government of Bengal made the Bengal Public Service Regulations 1937 and Regulation 34 thereof provided that it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission with respect to the filling of certain posts. Article 320 of the Constitution of India provided in the proviso to Clause (3) thereof that the President 'as respects the all-India services and also as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union, and the Governor, as respects other services and post in connection with the .affairs of a State, may make regulation specifying the matters in which either generally, or in any particular class of case or in any particular circumstances, it shall not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted. Similarly Article 188 of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan in Clause (2) therein provided that the President in respect of service and post in connection with the affairs of the Federation and the Governor of the Province in respect of service in connection with the affairs of the Province may make regulation in which it shall not be necessary for Public Service Commission to be consulted. Similarly, in the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan in Sub-Article (2) of Article 185 the President was authorized to provide by Order to dispense with Consultation with the Public Service Commission. 18. Thus it appears that the power to dispense with the consultation with the Public Service Commission in certain matters by the President is not unknown and the President or the Governor-General or Governor could dispense with consultation with the Public Service Commission by making regulation. No authority could be shown by Mr. Amirul Islam to show that making of a law by the Parliament is a pre-condition for making any regulation by the President nor is there anything to show that the law made by the Parliament or the requlations made by the President are only to regulate the manner of consultation with the Public Service Commission. The Parliament by making any law may dispense with consultation with the Public Service Commission in certain respect and the President, after consultation with the Commission, may also make regulation dispensing with the consultation with the Commission in certain respect. As such, it cannot be said that the provisions of Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1972 in particular Regulation No.8 is ultra vires of the Constitution. 19. It may be mentioned that apart from Regulations 4(a) and 8 of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission. (Consultation) Regulations 1979, Regulation 3(b) provides that it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission in regard to any matter mentioned in Sub-clauses (a) and (b) of clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution in the case of the post appointment to which requires the specific order of the President. The Rules of Business 1975 provides that all Secretariat appointments of and above the rank of Deputy Secretary are to be submitted to the President before issue of orders thereof. Therefore for appointments to the post of Deputy Secretary and above, consultation with the Public Service Commission is not necessary. Hence there is no substance in the contention that without consultation with the Public Service Commission no order of promotion can be passed by the President. 20. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate then submitted that since no law was made by the Parliament, the President, in the absence of such law, cannot make any regulation, the passing of any such law being pre-condition for making any regulation by the President in accordance with clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution. The learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, has referred to the Bangladesh Public Service Commission Ordinance, 1977 (Ordinance No. LVII of 1977) by which the Bangladesh Public Service Commission has been established. Section 4 of the said Ordinance provides that the exercise of the function of the Commission under Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution in respect of any matter referred therein shall be subject to the provision of this Ordinance, any regulation made under the Article or any other law for the time being in force affecting such matter. Section 5 of the said Ordinance excluded certain matters from the purview of the Commission which, inter alia provides that notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance or in any other law for the time being in force, consultation with the Commission shall not be necessary in respect of any appointment to, amongst other, any service or post, appointment of which was excluded from the purview of the Public Service Commission before the commencement of this Ordinance; The learned Attorney-General in this connection has referred to the Bangladesh Public Service Commission Order 1973 (President Order No. XXV of 1973) wherein in Article 5(2) and Article 6(2) it is provided that except to the extent that the Government after consulting with the Commission may provide otherwise by Regulation in relation to services and posts, shall consult the Commission in the matter relating to method of recruitment to such services and posts, the principle to be followed in making appointment to such services and posts and promotion of suitable candidate for such appointment and promotion. The learned Attorney-General also referred to similar provisions made in the Public Service Commission Ordinance 1977 (Ordinance No. VIII of 1977) which had been repealed by Ordinance No. LVII of 1977. In the repealing Ordinance it is provided in section 4 that subject to the provision of this Ordinance and Clause (2) of the Article 140 of the Constitution, the functions of the 2(two) Public Service Commissions shall be exercised in respect of Class I Civil Service Post and other Civil Services respectively. Thus it would appear from the President's Order No. XXV of 1973, Ordinance No. VIII of 1977 and Ordinance No. LVII of 1977 that the President by making regulation as mentioned in Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution may dispense with consultation with the Public Service Commission. Hence it cannot be said that the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 was made by-passing the Constitutional requirement or that the said Regulations are ultra vires under Clause (2) of the Article 140 of Constitution. 21. In this connection it may be mentioned that Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that Ordinance No. LVII of 1977 is not a law made by the Parliament; but the definition of law in Article 152 of the Constitution includes Ordinance as "law." Further, Ordinance LVII of 1977 was promulgated on 28.11.77 and the same has been protected in paragraph 18 of the 4th schedule of the Constitution by the Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act, 1979 (Act. 1 of 1979). 22. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate referred to the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 wherein it was provided that all posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries, Additional Secretaries and Secretaries of the Bangladesh Secretariat shall be filled by officers encadred in the Pool and encadrement of officers shall be made by the Government on the basis of selection made by the Public Service Commission from amongst the officers mentioned in sub-paragraph' (3) of Paragraph 3 of the Order. Then the learned Advocate referred to the Notification dated 17.7.89 by which Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 was repealed and the Senior Services Pool was abolished and in paragraph 6 of the said notification it has been mentioned that the guidelines for appointment and promotion to the post of Secretary, Additional Secretary and Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary would be notified by the Ministry of Establishment. Mr. Amirul Islam has submitted that the Senior Services Pool Order and Senior Services Pool Encadrement (Examination) Rules 1988 provided for written examination and viva voce examination and after the repeal of the Senior Services Pool Order the provision for holding written examination and viva voce examination has also been abolished and there is no legal basis for holding any examination or test for promotion of the officers and paragraph 6 of the said notification cannot delegate the power to hold examination and lest by issuing guidelines by the Ministry of Establishment. The learned Advocate has submitted that paragraph 6 of the aforesaid notification dated 17.7.89 cannot empower the Government to issue any guideline for holding test or examination for the purpose of promotion. The learned Advocate has further contended that Article 133 of the Constitution provided that the Parliament is to make law regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic and the proviso therein empowered the President to make rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of such persons and, as such, paragraph 6 of the notification dated 17.7.89 is ultra vires of Article 133 of the Constitution. According to Mr. Amirul Islam, paragraph 6 of the said notification is the source for making the notification dated 10.10.91 Annexure-K for constitution of the Council Committee for Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure. The learned Advocate further submitted that this notification Annexure-K is ultra vires being without any legal basis. Mr. Amirul Islam also challenged the reconstitution of the Superior Selection Board by the Notification dated 19.8.91, Annexure-J as without having any legal basis. 23. On the other hand the learned, Attorney- General has referred to the development of different committees including Superior Selection Board since 1972. He has referred to the resolution of the Ministry of Cabinet Affairs, Establishment Division which decided to constitute a Superior Selection Board by a resolution dated 1.3.72 to recommend for appointments to the rank of Section Officer and above. The learned Attorney-General has referred to the subsequent resolutions dated 24.3.72, 27.3.72, 29.8.75 and subsequent resolutions reconstituting Superior Selection Board dated 14.7.76, 29.5.78, 6.11.78 and 8.10.79. The learned Attorney-General has referred to the notification dated 5.7.82 dissolving the Superior Selection Board and then in reconstitution of the same by notifications dated 27.7.82 and 23.8.83. The learned Attorney- General then referred to the notification dated 24.7.88 by which the Superior Selection Board was decentralised and the notification dated 2.4.91 by which the Superior Selection Board has again been reconstituted and the impugned notification dated 19.9.91 Annexure-J by which the Superior Selection Board has again been reconstituted and in this notification earlier notifications dated 24.7.89 and 2.4.91 have been referred to. 24. As to that the basis for formation of the Council Committee the learned Attorney-General has drawn our attention to rule 16 of the Rules of Business 1975 framed under Article 55(6) of the Constitution which runs as follows: "16. Committee of the Council of Ministers (1)-The President/Council may constitute Standing Committees of the Council and assign necessary functions to them. The composition and functions of such Committees may be amended or, modified by the President if it is so desired. (2) In like manner, the President/Council may constitute Ad-hoc Committee for specific purposes and assign functions to them. (3) Any decision taken by such Committees which is not required to be ratified by the Council shall have the force of a decision of the Council when approved by the President. (4) The minutes of discussion and decision of a Committee of the Council shall be circulated to all members of the Council by the Cabinet Secretary/Joint Secretary, Cabinet. (5) Any Ministry can approach the President for a review of a decision of a Committee of the Council which is not required to be ratified by the Council. The President will decide whether the decision shall be reviewed or be referred to the Committee, or be taken up in a meeting of the Council. (6) Committee composed of Secretaries to the Government and such other officials as may be necessary, may be constituted to provide Secretariat and Administrative support to the Committees of the Council and also to co-ordinate activities between Ministries/ Divisions at the Official level. The President shall decide constitution, composition and functions of such Committees." 25. He then referred to the schedule 1 of the Rules of Business item 10 of the Ministry of Establishment. Paragraph 1 provides for formation policy on regulation of service and determination of the terms and conditions. He referred to Gazette Notification dated December 6, 1982 wherein the composition of Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure has been given with terms of reference amongst other, to consider all promotions and initial appointment to the posts of Joint Secretary and above duly processed through the Superior Selection Board and to make recommendation to the Chief Martial Law Administrator. 26. As to the formation of the Council Committee for Superior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure rule 16 of the Rules of Business 1975 framed under Article 55(6) of the Constitution provides that the President of Council of Ministers may constitute standing Committee of the Council and assign necessary function to them and the composition and functions of such Committee may be amended or modified by the President. The first Council Committee was formed on the 6th of December, 1982; it was reconstituted on the 25th of July, 1983 and again the Council Committee was reconstituted by the impugned notification dated 10.10.91 (Annexure H in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992) wherein the Council Committee was composed of 7 Cabinet Ministers and one Minister of State with the Minister for Education as its convener. 27. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that the constitution of the Superior Selection Board and the Council Committee is ultra vires and in violation of the Constitutional provisions as contained in Part IX Chapters I and II of the Constitution inasmuch as these are in direct conflict with the Constitutional provisions and, as such, are liable to be declared illegal and void. As has been stated earlier the Superior Selection Board as well as the Council Committee were constituted in pursuance of the direction of the Government as notified from time to time, in exercise of the powers under rule 16 of the Rules of Business. No specific provision of the Constitution as mentioned in Chapters I and II of Part IX of the Constitution has been pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner which is in conflict with the Superior Selection Board or Council Committee. The whole argument Of Mr. Islam is that any appointment or promotion in the service of the Republic must be done in consultation with the Public Service Commission but the learned Advocate has totally omitted the other provisions of law by which consultation with the Public Service Commission has been dispensed with. Therefore there is no substance in this contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. 28. The next contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the interview and marking system by the Council Committee is without any lawful authority and the interview system introduced in case of promotion to the post of Joint Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries is highly discriminatory and arbitrary and as such violative of Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution. 29. It is further submitted that the so-called interview system for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary has been introduced with the malafide intention for perpetuating nepotism and favouritism and thereby promoting the juniors of the petitioners superseding them in violation of the said rules. It is pointed out that the Council Committee most illegally introduced marking system allowing 40% marks for viva voce and 60% marks for 10-years Annual Confidential Reports. It is submitted that selection on the basis of ACRs is sufficient to judge the merit and suitability of the officer but the Council Committee introduced the interview system keeping 40% marks for viva voce which resulted in discrimination and arbitrary selection of the promotes which offended Article 27 of the Constitution which provides that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law, as well as clause (1) of Article 29 which provides that there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic. 30. The contention of Mr. Amirul Islam in this regard is that allotting 40% marks for interview is highly disproportionate in comparison with 60% marks on the evaluation of 10 years ACRs and, according to the learned Advocate, this has given rise to pick and choose leading to arbitrary selection of the officers for promotion. In support of his contention Mr. Islam has referred to the case of Ajoy Hasiah vs. Khalid Mojib Surwardi reported in. (1981) I SCC 722 AIR 1981 (SC) 487 and the case of Ashoke Kumar Yadob vs. State of Hariana reported in (1985) 4 sec 417. In the former case the petitioner applied for admission in the Engineering College and appeared in a written test of 100 marks as well as in interview of 50 marks but he was not selected and it was contended that allocation of as many as 50 marks for interview as against 100 marks for written test for assessment of suitability of the candidate was not proper which led to arbitrariness and offended the equality clause of Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. It has been observed therein by the Supreme Court of India that in the matter of admission to College or in the matter of public employment the oral interview test should not be relied upon as an exclusive test but it may be resorted to only as an additional or supplementary test and further observed that allocation of more that 50% of the total marks for interview would be unreasonable and would be liable to be struck down as constitutionally invalid. With this observation the Court dismissed the write petition. The later case relates to selection of officers by the Hariana Public Service Commission to the Civil Service Executive Posts in which 700 marks was for written examination and 200 marks for viva voce examination. In this case also the allocation of high percentage of marks for viva voce test was deprecated and the Court directed that thereafter in case of selection to be made to the Hariana Civil Service through competitive examination, the mark for viva voce test should not exceed 12.2% as is followed by the Union Public Service Commission of India for selection to the Indian Administrative service. The Division Bench of Punjab and Hariana High Court set aside the selection of the selected candidates on the ground, amongst others, that allocation of 200 marks for viva voce test was arbitrary but the Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the High Court. Both these judgments were delivered by Bhagobati, J and in both the cases the selection of the candidates were up held. 31. The learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, has referred to the case of Keshab Ram Pal vs. UP Higher Education Service Commission reported in AIR 1986 Supreme Court 597. In this case the petitioner along with 59 candidates was interviewed for selection in 8 posts of principals. As the petitioner was not selected he challenged the selection by the interview board on the ground that selection was arbitrary as marks were not separately allocated under each of the heads and the Supreme Court of India held that the interview board was under no obligation to sub-divide the marks under various sub-heads and accordingly, dismissed the writ petition. In this case apart from the 2 cases referred to above as reported in AIR 1981 (SC) 487 and (1985) 4 SCC 417 the Court considered two other cases reported in AIR 1971 (SC) 2303 and AIR 1981 (SC) 1777. The former case relates to selection of candidates for admission in the Medical College and the latter case relates to selection of officers by the Public Service Commission after holding a competitive examination for recruitment as Munsif. In the later case namely, Lila Dhar vs. State of Rajasthan 300 marks were allocated for, written examination and 100 marks for viva voce examination. 39 candidates were selected for appointment; the last candidate obtained a total of 190 marks in the examination comprising 185 in written examination and 55 in viva voce examination. The petitioner namely, Lila Dhar obtained a total of 189 marks, 159 in written test and 30 in viva voce and she was not selected for appointment. One of the contentions raised there was that the entire selection was vitiated by allocating more than 20% marks for viva voce examination. The writ petition was dismissed making the observation that the weight to be given to the interview test depends on the requirement of the service to which the recruitment was made. All the 4 decisions were considered in the case reported in AIR 1986 (SC) 597 wherein the following observations made in the case of Lila Dhar (AIR 1981 (SC) 1777) was quoted: “It is now well recognized that while a written examination assesses a candidate's knowledge and intellectual ability, an interview test is valuable to assess a candidate's overall intellectual and personal qualities. While a written examination has certain distinct advantages over the interview-test there are yet no written tests which can evaluate a candidate's initiative, alertness, resourcefulness, dependableness, cooperativeness, capacity for clear and logical presentation, effectiveness in discussion, effectiveness in meeting and dealing with others, adaptability, judgment, ability to make decision, ability to lead, intellectual and moral integrity. Some of these qualities may be evaluated, perhaps with some degree of error, by an interview-test, much depending on the constitution of the Interview Board....................” 32. In this case before us there was no written examination held for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary. Most of the cases of the Indian Supreme Court referred to above dealt with written examination and viva voce examination for the purpose of selection of candidates either to the Education Institution or to the administrative or judicial service. Only in the case of Keshab Ram Pal the candidates were interviewed for selection in eight post of Principals and the ground on which the selection was challenged as arbitrary was that the marks were not separately allocated under different sub-heads but the Supreme Court of India rejected the contention. In the case before us the candidates for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretaries were interviewed by the Council Committee consisting of 7 Cabinet Ministers and one Minister for State with the Minister for Education as its chairman and 40% marks has been allocated for the 8 Members of the Committee each having only 5 marks to be given to a particular candidate. Similarly, for the selection of candidates for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries the Selection Committee consisted of 5 Members including one Minister for State and 4 Secretaries of the Government with the Minister for State for Establishment as its Chairman. Both the committees interviewed the candidates after their cases have been processed through the Superior Selection Board. 60% of the marks are to be evaluated from 10 years ACR. The contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the interview and marking system by the Council Committee or Selection Committee for selection of Deputy Secretaries is without any lawful authority and that the so-called interview system for promotion has been introduced with the malafide intention for perpetuating favouritism and corruption. The learned Advocate further submitted that selection of the candidates on the basis of ACR is sufficient to judge the merit and the suitability of the officers and introduction of interview system allotting 40% marks for viva voce resulted in arbitrary selection of the promo tees. Nothing has been placed before us to show that the interview taken by such a high powered body was arbitrary or that the interview system has been introduced in order to politicise the Civil Service. It may be mentioned in this connection that 484 candidates were interviewed for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretaries of which 194 were promoted and out of 868 candidates for promotion for the posts of Deputy Secretaries 427 were promoted. The petitioners in response to the interview letters appeared before the Council Committee or the committee for selection of the Deputy Secretaries. They were given equal opportunities to appear before the Committee and they appeared; but since they were not found fit they were not promoted. 33. As has been observed by the Supreme Court of India as quoted above to evaluate a candidate's initiative, alertness, resourcefulness, dependableness, cooperativeness, capacity for clear and logical presentation, effectiveness in discussion, effectiveness in meeting and dealing with others, adaptability, judgment, ability to make decision, ability to lead, intellectual and moral integrity an interview-test is the best way to assess a candidate's over-all personal qualities. As such, it cannot be said that allocation of 40% marks for interview is dis-proportionate to 60% marks on evaluation of 10 years ACR There is hardly any scope for pick and choose by such a high powered body in selecting the officers for promotion. The respondents by filing a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition annexed a copy of the summary for consideration of the Cabinet decision dated 3.11.91 (Annexure-I) wherein the Ministry of Establishment submitted a guideline for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries allotting 40% marks for the Interview Board; and this has been approved by the Cabinet and signed by the Prime Minister on 11.11.91. This cabinet decision Annexure-I, was not published in the official Gazette and it is submitted by Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, that there is no legal basis for Annexure-I and, as such, the selection of the candidates for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries on the basis of such interview system is without any lawful authority. It is true that this Cabinet decision was not published in the official Gazette but this is an Executive order passed by the highest authority for the purpose of laying down the guide-line to be followed for the selection of the candidates by the Council Committee for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretaries and for selection of candidates by the Committee headed by the State Minister for Establishment for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretaries. Therefore it cannot be said that the Notification of the Government constituting the Special Promotion Committee, the Superior Selection Board and the Council Committee on Promotion relating to promotion of Superior Government Officials were made without any lawful authority. 34. To sum up, the petitioners have challenged the vires of Rule 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitments Rule, 1981 but the learned Advocate for the petitioner did not press this ground. The vires of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation 1979 was challenged on the ground of by-passing the Constitutional requirements of consultation in the matters of promotion to the Services of the Republic as provided under Article 140 (2) of the Constitution. But it cannot be said that the provision of Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation 1979, in particular Regulation 8 is ultra vires of the Constitution. As to the formation of the Council Committee, the Superior Selection Board and the Committee for Promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries, it cannot be said that these Committees were without any legal basis and, as such, the impugned notifications dated 19.8.1991, 9.10.91 and 4.12.91, cannot be said to be illegal. As such the notification dated 8.2.92 Annexure-M in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 and Notification dated 8.2.92 Annexure-E in writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 are valid and legal. For the reasons stated above both the Rules are discharged without any order as to cost and Writ Petition No. 813 of 1993 is rejected. The case of the petitioner Md. Mominul Islam is that at the relevant time he was serving as Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Rangamati Hills District and was superseded in the same manner as the original petitioner of the writ petition. 53. The case of petitioner Kazi Tariqul Islam is that he was originally appointed in the Industrial Management Service as a Class-I officer on the basis of Special Superior Service Examination, 1972 conducted by the Public Service Commission.
