It is further asserted that some officers who did not fulfill the above requirement were also promoted to the posts of Deputy Secretary. In this way, this petitioner was also superseded and many of his juniors were promoted to the posts of the Deputy Secretary in the Bangladesh Secretariat. 54. The case of petitioner Makimuddin Ahmed is that he was also appointed in the Industrial Management Service as a Class-I Officer on the basis of a Special Superior Service Examination, 1972 conducted by the Public Service Commission. He was subsequently absorbed in the Bangladesh Civil Service (Administration) Cadres as an Assistant Commissioner and was holding the post of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Khulna. His case is also that he was superseded in the same manner as the other petitioners, particularly, on the ground that he did not complete five years' service in the New National Scale Taka 1400.00-2225.00 in the post of senior Assistant Secretary or equivalent posts and his juniors were promoted to the posts of Deputy Secretary on the basis of the same arbitrary system of selection. 55. The case of petitioner Bimal Kumar Khundu is that he was also initially appointed in the Bangladesh Civil Service (Administration) Cadre as Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector on the basis of the Special Superior Service Examination, 1972 and was holding the post of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Netrakona at the relevant time. It is alleged by him that he was also recommended for promotion by the Superior Selection Board but despite this he was arbitrarily superseded in the same manner as the above petitioners and his juniors were promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary. 56. The respondent No. 1 challenged the claims of the above petitioners on similar grounds as the other writ petitions. 57. Mr. Amir-ul Islam argued at length in an attempt to assail the vires of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981, particularly, Rule 5 thereof. 58. Rule 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981, provides as follows: "Appointment by promotion-Subject to the provisions of Schedule II, appointment by promotion to a specified post of a service shall be made on the recommendation of the Council Committee on Promotion, Superior Selection Board or the Special Promotion Committee, as the case may be, constituted by the government in this behalf:' It, therefore, appears that in view of Rule 5 of the above rules appointment by promotion only to a "specified post" can be made according to the above Rules and the said promotion is also subject to Schedule II. "Specified post" is defined in clause (f) of Rule 2 of the above rules as follows: "Specified Post" means a post of the service specified in Schedule II." Schedule II annexed to these Rules shows that the post of Deputy Secretaries, Joint Secretaries and above are not included therein. By a subsequent amendment, however, promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary only from the post of Section Officers in the Secretariat was included in the Schedule but in the present writ petitions none of the petitioners case falls in this category as they did not seek promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary from the post of Assistant Secretary of the Bangladesh Secretariat. It, therefore, appears that the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 do not govern the case of the present petitioners and, as such, although lengthy argument was advanced challenging the vires of these Rules, particularly, Rules thereof, refrain from deciding the vires of these Rules as it is not necessary for the purpose of deciding the matters-in-issue in these writ petitions. 59. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam, the learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners, then challenged the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 (hereinafter called the Regulations) as ultra vires the Constitution. His attack on these Regulations has been two-fold. He has first of all, attacked these Regulations on the ground that these Regulations whereby certain posts which included the posts relating to the petitioners were kept out of the ambit of the Public Service Commission, were against the scheme of the Constitution and were also in contravention of a specific Article being Article 140 of the Constitution, in as much as, according to him, the tests and examination for selecting suitable candidates for appointment and promotion to any post in the service of the Republic cannot be conducted by any other body except the Public Service Commission in view of Clause (l) of Article 140 of the Constitution and appointment and promotion to any post in the service of the Republic cannot be made by the President without consulting the Public Service Commission in view of Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution. He has also attacked these Regulations on the ground that these Regulations could not be framed by the President before enactment of law by Parliament in view of clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution as, according to him, in view of the above clause Parliament must first enact law and then such Regulations may follow the law enacted by Parliament and since no law in respect of the matters covered by Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution was ever enacted by Parliament, making of the Regulations by the President was without jurisdiction and, therefore, illegal. Mr. Islam has next contended that Regulation 3 and Regulation 4 whereby the posts, with which the petitioners are concerned were kept out of the ambit of consultation with the Public Service Commission by the President regarding appointment and promotion to these posts, were absolutely illegal as, according to him, no post could be kept out of the ambit of consultation of the Public Service Commission in view of Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution. In other words, according to him, framing of these exclusion clauses was beyond the power of the President as these were in contravention of Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution. Mr. Islam wanted to say that in view of the above legal position the omission by the Government to consult the Public Service Commission regarding promotion of the petitioners 19 the post of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary respectively was illegal and ultra vires the Constitution and cannot, therefore, be sustained. 60. Mr. Aminul Huq, the learned Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.1, has, on the other hand, argued that the Regulations framed by the President were within his constitutional powers and these Regulations were by no means violative of Article 140 of the Constitution. The learned Attorney-General has taken pains to interpret both Clause (1) and Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution and has argued that Clause (1) of Article 140 simply lays down the functions of the Public Service Commission but Clause (1) of Article 140 of the Constitution does not make it mandatory on the part of the Government to ask the Public Service Commission to conduct tests and examinations and to seek advice of the Public Service Commission on all matters of appointment and promotion. He has also argued that the power to make Regulations by the President under Clause (a) of Article 140 of the Constitution is independent of the power of Parliament to enact law in matters covered by the said clause and it is not correct to say that the Regulations must follow an enactment in the matter passed by Parliament. He has also argued that the power to make Regulations by the President under Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution also includes the power to exclude any post or class of post in the service of the Republic from the obligation of consulting the Public Service Commission in matters of appointment and promotion to these posts. 61. It is undisputed that while considering the cases of promotion of the petitioners in these writ petitions no test and examination was conducted to judge their suitability for promotion by the Public Service Commission. It is also not disputed by the respondents that the Public Service Commission was not also consulted at the time of considering the cases of promotion of the petitioners to higher posts, such as, the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary respectively. It has, therefore, to be first decided whether holding of suitability test or examination for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary in the Bangladesh Secretariat is the exclusive power and jurisdiction of the Public Service Commission alone and is a constitutional mandate as has been argued by Mr. Amir-ul Islam. If the answer is affirmative, then it will follow that the procedure of test and examination adopted by the respondents in selecting candidates for appointing to the above posts superseding the petitioners was ultra vires the Constitution and, in that case, the other points pressed by the parties need not at all be considered. If the answer is in the negative, we have then to determine whether by omitting to consult the Public Service Commission while selecting candidates for promotion to the posts involved in these writ petitions the respondents violated any constitutional mandate and if the answer is in the affirmative, we need not enter into the other issues agitated by the parties. As such, I propose to take up the cases of the parties in respect of the above first of all. 62. In order to do so, it is necessary to reproduce Article 140 of the Constitution and the relevant Regulation in order to appreciate the stands taken by the petitioners and the respondents respectively in these writ petitions and in this connection, Regulation 3, Regulation 4 and Regulation 8 of the Regulations are relevant and the learned Attorney-General mainly depended on these Regulations in supporting the stand of the Government that no test and examination by, and no consultation with, the Public Service Commission was necessary in case of promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary; Article 140 of the Constitution runs as follows: "(1) The functions of a public service commission shall be- (a) to conduct tests and examinations for the selection of suitable persons for appointment to the service of the Republic. (b) to advise the President on any matter on which the commission is consulted under clause (2) or on any matter connected with its functions which is referred to the commission by the President; and (c) such other functions as may be prescribed by law. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, and any regulation (not inconsistent with such law) which may-be made by the President after consultation with a commission, the President shall consult a commission with respect to- (a) matters relating to qualifications for, and methods of recruitment to, the service of the Republic; (b) the principles to be followed in making appointments to that service and promotions and transfers from one branch of the service to another, and the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions and transfers; (c) matters affecting the terms and conditions (including pension rights) of that service; and (d) the discipline of the service." Clause (b) of Regulation 3, Clause (a) of Regulation 4 and Regulation 8 of the Regulations are also relevant and these run as follows: "3. It shall not be necessary to consult the Commission in regard to any matter mentioned in sub-clauses (a) and (b) of Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution in the case of- (a)............................. (b) the posts appointment to which requires the specific order of the President under the Rules of Business, 1975; 4. It shall not be necessary to consult the Government with regard to the selection for appointment- (a) to a Class I service or service or post of any officer who is already a member of a Class I service, or holding a Class I post; 8. It shall not be necessary to consult the Commission in cases of promotion within the same class of service." Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution lays down that subject to any regulation that may be made by the President after consultation with a Commission the President shall consult the Public Service Commission with respect to matters relating to qualifications for, and methods of recruitment to, the service of the Republic and the principles to be followed in making appointments, promotions and transfers and the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions and transfers, etc. 63. We have already seen that Clause (b) of Regulation 3 of the Regulations lays down that in case of appointment to the posts appointments to which requires the specific order of the President under the Rules of Business, 1975 no consultation with the Public Service Commission is necessary. 64. Rule 6 of the Rule of Business, 1975 lays down as follows: "All cases of the nature specified in Schedule III to these Rules shall, before issue of orders therefor be submitted to the President and no action on them will be taken otherwise than in accordance with the directions of the President." Item No. 23 of Schedule III of the Rules of Business, 1975 lays down as follows: "All Secretariat appointments of and above the rank of Deputy Secretary" 65. Consequently, in view of Clause (b) of Regulation 3 of the Regulations read with Rule 6 and Item No. 23 of Schedule III of the Rules of Business, 1975 no consultation with the Public Service Commission was necessary in case of appointment to the post of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary in question. It therefore, appears that in view of Rule 6 of the Rules of Business, 1975, since the specific order of the President was required to make appointments and promotions to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary in the Bangladesh Secretariat and as clause (b) of Regulation 3 excludes all posts appointments to which required the specific order of the President from the ambit of consultation with the Public Service Commission, it was not necessary to consult the Public Service Commission in case of appointments and promotions to the post of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary. Moreover, in view of Regulation 8 the case of promotion within the same class of service was also excluded from the ambit of consultation with the Public Service Commission. So, if these Regulations are found to be intra vires the Constitution the omission of the Government to consult the Public Service Commission before making promotions to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary cannot be said to have been illegal and ultra vires the Constitution. 66. Mr. Islam has launched a general attack on these Regulations as a whole on the ground that the scheme of the Constitution is that the Public Service Commission is the only body contemplated in the Constitution as empowered to select candidates for appointment, promotion, etc. to all posts in the service of the Republic and in this respect, Mr. Islam depended on Article 140 of the, Constitution. 67. A consideration of Clause (1) of Article 140 of the Constitution simply shows that the functions of the Public Service Commission have been enumerated therein and these functions are, (1) to conduct tests and examinations for selection of suitable persons for appointment to the service of the Republic, (2) to advise the President on any matter on which the Public Service Commission is consulted under Clause (2) of Article 140 or on any matter connected with its functions which is referred to the Public Service Commission by the President and also (3) to discharge such other functions as may be entrusted to it by law. We have not been able to persuade ourselves to hold that by enumerating the functions of the Public Service Commission in Clause (1) of Article 140 the Constitution-makers intended to say that it was the Public Service Commission alone having exclusive jurisdiction to conduct tests and examinations for selection of suitable persons for appointment to the service of the Republic and that in all cases of appointment and promotion to all posts in the service of the Republic it was mandatory on the part of the President to consult the Public Service Commission. Clause (1) and Clause (2) of Article 140 reading together imply that the President was empowered, by making Regulations, to exclude the question of consulting the Public Service Commission in case of promotion to any post in the service of the Republic. It also does not appear to us that the constitution-makers intended to vest exclusive jurisdiction in the Public Service Commission to select candidates for promotions to all posts in the service of the Republic. It appears to us that the Public Service Commission is a consultative body and it is for the Government to decide in which cases of appointment and promotion the Public Service Commission should hold tests and examinations and it also appears to us that in general, the President is required to consult the Public Service Commission in matters mentioned in sub-clauses (a) to (d) of Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution unless the President excludes any post from the ambit of such consultation by making Regulations under Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution. 68. Mr. Islam has next argued that in view of Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution the President could not make the Regulations before enactment of law by Parliament in view of the following words appearing in the said clause, "Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament and any Regulation (not inconsistent with such law)." 69. In order to appreciate the significance of Clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution we may trace the background and history of this particular provision. 70. In the Government of India Act, 1935 almost similar provision was made in section 266 thereof which provided as follows: "(1) It shall be the duty of the Federal and the Provincial Public Service Commissions to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Federation and the services of the Provinces respectively. (2) It shall also be the duty of the Federal Public Service Commission, if requested by any two or more Provinces so to do, to assist these Provinces in framing and operating schemes, of joint recruitment for their forest services, and any other services for which candidates possessing special qualifications are required. (3) The Secretary of State as respects services and posts in which appointments are made by him, the Governor-General in his discretion as respects other-services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Federation, and the Governor in his discretion as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of a Province, may make regulations specifying the matters on which either generally, or in any particular class of case or in any particular circumstances, it shall not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted but, subject to regulations so made and to the provisions of the next succeeding sub-section, the Federal Commission or, as the case may be, the Provincial Commission shall be consulted- (a) on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and for civil posts; (b) on the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers; (c) on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving His Majesty in a civil capacity in India, including memorials or petitions relating to such matters; (d) on any claim by or in respect of a person who is serving or has served His Majesty in a civil capacity in India that any costs incurred by him in defending legal proceedings instituted against him in respect of acts done or purporting to be done in the execution of his duty should be paid out of the revenues of the Federation or, as the case may be, the Province; (e) on any claim for the award the award of a pension in respect of injuries sustained by a person while serving His Majesty in a civil capacity in India, and any question as to the amount of any such award, and it shall be the duty of a Public Service Commission to advise on any matter so referred to them and on any other matter which the Governor-General in his discretion, or as the case may be, the Governor in his discretion, may refer to them. (4) Nothing in this section shall require a Public Service Commission to be consulted as respects the manner in which appointments and posts are to be allocated as between the various communities in the Federation or a Province or, in the case of the subordinate ranks of the various police forces in India, as respect any of the matters mentioned in paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section (3) of this section." 71. It appears from the above that sub-section (3) of section 266 of the Government of India Act, 1935 provided similar provision as Article 140 of the Constitution and sub-section (3) of section 266 made specific provision empowering the Secretary of State as respects services and posts to which appointments were made by him, the Governor-General as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Indian Federation and the Governor as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of a Province to make regulations specifying the matters on which it would be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted and subject to such regulations they were bound to consult the Public Service Commission in matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (e) of the above sub-section. 72. The corresponding Article in the Indian Constitution is Article 320 which runs as follows: "(1) It shall be the duty of the Union and the State Public Service Commissions to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Union and the services of the State respectively. (2) It shall also be the duty of the Union Public Service Commission, if requested by any two or more States so to do, to assist those States in framing and operating schemes of joint recruitment for any service for which candidates possessing special qualifications are required. (3) The Union Public Service Commission or the State Public Service Commission, as the case may be, shall be consulted- (a) on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and for civil posts; (b) on the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers; (c) on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India or the Government of a State in a civil capacity including memorials or petitions relating to such matters; (d) on any claim by or in respect of a person who is serving or has served under the Government of India or the Government of a State or under the Crown in India or under the Government of an Indian State, in a civil capacity, that any costs incurred by him in defending legal proceedings instituted against him in respect of acts done or purporting to be done in the execution of his duty should be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India, or, as the case may be, out of the Consolidated Fund of the State; (e) On any claim for the award of a pension in respect of injuries sustained by a person while serving under the Government of India or the Government of a State or under the Crown in India or under the Government of an Indian State, in a civil capacity, and any question as to the amount of any such award, and it shall be the duty of a Public Service Commission to advise on any matter so referred to them and on any other matter which the President, or, as the case may be, the Governor or Rajpramukh of the State, may refer to them: Provided that the President as respects the all-India services and also as respect other services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union, and the Governor or Rajpramukh, as the case may be, as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of a State, may make regulations specifying the matters in which either generally, or in any particular class of case or in any particular circumstances, it shall not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted. (4) Nothing in clause (3) shall require a Public Service Commission to be consulted as respects the manner in which any provision referred to in clause (4) of Article 16 may be made or as respects the manner in which effect may be given to the provisions of Article 335. (5) All regulations made under the proviso to clause (3) by the President or the Governor or Rajpramukh of a State shall be laid for not less than. fourteen days before each House of Parliament or the House or each House of the Legislature of the State, as the case may be, as soon as possible after they are made, and shall be subject to such modifications, whether by way of repeal or amendment, as both Houses of Parliament or the House or both Houses of the Legislature of the State may make during the session in which they are so laid." 73. In the Pakistan Constitutions of 1956 and 1962 similar provisions were made in Articles 188 and 185 respectively which run as follows: "188 (1) It shall be the duty of the Federal Public Service Commission and a Provincial Public Service Commission to conduct examinations for appointment to the services and posts concerned with the affairs of the Federation, or the Province, as the case may be. (2) The President, in respect of services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Federation, and the Governor of a Province, in respect of services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Province may make regulations specifying the matters in which generally or in any particular class of case, or in any particular circumstances, it shall not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted; but, subject to such regulations, the appropriate Public Service Commission shall be consulted- (a) on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and posts and qualifications of candidates for such services and posts; (b) On the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another, and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers; (c) on all disciplinary matters affecting a person in the service of the Federal or a Provincial Government in a civil capacity, including compulsory retirement whether for disciplinary reasons or otherwise, and memorials or petitions relating to such matters; (d) on any claim by or in respect of a person who is serving or has served under the Federal or a Provincial Government in a civil capacity that any costs incurred by him in defending any legal proceedings instituted against him in respect of acts done or purported to be done in the execution of his duty should be paid out of the general consolidated fund or the Provineial Consolidated Fund, as the case may be; (e) on any proposal to withhold a special or additional pension or to reduce any ordinary pension; and (f) on any claim for the award of a pension or allowance in respect of injuries sustained while serving under the Federal or a Provincial Government in a civil capacity, and any question as to the amount of any such award; and it shall be the duty of the Public Service Commission to advise on any matter so referred to them, and on any other matter which the President or the Governor, as the case may be, may refer to the Commission. (3) Where under the Constitution or any law, rules are made for regulating the appointment or conditions of service of persons in the service of Pakistan, but not under the control of the Federal Government or a Provincial Government, such rules may provide for consultation with the appropriate Public Service Commission; and, subject to any express provision of the Constitution or of the said law, clause (2) shall apply mutatis mutandis." "185. (1) The functions of the Central Public Service Commission shall be- (a) to conduct tests and examinations for the selection of suitable persons for appointment to the All-Pakistan Services, the civil services of the Centre and civil posts connected with the affairs of the Centre; (b) to advise the President on any matter on which the Commission is consulted under clause (2) of this Article or which is referred to the Commission by the President; and (c) such other functions as may be prescribed by law. (2) Except to the extent that the President, after consulting the Commission, may provide otherwise by Order, the President shall, in relation to the All-Pakistan Services, the civil services of the Centre and civil posts connected with the affairs of the Centre, consult the Central Public Service Commission with respect to- (a) matters relating to qualifications for, and methods of recruitment to, services and posts; (b) the principles on which appointments and promotions should be made; (c) the principles on which persons belonging to one service should be transferred to another; (d) matters affecting terms and conditions of service and proposals adversely affecting pension right; and (e) disciplinary matters." 74. It, therefore, appears that the provision contained in clause (2) of Article 140 of our Constitution in fact followed from sub-section (3) of section 266 of the Government of India Act, 1935. It also appears that in the proviso to clause (e) of Article 320 of the Indian Constitution, in clause (2) of Article 188 of the Pakistan Constitution, 1956 and in clause (2) of Article 185 of the Pakistan Constitution. 1962 similar provisions were made empowering the Parliament to exclude any post or class of post from the ambit of consultation with the Public Service Commission in respect of appointments, promotions, etc. to such posts. Sub-section (3) of section 266 of the Government of India Act, 1935 is very clear empowering the Secretary of State, the Governor-General of India and the Governors of the Provinces to make regulations specifying the matters on which either generally or in any particular class of case or in any particular circumstances it would not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted. So, it appears that in the Regulations framed under the Government of India Act, 1935 the matters in respect of which consultation would not be necessary were to be specifically specified. In the proviso to clause (e) of Article 320 of the Indian Constitution the President of India and the Governor of the State, as the case may be, are empowered to make regulations specifying the matters in which either generally or in any particular class of case or in any particular circumstances it shall not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted. It may be noticed that the language used in sub-section (3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 and the language in the proviso to sub-clause (e) of Article 320 of the Indian Constitution are similar so far as the exclusion clauses are concerned. The latter appears to be exact reproduction of the former. Similarly, in the Pakistan Constitution, 1956 the same words as in the Government of India Act, i935 and the Indian Constitution were borrowed for providing for the exclusion clause in clause (2) of Article 188 thereof. There was subsequently a departure in the Pakistan Constitution, 1962 in which in clause (2) of Article 185 the exclusion clause was provided by using different words which ran as follows: "Except to the extent that the President, after consulting the Commission, may provide otherwise by Order.........................." In our Constitution, however, the exclusion clause was provided in clause (2) of Article 140 by using somewhat different language as follows: "Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parlament and any regulation (not inconsistent with such law) which may be made by the President after consultation with a Commission............................." Subject to the above provision, the President was enjoined to consult the Public Service Commission in matters of appointments, promotions, etc. of the persons in the service of the Republic. 75. From an analysis of the above provisions, it appears to me that in the Government of India Act, 1935 the Secretary of State, 'the Governor-General and the Governors of the Provinces, as the case might be, and in the Indian Constitution and Pakistan Constitution, 1956, the President of India and the President of Pakisten respectively were empowered to make Regulations and in such regulations were empowered to provide for exclusion clauses by specifying the matters or particular class of cases or particular circumstances in which consultation with the Public Service Commission would not be necessary. In the Pakistan Constitution, 1962 wider powers appear to have been vested in the President by removing the requirement of specifying the post, class of post or circumstances, in which consulation would not be necessary. In our Constitution also wider power appears to have, been given to the President by providing that Consultation would be subject to such regulations but such regulations would be subject to any provision of law made by Parliament. In other words, in the Government of India Act, 1935, the Indian Constitution and the Pakistan Constitution, 1956, the Governor-General of India, the President of India and the President of Pakistan respectively, were only empowered to exclude certuin specified matters from the ambit of consultation with the Public Service Commission by making Regulations whereas, in the Bangladesh Constitution consultation in all respects as a whole was subject to Regulations made by the President which were, however, subject to law that may be made by Parliament. 76. Mr. Islam has also argued that the President is not empowered to make regulations before Parliament enacts law. 77. In this connection, it appears to me that the power to enact law and the power to make Regulations under clause (2) of Article 140 of the Constitution are absolutely independent powers subject to the condition that the Regulations would be subject to any provision of law that may be enacted by Parliament which means that if any Regulation is in conflict with any provision of law made by Parliament the provision of law will prevail whether the law was enacted earlier than the Regulation or later than the Regulation. This provision does by no means mean that the President cannot make Regulations unless and until law is enacted by Parliament as has been argued by Mr. Islam attaching great emphasis on the words, "subject to the provision of any law made by Parliament." By using the above words, the Constitution-makers did not, it appears, mean that law must first of all be enacted by Parliament and then Regulations by the President may follow as contended by Mr. Islam. The plain meaning of the above words is that any Regulation made by the President shall be subject to law enacted by Parliament whether the enactment has taken place earlier than the Regulation or later. 78. It, therefore, appears to us that the Regulations whereby appointment to the posts of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary were excluded from the ambit of consultation with the Public Service Commission were not ultre vires Article 140 of the Constitution. We, accordingly, find these Regulations intra vires the Constitution and, therefore, lawful. 79. It therefore, appears to us that the respondents did not commit any illegallity by omitting to consult the Public Service Commission while considering the cases of promotions of the petitioners to the posts of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary. We do not also find any substance in the contention of the petitioners that the Public Service Commission alone and no other agency was competent to test the suitability of candidates for promotion to the above posts. 80. Mr. Islam has also drawn our attention to Article 133 of the Constitution and has argued that this Article empowers Parliament to enact law for regulating appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic and, as such, no other authority in the Republic has the power to determine the conditions of service of the persons in the service of the Republic which included appointments and promotions which are in dispute in these writ petitions. He has also argued that by assuming the power of Parliament and by determining the conditions of service of the persons in the service of the Republic the Executive branch of the Government acted without jurisdiction and illegally. 81. The learned Attorney-General has tried to refute the above contention of Mr. Islam by arguing that although Article 133 of the Constitution made provisions empowering Parliament to make law to regulate appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic, the proviso to the said Article empowered the President to make rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic until such law is enacted by Parliament and as Parliament has not yet acted under Article 133 of the Constitution the President made various rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of the persons in the service of the Republic including the petitioners. 82. Article 133 of the Constitution runs as follows: "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution Parliament may by law regulate the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic: Provided that it shall be competent for the President to make rules regulating the appointment and the conditions of service of such persons until provision in that behalf is made by or under any law, and rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any such law." From the above, it appears that the intention of the Constitution-makers was that Parliament should take steps to enact law for regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic and the proviso to the above Article empowered the President to made rules for regulating such appointment and conditions of service. The proviso to the above Article appears to me to be an exception providing for arrangement to be made by the President for regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic for an interim period until law is enacted by Parliament according to Article 133 of the Constitution. It also appears to me that the proviso which is an exception to Article 133 was an arrangement to avoid a vacuum which might be created during the period taken by Parliament to enact law under Article 133 of the Constitution. It is unfortunate that although more than two decades after enactment of the Constitution have passed, the main provision of enacting law under Article 133 of the Constitution has not been implemented and the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic are being regulated and determined by the power vested in the President under the proviso which, we have already observed, is an exception to the main Article. It, however, appears that the proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution empowered the President to make rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic until law is enacted. The President did not therefore, illegally assume the power of Parliament while making rules and regulations for regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic and, therefore, did not act without jurisdiction, as has been argued by Mr. Islam. 83. Mr. Amir-ul Islam, the learned Counsel for the petitioners, then attacked the Notification No. 4(1) /90/217-Committee dated 9th October, 1991 as at Annexure-'X' to Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 whereby the Council Committee regarding promotions to the post of Joint Secretary and also Notification No. সম/ উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-৯৮ dated 4th December, 1991 as at Annexure-A to Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 whereby the Committee for considering the promotions to the post of Deputy Secretary were constituted. Mr. Islam has also attacked the procedure adopted by these two Committees for selecting candidates for promotions to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary respectively as absolutely arbitrary and, therefore, violative of Article 27 and Article 29 of the Constitution. 84. The learned Attorney-General has asserted that the Government have inherent powers to decide as to how promotions to various posts should be made and also to constitute bodies or committees to consider the suitability of candidates for promotion to various posts including the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary in the Bangladesh Secretariat and particularly so, in absence of any provision in any law made by parliament under Article 133 of the Constitution. The learned Attorney-General has also contended that the aforesaid Committees' fixed certain objective standards of assessing the suitability of the candidates for promotion to the above posts and introduced marking system and took test and interview and did not adopt any arbitrary procedure of selection and, as such, according to him, there is no substance in the contentions raised by the petitioners. He has also argued that after the petitioners submitted themselves to the above procedure and actually appeared at the test and interview there is no scope for them to challenge the constitution of the above Committees and the prooedures respectively followed by them. He has also contended that the petitioners having been found unsuitable they were rightly rejected by the above Committees which considered their cases. 85. We have first to consider whether the Government had any authority to constitute the Council Committee as per Notification No.4 (1) 90-217-Committee dated 9th October, 1991 and whether this Committee was legally empowered to consider the case of promotion of the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 and Writ Petition No. 813 of 1993 to the posts of Joint Secretary and also the Committee constituted under Notification No. সম/ উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-৯৮ dated 4th December, 1991 to consider the case of promotion of the petitioners of the other writ petition to the post of Deputy Secretary and whether this Committee was empowered to consider the cases of promotion of the above persons. 86. Both Mr. Amir-ul Islam and the learned Attorney-General and, particularly, the learned Attorney-General assisted us by furnishing various notifications which gave us an idea as to the origin and history of these Committees on promotion. From these notifications it appears that Superior Selection Board was constituted by the Government of Bangladesh by Notification No. BD 1-165/72-613 dated the 1st March, 1972 and this Superior Selection Board considered the cases of appointments and promotions to and above the rank of Section Officer (later redesignated as Assistant Secretary) in the Bangladesh Secretariat. It appears from this Notification that the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister was the Chairman of this Superior Selection Board and five Secretaries of five different Ministries respectively were Members and the Deputy Secretary, establishment Division was the Member-Secretary of this Superior Selection Board. The procedure to be followed by this Superior Selection Board and the procedures of selection for promotion to the above posts were enumerated in this Notification and these ran as follows: "3. The following will be the procedure of the Selection Board: (1) For Secretariat posts, Ministries will not make any recommendation at all. They will simply report the occurrence of the anticipated vacancy together with the qualifications and experience which the officers required for vacancy should possess. Officers will be selected in the following manner: (a) If any officer who had already been approved by the Selection Board for appointment to the grade in which the vacancy will occur or who was already serving in that grade in another Ministry, is likely to be available, the Establishment Secretary will arrange for his transfer to that Ministry. (b) If no such officer is available, the Establishment Secretary will look up the list of officers suitable for appointment in the vacancy in question and place their names before the Selection Board to determine their suitability and communicate the name of the officer thus approved. 2.(2) Where it is proposed to fill an appointment by promotion within the Department the proposal duly supported with the record of service and the Character Rolls of all the candidates who, could properly be considered, should be forwarded to the Establishment Secretary. It should not be merely stated that a particular officer is considered most suitable for the post. If it is proposed to pass over any officer, the reason for that should also be stated. (3) All correspondence regarding matters requiring orders of the Selection Board should be by means of semi-official letters addressed to the Establishment Secretary.• Self-contained summary should accompany all cases. (4) Appointments to casual vacancies for periods of less than two months will not require the approval of the Selection Board. Such appointments should be referred forthwith to the Board if the period is extended beyond two months. (5) The decision of the Superior Selection Board will be communicated to the Ministries/ Divisions concerned. Thereafter they will submit summaries to the Prime Minister through respective Ministers for the approval of the Prime Minister. When the approval of the Prime Minister is obtained, the same will be communicated to the Establishment Division in respect of Secretariat appointments. (All Secretariat appointments will be notified by the Establishment Division). In cases where expeditious action is necessary, the approval of the Prime Minister will be obtained by the Establishment Division. (6) The Selection Board should deal with appointments to higher posts in the Secretariat even in the rare cases when such appointments are made from persons not in Government service, i.e. all appointments which are within the purview of the Selection Board would be made on the recommendation of the Board irrespective of the fact whether or not they are made from among persons in Government service. The Board, however, will not be concerned with the appointments which are within the purview of the Public Service Commission." From the above, it appears that by this Notification which was the first Notification as conceded by the learned Advocate for the petitioners as well as the learned Attorney-General, it was provided that all proposals for promotions were to be supported with the records of service and Character Rolls of all the candidates. It appears that no system of test or examination was provided in this Notification and candidates for promotion used to be selected solely on the basis of their records of service and character rolls. It also appears that in the Notification it was also specifically directed that if a particular officer was proposed to be passed over the reason thereof should clearly be stated. So, it appears that a more or less objective method of selection was followed under this Notification. 87. The next Notification that has been placed before us is a resolution bearing No. স, বি/এ৯-২২৪/৭৫-৬২৯ dated 29th August, 1975. By this the Superior Selection Board was reconstituted with seven members of whom the Secretary, Ministry of Cabinet Affairs was the Chairman and five Secretaries of different Ministries were Members and one Secretary of the concerned Ministry was also a Member. This Superior Selection Board was empowered to-select candidates for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary and above in the Bangladesh Secretariat and some posts in Corporations and Semi-Government Organizations. The procedure to be followed by this Selection Board were also clearly specified in paragraph 3 of the Notification which runs as follows: ৩। বোর্ডের কার্যপ্রনালী নিম্নরুপ হইবেঃ (ক) সচিবালয়ের পদের জন্য মন্ত্রালয় বা বিভাগ আদৌ, কোন সুপারিশ করিবেন না। তবে শুধুমাত্র পদের শূন্যতা সম্পর্কে রির্পোট করিবেন এবং শূন্য পদ পূরণের জন্য অফিসারের যোগ্যতা এবং অভিজ্ঞতা সম্পর্কে তথ্যাদি পাঠাইবেন নিম্নবর্নিত কার্যরত থাকেন এবং সহজলভ্য হল, তাহা হইলে সংস্থাপন বিভাগের সচিব উক্ত অফিসারকে সংশ্লিষ্ট মন্ত্রানালয়ে বদলীর জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করিবেন। (২) যদি উপরোক্ত শ্রেনীর কোন অফিাসার না পাওয়া যায়, তাহা By another Notification dated 13th September, 1975 under Memo No. স, বি/এ১-২২৪/৭৫-৬৭৩ the Selection Board was empowered to reconsider the cases of superseded officers. 89. Thereafter, the Superior Selection Board was reconstituted by various Notifications from time to time. It is not necessary to quote these numerous notifications. The procedures laid down in the earliest Notification dated 1st March, 1972 for selecting candidates for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary and above remained almost the same until 1979 when the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 was made where under a different procedure for selection to the post of Deputy Secretary, Joint Secretary, Additional Secretary and Secretary was provided. It is not necessary to describe in detail the procedure laid down in the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 as this Senior Services Pool Order was subsequently repealed. In short, by the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 a pool cadre was created and different posts were included in the pool cadre and quota was fixed for encadrement in the pool from various services. It was also provided that the suitability for encadrement would be decided on the basis of examinations and tests conducted by the Public Service Commission. This Senior Services Pool Order continued until 17th July, 1989 when by Notification No. এস, আর, ও ২৬১-আইন/৮৯/সম(বিধি-২)/ এস, এসপি-১/৮৯ dated 17th July, 1989 the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 was repealed and the Senior Services Pool was abolished. The senior services pool order also empowered the Government to constitute Selection Boards for selection of pool officers for the posts which were to be filled in only by pool officers and also for selection of persons for encadrement as pool officers. After the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 the Superior Selection Board was reconstituted by Notification No. ED/ SSB-13/78-648 dated 8th October, 1979. Then after promulgation of Martial Law on 24th March, 1982, the Superior Selection Board was abolished by an order passed by the Chief Martial Law Administrator under No. 7053/ 1/Civ II dated 5th July, 1982 and the functions of the Superior Selection Board were entrusted to the Establishment Division with the direction that all proposals for promotion, etc. should be placed before the Chief Martial Law Administrator for decision. Twenty two days after this Notification this order dated 5th July, 1982 was repealed by another order issued by the Chief Martial Law Administrator's Secretariat under No. 7053/1/Civ II dated 27th July, 1982 and the Superior Selection Board was restored and directed to function as before until further orders. The Superior Selections Board was again reconstituted vide Notification No. ইউ/এস,এস,বি-১/৭৯-৪৫৪ dated 23.2.83 and it was directed to consider the cases of promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary outside the Senor Services Pool and the cases of promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and above in the Bangladesh Secretariat. The procedure laid down for selecting candidates were almost similar to those laid down in the Notification dated 1st March, 1992 with the difference that the proposal should be forwarded to the Chief Martial Law Administrator for his decision. It appears that this procedure continued for some time and thereafter, the Superior Selection Board was decentralised vide Notification No. উনি-৪/৯-১৪/৮৯-৩২৫ dated 24.7.89. The Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 was repealed vide Notification No. এস,আর,ও ২৬১-আইন/৮৯সম (বিধি-২) এস,পি-১/৮৯ dated 17th July, 1989 and the Senior Services Pool was abolished. It was laid down in the repealing notification that the Establishment Division would issue the principles to be followed for promotion and appointment to the posts of Secretaries, Additional Secretaries, Joint Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries separately (Paragraph 6 of the Notification). It, however, appears that no such principles were fixed by the Establishment Division immediately. Then followed Notification No. সম/উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-২৩ dated 19th August 1991, By this Notification the Superior Selection Board was reconstituted with the Secretary, Ministry of Cabinet Affairs as the Chairman and eight others including six Secretaries and two Additional Secretaries of different Ministries as Members. By this Notification the Superior Selection Board was empowered to recommend cases of appointment and promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and above in the Bangladesh secretariat. By this Notification departmental promotion/ appointment Board was also constituted empowering this Board to consider promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary in the Bangladesh Secretariat. Paragraph 6 of this Notification is very important and I am tempted to quote this paragraph which provides the guide-lines for the above Board for considering the suitability of candidates for promotion to the above posts and these guide-lines are in paragraph 6 which runs as follows: “৬। পদোন্নতি, নিয়োগ সিলেকশন গ্রেড ও উচ্চতর টাইম স্কেল প্রাপ্যতার ভিত্তিতে শুধু বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন ও সার্ভিস রেকর্ড (শৃঙ্খলা, আচরণ, দুনীর্তি ইত্যাদি সংক্রান্ত রেকর্ড) এর ভিত্তিতে বিবেচিত হইবে। এতদসংক্রান্ত প্রস্তাবাদি বিবেচনাকালে সংশ্লিষ্ট বোর্ড/কমিটি পৃথকভাবে কোন পরীক্ষা বা সাক্ষৎকার গ্রহণ করিবে না। তবে বি সি এস (পদোন্নতির জন্য পরীক্ষা) বিধি, ১৯৮৬, সংশ্লিষ্ট নিয়োগবিধি অথবা অন্য কোন বিধিতে যদি কোন পরীক্ষা বা সাক্ষাৎকারের ব্যবস্থা থাকে, তবে উক্ত বিধি যথারীতি অনুসরণ করিতে হইবে।” This Notification was issued during the tenure of the Acting President The guide-lines laid down in paragraph 6 above clearly show that the system of test and interview was discouraged and the Boards were debarred from holding any test or interview for selecting candidates and the Boards were enjoined to consider only the annual confidential reports and service of the officers who were to be considered for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and above. The Council Committee was also empowered to consider the proposals of the Superior Selection Board for promotion to the above posts. It is patent that in this Notification no guide-lines to be followed by this Council Committee was provided. 90. Similarly, by Notification No. সম/উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-৯৮ dated 4th December, 1991 as at Annexure- 'A' to Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 another Committee was formed for considering the cases of promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and this Notification runs as follows: প্রজ্ঞাপন বিষয়ঃ উচ্চতর সরকারী পদে ও স্ব-শাসিত সংস্থার পদে নিয়োগ। পদোন্নতি। উপরোক্ত বিষয়ে সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয়ের ১৯-০৮-১৯৯১ ইং (০৩ রা ভাদ্র, ১৩৯৮ বাংলা) তারিখের নঙ-সম/উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-২৩ নম্বর প্রজ্ঞাপনের ২(৩) উপ-অনুচ্ছেদ নিম্নরুপ সংশোধন করা হইলঃ (ক) সচিবালয়ের উপ-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতি প্রদানের উদ্দেশ্যে সাক্ষাৎকার গ্রহনপূর্বক সুপারিশ করার জন্য এবং উপ-সচিবগণের উচ্চতর টাইম স্কেল বিবেচনার জন্য নিম্নরুপ কমিটি গঠন করা হইলঃ (১) সংস্থাপন প্রতিমন্ত্রী (২) মন্ত্রী পরিষদ সচিব (৩) সংস্থাপন সচিব (৪) সচিব, প্রধানমন্ত্রীর কার্য্যালয় (৫) সংশ্লিষ্ট ক্যাডার নিয়ন্ত্রনকারী মন্ত্রণালয় এবং বিভাগের সচিব চেয়ারম্যান সদস্য সদস্য সচিব সদস্য সদস্য (খ) উপ-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতি ও উপ-সচিবগণের টাইম স্কেল সংক্রান্ত এস এস বি-র সুপারিশ এই কমিটি বিবেচনা করিবে এবং এই কমিটির সুপারিশ প্রধান মন্ত্রীর অনুমোদনের জন্য সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় পেশ করিবে। সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় পেশ করিবে। সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় এই কমিটিকে সচিবিক সহায়তা প্রদান করিবে। ২। সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় ১৯.০৮.১৯৯১ ইং তারিখের পূর্বোক্ত প্রজ্ঞাপনের ৬ নম্বর অনুচ্ছেদ এতদ্বারা বাতিল করা হইল। উক্ত প্রজ্ঞাপনে সকল স্থানে “রাষ্ট্রপতি” এর স্থলে প্রধানমন্ত্রী” পড়িতে হইবে। ৩। এই আদেশ অবিলম্বে কার্যকর হইবে। 91. It appears from the above Notification that the Minister of State for the Ministry of Establishment was made the Chairman and four Secretaries were made members of the above Committee. It is also provided in Paragraph (Ka) that this Committee would take interview of the candidates for promotion and then make recommendation. It was also provided by Paragraph (Kha) that this Committee would also consider the proposal and recommendation of the Superior Selection Board regarding the suitability of candidates for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary. Obviously, in Paragraphs (Ka) and (Kha) quoted above no guide-lines were provided. 92. Mr. Amir-ul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, has challenged the above two Notifications on two grounds and these grounds are: (1) That the Government have no constitutional or legal authority to constitute such Committees and (2) that no guide-lines were provided to these Committees and thereby arbitrary powers were vested in these Committees to select candidates for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary respectively and, as such, these Notifications were violative of Article 27 and Article 29 of the Constitution as want of guide-lines in these Notifications left ample scope to the members of these Committees to select candidates according to their whims and caprices and without following any objective standard of selection. 93. The learned Attorney-General, has, in reply, contended that in absence of any law made by Parliament under Article 133 of the Constitution the Government was competent to constitute the above Committees for selecting candidates to fill up various posts in the Bangladesh Secretariat and the constitution of such Committees was not in contravention of any constitutional provision or any provision of law. The learned Attorney General has also argued that the Government possessed inherent powers to constitute such Committees for considering the suitability of candidates for filling up different posts under it. 94. The next contention of the learned Attorney-General is that the above Committee followed a definite procedure which had been approved by the Cabinet and in support of his submission he has produced before us a summary that was submitted to the Cabinet by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment and an endorsement of the Prime Minister on this summary. We will consider this latter aspect after we consider the first contention of Mr. Islam. 95. We have already mentioned that there is virtually no law enacted by Parliament in exercise of its power under Article 133 of the Constitution regulating and determining the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic and these were determined by orders passed by the President and the Executive Branch of the Government from time to time. We have also observed that to regulate the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic was primarily the function of Parliament according to the scheme of Article 133 of our Constitution but Parliament has not so far used its powers vested in it under Article 133 and the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic are being regulated by the President and the Executive Branch of the Government in exercise of the exceptional power vested in them by the proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution. In view of the above situation, it appears to us that the President and the Executive Branch of the Government did not act unconstitutionally or illegally while constituting the above Committees by the impugned Notifications for considering the suitability of candidates for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary and above, as the case may be. We, therefore, do not find any substance in the contention of Mr. Islam that the Government had no jurisdiction to constitute the above two Committees by the impugned Notifications. 96. In order to appreciate the second contention of Mr. Islam that want of guide-lines in the above two impugned Notifications has rendered them arbitrary by vesting arbitrary powers in the two Committees and has thereby violated the equality clauses enshrined in Article 27 and Article 29 of the Constitution, we have to examine first, the effect of arbitrariness on Article 27 and Article 29, secondly, whether want of guide-lines in any instrument for exercise of powers by any public authority amounted to arbitrariness and thirdly, whether in the two instruments before us i.e. in the impugned Notifications, there is absence of any guidelines for exercise of powers by the authorities set up under those two Notifications 97. Mr. Islam has relied on a number of decisions in order to show that arbitrariness violates Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 98. The two of quoted Articles 27 and 29 of our Constitution are as follows: "27. All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law." "29. (1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office in the service of the Republic. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the state from- (a) making special provision in favour of any backward section of citizens for the purpose of securing their adequate representation in the service of the Republic; (b) Giving effect to any law which makes provision for reserving appointments relating to any religious or denominational institution to persons of that religion or denomination; (c) reserving for members of one sex any class of employment or office on the ground that it is considered by its nature to be unsuited to members of the opposite sex." 99. It had been a well settled principle for long, and is still so, that discrimination for want of reasonable classification i.e. such classification which does not fulfill two conditions, namely, "(i) that the classification is founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group and (ii) that the differential has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the legislative or executive action" is violative of the equality clause. Ajay Hasia vs. Khalid Mujib, AIR 1981 (SC) 487 (para 16) (Also see DS Nakara vs. Union of India AIR 1983 (SC) 130 and IA Shawani and others vs. Government of Pakistan, 1991 SCMR 1041 which are two of the latest of numerous decisions on the point by the Indian Supreme Court and the Pakistan Supreme Court respectively). 100. The effect of arbitrariness on the equality clause as enshrined in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution was probably examined for the first time by the Indian Supreme Court in KP Royappa vs. State of Tamil Nadu, 1974 2 SCR 348 and before that Article 14 had only come "to be identified with the doctrine of classification because the view 'taken was that Article forbids discrimination." (See Ajay Hasia vs Khalid Mujib, AIR 1981 SC 487, Para 16) In KP Royappa's case the Supreme Court of India" laid bare a new dimension of Article 14 and pointed out that that Article has highly activist magnitude and it embodies a guarantee against arbitrariness." (per Bhagwati, J., in Ajay Hasia's case, para 16). The following para in KP Royappa's case enunciated the principle as follows: "Article 16 embodies the fundamental guarantee that there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. Though enacted as a distinct and independent fundamental right because of its great importance as a principle ensuring equality of opportunity in public employment which is so vital to the building up of the new classless egalitarian society envisaged in the Constitution, Article16 is only an instance of the application of the concept of equality enshrined in Article 14. In other words, Article 14 is the genus while Artic1e l6 is a species, Article 16 gives effect to the doctrine of equality in all matters relating to public employment. The basic principle which therefore, informs both Articles14 and 16 is equality an inhibition against discrimination. Now, what is the content and reach of this great equalising principle? It is a founding faith, to use the words of Pose, J.," a way of life", and it must not be subjected to a narrow pedantic or lexicographic approach. We cannot countenance any attempt to truncate its all-embracing scope and meaning, for to do so would be to violate its activist magnitude and dimensions and it cannot be "cribbed, cabined and confined" within traditional and doctrinaire limits. From a positivistic point of view, equality is antithetic to arbitrariness. In fact equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies: one belongs to the rule of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch. Where an act is arbitrary it is implicit in it that it is unequal both according to political logic and constitutional law and is therefore violative of Article 14, and if it affects any matter relating to public employment it is also violative of Article 16. Articles 14 and 16 strike at arbitrariness in State action and ensure fairness and equality of treatment. They require that State action must be based on relevant principles applicable alike to all similarly situated and it must not be guided by any extraneous or irrelevant considerations because that would be denial of equality. Where the operative reason for State action, as distinguished from motive inducing from the antechamber of the mind, is not legitimate and relevant but is extraneous and outside the area of permissible considerations, it would amount to malafide exercise of power and that is hit by Articles 14 and 16. Malafide exercise of power and arbitrariness are different lethal radiations emanating from the same vice: in fact, the latter comprehends the former. Both are inhibited by Articles 14 and 16." (page 386). 101. Then followed Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India, 1978 2 SCR 621 in which the above proposition was further reiterated in the following words: "Now, the question immediately arises as to what is the requirement of Article 14: what is the content and reach of the great equalising principle enunciated in this Article? There can be no doubt that it is a founding faith of the Constitution. It is indeed the pillar on which rests securely the foundation of our democratic republic. And, therefore, it must not be subjected to a narrow, pedantic or lexicographic approach. No attempt should be made to truncate its all-embracing scope and meaning, for to do so would be to violate its activist magnitude. Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions and it cannot be imprisoned within traditional and doctrinaire limits. We must reiterate here what was pointed out by the majority in EP Royappa vs. State of Tamil Nadu & another (1) namely, that "from a positivistic point of view, equality is antithetic to arbitrariness. In fact equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule of law in a republic, while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch. Where an act is arbitrary it is implicit in it that it is unequal both according to political logic and constitutional law and is therefore violative of Article 14". Article 14 stikes at arbitrariness in State action and ensures fairness and equality of treatment. The principle of reasonableness, which legally as well as philosophically, is an essential element of equality or non-arbitrariness, pervades Article 14 like a brooding omnipresence and the procedure contemplated by Article 21 must answer the test of reasonableness in order to be in conformity with Article 14. It must be "right and just and fair" and not arbitrary fanciful or oppressive;" (pages 673-674). 102. This principle was again reaffirmed in Kamana Dayaram Shetty vs. The International Airport Authority of India and others (1979) 3 SCR, 1014 in the following manner "This rule also flows directly from the doctrine of equality embodied in Article 14. It is now well settled as a result of the decisions of this Court in EP Rayappa vs. State of Tamil Nadu (1) and Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India (2) that Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness in State action and ensures fairness and equality of treatment. It requires that State action must not be arbitrary but must be based on some rational and relevant principle which is nondiscriminatory; it must not be guided by any extraneous or irrelevant considerations because that would be denial of equality. The principle of reasonableness and rationality which is legally as well as philosophically an essential element of equality or non-arbitrariness is protected by Article 14 and it must characterise every State action, whether it be under authority of law or in exercise of executive power without making of law. The state cannot, therefore, act arbitrarily in entering into relationship, contractual or otherwise, with a third party, but its action must conform to some standard or norm which is rational and non-discriminatory. This principle was recognized and applied by a Bench of this Court presided over by Ray C.J. in Erusian Equipment and Chemicals vs. State of West Bengal (supra) where the learned Chief Justice pointed out that "the State can carryon executive function by making a law or without making a law. The exercise of such powers and functions in trade by the State is subject to Part III of the Constitution. Article 14 speaks of equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. Equality of opportunity should apply to matters of public contracts. The State has the right to trade. The State has there the duty to observe equality. An ordinary individual can choose not to deal with any person. The Government cannot choose to exclude persons by discrimination. The order of blacklists has the effect of depriving a person of equality of opportunity in the matter of public contract. A person who is on the approved list is unable to enter into advantageous relations with the Government because of the order of black-listing ... A citizen has a right to claim equal treatment to enter into a contract which may be proper, necessary and essential to his lawful calling ... It is true that neither the petitioner nor the respondent has any right to enter into a contract but they are entitled to equal treatment with others who offer tender or quotations for the purchase of the goods." It must, therefore, follow as a necessary corollary from the principle of equality enshrined in Article 14 that though the State is entitled to refuse to enter into relationship with anyone, yet if it does so, it cannot arbitrarily choose any person it likes for entering into such relationship and discriminate between persons similarly circumstanced, but it must act in conformity with some standard or principle which meets the test of reasonableness and non-discrimination and any departure from such standard or principle would be invalid unless it can be supported or justified on some rational and non-discriminatory ground." (pages 1042-1043). Again, in Air India vs. Nergesh Metrza and others (transfer case) and six. other writ petitions, reported in (1981) 4 sec., 335 the Indian Supreme Court elaborately dealt with the equality clause enshrined in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution, and lucidly interpreted -what is meant by hostile discrimination with reference to the equality clause and then observed, "We might mention here that even though the conditions mentioned above may not be violative of Article 14 on the ground of discrimination but if it is proved to our satisfaction that the conditions laid down are entirely unreasonable and absolutely arbitrary then the provisions will have to be struck down." (para 71). Lastly, in Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab, (1982) 3 see, 24, the discretion vested in Courts to impose death penalty (or imprisonment for life) in case of conviction under section 302 of the Penal Code without laying down any guide-lines for exercise of the said discretion was held in the dissenting opinion (minority opinion) of Bhagwati, J. as unconstitutional being violative of Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. 103. Let us now again refer to Ajay Rasia vs. Khalid Mujib, AIR 1981 (SC) 487 in which the principle of selection was disputed as in the present writ petitions and on which the learned Attorney-General also depended in order to formulate his point that the interview system cannot be deemed to be arbitrary by itself. We shall, however, consider the decision in this case on interview system and the arguments of the learned Attorney-General in this respect when we discuss the interview system evolved by the Council Committee and the Committee on Deputy Secretary for selecting their respective candidates. So far as the equality clause enshrined in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution is concerned, reiterating the above decisions the Indian Supreme Court again held in Ajay Hasia's case: "It must therefore now be taken to be well settled that what Article 14 strikes at is arbitrariness because an action that is arbitrary, must necessarily involve negation of equality. The doctrine of classification which is evolved by the Courts is not paraphrase of Article 14 nor is it the objective and end of that Article. It is merely a judicial formula for determining whether the legislative or executive action in question is arbitrary and therefore constituting denial of equality. If the classification is not reasonable and does not satisfy the two conditions referred to above, the impugned legislative or executive action would plainly be arbitrary and the guarantee of equality under Article 14 would be breached. Wherever therefore there is arbitrariness in State action whether it be of the legislature or of the executive or of an "authority" under Article 12, Article 14 immediately springs into action and strikes down such State action. In fact, the concept of reasonableness and non-arbitrariness pervades the entire constitutional scheme and is a golden thread which runs through the whole of the fabric of the Constitution." (para 16, page 499). 104. Although in Ajay Rasia's case the principle involved related to selection procedure of candidates for admission in an Engineering College, the principle laid down was held to be equally applicable to selection procedure for appointment and promotion in public employment as well. 105. Mr. Islam also relied on Dr. Nurul Islam vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201 in which Articles 27 and 29 of our Constitution were elaborately interpreted. In the above well-known case Professor Nurul Islam, an eminent physician, was retired from service by applying section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act (Act No: XII of 1994). In the said Act no guideline was provided as to when and how the Government could invoke the aforesaid Act for retiring Government servants and, as such, it was held that the said Act vested arbitrary powers in the Government for exercise of the said power and was, therefore, violative of the equality clauses as enshrined in Article 27 and Article 29 (1) of the Constitution. 106. So far as the second contention of Mr. Islam is concerned, both the Notifications show that no guide-lines were provided to the Council Committee set up for considering the case of promotion to the post of Joint Secretary and above and the Committee headed by the Minister of State, Ministry of Establishment, for considering the suitability of candidates for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary in the Bangladesh Secretariat The petitioners have asserted in their writ petitions by swearing affidavits that the Council Committee introduced a system of test and interview for considering candidates for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary and also introduced marking system allotting 40 marks for interview, 10 marks for pen picture and 50 marks for ten years ACR out of a total of 100 marks and, according to Mr. Islam, this system of test and interview and the allotment of marks in the above manner was resorted to with ulterior motives and with the intention of exercising the power of selection arbitrarily without any objective standard and, excluding men of merit, for selecting unworthy henchmen of the party in power. Mr. Islam has also argued that the Council Committee was not vested with any power to hold test and examination and allot marks in the manner in which this had been done in the case of considering candidates including the petitioners in Writ Petitions Nos. 2738 of 1992 and 813 of 1993 for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary. 107. The respondent No.1 did not deny in its affidavit-in-opposition that the Council Committee evolved the system of test and examination and allotted marks as alleged by the petitioners and described above. On the other hand, in paragraph 12 of the affidavit-in-opposition in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 filed by the respondent No.1 it is specifically admitted as follows: "The Council Committee took interviews to determine merit and suitability of officers for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary on the basis of guide-lines given by the Government and prevailing practices in ibis regard. Interview and marking system was followed by Council Committees in accordance with guide-lines and prevailing practices in order to assess the suitability of officers for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary." In paragraph 13 the respondent No. 1 of the above writ petition also specifically admitted as follows: "That it is stated that Council Committee itself introduced interview and examination system for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary and introduced system of allotting 40% marks for viva, 10% for penpicture and 50% for 10 years ACR. As a matter of fact, the Council Committee followed the interview system and marking system as per Government guide-lines in this respect." So, it is.an admitted position that the Council Committee took test and interview allotting 40% marks for viva. 10% for penpicture and 50% for 10 years ACR and according to the admission in the affidavit- in-opposition the Council Committees followed the interview system and the marking system as per "guidelines" provided by the Government. 108. The guide-lines referred to in the affidavit-in opposition by the respondent No.1 could not, however, be produced before us by the learned Attorney-General. Instead, the learned Attorney-General produced before us a summary submitted to the Cabinet by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment, and the endorsement of the Prime Minister thereon. 109. The summary is very important and it runs as follows: (অতি গোপনীয়) গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় উধ্বর্তন নিয়োগ ১ শাখা মন্ত্রিপরিষদের জন্য সার সংক্ষেপ। নং সম/ উনি ১-১/৮৯-৩৫৭ তারিখঃ ৩.১১.৯২ ইং ১৮.৭-৯৮ বাং। বিষয়ঃ উপ-সচিব ও যুগ্ন-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য বাছাই পদ্ধতি সংশোধন। যুগ্ন-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য কর্মকর্তা বাছাই এর কাজ প্রাথমিকভাবে সুপিরিয়র সিলেকশন বোর্ড ও চূড়ান্তভাবে
