উধ্বর্তন নিয়োগ, পদোন্নতী ও চাকুরী কাঠামো সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রি পরিষদ কমিটি করিয়া থাকেন । উপ-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য কর্মকর্তা বাছাইয়ের দায়িত্ব কয়েকজন সচিব সমন্বয়ে গঠিত একটি কমিটির উপর ন্যাস্ত। ২। পূর্বে উপরোক্ত পদ সমূহে পদোন্নতি জন্য কর্মকর্তা বাছাইয়ের জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্মকর্তাদের বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন ও শিক্ষাগত যোগ্যতা বিবেচনা ছাড়াও তাঁহাদের ইন্টারভিউ লওয়া হউক। পরবর্তীকালে উপদেষ্টা পরিষদের ২৪.২.৯১ তারিখের নং উপরে ১৩(২)/৯১ বৈঠকে পদোন্নতির সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহীত হয় এবং তদনুযায়ী সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় হইতে ১৯.৮.৯১ তারিখে নং সম/উনি- ৪/২/৯১-২৩ প্রজ্ঞাপন জারী করা হয়। ইন্টারভিউ ব্যবস্থা রহিত করার বিষয়টি উধ্বর্তন নিয়োগ, পদোন্নতী ও চাকুরী কাঠামো সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিপরিষদ কমিটির ৩.১১.৯১ ইং তারিখের সভায় পুনঃ পর্যালোচনা করাপ হয় এবং সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহীত হয় যে, পদোন্নতির জন্য দক্ষ ও মেধাবী কর্মকর্তা বাছাইয়ের জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্মকর্তাদের বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন যাচাই ছাড়াও ইন্টারভিউ লওয়া আবশ্যক। কর্মকর্তা বাছাইকল্পে একজন কর্মকর্তার উপযুক্ততা ১০০ নম্বরের ভিত্তিতে মূল্যায়ন করা যাইতে পারে। এবং তম্নধ্যে ৬০ নম্বর বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদনের জন্য ও ৪০ নম্বর ইন্টারভিউয়ের জন্য নির্ধারিত থাকিতে পারে। ৩। উর্ধ্বতন পদসমূহ সিলেকশন পদ বিধায় উক্ত পদ সমূহে মেধা ভিত্তিতে পদোন্নতি দিবার বিধানই চালু রহিয়াছে। উর্ধ্বতন নিয়োগ, পদোন্নতি ও চাকুরী কাঠামো সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিপরিষদ কমিটির উপরোক্ত সুপারিশের প্রেক্ষিতে মেধা ভিত্তিতে/উপ-সচিব ও যুগ্ন-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতি প্রদানের উদ্দেশ্যে নিম্নরুপ বাছাই পদ্ধতি অনুসরণ করা যাইতে পারেঃ (ক) উপ-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য গঠিত কমিটি/সুপিরিয়র সিলেকশন বোর্ড/ কাউন্সিল কমিটি কর্মকর্তাগণের কার্যাবলী ও উপযুক্ততা ১০০ নম্বরের ভিত্তিতে মূল্যায়ন করিবে। তনমধ্যে ৬০ নম্বর বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদনের জন্য নির্ধারিত থাকিবে এবং এরুপ প্রতিবেদনের মানের ভিত্তিতে কর্মকর্তাগনের প্রাপ্য নম্বর নিরুপন করা হইবে। বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদনের যথাসম্ভব বস্তনিষ্ঠ মূল্যায়নের জন্য ১০ বছরের গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন বিবেচনা করা হইবে। (খ) সংশ্লিষ্ট কমিটি অবশিষ্ট ৪০ নম্বরের জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্মকর্তাগণের ইন্টারভিউ লইবেন। এবং ইন্টারভিউয়ের ফলাফলের ভিত্তিতে কর্মকর্তাগণকে তাহাদের প্রার্প নম্বর প্রদান করিবেন। (গ) বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন ও ইন্টাভিউ এ প্রাপ্ত নম্বরের ভিত্তিতে কর্মকর্তাগণের একটি প্যানেল তৈয়ার করা হইবে এবং বিদ্যমান শূন্যপদ এই প্যানেল হইতে পদোন্নতি দিয়া পূরণ করা হইবে। ৪। ৩নং অনুচ্ছেদে (ক), (খ) ও (গ) প্রস্তাব মন্ত্রিপরিষদের সদয় বিবেচনা ও অনুমোদনের জন্য উপস্থাপন করা হইল। ৫। এই সার সংক্ষেপ সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয়ের মাননীয় প্রতিমন্ত্রী অনুমোদন করিয়াছেন। স্বাক্ষর/= ৩.১১.৯১ (মোঃ হাসিনুর রহামান) সচিব। গোপনীয় বিষয়ঃ সম্পূরক বিষয়সূচী-৩ ঃ উপ-সচিব ও যুগ্ন সচিব পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য বাছাই পদ্ধতি সংশোধন। সিদ্ধান্তঃ ১৬। (ক) সার সংক্ষেপের ৩ নম্বর অনুচ্ছেদের প্রস্তাবসমূহ অনুমোদন করা হইল। (খ) একটি পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য তিনজন কর্মকর্তাকে অর্থাঃ ১:৩ অনুপাত বিবেচনা বা মূল্যায়ন করিতে হইবে। (গ) উধ্বর্তন কর্মকর্তাগন যাহাতে অধস্ত কর্মকর্তাদের বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন যথাসময়ে লিপিবদ্ধ করিয়া সংশ্লিষ্ট দপ্তরে জমাদেন উহা নির্বাচিত করিবার জন্য সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করিবে এবং বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন যথাসময়ে লিপিবদ্ধ করিতে যাহারা ব্যর্থ হইবেন তাহাদের বিরুদ্ধে ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করিতে হইবে। স্বাক্ষরঃ- খালেদা জিয়া প্রধানমন্ত্রী ১১.১১.৯১ The summary shows that certain proposals were made to the Cabinet by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment and the endorsement of the Prime Minister thereon shows that paragraph 3 of the Summary was approved by the Cabinet. The above quoted Summary shows that in paragraph 3 it was proposed that out of 100 marks 60 marks should be allotted for ACR of the officer concerned and 40 marks should be alloted for interview and this proposal was accepted by the Cabinet as per the Prime Minister's endorsement thereon dated 11.11.91. It is clear from the admitted facts that the Council Committee did not at all follow the decision of the Cabinet and instead of allotting 60 marks for ACR the Council Committee allotted 50 marks for ACR, 40 marks for interview and 10 marks for pen picture. It followed the decision of the Cabinet appearing from the Summary and the endorsement of the Prime Minister thereon placed before us by the learned' Attorney-General. In the next place, the Summary shows that it was a "অতি গোপনীয়" the English rendering of which is "top secret," document. There is nothing to show that the Government issued any Notification on the basis of this "top secret" document for information of the candidates who were supposed to be affected by the procedure of selection mentioned therein. There is also nothing to show that this Cabinet decision was circulated to the Council Committee. The "top secret" decision of the Cabinet cannot be regarded an guide-lines provided by the Government as has been argued by the learned Attorney-General. If the Government issued a Notification on the basis of this "top secret" document for public consumption and particularly, for information of those who were affected by it, it could be said that the Government provided guide-lines to the Committee for adopting a procedure for selecting candidates for the above post. Moreover, as we have already seen, these "guide-lines" were also not followed by the Council Committee. So these "guide-lines" lose all relevancy. 110. It, therefore, appears that the Council Committee itself determined the procedure to be followed by it and while doing so, reserved 50% marks for ACR and allotted 10% marks for pen-picture and 40% marks for interview i.e. reserved as much as 50 marks for selecting candidates on the basis of interview and pen-picture. 111. Similarly, the Committee constituted considering the suitability of candidates for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary vide Notification No 4/2-4/91-98 dated 4th December, 1991 as at A to Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 which runs as follows: বিষয়ঃ উচ্চতর সরকারী পদে ও স্ব-শাসিত সংস্থার পদে নিয়োগ/ পদোন্নতি। উপরোক্ত বিষয়ে সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয়ের ১৯.০৮.১৯৯১ ইং (০৩রা ভাদ্র, ১৩৯৮বাংলা) তারিখের নং-সম/ উনি ৪/২/-৪/৯১ ইং নম্বর প্রজ্ঞাপনের ২(৩) উপ-অনুচ্ছেদ নিম্নরুপ সংশোধন করা হইল। (ক) সচিবালয়ের উপ-সচিব পদে পদোন্নতি প্রদানের উদ্দেশ্যে সাক্ষাৎকার গ্রহণ পূর্বক সুপারিশ করার জন্য এবং উপ-সচিবগণের উচ্চতর টাইম স্কেল বিবেচনার জন্য নিম্নরুপ কমিটি গঠন করা হইলঃ (১) সংস্থাপন প্রতিমন্ত্রী (২) মন্ত্রী পরিষদ সচিব (৩) সংস্থাপন সচিব (৪) সচিব, প্রধান মন্ত্রীর কার্য্যালয় (৫) সংশ্লিষ্ট কাজের নিয়িন্ত্রকারী সদস্য মন্ত্রণালয় এবং বিভাগের সচিব চেয়ারম্যান সদস্য সদস্য-সচিব সদস্য ২। সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণ য়ের ১৯.৮.১৯৯১ ইং তারিখের পূর্বোক্ত প্রজ্ঞাপনের ৬ নম্বর অনুচ্ছেদ এত দ্বারা বাতিল করা হইল। উক্ত প্রজ্ঞাপনে সকল স্থানে “রাষ্ট্রপতি” এর স্থলে “প্রধানমন্ত্রী” পড়িতে হইবে। ৩। এই আদেশ অবিলম্বে কার্য্যকর হইবে। It appears from the above that the Committee was constituted with the Minister of State, Ministry of Establishment, as Chairman and four Secretaries as Members. Paragraphs (Ka) and (Kha) of the above Notification are relevant which laid down that the above Committee would take interview of the candidates, consider the recommendation of Superior Selection Board and the candidates' suitability for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and then submit recommendation to the Establishment Division for submission to the Prime Minister. In this Notification also, as it is clear from its contents, no guideline was provided to the Committee as to how selection was to be made. 112. In the above context, it is alleged by the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992, the said Committee arbitrarily decided to take written test and interview fixing 60 marks for written test and 40 marks for interview out of a total of 100 marks. (Paragraph J of the writ petition). This allegation has been denied by the respondent No. 1 in its affidavit-in-opposition. The respondent No.1 asserts in its affidavit-in-opposition that no written test was held for selecting candidates for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary as has been alleged by the petitioners. The respondent No.1 however, admitted in its affidavit-in-opposition that the Committee took interview of the candidates fixing 40 marks for it and allotted 60 marks for assessment on the basis of ACRs of the officers concerned out of a total of 100 marks (paragraphs 13 and 14 of the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No. 1 in Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992). We accept the averment in the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No.1 as correct since this averment in the affidavit-in-opposition has not at all been disputed by Mr. Islam at the time of hearing of the writ petitions. 113. It, therefore, appears that the Committee determined its own procedure of selecting candidates for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary allocating 60% marks for ACR and 40% marks for interview. 114. It is patent from the above that in the two impugned Notifications no guideline was provided by the Government as to how selection of candidates for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary should be made except a general direction to the effect that the Committee on Deputy Secretary would take interview of candidates and, as such, the Council Committee and the Committee for selecting Deputy Secretaries laid down its own procedure. We shall examine the implications of these procedures later on and before doing so, it must be said that in absence of any guideline in the impugned Notification Annexure-'K' in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 regarding the procedure to be followed for selecting candidates for promoting to the posts of Joint Secretary the Council Committee on promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and above and also in the Notification as at Annexure-'A' to Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 for selecting Deputy Secretaries regarding the procedure as to how candidates should be selected for promoting to the posts of Deputy Secretary the Committee on promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary were vested with unguided and arbitrary powers and, as such, these two Notifications so far as the reference portions of these Notifications contained in sub-paras (1) and (2) of para (Ga) of the Notification No. 4 (1)/90/217- Committee dated 9th October, 1991 as at Annexure- 'K' to Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 and in paras (Ka) and (Kha) of the Notification No. সম/ উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-৯৮ dated 4th December, 1991 as at Annexure-'A' to Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 were violative of Article 27 of the Constitution as well as Article 29(1) of the Constitution. 115. Since it is palpable that the Council Committee and the Committee on Deputy Secretaries set up for recommending candidates for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and above and to the posts of Deputy Secretary respectively were not given guide-lines or principles to be followed in making selection of candidates, were vested with arbitrary powers to select or reject any persons irrespective of their suitability judged on the basis of objective assessment of their merits and performance. 116. As such, although we find that the formation of the Council Committee for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and above and the Committee for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary was within the competence of the Government, the vesting of powers to select candidates without providing any uniform guide-lines or yardsticks or principles to be followed was without lawful authority being arbitrary powers and, therefore, violative of Article 27 of the Constitution as well as Article 29 (1) of the Constitution, because, scope for arbitrary exercise of powers means conflict with equal treatment of the candidates who were concerned with promotion in the instant cases, with equal protection of law and lastly, with equality of opportunity of all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic. 117. It is patent that the above powers were also in fact exercised arbitrarily, because, the Council Committee did not think it necessary to abide by the Cabinet decision as evident from the endorsement dated 11.11.91 of the Prime Minister on the Summary submitted to the Cabinet under memo No. সম/অনি ১-১/৮৯-৩৫৭ dated 3.11.91 and ignoring the Cabinet decision to allot 60 marks for ACR and 40 marks for interview, allotted 50 marks for ACR., 40 marks for interview and 10 marks for pen-picture and secondly, this Committee devised the above method, whereas the Committee on promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary devised a separate method by allotting 60 marks for ACR and 40 marks for interview. The two Committees devised two different methods for promotion to the posts in the same service i.e. the Secretariat service, (although the posts in the one were higher being the post of Joint Secretary and the posts in the other were lower than the former being the posts of Deputy Secretary). This also shows that absence of any general guide-lines in the two impugned Notifications the above two Committees devised two different methods for promotion of officers in the same service i.e. Bangladesh Secretariat service. In this connection, I am again tempted to refer to the previous Notifications regarding the constitution of the Superior Selection Board, etc. (which have already been referred to once) in which distinct guide-lines were provided to the aforesaid Boards and Committees as to how selection should be made. 118. We shall now examine the implications of the methods devised by the aforesaid two Committees. 119. The learned Attorney-General has argued that the interview system for selecting candidates for promotion cannot be said to be an arbitrary system and it is a widely accepted method of selection. In support of his contention he referred to the following observations of the Supreme Court of India in Ajay Hasia's case: "It is, therefore not possible to accept the contentions of the petitioners that the oral interview test is so defective that selecting candidates for admission on the basis of oral interview in addition to written test must be regarded as arbitrary." As already stated earlier, we will presently see the fundamental aspects of the opinion of the Supreme Court of India expressed in Ajay Hasia's case about oral interview test. 120. The petitioners have produced before us the model of Annual Confidential Report forms. It appears from these forms that a very objective and scientific method of assessment of the merits of an officer has been provided in these forms. There are as many as 15 columns and there is marking system for each column. The reporting officer is required to put marks on various aspects of the quality of the officer, such as, discipline, judgment, intelligence, public relation, co-operation, personality, sense of security, consciousness, etc. There are also other columns for marking system such as, professional knowledge, quality of work, quantity of work, punctuality, etc. It also appears from the form of annual confidential report that on the basis of total marks received by an officer on each of the above items his merit as an officer is decided. It further appears that there is also a portion for noting the pen-picture consisting of various aspects of the character, appearance, etc. of the officer. We have found that this annual confidential report provided a very effective means of assessing the quality and merit of an officer and the assessment was mostly objective. I am, however, not unmindful of the fact that the assessment in the annual confidential report may not be invariably and always objective and in some cases the opinion expressed in the annual confidential report might be actuated by subjective opinion of the reporting officer followed from bias either in favour of or against an officer. Assuming that such possibility is there, it must be acknowledged that it is there to a much lesser degree, because, the annual confidential reports for 10 years are considered and it cannot be said that all the reporting officers would give subjective assessment of a candidate's suitability. Such possibility is extremely rare and exceptional. On the other hand if the subjective interview system is made the determining factor, possibility of arbitrariness is unlimited and, as such, is in direct conflict with Article 27 and Article 29 of the Constitution. In this connection, I should not be understood to mean that the system of interview is entirely arbitrary and has to be totally rejected as a method of selection of candidates for promotion. What I mean to say is that the subjective interview system cannot be made such as to create scope for totally frustrating the objective system of assessment of the suitability of candidates appearing in their respective annual confidential reports. I do not also say that there should not be any marking system at the interview tests. What I want to say is that the subjective marking system at interview should not be such as to totally nullify the objective marking system of the candidates in their respective annual confidential reports. The marking system at the interview tests should only be such as to be the determining factor only in such cases of candidates as are found equally suitable on the basis of the objective assessment in their respective annual confidential reports. 121. Let us now see whether the methods respectively evolved by the above two Committees met the above tests. It appears that 50% marks were allocated to make assessment on the basis of annual confidential report and 40% marks were fixed for making assessment on the basis of interview and 10% marks were fixed for pen-picture by the Council Committee for selecting candidates for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary. It is not understood, and no submission was advanced in this respect, as to what is meant by 10% marks for pen-picture. There is a separate column for pen-picture in the annual confidential report forms. It appears that in addition to the above pen-picture, the Council Committee itself also made assessment of the pen-picture of an officer at an interview of a few minutes although the pen-picture in the annual confidential report is the result of observation of an officer by the reporting officer for a considerably long time i.e. one year. It also appears that the Council Committee as well as the Committee on promotion of Deputy Secretary allotted 40 marks for interview and presumably awarded marks to the candidates on the basis of a few minutes interview. In this connection, I would like to refer that I asked the learned Attorney-General to produce the mark-sheets before this Court so that this Court, in its anxiety to see that no arbitrary way of selecting candidates was resorted to, may look into the method of awarding marks by the Committees consisting of as many as eight members in case of the Council Committee and five Members in case of the Committee for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary. The learned Attorney-General took one day's time and on the following day submitted that he was unable to produce the mark-sheets and also contended that the mark-sheets were not at all necessary for deciding these writ petitions. So, the respondents could not produce any materials before us to show on what basis the above Committees awarded marks to each candidate and could not satisfy ourselves that no arbitrary marking system was adopted. Mr. Islam, however, alleged that in many cases no marks had at all been given and in many cases candidates were interviewed for only 2-3 minutes and in some other cases marks once allotted were subsequently altered. These allegations could only be refuted had the marks sheets been produced before us. Withholding of the marks-sheets rather strengthens Mr. Islam's allegations. 122. It is, however, patent that since only 50 marks were allocated for assessment on the basis of annual confidential report and 50 marks were allocated for awarding marks on the basis of subjective method of assessment by interview and pen-picture by the Council Committee, it appears to me that the interview system could be used to frustrate the merit of an officer who had received even 100% marks in his annual confidential report which is, as we have already observed, one of the most objective methods of assessing the merit of an officer. Similarly, by allocating 40 marks for selecting candidates for the post of Deputy Secretary, the assessment of the quality of an officer on merit on the basis of his annual confidential report could be easily frustrated by allocating arbitrary marks at interview. 123. Although allegations were made in the writ petitions that the said Committees selected only those who were sympathetic to the political party in power, no materials could be produced before us to show that was so. But, the fact remains that in the system evolved by the above Committees there was scope for arbitrary exercise of power and, as such, these methods were, to my view, violative of Article 27 of the Constitution and Article 29(1) of the Constitution, because, these methods left scope for unequal treatment of candidates by the above Committees. 124. In the affidavits-in-opposition of the respondent No.1 also it has been simply stated that the Council Committee and the Committee for selecting candidates for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary selected candidates objectively by interviewing them. There is nothing in the affidavits-in-opposition as to what criteria, method, or yardstick was followed for awarding marks to the candidates at the interview. In the Notifications creating the above Committees also no guidelines criteria or yardsticks for selection of some from many candidates who were equally situated having fulfilled the conditions for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary respectively were given. Selection of some from many equally situated itself involved classification and there being no uniform guidelines, yardstick or criteria of making the classifications the whole process of selection became arbitrary and, therefore, the consequent classification also became arbitrary having failed to pass the "reasonableness" test thereby rendering such classification violative of the equality clause as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution. In the present case, the petitioners were superseded and others equally placed with them and in some cases junior to them were promoted to higher posts and thereby a classification was made and since we have found that this classification was made by the above Committees set up for considering their cases without any uniform guidelines, yardsticks or criteria, the classification was unreasonable and, therefore, violated both Article 27 and clause (1) of Article 29 of the Constitution. 125. We now revert to Ajay Hasia’s case. In this case exclusion of several candidates from admission to the Regional Engineering College, Srinagar and selection of other candidates for admission therein on the basis of written test examination, marks obtained in qualification examination and oral interview were challenged by the excluded candidates on the ground, inter alia, that substantial marks (33-1/3%) were allotted for oral interview in order to exclude candidates who had secured very high marks in written examination by arbitrarily awarding marks at the interview and, as such, the method of oral interview having created scope for arbitrary selection was violative of the equality clause as enshrined in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. The Supreme Court of India discussed the pros and cons of the oral interview system in detail. It said: "The second ground of challenge questioned the validity of viva voce examination as a permissible test for selection of candidates for admissions to a college. The contention of the petitioners under this ground of challenge was that viva voce examination does not afford a proper criterion for assessment of the suitability of the candidates for admission and it is a highly subjective and impressionistic test where the result is likely to be influenced by many uncertain and imponderable factors such as predilections and prejudices of the interviewer, his attitudes and approaches, his preconceived notions and idiosyncrasies and it is also capable of abuse because it leaves scope for discrimination, manipulation and nepotism which can remain undetected under the cover of an interview and moreover it is not possible to assess the capacity and calibre of a candidate in the course of an interview lasting only for a few minutes and, therefore, selections made on the basis of oral interview must be regarded as arbitrary and hence violative of Article 14. Now this criticism cannot be said to be wholly unfounded and it reflects a point of view which has certainly some validity. We may quote the following passage from the book on "Public Administration in theory and Practice by WP Sharma which voices a fair and balanced criticism of the oral interview method. "The oral test of the interview has been much criticised on the ground of its subjectivity and uncertainty. Different interviewers have their own notions of good personality. For some, it consists more in attractive physical appearances and dress rather than anything else, and with them the breezy and shiny type of candidate scores highly while the rough uncut diamonds may go unappreciated. The atmosphere of the interview is artificial and prevents some candidates from appearing at their best. Its duration is short, the few questions of the hit or miss type, which are put, may fail to reveal the real worth of the candidate. It has been said that God takes a whole life-time to Judge a man's worth while interviewers have to do it in a quarter of an hour. Even at its best, the common sort of interview reveals but the superficial aspects of the candidate's personality like appearance, speaking power, and general address. Deeper traits of leadership, tact, forcefulness, etc. go largely undetected. The interview is often in the nature of desultory conversation. Marking differs greatly from examiner to examiner. An analysis of the interview results show that the marks awarded to candidates who competed more than once for the same service vary suprisingly. All this shows that there is a great element of chance in the interview test. This becomes a serious matter when the marks assigned to oral test constitute a high proportion of the total marks in the competition. " OL Glenn Stahl points out in his book on Public Personnel Administration that there are three disadvantages from which the oral test method suffers, namely, "(1) the difficulty of developing valid and reliable oral tests (2) the difficulty of securing a reviewable record on an oral test and (3) public suspicion of the oral test as a channel for the exertion of political influence" and, we may add, other corrupt, nepotistic or extraneous considerations. The learned author then proceeds to add in a highly perceptive and critical passage "The oral examination has failed in the past in direct proportion to the extent of its misuse. It is a delicate instrument and in inexpert hands, a dangerous one. The first condition of its successful use is the full recognition of its limitations. One of the most prolific sources of error in the oral test has been the failure on the part of examiners to understand the nature of evidence and to discriminate between that which was relevant, material and reliable and that which was not. It also must be remembered that the best oral interview provides opportunity for unalysis of only a very small part of a person's total behaviour. Generalisations from a single interview regarding an individual's total personality pattern have been proved repeatedly to be wrong. But, despite all this criticism, the oral interview method continues to be very much in vogue as a supplementary test for assessing the suitability of candidates wherever test of personal traits is considered essential. Its relevance as a test for determining suitability based on personal characteristics has been recognized in a number of decisions of this Court which are binding upon us. In the first case on the point which came before this Court, namely, R. Chitra Lekha vs. State of Mysore, (1964) 6 SCR 368 : (AIR 1964 SC 1823) this Court pointed out. "In the field of education there are divergent views as regards the mode of testing, the capacity and calibre of students in the matter of admissions to colleges. Orthodox educationists stand by the marks obtained by a student in the annual examination. The modern trend of opinion insists upon other additional tests, such as interview, performance in extra-curricular activities, personality test, psychiatric tests, etc. Obviously we are not in a position to judge which method is preferable or which test is the correct one................The scheme of selection, however, perfect it may be on paper, may be abused in practice, That it is capable of abuse is not a ground for quashing it. So long as the order lays down relevant objective criteria and entrusts the business of selection to qualified persons, this Court cannot obviously have any say in the matter." and on this view refused to hold the oral interview test as irrelevant or arbitrary. It was also pointed out by this Court in A. Peeriakaruppan vs. State of Tamil Nadu, (1971) 2 SCR 430: (AIR 1971 SC 2303): "In most cases, the first impression need not necessarily be the best impression, but under the existing conditions, we are unable to accede to the contentions of the petitioners that the system of interview as in vogue in this country is so defective as to make it useless." It is therefore not possible to accept the contentions of the petitioners that the oral interview test is so defective that selecting candidates for admission on the basis of oral interview in addition to written test must be regarded as arbitrary. The oral interview test is undoubtedly not a very satisfactory test for assessing and evaluating the capacity and calibre of candidates, but in the absence of any better test for measuring personal characteristics and traits, the oral interview test must, at the present stage, be regarded as not irrational or irrelevant though it is subjective and based on first impression, its result is influenced by many uncertain factors and it is capable of abuse. We would, however like to point out that in the matter of admission of college, or even in the matter of public employment the oral interview test as presently held should not be relied upon as an exclusive test but it may be resorted to only as an additional or supplementary test and, moreover, great care must be taken to see that persons who are appointed to conduct the oral interview test are men of high integrity, calibre and qualification," (para 18, pages 500-501): 126. Thereafter, the Court considered the propriety of allotting 33-1/3% marks for oral interview and held "So far as the third ground of challenge is concerned, we do not think it can be dismissed as unsubstantial. The argument of the petitioners under this head of challenge was that even if oral interview may be regarded in principle as a valid test for selection of candidates for admission to a college, it was in the present case arbitrary and unreasonable since the marks allocated for the oral interview were very much on the higher side as compared with the marks allocated for the written test. The marks allocated for the oral interview were 50 as against 100 allocated for the written test, so that the marks allocated for the oral interview came to 33-1/3% of the total number of marks taken into account for the purpose of making the selection. This, contended the petitioners, was beyond all reasonable proportion and rendered the selection of the candidates arbitrary and violative of the equality clause of the Constitution. Now there can be no doubt that, having regard to the drawbacks and deficiencies in the oral interview test and the conditions prevailing in the country, particularly when there is deterioration in moral values and corruption and nepotism are very much on the increase, allocation of a high percentage of marks for the oral interview as compared to the marks allocated for the written test cannot be accepted by the Court as free from the vice of arbitrariness. It may be pointed out that even in Peeriakaruppan’s: case (AIR 1971) SC 2303) (supra), where 75 marks out of a total of 275 marks were allocated for the oral interview, this Court observed that the marks allocated for interview were on the high side. This Court also observed in Miss Nishi Meghu's case (AIR 1980 SC 1975 (supra) "Reserving 50 marks for interview out of a total of 150 ........Does seem excessive, especially when the time spent was not more than 4 minutes on each candidate". There can be no doubt that allocating 3- 1/3 of the total marks for oral interview is plainly arbitrary and unreasonable. It is significant to note that even for selection of candidates for the Indian Administrative Service, the Indian Foreign Service and the Indian Police Service, where the personality of the candidate and his personal characteristics and traits are extremely relevant for the purpose of selection, the marks allocated for oral interview are 250 as against 1800 marks for the written examination, constituting only 12.2% of the total marks taken into consideration for the purpose of making the selection. We must therefore regard the allocation of as high a percentage as 33-1/3 of the total marks for the oral interview as infecting the admission procedure with the vice of arbitrariness and selection of candidates made on the basis of such admission procedure cannot be sustained. But we do not think we would be justified in the exercise of our discretion in setting aside the selection made for the academic year 1979-80 after the lapse of a period of about 18 months, since to do so would be to cause immense hardship to those students in whose case the validity of the selection cannot otherwise be questioned and who have nearly completed three semesters and, moreover, even if the petitioners are ultimately found to be deserving of selection on the application of the proper test, it would not be possible to restore them to the position as if they were admitted for academic year 1979-80, which has run out long since. It is true there is an allegation of mala fides against the Committee which interviewed the candidates and we may concede that if this allegation were established, we might have been inclined to interfere with the selections even after lapse of a period of 18 months, because the writ petitions were filed as early as October-November, 1979 and merely because the Court could not take up the hearing of the writ petitions for such a long time should be no ground for denying relief to the petitioners, if they are otherwise so entitled. But we do not think that on the material placed before us we can sustain the allegation of mala fides against the Committee. It is true, and this is a rather disturbing feature of the present cases, that a large number of successful candidates succeeded in obtaining admission to the college by virtue of very high marks obtained by them at the viva voce examination tilted the balance in their favour, though the marks secured by them at the qualifying examination were much less than those obtained by the petitioners and even in the written test, they had fared much worse than the petitioners. It is clear from the chart submitted to us on behalf of the petitioners that the marks awarded at the interview are by and large in inverse proportion to the marks obtained by the candidates at the qualifying examination and are also, in a large number of cases, not commensurate with the marks obtained in the written test. The chart does create a strong suspicion in our mind that the marks awarded at the viva voce examination might have been manipulated with a view to favouring the candidates who ultimately came to be selected, but suspicion cannot take the place of proof and we cannot hold the plea of mala fides to be established. We need more cogent material before we can hold that the Committee deliberately manipulated the marks at the viva voce examination with a view to favouring certain candidates as against the petitioners. We cannot, however, fail to mention that this is a matter which required to be looked into very carefully and not only the State Government but also the Central Government which is equally responsible for the proper running of the college, must take care to see that proper persons are appointed on the interviewing committee and there is no executive interference with their decision-making process. We may also caution the authorities that though, in the present case, for reasons which we have already given, we are not interfering with the selection for the academic year 1979-80, the selections made for the subsequent academic years would run the risk of invalidation if such a high percentage of marks is allocated for the oral interview. We are of the view that under the existing circumstances allocation of more than 15% of the total marks for the oral interview would be arbitrary and unreasonable and would be liable to be struck down as constitutionally invalid." (para 19). 127. Consequently, Ajay Hasia does not support the stand taken by the learned Attorney-General but it is a decision supporting the view taken by us. Respectfully agreeing with the above view we also hold that allocation of such a high percentage of marks as 40% and 50% respectively at the oral interviews was arbitrary and unreasonable and is, therefore, "liable to be struck down as constitutionally invalid." (Ajay Hasia, para 19). If the system of interview for making promotion to such high posts as the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary in the Bangladesh Secretariat is at all followed, then as in case of admission to educational institutions as decided in Ajay Hasia's case so also in case of promotion to the above posts, allocation of more than 15% of the total marks for oral interview will create scope for arbitrariness in selecting candidates for promotion. 128. I am, therefore of opinion that the procedure evolved by the Council Committee on promotion and also by the Committee for promotion to the post of the Deputy Secretary for selecting candidates for promotion to the posts of the Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary respectively were violative of Article 27 of the Constitution and Article 29 (1) of the Constitution and, therefore, without lawful authority. Consequently, the supersession of the petitioners on the basis of the above methods by the Council Committee and the Committee on Deputy Secretary respectively, were illegal and without lawful authority and cannot, therefore, be sustained. 129. The learned Attorney-General has placed a decision of our Court in support of his contention that promotion cannot be claimed by a Government servant as a matter of right. 130. The case referred to by him is Ghazi Md. Ekhlas Mia vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 28 DLR 397. In this case an order of reversion of the petitioner from the post of Station Engineer to that of an Assistant Engineer was calied in question by a writ petition. The petitioner who was substantively an Assistant Engineer was appointed to act at Station Engineer in the Inland Water Transport Authority temporarily and until further orders. The post of Station Engineer was subsequently upgraded but in the new grade the petitioner was not appointed although he had continuously held the post for 6 years and in his place another person was appointed as Station Engineer on adhoc basis. He challenged this reversion on the ground that he has a right to be promoted. In this case, a Division Bench of this Court presided over by Shahabuddin Ahmed, J. (as his Lordship was then) held that promotion is not a right of a Government servant. To use the words used by his Lordship, it was observed as follows: "Promotion is not a right of a Government servant; it is to be earned by good performance. Promotion is made at the discretion of the authority but that discretion must be exercised in accordance with rules if any and established practices taking into consideration seniority efficiency, temperamental suitability honesty integrity etc. of the officers concerned. Seniority is not the sole determining factor in this case of promotion. To be promoted is not a right guaranteed by the Constitution of Bangladesh nor is it a condition of service of a Government employee." Ultimately while discharging the Rule the Court observed as follows: "In view of the petitioner's long service in the post of Station Engineer the authorities concerned should, in all fairness, examine his case while making final selection for substantive appointment to the post." 131. The above case clearly lays down the principles which we have enunciated above. We do not say that the petitioners are entitled to be promoted as a matter of right and on the basis of their respective seniority. Seniority is doubtless a factor but not the sole determining factor. We also agree with the learned Attorney-General that merit should be one of the main determining factors in case of promotion of Government officers and this question has not also been disputed by the petitioners of these writ petitions. What is in fact challenged in these writ petitions is the arbitrary method adopted in assessing the merits of the candidates and none of the petitioners has claimed promotion as a matter of right on the basis of seniority alone. As such, the above decision, instead of assisting the respondents supports the view that arbitrary method of selection has to be shunned and selection of candidates for promotion has to be made by taking into consideration seniority, efficiency, temperamental suitability, honesty, integrity, etc. as observed by their Lordships in the above case and this cannot be determined on the basis of a few minutes' interview of the candidates but mainly on the basis of their long service records and annual confidential reports. 132. The next decision cited by the learned Attorney-General during his course of arguments which I will refer is Sant Ram Sharma, Appellant vs. State of Rajasthan and others, Respondents, AIR 1967 (Supreme Court) 1910. In this case, the appellant who was an officer in the Indian Police Service and was a Deputy Inspector General of Police challenged his supersession to the post of Inspector General of Police by another officer. In the same writ petition he also challenged his appointment as Deputy Inspector General of Police subsequent to the superseding officer contending that in the original gradation list his position was above the superseding officer and he being the senior-most ought to have been appointed as Deputy Inspector General of Police and also as Inspector General of Police before the superseding officer. Since he was superseded he took the position that his fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 16 of the Indian Constitution providing for equal treatment of all citizens before law, equal protection of law and equal opportunity of all citizens for employment in the service of the State were violated. In this case, it was held that seniority alone could not be the sole factor for determining the suitability of an officer for a selection post and it was also held that the claim for promotion is primarily based on merit and not on seniority alone. The Indian Supreme Court also observed: "The circumstance that these posts are classed as Selection Grade Posts itself suggests that promotion to these posts is not automatic being made only on the basis of ranking in the Gradation List but the question of merit enters in promotion to selection posts. In our opinion, the respondents are right in their contention that the ranking or position in the Gradation List does not confer any right on the petitioner to be promoted to selection post and that it is a well-established rule that promotion to selection grades or selection posts is to be based primarily on merit and not on seniority alone. The principle is that when the claims of officers to selection posts is under consideration, seniority should not be regarded except where the merit of the officers is judged to be equal and no other criterion is, therefore, available." 133. We also subscribe to the above principles enunciated by their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India in the above case. I have failed to understand as to how this case helps the case of the respondents. The petitioners in the present writ petitions as we have already observed, do not claim promotion on the basis of seniority alone and their main grievance is about the method of assessment of merits evolved by the Government which, according to them, was arbitrary and, therefore, violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 134. Let us now consider the maintainability of these writ petitions. 135. The learned Attorney-General has submitted, with considerable emphasis, that the matters involved in these writ petitions being matters relating to the conditions of service and promotion of the persons in the service of the Republic, these writ petitions are not maintainable in view of Article 117 of the Constitution and the proper forum for the petitioners is the Administrative tribunal set up under the said Article. 136. Mr. Islam has contended that these writ petitions having been filed for enforcement of fundamental rights as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution and Article 29 of the Constitution and since in these writ petitions the vires of certain enactments as well as Notifications issued by the Government are challenged as ultra vires the Constitution invoking Article 27 and Article 29 of the Constitution an Administrative Tribunal cannot have jurisdiction to entertain this matter and the Constitution Bench of this Court alone is the proper forum to decide the matters agitated in these petitions. Article 117 of the Constitution runs as follows: "117 (1) Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of- (a) The terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic, including the matters provided for in part IX and the award of penalties or punishment; (b) the acquisition, administration, management and disposal of any property vested in or managed by the Government by or under any law, including the operation and management of, and service in any nationalised enterprise or statutory public authority; (c) any law to which clause (3) of Article 102 applies. (2) Where any administrative tribunal is established under this Article, no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal: Provided that Parliament may, by law, provide for appeals from, or the review of decisions of any such tribunal." 137. It therefore, appears that where the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic are matters-in-issue the Administrative Tribunal is the normal forum for deciding such issues and the jurisdiction of all other Courts including this Court is ousted in view of clause (2) of Article 117 of the Constitution. 138. It must. however, be observed that when simple terms and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic are matters-in-issue Article 117 of the Constitution applies but when the question of enforcement of fundamental rights, as in the present writ petitions, is involved this Court must assume jurisdiction in view of the mandate in Article 44 of the Constitution which runs as follows: "44 (1) The right to move the High Court Division in accordance with clause (1) of Article 102, for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part is guaranteed. (2) Without prejudice to the powers of the High Court Division under Article 102, Parliament may by law empower any other Court within the local limits of its jurisdiction, to exercise all or any of those powers." From the pleadings in these writ petitions we find that the petitioners filed these writ petitions for enforcement of their fundamental rights as enshrined in Article 27 and Article 29 of the Constitution and challenged several enactments and Notifications issued by the government invoking the above Articles containing fundamental rights. As such, we are of opinion that this Court rightly assumed jurisdiction to decide the issues agitated in these writ petitions and as the question of enforcement of fundamental rights is involved the Administrative Tribunal cannot decide the issues raised in these writ petitions. 139. Moreover, assuming that these matters could also be agitated before the Administrative Tribunal in a different manner, since the petitioners diligently pursued these matters in this Court for a number of years and this Court heard these matters at length, it would not be proper use of discretion to relegate the parties to another prolonged litigation before the Administrative Tribunal on the technical ground of locus standi of this Court. Hence, in my opinion, the writ petitions are maintainable. 140. Now, as to the final order. 141. Mr. Islam contended that the entire promotion procedure being illegal, all promotions made to the posts of Joint Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries respectively pursuant to the two impugned Notifications should be declared illegal and should be struck down. We are afraid this cannot be done for two reasons. The first reason is that those who have been promoted are not before us as parties and we have had no opportunity of hearing them. The second reason is that considerable time (about three years) has already elapsed after their promotion and an order clearing their promotion as illegal will have far-reaching effect on the entire administrative set-up and functioning of the administrative machinery. So, we have decided to refuse this particular prayer of Mr. Islam. But, we would at the same time like to observe that in order to avoid multiplicity of litigation in future, the Government may, if so advised, consider the cases of all those officers who were superseded by their juniors from being promoted to the posts of Joint Secretary and Deputy Secretary respectively pursuant to the above two impugned Notifications. 142. With the above observations, the rules in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 and Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 are made absolute and the petition in Writ Petition No 83 of 1993 is allowed. 143. Sub-paras (1) and (2) of Para (Ga) of Notification No 4(1) /90/217-Committee dated 9th October, 1991 and sub-paras (Ka) and (Kha) of the first para of Notification No সম/ উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-৯৮ dated 4th December, 1991 are hereby declared to be illegal, without lawful authority and of no legal effect being ultra vires Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution and are struck down. 144. The procedures of selection of officers adopted by the Council Committee on Promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and above for making promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary pursuant to Notification No. 4(1)/90/217-Committee dated 9th October, 1991 and by the Committee on Promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary for making promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary pursuant to Notification No সম/ উনি-৪/২-৪/৯১-৯৮ dated 4th December, 1991 are declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 145. The supersession of petitioner Mr. Shafiuddin Ahmed of Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 and petitioner Mr. Md. Sarwar-e-Alarn of Writ Petition No 813 of 1993 and their exclusion from promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary are declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 146. The supersession of petitioners Mr. Shaikh Mozahar Uddin, Mr. Md. Mominul Islam, Mr. Kazi Tariqul Islam, Mr. Makimuddin Ahmed and Mr. Bimal Kumar Khundu of Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 and their exclusion from promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretary are declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 147. The respondents are directed to consider the cases of all the above petitioners for promotion to the above respective posts according to law and in the light of the observations made in this judgment within six months from this date. If they are found fit for promotion, they shall be promoted with restoration of their respective seniority as per the gradation list. 148. The parties are directed to bear their respective costs. This judgment shall govern Writ Petition No 2738 of 1992, Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 and Writ Petition No 813 of 1993. Md. Hamidul Haque J. In these writ petitions, the petitioners challenged the vires of section 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1985 and of the provisions of the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations of 1979. The petitioners also challenged the constitution of the Superior Selection Board, the Committee on appointment and promotion of Deputy Secretaries and the Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service structure. The petitioners further challenged the procedure followed by the two Committees while making recommendation for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries. Facts of the case have been stated by my learned brothers Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker and Naimuddin Ahamed and, as such, I do not like to state the facts. I agree with the views of my learned brothers regarding interpretation of section 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1985 and of the provision of the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations 1979 and the maintainability of the writ petitions. While I agree with my learned brother Naimuddin Ahmed J, that the Rule be made absolute, I like to add my views about the constitution of the Committees in question and also about the procedure followed by the Committees while making recommendation for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries. 151. At the very early stage of hearing of these petitions a question arose as to the legal basis and origin of the two committees constituted by the Government for the purpose of making recommendation for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries. The learned Attorney-General, Additional-Attorney General and the learned Advocate for the petitioners Mr. Amirul Islam laboured hard to trace out the history and origin of these Committees and helped the Court in this regard to arrive at a decision. From the submission of the learned Advocates of both the parties and also from the Gazette Notifications furnished at the time of hearing by both the parties, it appears to us that these Committees were not constituted under any provision of any "law enacted by the Parliament or under any Rules framed by the Government or by the President under Article 133 of the Constitution. 152. In this regard the learned Attorney-General submitted that the posts of Deputy Secretaries and above were always considered as "selection posts" and, as such, the Government used to determine the procedure for appointment to such posts by issuing notifications from time to time. On the other hand, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, Mr. Islam, submitted that in view of the provisions of Article 133 of the Constitution which provided for enactment of law to regulate the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic and also framing Rules by the President until provision in that behalf is made by or under any law enacted by the Parliament. According to him, as there is no law or rules as contemplated under Article 133 there is no scope for giving appointment to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries by determining any procedure arbitrarily by the Government by issuing notifications. He has also argued that while giving appointment to these posts, consultation with the Public Service Commission as provided under Article 140 is also a must. Further, according to him, promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries or Joint Secretaries is very much a condition of service and, as such, the procedure relating to promotion to these posts must also be laid down by law or by rules framed under Article 133. So, he has argued that laying down of any procedure for promotion by the Government by issuing notifications is violative of Article 133. The learned Attorney-General however in reply, submitted that in the absence of any such law or rules, the Government cannot sit idle if the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries fall vacant due to retirement or otherwise. According to him, for the sake of running the administration smoothly, vacant posts must be filled up and for that purpose the Government can take appropriate steps in exercise of its inherent power and, in fact, the Government constituted the Committees and also laid down the procedure for promotion to those posts to meet such a situation. Moreover, he has submitted that the Committees were constituted on the basis of Cabinet decision and the procedure followed by these Committees was also the decision of the Cabinet and not of any particular Ministry. 153. From the history of services as furnished before us and from some of the cases cited by the learned Advocates of both the sides, it appears to us that some posts under the Government including the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries, Additional Secretaries and Secretaries are considered as selection posts" in this sub-continent. Unfortunately, in spite of the best efforts of the learned Advocates of both sides, we could not be supplied with the information as to when at first these posts were considered as Selection Posts or as to under what authority the posts were so considered. We also do not find anything in our Constitution to show that these posts are considered as Selection Posts and are kept outside the purview of Article 133 of the Constitution. But surprisingly we find that though various Recruitment Rules for different cadres have been framed under Article 133, these posts have not been included nor separate Rules have been framed in respect of these posts. Even if these posts are considered to be Selection posts, there is no reason as to why some rules could not be framed during last 22 years in respect of these posts. On perusal of Article 133, it is clear to me that these posts definitely are posts in the service of the Republic and, as such, cannot be considered outside the purview of Article 133. 154. However, the fact remains that no Rules have been framed as regards the procedure for promotion to these posts, So, the question arose as to whether the Government can formulate any procedure in the absence of any law or rules as contemplated under Article 133 of the Constitution. It appears to me that the answer to this question should be in the affirmative and the argument put forward in this regard by the learned Attorney- General may be accepted. If some of the Selection Posts fall vacant, such posts must be filled up for the sake of better and smooth administration. It cannot be conceived of that as there is no law or rules regulating the procedure for promotion to these posts, the posts should remain vacant. If such posts are not filled up, certainly it will lead to a crisis in the administration. Under such circumstances, the Government may come forward to fill up the vacuum by formulating some procedure or guideline for appointment of officers to these posts by way of promotion. 155. We find support to the above view in the observations made by their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Sant Ram Sharma vs. State of Rajasthan and others as reported in AIR 1967 (SC) 1910. The relevant observations are as follows: "We proceed to consider the next contention of Mr. NC Chatterjee that in the absence of any statutory rules governing promotions to selection grade posts the Government cannot issue administrative instructions and such administrative instructions cannot impose any restictions not found in the Rules already framed. We are unable to accept this argument as correct. It is true that there is no specific, provision in the Rules laying down the principle of promotion of junior or senior grade officers to selection grade posts. But that does not mean that till statutory rules are framed in this behalf, the Government cannot issue administrative instructions regarding the principle to be followed in promotions of the officers concerned to selection grade posts. It is true that Government cannot amend or supersede statutory Rules by administrative instructions, but if the rules are silent on any particular point, Government can fill up the gaps and supplement the rules and issue instructions not inconsistent with the rules already framed." The Appellate Division of our Supreme Court also was pleased to make similar observation in the case of Sharping, Matshajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd. liS Btmgladesh and others as regards settlement of fisheries which is reported in 39 DLR (AD) 85 wherein it has been observed as follows: "Under section 76 of this Act it lies at the disposal of the Government who may either manage it khas or make settlement thereof in accordance with rules to be made by them. In the absence of any such rules, the Government must follow certain fixed standards; principles or guidelines applicable to all persons seeking settlement and shall not act arbitrarily or in discriminatory manner". 156. Though the facts and circumstances of the case reported in 39 DLR (AD) 85 is not similar but the observation appears to be applicable. In this case, under section 76 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the Government is required to dispose of fisheries by way of settlement in accordance to the rules made by it. It has been clearly stated that in the absence of any such rules, the Government must follow certain standards, principles or guide-lines. Under Article 133 of the Constitution, Parliament may, by law, regulate the appointment and conditions of service but till such law is made by the Parliament, it shall be competent for the President to make rules regulating such appointment and conditions of service. In fact, no law has been passed by the Parliament nor any rules were framed by the President regulating appointment to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and above. Under such circumstances, the Government is empowered to formulate any principle, procedure or guide-line for appointment to those posts by promotion. Thus, in my opinion, the formulation of any procedure or principle along with the Constitution of the committees for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries cannot be said to have been made without any lawful authority. 157. Now, from the notifications and other papers made available to us at the time of hearing by both the parties, it appears that after the independence of Bangladesh, Superior Selection Board was constituted for the first time oil the basis of Cabinet Resolution No. ED 1-165/72-613 dated 1.3.72. This Board was required to recommend appointments to the posts of Sect-ion Officers and above in the Secretariat and some other higher posts of other departments. In this Resolution, the procedure for appointment of officers to the above posts by way of promotion was laid down and the Board was required to consider service records and character roll of each officer while making recommendation for promotion to the above posts. Thereafter, from time to time the Superior Selection Board was reconstituted by issuing notifications on different dates. The first departure from the procedure laid down in the earlier resolution was made by introducing a Senior Service Pool in 1979 by promulgating the Senior Service Pool Order, 1979. This Pool Order also provided for the constitution of Superior Selection Board and such Selection Board was reconstituted on 8.10.79. This Selection Board was dissolved by an order of the then Chief Martial Law Administrator on 5.7.82 but after few days it was revived by an order 27.7.82. Thereafter, on the basis of the Cabinet Resolution dated 23.2.83, another Superior Selection Board was constituted for appointment of Joint Secretaries and above in the Secretariate. The detailed procedure was laid down and the criterion of making recommendation on the basis of service record and ACR was retained. In the meantime, on 17.7.89 Senior Service Pool was abolished and quota system was adopted for the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries for each cadre and the posts of Additional Secretaries and Secretaries were kept open for officers of all cadres. Then by a notification dated 24.7.89 the Superior Selection Board constituted by resolution dated 22.3.83 was abolished and it was decentralised. But again by another notification dated 2.4.91, the procedure introduced by the notification dated 24.7.89 was cancelled and Superior Selection Board was revived and reconstituted. This time again detailed procedure was laid down and it was provided for the first time that the Superior Selection Board would make recommendation for appointment to the posts of Joint Secretaries and above to the Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service structure. Another departure was also made-a separate Committee was constituted to recommend the cases of promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries. On 10.7.91 Superior Selection Board was again reconstituted retaining the procedure laid, down 'in the notification dated 2.4.91. Thereafter; to remove any doubt which might have been created due to the notifications dated 24.7.89 and 2.4.91, another notification was issued on 19.8.91 by way of clarification. By this notification the earlier two notifications dated 27A.89 and 2.4.91 were cancelled and Superior Selection Board' and other Committees were constituted again. The vires of this notification dated 19.8.91 has been challenged which has been marked as Annexure-J in the Writ Petition No 2738 of 1992. 158. Now let us consider the grounds on which the legality of this notification has been challenged. Before going into details, it may be mentioned that sub-paragraph (3) of paragraph 2 of this notification was amended by the notification dated 4.12.91 arid paragraph 6 of the notification dated 19.8.91 was also cancelled by the notification dated 4.12.91. Under Paragraph 3(Ka) of the notification dated 19.8.91, it Committee was constituted with the Cabinet Secretary as the Chairman and four other Secretaries as members. Under sub-para (Kha) of this paragraph, the Committee was required to send its recommendation through the Minister of Establishment to the President for his approval. By the notification dated 4.12.91, both sub-paras (ka) and (kha) of the original notification dated 19:8.91 was amended and the Minister of State-in-charge of Establishment was made Chairman and four other Secretaries were made Members of the Committee. Sub-paragraph (kha) was amended by providing that the Committee would consider the recommendation of the Superior Selection Board for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and send its own recommendation to the Prime Minister for approval. By paragraph 2 of this notification, paragraph, 6 of the earlier notification dated 19.8.91 was cancelled. 159. Now, let us see what was in paragraph 6 of the earlier notification dated 19.8.91 the paragraph is quoted below: ৬। পদোন্নতি, নিয়োগ, সিলেকসন গ্রেড উচ্চতর টাইমস্কেল প্রাপ্য ভিত্তিতে শুধু বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন ও সার্ভিস রেকর্ড (শৃঙ্খলা, আচরন, দুর্নীতি ইত্যাদি সংক্রান্ত রেকর্ড) এর ভিত্তিতে বিবেচিত হইবে। এতদসংক্র��ন্ত প্রস্তাবাদি বিবেচনাকলে সংশ্লিষ্ট বোর্ড/কমিটি পৃথকভাবে কোন পরীক্ষা বা সাক্ষাৎকার গ্রহন করিবে না তবে বিসিএস (পদোন্নতির জন্য পরীক্ষা) বিধি, ১৯৮৬, সংশ্লিষ্ট নিয়োগবিধি অথবা অন্য কোন বিধিতে যদি কোন পরীক্ষা বা সাক্ষাৎ কারের ব্যবস্থা থাকে, তবে উক্ত বিধি যথারীতি অনুসরন করিতে হইবে। So it is clear that in paragraph 6, emphasis was given on the ACR and the service record of each officer for the purpose of consideration of the cases of promotion and the Committee was directed not to hold any examination or interview unless required by any rules. Now, this paragraph 6 was cancelled by the notification dated 4.121.91 without substituting any alternative procedure for consideration by the Committee. So, after cancellation of paragraph 6 of the notification dated 19.8.91, there was no guide-line before the Committee because that paragraph was not substituted by providing any new guideline. 160. The respondents however, by filing a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition on 17.11.93 submitted a copy of a summary dated 3.11.91 prepared by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment for consideration of the Cabinet which has been marked Annexure-I. In this summary, at paragraph 3(ka), a proposal was placed for consideration of the Cabinet to the effect that the Committees cons-tituted for consideration of the cases of promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and Joint Secretaries would make evaluation of the officers on the basis of allotment of 100 marks-60 marks for ACK and 40 marks for interview. This new proposal was approved by the Cabinet on 11.11.91. Thus it is quite clear that the Cabinet sought to introduce a new procedure of allotment of marks in place of the earlier procedure contained at paragraph 6 of the notification dated 19.8.91. It is surprising to note that the amending notification dated 4.12.91 though issued after approval of the new procedure by the Cabinet, it did not include the new procedure. 161. The learned Attorney-General submitted that the Committee while making recommendation for promotion actually followed this new procedure. The learned Attorney-General has also submitted that a Cabinet decision need not be published in the official Gazette. In this connection, he referred to the case reported in AIR 1959 (Andhra Pradesh) 437 and another case reported in P1.1) 1971 (SC) 667. The facts and circumstances of both the reported cases are different from the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the instant case, we find that the Government by issuing a notification dated 19.8.91 laid down a procedure requiring the Committee concerned to follow a particular procedure while making recommendation for promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries. Once a procedure is published in the official Gazette, if it is modified subsequently, the modification must also be notified and published in the Official Gazette. There was no necessity of publication of the Cabinet decision dated 11.11.91 introducing a new procedure, had the procedure contained at paragraph 6 of the earlier notification was not published in the Gazette when the earlier Gazette notification was amended by issuing a Gazette notification at a subsequent date, the new procedure being totally different from the earlier procedure, the new procedure ought to have been incorporated in the amending notification. In view of this position, it is clear to me that it was incumbent upon the Government to publish the new decision by issuing a Gazette notification in substitution of paragraph 6 of the earlier notification dated 19.8.91. As the new Cabinet decision was not published in the official Gazette to substitute paragraph 6 of the earlier notification, it can be said that the new procedure had no legal existence. 162. The learned Attorney-General, however argued that the petitioners and all other officers were fully aware of the new procedure of allotment of marks and in support of his contention he referred to paragraph 7(u) of Write Petition No. 2738 of 1992. In sub-pars (u) of paragraph 7, it has been stated by the petitioner that the Council Committee most illegally introduced marking system allotting 40% marks for viva, 10% marks for penpicture and 50% marks for 10 years ACR. I have perused this sub-paragraph but from the statements made in this sub-paragraph it cannot be said that the petitioner was fully aware of the new procedure. In the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No.1 there is no mention of the Cabinet decision dated 11.11.91. At paragraph 13 of the affidavit-in-opposition, it has been stated that the Council Committee followed the interview system and marking system as per Government guide-lines in this respect. But what was the guide-line has not been specifically mentioned. Now, it is said that the guideline was the guideline approved by the Cabinet on 11.11.91. The proposal approved is that of allotment of 100 marks-60 marks for ACR and 40 for' interview. But this is not the case of the petitioners. The petitioners nowhere stated that 60% marks for ACR and 40% marks for interview was fixed. The petitioners were not at all sure about the new procedure and this is evident from the fact that they mentioned in sub-paragraph (u) of paragraph 7 that 50 marks was for ACR, 40 for viva and 10 for pen-picture. From Annexure I, the summary, I do not find that 10 marks was allotted for pen-picture. The new procedure was never published. Naturally, the petitioners could know nothing definitely about the new procedure. Even if the petitioners were aware unofficially, this cannot preclude the petitioners from challenging the action of the Committees in following the new procedure. 163. So, from my above discussion, it is clear that though the Committee constituted for consideration of the cases of promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries was constituted legally, the same Committee acted arbitrarily while making recommendation by following a procedure which had no legal existence. 164. So long I confined my discussion on the constitution of the Superior Selection Board and the Committee constituted under paragraph 2(3) of the notification dated 19.8.91 as modified by notification dated 4.12.91. Now, I shall discuss about the Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure. As regards this Committee, the learned Advocates of both parties could not show any notification as to when at first such Council Committee was constituted. However, from the papers submitted by both the parties, we find that a Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure was reconstituted along with other National Councils and Committees on the basis of Cabinet resolution dated 6.12.82. The then Deputy Martial Law Administrator and the Chief of Naval Staff was the Convenor of that Committee and six other Ministers were Members of that Committee. The relevant terms of reference of that Committee were as follows: "(i) Review cases of supersession and promotion of officers of the level of Joint Secretary and above; (ii) Consider all proposals for promotion and initial appointments to the post of Joint Secretary and above and Head of Departments/ Autonomous Bodies/Corporations duly processed through the Superior Selection Board and to make recommendations to the CMLA" 165. it appears from the Resolution that no detailed procedure was laid down regarding the criterion to be followed by the Council Committee while making recommendation for promotion. This Council Committee was again reconstituted by resolution of the Cabinet dated 25.7.83. It is mentioned in this Resolution that the terms of reference and other instructions remained unchanged but no notification could be made available to us to show what are those other instructions. We find no other notification relating to Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotions and Service Structure before 10.10.91 i.e. before the impugned notification (Annexure-K) of Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992) was issued. From this notification, we find that the Minister-in-charge of Education is the Convener, six other Cabinet Ministers, one Minister of State and the Minister of the relevant Ministry are Members of that Committee. No procedure has been laid down in this notification as to how the Committee will make its recommendation. The scope of this Committee is as follows: গ (১) যুগ্ন সচিব ও তদুর্ধ্ব পর্যায়ের কর্মকর্তাদের পদোন্নাতি বিবেচনা এবং অতিক্রমন পুনবির্বেচনা। (২) যুগ্ন-সচিব ও তদুর্ধ্ব পর্যায়ের পদে এবং বিভাগীয় প্রধান, স্বয়ত্বশাসিত সংস্থার প্রধান ও পরিচালনা পরিষদের সদস্য/পরিচালক পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য সুপারিশ সিলেকশন বোর্ডের মাধ্যমে প্রক্রিয়াকৃত প্রস্তাব সমূহ বিবেচনা করা এবং প্রধানমন্ত্রির সুপারিশ পেশ করা.. 166. From the above we find that this Council Committee was required to consider the cases of the officers for promotion to the post of Joint Secretaries which were processed by the Superior Selection Board and to make its own recommendation to the Prime Minister. No authority was given to this Committee to hold any examination or to hold any interview. The paragraph "Ga" of this notification was not amended after the Cabinet decision dated 11.11.91. So, this Committee also acted arbitrarily by following a procedure which was not included in its terms of reference or in its scope as determined in the notification on the basis of which the Committee itself was constituted. As such, the recommendation of this Committee for promotion of the officers to the posts of Joint Secretaries by following procedure of allotment of marks-60% for ACR and 40% for interview is also without any lawful authority. 167. Besides the question of legality of the procedure followed by the two Committees, Mr. Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, also questioned the validity of allotment of 40% marks for the interview or viva. According to him,' allotment of such high marks for viva without laying down any guide-line or standard for allotting such marks led to nepotism and favouritism. He further argued that this new system was introduced with a view to create political loyalists in the service of the Republic. In this connection, he also submitted that with the introduction of scientific ACR system, merit of the officers could easily be assessed on the basis of ACR itself and there was no necessity for holding any interview or viva. Lastly, he submitted that the system, created scope for arbitrary exercise of power by the Committees and, as such, it was violative of equality clause of the Constitution. In support of his views, Mr. Islam referred to two cases of the Supreme Court of India. In these cases, high marks were allotted for, interview or viva in admission tests and, as such, appears to be not applicable in the instant case. 168. As against the views of Mr. Islam, the learned Attorney-General has submitted that for filling up the Selection posts, merit should be the criterion and merit can be best assessed by interview of the candidates in addition to consideration of the ACR According to him, it is not violative of equality clause because all the candidates including the petitioners were asked to appear before the Interview Board and their cases were duly considered by the Committees but as they were not found fit, they were not recommended for promotion. He is also of the view that there is nothing wrong in the interview system itself specially when the candidates are all matured persons and in support of his views, he cited the case of Keshav Ram Pal vs UP Higher Education Services Commission, Allahabad and others as reported 'in' AIR 1986 (SC) 597. In that case, the Supreme Court of India was pleased to observe as follows:" "On the other hand, in the case of services to which recruitment has necessarily to be made from persons of mature personality, interview test may be the only way, subject to basic and essential academic and professional requirements being satisfied. To subject such persons to a written examination may yield unfruitful and negative results, apart from its being an act of cruelty to those persons.
