full_judgment: This Revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 27.2.92 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 173 of 1989, affirming those dated 8.6.89 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 27 of 1989. 2. The Rule was issued at the instance of defendant Government calling upon the plaintiff-opposite party to show cause as to why the aforesaid judgment and decree of the courts below should not be set aside. 3. The opposite party instituted the title suit of against the petitioner for a declaration that the treating the suit property as abandoned one and granting lease of the same by the petitioner are illegal, void, without jurisdiction, inoperative and of no legal effect and, as such, the action of the petitioner taken in respect of the suit property is not binding upon the opposite party. 4. The case of the plaintiff-opposite party, in short, is, that the suit property originally belonged to one Abdul Jalil, during the war of liberation, the said owner along with his family members took shelter in the Murapara camp under Dhaka district and taking advantage of their absence some miscreants took possession of the suit property illegally and got it declared as an abandoned property; the further case was that the said Abdul Jalil, in the meantime, died leaving behind two sons namely, Abdul Karim and Abdul Khaleque as his legal heirs. The said sons of late Abdul Jalil obtained nationality certificate from the Ministry of Home Affairs and made a representation to the authority concerned for not treating the property in question as abandoned but it was of no effect The said sons of Abdul Jalil sold the said property to the father of the plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 30.6.80, but the plaintiffs father was not aware of the fact that the suit property was an abandoned property. Hence the suit was filed for aforesaid declaration with a prayer for mandatory injunction directing the petitioner to restore possession of the property in favour of the opposite party. 5. The defendant-petitioner contested the said suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation. The property has been vested in the government as an abandoned property within the meaning of the President's Order No. 16 of 972, as such, the plaintiffs suit is barred under Articles 14(c), 23 and 24 of the said President's Order. The defendant's case is that since after liberation of the country the said owner late Abdul Jalil was found absent from the suit property to possess, control, manage and supervise the property and, as such, the suit property was rightly declared as an abandoned property, the petitioner further stated that he possessed the property by leasing out the same and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 6. The trial Court decreed the suit of the plaintiff against which the petitioner preferred appeal and the lower appellate Court affirmed the decree of the trial Court. The petitioner being aggrieved moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 7. Mr. Farid Ahmed, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, firstly, submits that the suit property has been rightly declared as an abandoned property under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 as the original owner left the property during the war of liberation of the country and his whereabouts was not known. It has been further submitted that the government having taken over the suit property possessed the same through its lessee/tenant, the transfer of the suit property to the plaintiffs' father on 30.6.80 was null and void under Article 7 of the President's Order 142 of 1972 and the plaintiff-opposite party cannot be said to have acquired any right, title or interest on the basis of such transfer, and, as such, the court of appeal below committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision causing failure of justice in affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The learned Assistant Attorney-General, lastly, argued that since the plaintiff-opposite party cannot be said to have acquired any right, title and interest in the suit property on the basis of the said kabala dated 30.6.80, she is not entitled to a decree of mandatory injunction and, as such, the findings and decisions arrived at by the courts below cannot be sustained in law and the Rule should be made absolute. 8. Mr. Azizul Hoq, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, contends that admittedly the original owner of the property was late Abdul Jalil who left the suit premises and took shelter in Murapara camp within the country during the war of liberation. He did not leave Bangladesh and, as such, his absence cannot be prejudicial to the interest of the country and for the temporary absence, the property cannot be declared as an abandoned property. It has been further submitted that it has been consistently held in the judicial pronouncement by the highest court of this country that mere absence of the owner of the property during the war of independence cannot be a ground for declaring the property as an abandoned property under provision of President's Order 16 of 1972 unless the government formed an opinion to the effect that the absence of the owner of any property was prejudicial to the interest of the country. Mr. Hoq lastly argued that the original owner of the property did not leave this country during war, he took shelter in a place within the country along with his family members. After his death Abdul Karim and Abdul Khaleque, the two sons of Abdul Jalil, inherited his property as his legal heirs. In support of his above contention the learned Advocate has referred to a decision in the case of Abdur Rashid and others vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 27 DLR 614. In that case it has been held that the owner may be absent or whereabouts may not be known but if his family members or heirs, as the case may be, are present in Bangladesh on the relevant date, his property cannot be treated as an abandoned property. 9. I have heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the relevant records and gone through the impugned judgments of the courts below. 10. The whole argument of the learned Assistant Attorney-General was that since the whereabouts of the original owner was not known, the property in question automatically vested in the government as an abandoned property under the provision of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and the plaintiff acquired no right, title and interest in the suit property on the basis of purchase the kabala (deed of sale) dated 30.6.80. 11. It is true that the government after declaring the suit property as abandoned property took possession. The possession of the government is not as owner of the property but as a caretaker of the same. It has already been settled that mere absence from the property at the time of Liberation War of Bangladesh cannot be only ground for declaring the property as an abandoned property. Before declaring the property as such, the government must form an opinion to the effect that the activities of the owner during his absence were prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh and without formation of any such opinion, the property cannot be declared as an abandoned property. There is nothing on record to show about any such formation of opinion in respect of the suit property. 12. In the instant case the original owner Abdul Jalil did not leave Bangladesh for any country, rather he was within Bangladesh taking shelter elsewhere and he was found absent from the property at the relevant time. It also appears that after his death Abdul Karim and Abdul Khaleque, the two sons of the deceased, obtained nationality certificate vide Ext. 4 and they were granted succession certificate as the legal heirs vide Ext 5 and those documents were accepted by the government without challenging them. 13. The trial Court upon consideration of the oral and documentary evidence on record found that the original property belonged to late Abdul Jalil and after his death the two sons, being the nationals of Bangladesh, inherited the property and the present plaintiff, on the basis of valid document, acquired title in the suit property. The lower appellate Court as final court of fact also rightly considered the provisions of law and the evidence on record and quite rightly affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 14. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the aforesaid decision I find substance in the contention of the learned Advocate of the opposite party. On perusal of the impugned judgments of the courts below I find that both the courts below considered the provision of law correctly and their findings and decisions are concluded by concurrent findings of fact and law and there is no legal infirmity for interference by this court. 15. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. Send down the records at once. End.

lawyer:
Masood R Sobhan, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
Saifuddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Lalima Begum and another ----- Petitioners
Vs
Chairman, Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Shaha J: This application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is directed against the judgment and order dated 29-3-92 passed by the Court of Settlement, First Court, Dhaka in Case No. 776 of 1987 dismissing the petitioners' case.

2. This case was filed by the petitioners under section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) against respondent No. 2 Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development, praying for exclusion of the case property in Holding No. 8B/B, 2nd Colony, Mirpur, Dhaka from the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings published in the Bangladesh Gazette (Extraordinary) dated 29th September, 1986 under the provisions of the above Ordinance.

3. The case of the petitioners, in short, is that the case property was leased out to Ahmed Reza on 7 -9-1961 by the then ADC, Dhaka as "Relief Plot" and since then Ahmed Reza had been possessing the same till his death in November, 1973 on the basis of a registered deed of lease dated 7th September, 1961. After his death his two sons Muktar Ahmed and Iqbal Hussain and two daughters Fahmida Khatun and Akbari Khatun have been possessing the case property as Ahmed Reza's heirs and heiresses and while they were thus the rightful owner in possession of the property in question they sold the same to the petitioners by two separate sale deeds dated 4-10-1978 and since then the petitioners have been owing and possessing the same by constructing 3 semi-pucca structures thereon and letting our the same to monthly bharatias. Their further case is that their vendors and their predecessor-in-interest had all along been in peaceful possession of the case property till they sold the same to them and there was no occasion whatsoever to treat it as an abandoned property at any point of time. The Government did never take over possession of the case property nor did it serve the statutory notice upon the occupiers as required under Article 7(3) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 for surrendering possession before including it in the list of Abandoned Buildings. The further case of the petitioners is that the property in question cannot be included in the list of the abandoned buildings as they are the rightful owners of the same by way of purchase for valuable consideration from Bangladeshi citizens and there was no occasion for the Government to treat it as abandoned property at any point of time under President's Order 16 of 1972 till before 23rd September, 1986 when the respondents arbitrarily enlisted the case property in the list of abandoned buildings.

4. The respondents opposed the petitioners case before the Court of Settlement but they did not file any written statement-objection denying the material allegations of the petition.

The learned Court of Settlement by its impugned judgment and order dated 29-3-1992 has been pleased to dismiss the petitioners case on findings that there is no evidence on record to prove that Ahmed Reza and his sons and daughters had been living in Bangladesh during and after the War of Liberation and that Ahmed Reza died in Bangladesh after the War of Liberation leaving behind heirs and heiresses.

5. Mr. Masood R Sobhan, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners, submitted that in view of the fact that allottee Ahmed Reza all along lived in Bangladesh till his death in November, 1973 and owned and possessed the case property all through on payment of "Annual Land Rent" to the Government in his name up to 1974 as evidenced by Annexure-"C" serial and the Burial Certificate Annexure-"T" proving that he died in Bangladesh on 8th November, 1973 and he was duly succeeded by his two sons and two daughters, vendors of the petitioners, there was no occasion for the Government for enlisting the case property in the list of abandoned buildings and, as such, the impugned Gazette Notification is illegal, arbitrary and without lawful authority. Mr. Masood R Sobhan further submitted that having regard to the admitted fact that petitioners have been in possession of the case property through bharatias and the respondents did not serve the statutory notice upon the occupiers asking them to surrender possession of the case property as required by Article 7(3) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 before including the case property in the list of abandoned buildings leading to the impugned Gazette Notification dated 29th September, 1986 it is evident that the property in question cannot be included in the list of abandoned properties-"kha" list and, as such, the purported Gazette Notification dated 29th September, 1986 is illegal, arbitrary, and without any lawful authority.

6. The learned Counsel for the petitioners further submitted that the learned Court of Settlement was manifestly wrong in passing the impugned judgment and order totally ignoring the legal incidence of payment of "Annual Land Rent" to the Government in the name of Ahmed Reza for the years of 1973 and 1974, the Joint Survey Report dated 27-6-1979 Annexure-"E" made by two responsible Officers of the Government clearly showing that the case property was never an abandoned property and that Moktar Hussain, Iqbal Hussain, Fahmida Khatun and Akbari Khatun, sons and daughters of allottee Ahmed Reza, duly obtained succession certificate in respect of the properties left by their father Ahmed Reza in Succession Certificate Case No. 768 of 1978 proving that the vendors of the petitioners are the heirs and heiresses of Ahmed Reza and they own the property left by the father Ahmed Reza as citizens of Bangladesh and while being the rightful owners in possession they sold the same to the petitioners by two registered sale deeds dated 4-10-1978 un-mistakeably proving that the case property is not an abandoned property. The learned Counsel further submitted that non-consideration of these material pieces of evidence and the legal aspect of the case on the question of statutory notice under Article 7(3) of Ordnance No. 54 of 1986 have materially affected the impugned decision of the learned Court of Settlement

7. The matter was heard by us on 1-3-1997 when none appeared for the respondents and after conclusion of the hearing 6-3-1997 was fixed for delivery of the judgment. On 6-3-1997 when we were about to deliver the judgment Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, appeared before us with Mr. KH Saifuddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, and prayed for a short accommodation for filing an affidavit-in-opposition for contesting the case and his prayer for adjournment was allowed and 12-3-1997 was fixed for hearing the case. On 12-3-1997 we took up the case for hearing at about 12-30 PM but none was present on behalf of the respondents. After hearing Mr. Masud R Sobhan, the learned Counsel for the petitioners, we learnt that he was not served with any copy of affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the respondents. Since there was none to oppose the Rule on behalf of the respondents we started delivering the judgment. After we finished a substantial part of the judgment Mr. KMS Saifuddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appeared before us and prayed for time for filing an affidavit-in-opposition which, according to him, was under process of preparation, but his prayer at that stage of the proceedings was refused. Mr. Saifuddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, then made over to u the rile of the Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh in respect of the case property and urged upon us to consider the materials in the file in deciding the case. Mr. KM Saifuddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General only submitted that the file of the Ministry of Works would fully justify the inclusion of the case property in the list of the abandoned properties and he has nothing more to add.

8. We went through the file of the Ministry in question and found that it was only on 28th of June, 1979 that for the first time some sporadic efforts were made by an over zealous officer for fishing out a case of abandoned property by bringing the case property within the mischief of abandoned property laws. In pursuance of the said move the Government formed a Joint Survey Team consisting of an Assistant Settlement Officer and an Assistant Engineer to enquire into the matter by conducting a joint survey on the spot for ascertaining the character of the case property and to submit its report to the Superintending Engineer, Abandoned Buildings. The Survey Team submitted its report dated 21st July, 1979 marked Annexure-"E" to the petition and it reads as follows:

মাননীয়

তত্ত্ববধায়ক প্রকৌশলী

পরিত্যক্ত বাড়ী ঘর সার্কেল

৮৮, মতিঝিল বাণিজ্যিক এলাকা, ঢাকা।

বিষয়ঃ ৮ ঔ-বি/বি, ২য় কলোনী মিরপুর বাড়ী প্রসঙ্গে।

স্বারক নং-এপি ১৮-বাসা-১৬৩/৭৯/৪৭৭ তারিখ-২৭-৬-৭৯ ইং-

মহাতন,

উল্লেখিত স্মারকে, অদিষ্ট হইয়া যথারীতি সরেজমিনে তদন্তকার্য্য সম্পূর্ণ করিয়াছি। তদন্তে প্রতিয়মান হয় যে বিগত ৭-৮-৬১ ইং তাং-পর ১৪৬৬ ৩ নং লিজ দলিল বলে জনাব আহম্মেদ রেজা পিতা মৃত আলী কেস এই সম্পত্তির লিজ গ্রহীতা হন।

তদন্তে প্রকাশ পায় যে মূল লিজ গ্রহিতা বিগত ১৯৭২ ইং তাং ২ পুত্র ও ২ কন্যাকে ওয়ারিশ রাখিয়া মারা যান। যথা-(১) মোকতার আহম্মেদ (২) ইকবাল হোসেন (৩) ফাহামিদা খাতুন (৪) আকতারী বেগম। উল্লেখ সাকসেসন সার্টিফিকেট নং-৭৬০/৭৮।

এই বাড়ীটি ২টি অংশে বিভক্ত। সামনের অংশে ৩টি দোকান এবং পিছনে ২টি বেডরুম সহ ১টি বাড়ী। উল্লেখিত বাড়ী এবং দোকান ভাড়াটিয়ার মাধ্যমে বাড়ীর ওয়ারিশ সহ এ মালিকগণের দখলে বর্তমান বাড়ীটি পরিত্যক্ত সম্পত্তির আওতায় আসে নাই।

অবগতি কল্পে এই সাথে বাড়ীটির হাত নকসা সংযুক্ত হইল।”

The above report dated 21st July, 1979 convincingly proves that the case property is not an abandoned property and it does not come within the mischief of an abandoned property as embodied in Article 2 of President's Order 16 of 1972. It appears that the case property was included in the list of "Abandoned Buildings" only on 23rd September, 1986 without any further material on record to justify its inclusion in the list of abandoned properties.

9. In this Rule the respondents have not filed any affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the petition, although the respondents were given sufficient opportunity to do so. The result is that the assertions made in the petition stand uncontroverted.

10. The petitioners in support of their claim have filed the photo copy of the two registered sale deeds dated 4th October, 1978 as contained in Annexure-"B" and B(1) to the petition. They have also filed the Clearance Certificate and rent receipts showing payment of "Annual Land Rent" to the Government in the name of Ahmed Reza up to 1974. This Annexure-"e" series clearly proves that "Annual Land Rent" for the case property was paid to the Government for the years 1973 and 1974 in the name of allottee Ahmed Reza. The Joint Survey Report submitted by Assistant Settlement Officer and Assistant Engineer dated 21st of July, 1979 Annexure-E proves, beyond doubt, that the case property is not an abandoned property and it does not come within the purview of abandoned property laws. Annexure-I, dated 12th November, 1973 is the Burial Certificate issued by the General Secretary, KalshiJame Mosque, Madrasha, Eidgah and Graveyard Committee showing that Ahmed Reza, the original allottee, had died in Dhaka on 8th November, 1973 and he was buried at the Kalshi Graveyard. The Joint Survey Report Annexure-"E" and the Burial Certificate Annexure- "I", therefore, go unchallenged. All these papers, which remained uncontroverted, unmistakably prove that Ahmed Reza, the original allottee, had been living in Bangladesh till his death on 8th November, 1973 and after his death his 2 sons and 2 daughters, vendors of the petitioners, stepped into his shoes and since then they have been in uninterrupted and peaceful possession of the property in question. While thus being in peaceful possession they sold the case property to the petitioners by two registered sale deeds dated 4th October, 1978. Under such circumstances, we are of the view that the learned Court of Settlement was not at all justified in holding that the case property was rightly declared as an abandoned property on the finding that the petitioners did not produce any oral and documentary evidence showing that Ahmed Reza was living in Bangladesh during and after the War of Liberation.

<u>11. It is true that if a property comes within the definition of "Abandoned Properties" as contemplated in Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972, it automatically vests in the Government in terms of Article 4 thereof on the commencement of the said Order. But an abandoned property even in possession of any person can only be included in the list of "Abandoned Properties", called "Kha" list in respects of which notices for surrender have been issued and possession taken over as "Abandoned Property". This notice must be the notice as required by Article 7(3) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) and as prescribed by Rule 3(8) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property. (Taking Over Possession) Rules, 1972. The listing of the properties in the list of Abandoned Properties viz. "Kha list" and publication thereof in the Official Gazette in respect of which notices under Article 7(3) of President's Order 16 of 1972 have not been issued will be clearly illegal. Moreover, section 4 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 provides that notices for surrender for taking over possession of any property as "Abandoned Properties" shall not be issued under the said Ordinance after 31st of October, 1986, Article 5 of President's Order No. 54 of 1985 provides as follows:</u>

<u>5. Publication of lists of buildings-(I) The Government shall, after the 31st day of March, 1986 and before the 30th day of April, 1986, publish-in the Official Gazette-</u>

<u>(a) a list of building the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order;</u>

<u>(b) a list of buildings in respect of which notices for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said Order have been issued;</u>

<u>Provided that no such list shall include any building in respect of which-</u>

<u>(a) any decree or order has been passed, at any time before the publication of the list in the Official Gazette, by any court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not to have vested in the Government under the President's Order or declaring the possession by the Government of the building as an abandoned property under that Order to be illegal or invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person, or</u>

<u>(b) a suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding is pending before any court immediately before the date of publication of the list in the Official Gazette, in which the vesting in, or possession of, the Government of the building as abandoned property under the President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the building by the Government or by any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person.</u>

<u>(2) The lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such.</u>

12.It is thus evident that once a property is enlisted as an "Abandoned Property" by observing the legal formalities it becomes conclusive evidence as regards the character of the property in question but the requirement of law is that before a property is enlisted as an "Abandoned Property" notice under Article 7(3) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 must be given to the occupiers. In this case, no notice as required by the Article 7(3) of President's Order 16 1985 appears to have been issued to the occupiers. Admittedly, the case property is still in possession of the petitioners through bharatias. There is absolutely nothing on record to rebut the clear assertions of the petitioners that the statutory notice as required under Article 7(3) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 was never issued by the Government before treating the property as an abandoned property leading to the ultimate publication in the Official Gazette. The impugned judgment of the Court of Settlement does not at all indicate as to whether it at all considered the vital question of the statutory notice as required by law. In the face of the clear assertion by the petitioners that no such statutory notice was ever served upon the occupiers of the case property before treating it as "Abandoned Property and in the absence of any evidence whatsoever to prove to the contrary, it must be held that notice as required under Article 7(3) of the Ordinance was never issued to the occupiers of the case property, leading to the impugned publication in the Official Gazette on 23rd October, 1986. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record the whole exercise appears to be illegal, malafide and without any lawful authority. Since the essential requirements of law as required by President's Order 16 of 1972 and Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 were not complied with before enlisting the case property as an "Abandoned Property" in late September, 1986 it must be held that the respondents acted illegally, arbitrarily and without any lawful authority in making the impugned publication in the Official Gazette treating the case property as an abandoned property. The learned Court of Settlement appears to have totally ignored these vital aspects of the case, the material evidence on record and the law bearing on the subject. Moreover, the learned Court of Settlement also failed to consider the legal incidence of payment of "Annual Land Rent" in the name of allottee Ahmed Reza upto 1974 and the question of uninterrupted and peaceful physical possession of the case property by the original allottee Ahmed Reza and after him by his successors-in-interest, vendors of the petitioners. Failure of the learned Court of Settlement to consider the vital documents in Annexure-"C" series, Annexure-"E" and Annexure "I" to the petition fully supporting the claim of the petitioners must have materially affected the impugned decision. The learned Court of Settlement also failed to take into consideration the Joint Survey Report submitted by two responsible Government Officers clearly certifying that the case property was not an abandoned property and it does not come within the purview of President's Order 16 of 1972. In the context of proved facts the Government has no right to disown the said Joint Survey Report without any fresh convincing materials justifying the cancellation of the said report. The inclusion of the case property in the list of "Abandoned Property" on 23-9-1986 without serving the statutory notice upon the occupiers as required by Article 7(3) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 appears to be wholly illegal and arbitrary.

13. The principles of fairness in government action requires that government functionaries must act according to law and must perform their duties in good faith. Public accountability and acceptance demand that government actions must correspond to good conscience and fair play. In the instant case, we are constrained to hold that even minimum fairness was not exhibited in dealing with the case property belonging to a citizen of the country, whose right to property is guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution. The enlisting of the case property in the list of "Abandoned Property", in the circumstances of the case, thus must be held to be illegal, mala fide and without lawful authority.

<u>14. We are conscious that the High Court Division in deciding the case is not acting as the court of appeal with the power to lightly interfere with findings of facts arrived at by the learned Court of Settlement. But since the learned Court of Settlement failed to consider material pieces of evidence in Annexures-"C" series, "E" and "T" and the fact of non-service of the statutory notice as required under Article 7(3) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 upon the occupiers of the case property, we are of the opinion that the learned Court of Settlement acted illegally and without jurisdiction in finding that the petitioners have failed to show that the allottee Ahmed Reza and his sons and daughters have been living in Bangladesh during and after the War of Liberation of Bangladesh and that he died in Bangladesh leaving behind legal heirs and heiresses, which are evidently against materials on record.</u>

15. In fact, we do not find in the four comers of the record and the file of the concerned Ministry, which we returned to the learned Deputy Attorney-General after our inspection, the existence of any magic wand which whipped up an ordinarily non-enterprising administration to suddenly wake up from its slumber to be galvanised into action for suddenly treating the case property as an abandoned property in late September, 1986. This leads us to conclude that the whole exercise in enlisting the case property as an abandoned property is ill-conceived, malafide and without any lawful authority.

<u>16. On consideration of the Annual Rent Receipts-Annexure-"C" series, the Burial Certificate- Annexure- "I", the Joint Survey Report -Annexure- "E" and the succession certificate granted in Case Succession Certificate Case No. 768 of 1978 in favour of the 2 sons and 2 daughters of allottee Ahmed Reza, who are the vendors of the petitioners, we are firmly of the view that there is absolutely no reason to hold and believe that allottee Ahmed Reza was not in Bangladesh when President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into existence and that his whereabouts were not known and he and after him his successors-in-interest were not possessing the case property, providing the legal basis for treating the case property as an abandoned property, The learned Court of Settlement erred in law in passing the impugned judgment without properly considering the legal effect of all these material pieces of evidence and the same has materially affected the impugned decision.</u>

17. For the reasons stated above, we are of the view that the learned Court of Settlement acted illegally and without jurisdiction in dismissing the case of the petitioners on an erroneous view of law and facts, ignoring material pieces of evidence, affecting the ultimate decision of the case and, as such, the same is liable to be set aside in the interest of justice.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost which we assess of Taka 2,000.00 (two thousand) only. The impugned judgment and order dated 29-3-92 passed by the learned Court of Settlement, First Court, Dhaka in Case No. 776 of 1987 are hereby declared to be illegal, arbitrary and without any lawful authority. We further declare that the inclusion of the case property in Holding No. 8B/B, 2nd Colony, Mirpur, Dhaka in the "Kha" list of abandoned properties, (published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 29th September, 1986), has been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

End.

full_judgment:
The first Miscellaneous Appeal under section 35(3) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 arises out of an order dated 21-10-95 passed by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 2 of 1994 affirming those dated 12-10-93 of the Deputy Administrator of Waqf, Dhaka on an application under section 50 of the said Ordinance.

2. The appellant filed an application under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance stating, inter alia, that the property described in the schedule thereto originally belonged to late Helimullah, the predecessor-in-interest of the appellant and the respondent who while in such possession and enjoyment of the suit property created a mortgage in favour of one Babu Bimala Charan Sharma by a Deed of Mortgage dated 5th Aswin, 1319 BS. The said Helimullah had 4 sons who were having independent income of their own and in order to redeem the mortgage Helimullah proposed to sell the case land at a consideration of Taka 1500.00 and they agreed to purchase the same and in pursuance thereof Taka 500 was paid as advance for redemption of the mortgage and accordingly redeemed the same. Thereafter on receipt of Taka 1000.00 on different dates Helimullah executed a sale deed on 19-11-18 corresponding to 3rd Agrahayan, 1325 BS in favour of his said 4 sons who on purchase have been possessing the same having mutated their names in the record of right. A part of the suit property devolved upon the petitioner as the heir of Ishaque Rashid, one of the recipients of the kabala who has been in possession of the suit land exclusively by way of family arrangement among the co-sharers. The respondent No.1 has filed Title Suit No.237 of 1983 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet alleging the suit land to be waqf property styling himself as the mutwalli thereof and prayed for permanent injunction against the petitioner and on receipt of the summons for the first time learnt from the disclosure in the plaint that the original owner Halimullah by a deed dated 28th Kartik, 1323 RS made a waqf in respect of the case property and that the mutwalli has got the same enrolled as EC No.13201. The said Deed of Waqf is collusive, spurious and was never acted upon by the enrolment made by the opposite party collusively. The property is not a waqf property but a personal property of the petitioner and others in whose name the case land has been recorded. Since the suit land was under an agreement for sale with the said sons, late Halimullah was not legally competent to make the waqf and the subsequent disposition in favour of his sons also goes to show that the waqf was not intended. The appellant accordingly prayed for recalling the said order of enrolment treating the property to be a waqf property. The Waqf Administrator heard the said application and dismissed the same holding that the property is a waqf property though he made certain redundant remarks directing the parties to take resort to the civil Court regarding the genuineness of the documents filed by the parties.

3. On appeal before the learned District Judge the same was heard by the learned Additional District Judge who by the impugned order has dismissed the appeal.

4. Thereafter, the appellant has preferred this appeal before this court.

5. The Civil Revision No; 250 of 1991 is also heard along with the appeal because the said Rule arises out of an application for stay of the Title Suit No.237 of 1982 till final disposal of the application filed before the Waqf Administrator which now is the subject matter of the instant first miscellaneous appeal and an order of stay of further proceeding of Title Suit No.237 of 1982 was obtained in the said Rule pending disposal thereof.

6. Mr. Fazlul Haque, learned Advocate for the appellant, has submitted that the alleged waqf deed dated 28th Kartik, 1323 BS was never acted upon as the waqif did not intend to create a waqf in respect of the suit property as he pursuant to an agreement for sale with his sons had meanwhile obtained an amount of Taka 500.00 to redeem the suit property from mortgage and disposed of the same on 19-11-1918 corresponding to 3rd Agrahayan, 1325 BS. The learned Advocate further submitted that the property since purchased by the 4 sons of Helimullah, the alleged waqif, who have been possessing the same as a secular property by mutating their names in the Khatian and as such, the suit property is not a waqf property as has been illegally found by the learned Additional District Judge, and the Waqf Administrator.

7. Mr. B K Das, learned Advocate for the respondent No.1, however, has supported the impugned order of the Waqf Administrator and the order passed by the learned Additional District Judge with reference to the finding that the property is a waqf property. The learned Advocate further submitted that the Deed of Waqf was acted upon which is apparent from the finding of the court of appeal below that the father of the appellant Ishaque Rashid has realised by way of Title Suit No.67 of 1940 the beneficial interest of the waqf property and also filed Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1959 before the Waqf Administrator which go to show that the waqf deed was acted upon. The learned Advocate further submitted that in view of the receipt of the beneficial interest by the father of the petitioner in the waqf property which has not devolved upon the petitioner upon his death, the petitioner is estopped from denying the character of waqf of the case property.

8. Mr. Fazlul Haque, learned Advocate for the appellant has, however, tried to repel the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 stating that there is nothing on record to show that the alleged suit was for beneficial interest in respect of suit property or that the alleged miscellaneous case before the Administrator of Waqf was also to that effect as no paper has been exhibited in the case inasmuch as the petitioner who is in possession of the suit property is a person contemplated under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance to claim that the property is not a waqf property and, as such, no estoppel is operating against the petitioner. The learned Advocate further submitted with reference to evidence on record that even the mutwalli's brother has sold a part of the suit property treating the same to be secular property and that the record of right has also supported his contention that the property was treated to be secular property as though the waqf was allegedly created in 1916 but the mutwali has allowed the suit property to be recorded in the names of the sons of the Waqif Helimullah as secular property.

9. On perusal of the judgment of the Waqf Administrator, it appears that the Waqf Administrator without discussing the evidence on record has arrived at a finding that:

এমতাবস্থায় নথি পর্যালোচনা এবং পক্ষগণের নিয়োজিত বিজ্ঞ কৌশলীদের যুক্তিতর্ক পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় যে ৬টা চা বাগানের শেয়ারসহ সম্ভাবনাময় ওয়াকফ এষ্টেটটির ১৩২৩ বাংলা সনে ওয়াকফ দলিল মূলে বিধি সম্মতভাবেই অত্র অফিসে তালিকাভূক্ত করা হইয়াছে এবং ইতিমধ্যে সমুদয় সম্পত্তি ওয়াকফ ভূক্ত করা হইয়াছে এবং ইতিমধ্যে সমু���য় সম্পত্তি ওয়াকফ অধ্যাদেশ ৫০ ধারামতে ওয়াকফ সম্পত্তি হিসাবে প্রমাণিত হইয়াছে।

The said finding of the Waqf Administrator was on the basis of the respective cases of the parties but was not based on any consideration or appreciation of the evidence on record.

10. The court of appeal below as well affirmed the said finding without any paper before the court regarding Title Suit No.67 of 1940 and the Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1959. But the Court of appeal below has taken exception to the finding of the Waqf Administrator regarding referring the parties to the civil Court. The Court of appeal below has not however, found the submission of the appellant that the suit property was encumbered at the time when the Waqf Deed was executed as nothing could be placed to show that there was a prior agreement for sale in respect of the waqf property or that the suit property was encumbered to the sons of the Waqif for sale of the same. The court of appeal below also arrived at a finding that even if it is established that the waqf was not acted upon by the settler himself would not detract from its validity in the least but would be only an evidence of trust on the part of the settler relying upon the Title Suit No.67 of 1940 and Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1959 (EC 13201). The Court of appeal below has, however, found that there was no evidence that the property of India was divided with Sylhet town property and repelled the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the intention is the governing factor to show whether the Waqf Deed was ever acted upon or not and concurred with the finding of the Administrator of Waqf that the suit property is the property of Helimullah Waqf Estate.

11. In the instant case certain salient features shall appear from the deposition of the parties, inter alia, that the enrolled property is a secular property, that the suit property was initially mortgaged with Babu Bimala Charan Sharma; that in order to redeem the property Helimullah entered into an agreement for sale on 17th Bhadra, 1322 BS with his sons to sell the property at a consideration of Taka 1500.00 and obtained Taka 500.00 as advance in order to redeem the suit property from Bimala Sharma and accordingly, executed a sale deed in favour of his 4sons on 3rd Agrahayan, 1325 BS corresponding to 19-11-1918 (Exhibit-2) stating the fact of the agreement in the sale deed; that the record of right (Exhibit-4) stood in the names of the sons of Helimullah and Exhibit-5 is the Mortgage Deed. The appellant deposed that nobody knew about the alleged enrolment and the said Waqf Deed was never acted upon. The property was always treated to be secular property in which the homestead of the appellant is situated. The appellant learnt about the alleged Waqf Deed from the suit being Title Suit No. 237 of 1982 for the first time. In cross examination the said witness denied that the suit property has been recorded in the name of the waqf estate but the mutwalli for his own interest got the suit property enrolled as waqf property and denied that his father Ishaque Rashid filed the suit for getting the beneficial interest from the waqf estate and also filed the miscellaneous case before the Administrator of Waqf. The said witness further deposed that Matiar Rashid and M Ali, the brothers of the mutwalli, have also disposed of certain property out of alleged waqf property and denied the suggestion that the mutwalli has filed a suit for cancellation of the sale deed. The attorney of the mutwalli Mamunur Rahman has deposed for the respondent stating that Helimulla made a waqf in respect of the suit property on 20th Kartik 1323 BS and he was the first mutwalli and subsequently his son Shamsur Rashid became mutwalli and he was the attorney of said Shamsur Rashid but on a suggestion to show any paper to that effect he declined to file any such paper. He has also stated that he does not know whether the waqf is waqf al Awlad of waqf al Lillah. He also stated that he will not file any paper regarding Title Suit No.67 of 1940 and Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1969. He also stated that he does not know whether the suit property is recorded in the Tahsil office as secular property. He also said that the quantum of waqf property is 0.252 decimals but he does not remember what is the exact quantum now though he has stated that he is acting as mutwalli of the suit property. He has denied that the suit property was mortgaged and that same was redeemed with the money of the sons of Helimullah to whom the latter subsequently sold the suit property. He also stated that the suit property was enrolled on 20th Kartik, 1323 BS but denied the same to have been enoIIed in 1956. He has further deposed that he has not filed any income or expenditure return in respect of the suit property for the last 10 years.

Section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance reads as under:

"Property or not shall be decided by the Administrator: Provided that the mutwalli or any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Administrator in this behalf may, within three months from the date of such decision or order, submit a petition to the District Judge in accordance with the provision of sub-section (1) of section 35; and if such a petition is filed, the provisions of section 35 shall apply."

In view of the said provision a petition envisaged under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance lies when a person is aggrieved by a decision or order of the Waqf Administrator.

12. In the instant case the appellant has been aggrieved by enrolment of the suit property as waqf property vide EC 13201. It is the consistent case of the petitioner-appellant, as revealed from the deposition, that the suit property was treated to be a secular property on the basis of purchase from Helimullah and the suit property was originally subject to mortgage which was redeemed upon an agreement for sale with the sons of Helimullah and in consequence thereof obtained Taka 500.00 from the said sons and redeemed the mortgage and sold the same to the sons of Helimullah on 19-11-1918 corresponding to 3rd Agrahayan, 1325 BS but meanwhile on 20th Kartik 1323 BS said Helimullah was alleged to have executed a waqf deed in respect of the suit property. The appellant has asserted that the said recipients of the Kabala possessed the suit property as secular property and the same was recorded in their names. No step was ever taken to get the same enrolled as waqf property and that the waqf deed was never acted upon as the waqif did not intend to create the waqf in respect of the suit property. Exhibit-4 which is the printed form of the record of right, shows that the suit property was recorded as a secular property in the names of the heirs of Helimullah. It may be mentioned here that the waqf deed was dated 20th Kartik. 1323 BS i.e. prior to the execution of the sale deed in favour of the sons of Helimullah. In view of the poor execution of the waqf deed and subsequent execution of a sale deed by the waqif the intention of the waqif to create a waqf was to be considered in order to determine the suit property as waqf property or not. In that view of the matter, the intention of the waqif is very material. Although the agreement for sale was not filed in this case but the sale deed dated 19-11-1918 corresponding to 3rd Agrahayan, 1325 BS was filed to show that it recited about the agreement dated 17th Bhadra 1322 BS i.e. prior to the execution of the Waqf Deed on 20th Kartik, 1323 BS. Had the waqif intended to create a waqf in respect of the suit property he would definitely not have disposed of the suit property in favour of his sons redeeming the property from mortgage by taking advance from his sons. This fact also finds support from the fact that the waqf was never enrolled with the Administrator of Waqf during his lifetime. It is in evidence that the same was enrolled in 1956 during the life of Ishaque Rashid, the father of the petitioner. Though it has been claimed by the respondent that the father of the petitioner has filed Title Suit No.67 of 1940 and Miscellaneous Case NO.16 of 1959 for beneficial interest but no paper has been filed in the case as appears from the deposition of the parties but the court of appeal below has based its decision as to the nature of the waqf property on the basis of Title Suit No. 67 of 1940 and Miscelleous Case No.16 of 1959.

13. As regards the record of right, the said attorney of the mutwalli has said that he has never enquired as to whether the suit property was recorded as secular property in the tahsil office and that he does not know the present quantum of land although the land in waqf was 0.25’2 BS decimals. Although he has said that the waqf property was enrolled in 1325 BS but from the paper it appears that it was enrolled in 1956.

<u>14. In view of the fact that the waqif himself disposed of the property after creation of the alleged waqf and that there is nothing on record to show that as per terms of the Waqf Deed he acted as mutwali during his lifetime or that he got the same enrolled as waqf or got the same mutated as waqf but treating the same as secular property and disposing of the same to his sons who are admittedly in possession of the same on mutation of their names, go to show that the waqf was not a real one and that it was never intended to be acted upon because the conduct of the settler himself at the time of transaction and also his subsequent conduct shows that the waqif himself did not intend to create the waqf in respect of the suit property and, as such, the Waqf Deed was not acted upon.</u>

<u>15. In the case referred to by the Court of appeal below reported in 37 CWN 892 (Srimati Ebratunnessa Bibi & ors vs. Debendra Nath Sen & ors) it has been held that:</u>

<u>The question in such circumstances is the question of intention. The law in this respect is well settled. The intention of the settler has to be inquired into in order to make out whether the waqf was real or not, and for the purpose of such enquiry, facts and circumstances showing for suggesting that it was never intended to be acted upon are relevant. The conduct of the settler himself at the time of the transaction, as also his subsequent conduct if it is merely in continuation of his conduct at the time and of a place with it are relevant in such an enquiry:</u>

<u>It is in evidence that even the mutwalli's brother has sold part of the suit property and that the attorney of the mutwalli has admitted that for the last 10 years there is no statement-retum of income of expenditure filed before the Administrator of Waqf in respect of the suit property and that the suit property is in possession of the co-sharers as would appear from the evidence of PW1 and the same was recorded in the names of the co-sharers as in Exhibit-4.</u>

<u>16. As regards the finding of Waqf Administrator duly affirmed by the court of appeal below that the question of various deeds filed in support and against the waqf and referring the same to the civil Court by the Waqf Administrator is also not sustainable in law in view of the fact that if the dispute as to the waqf character of the property is raised either before or at the time of enrolment or after the enrolment the jurisdiction to decide the waqf character is with Waqf Administrator. The Waqf Ordinance being a special procedure is to be followed and the cognisance of the civil Court is excluded. The aforesaid view has been expressed in the case of Syed Masud Ali &ors vs. Asmatullah & ors reported in 31 DLR (AD) 249.</u>

17. In view of the aforesaid decision, I am of the view that the Administrator of Waqf is competent to decide the various documents filed for and against the nature of the property in question and to decide once and for all under the special provision of law as to whether the property is waqf or not.

<u>18. It may be mentioned that the record of right standing in the names of the sons of the waqif as secular property though not conclusive evidence of fact but due weight is to be given attaching that they have been allowed by those who were going to be adversely affected by them to remain unaltered for such a large number of years even though they were aware of the entries in the records. The aforesaid view has been expressed in the case of Chief Administrator of Auqaf vs. Miah Ghutam Fareed & ors, reported in SCMR 1993, 643.</u>

19. In view of the above, I am of the view that the property is not a Waqf property.

20. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and order of the court of appeal below are set aside. There will, however, be no order as to costs.

Since the application under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance before the Waqf Administrator has been disposed of by this Judgment, the Rule in Civil Revision No. 250 of 1991 for stay has become infructuous and the same is, accordingly, discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 9th April, 1987, Passed by the High Court Division, in Writ Petition No. 93 of 1985.)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal J: This appeal by leave is from Judgment and Order dated 9 April, 1987, passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka, in Writ Petition No. 93 of 1985 discharging the Rule.

2. The appellants filed the aforesaid writ petition against respondents Nos. 1-4 challenging the legality of the Memo No. Da-73/84/202 Acqn. dated 28.2.85 (Annexure-M to the writ petition) issued under the signature of respondent No. 3, setting aside, inter alia, the deed of settlement (Annexure-G) dated 9.10.79 and declaring further that the property, Holding No. 7 Wiseghat, shall remain as vested property under the management and control of the Government with the present occupant as lessee/tenant until further orders. The appellants' case in the Writ petition was that they are citizens of Bangladesh having migrated from Murshidabad, India, in 1964, after exchanging their Indian property with the aforesaid premises at 7 Wiseghat Road, Lhaka, which originally belonged to one Akhanda Dumar Bose alias Ajit Kumar Bose. On his death the said property devolved on his son Proddyut Kumar Bose (Respondent No. 5). In the CS Record, it was recorded in the name of Akhanda Kumar Bose and in the SA Record in the name of his son Proddyut Kumar Bose, son of Ajit Kumar Bose. In 1950 the then Government of East Pakistan requisitioned the said property of aforesaid Proddyut Kumar Bose for accommodation of Government employees.

3. By a deed of exchange executed and registered on 28.4.64 (.1`.1inexure C) the appellants exchanged their property in Murshidabad with said Proddyut Kumar Bose for his aforesaid Wiseghat property in Dhaka, Bangladesh. On 13.2.64 Proddyut Kumar Bose executed and registered a power of attorney (Annexure D) authorising appellant No. 1, who is the brother of appellant No. 2, to execute and register a deed of exchange in respect of the said property in favour of the appellants. The said exchange power of attorney was revalidated in East Pakistan on 6.6.64.

4. On coming to the then East Pakistan, the appellants found that the said Wiseghat property under requisition was in the possession of respondent No. 4 Bulbul Lalit Kala Academy as an allottee of the Government on a monthly rental. Theappellants applied on 8.9.66 to the Relief Commissioner, Dhaka, under the provisions of the Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance 1964, for permission for execution and registration of the deed of exchange in their favour on the basis of the Power of Attorney executed by said Proddyut Kumar. But the Relief Commissioner could not grant the necessary permission as war already broke out between India and Pakistan on 6 September, 1965; the Relief Commissioner expressed his inability to do anything in the matter and asked the appellants to apply to the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, which they did on 20.1.1967, who in his turn directed them to apply to the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, respondent No. 2. Accordingly in 1972 the appellants filed a petition to respondent No. 2 for execution and registration of the deed of exchange. Respondent No. 2 by Memo No. 419 XVII-318/73 Exchange dated 13.8.73 (Annexure E) sent the petition of the appellants to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Dhaka, for taking necessary action in the matter.

5. While the matter was pending consideration by the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka, Memo No. 5177(18) VP 497 dated 29.11.77 (Annexure F) was circulated by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms on the subject of exchange of migrants' immovable property with bonafide Muslim refugees/expellees from India authorising the ADC (Rev.) on behalf of the Government to execute and register the deed of conveyance. Accordingly the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka, after consultation with the Government Pleader, Dhaka, executed on 10.9.79 a deed of settlement in respect of the said Wiseghat property in favour of the appellants which was registered on 20.10.79. The appellants mutated their names in the revenue records on 17.6.84 and paid rent to the Government (Annexures H and I).

6. In April, 1984, the appellants applied to the ADC (LA) Dhaka for de-requisition and restoration of possession of the said property. At that time Mr. Amanullah Chowdhury. Secretary, Bulbul Lalit Kala Academy, filed a petition on 28.2.84 (Annexure J) to the same office challenging the appellants' deed of settlement (Annexure G). A notice dated 2.5.84 (Annexure K) was issued to the constituted Attorney of the appellants for a hearing on the matter by the ADC (LA) on 17.5.84. A hearing took place on that day and the appellants' advocate produced all the papers and also filed an application (Annexure-L) o the same date.

7. The appellants, however, to their surprise received the memo dated 28.2.85 (Annexure M) by which the Government set aside the order passed by the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka on 9.10.79 in Exchange Case No. 21/77-78 and the order dated 17.6.84 passed in Misc. Case No. 25/84. It meant that the deed of settlement in favour of the appellants and the order mutating their names in respect of the property in question were set a side. This order dated 28.2.85 had been impugned in the writ petition.

8. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in their affidavit-in-opposition denied that Akhanda Kumar Bose was also called by the other name i.e. Ajit Kumar Bose. It was stated that the disputed property was requisitioned in 1974 for the accommodation of Intelligence Branch Office and, thereafter, it was allotted in favour of respondent No. 4 in 1955 on a monthly rent of Tk. 300/-. Proddyut Kumar Bose filed a written objection on 7.4.80 to the ADC (Rev.), Dhaka, challenging the genuineness of the deed of exchange (Annexure C) and denying the execution thereof. It was stated that on consideration of the petition dated 9.12.84 filed by respondent No. 4 to the President and Chief Martial Law Administrator and the petition filed by the appellants on 10.10.84, the respondents set aside the order of settlement of the disputed property by the impugned order on the grounds mentioned therein which will speak for itself.

9. In their affidavit-in-reply the appellants, inter alia, stated that Proddyut Kumar Bose did not pursue his objection and it was ultimately rejected on 28.3.83 for non-prosecution.

10. Respondent No. 4 also filed an affidavit-in-opposition alleging mainly that the disputed property was a Debottar Property, that the name of Akhanda Kumar Bose was recorded as Shebayet in the C.S. Khatian, that on his death his son Proddyut Kumar Bose continued as the Shebayet (trustee), that he is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and has been living here, that the alleged deed of exchange and the power of attorney purported to have been executed by Proddyut Kumar Bose were fraudulent and not genuine and that the deed of Settlement in favour of the appellants was rightly set aside.

11. The appellants by filing affidavit-in-reply denied the assertions made by respondent No. 4 and annexed an affidavit dated 13.10.80 by Proddyut Kumar Bose in which he admitted the genuineness of the Power of Attorney and the exchange deed.

12. Respondent No. 5, Proddyut Kumar Bose was added as respondent in the writ petition on his application. He in his affidavit-in-opposition also stated that his father's name is Akhanda Kumar Bose and he had no alias as Ajit Kumar Bose. He denied the deed of exchange and the power of attorney said to be executed by him and maintained that the disputed property was neither an enemy property nor a vested property. On 31.1.75 he entered into an agreement with respondent No. 4 for sale of the disputed property and received Tk. 3,85,000/-. He disputed the authority of the ADC (Rev.) to grant settlement of the property in question to the appellants.

13. By filing another affidavit-in-reply, the appellants denied the assertions made by respondent No. 5.

14. On behalf of the appellants it was argued before the High Court Division that the deed of settlement having been executed by the ADC (Rev.), Dhaka, in exercise of powers conferred by the Government by Memo dated 29.11.77 (Annexure F) and the said settlement having been confirmed by mutation of the name of the appellants in the records of the Government and by realising rent, the appellants acquired a vested right in the disputed property and it could not be taken away by the Government because there was no authority left in the Government to defeat the right of the appellants by retracting the steps already taken. The learned Judges, however, disagreed with the submission and referred to clause 12 of the deed of settlement which provides as follows:

"12. It shall be lawful for the lessor at any time during the period of lease to determine the lease by a written notice in case any fraud on the part of the lessee is detected or the deed of exchange is found fraudulent and the lessee shall have no right or title to the lease hold properties."

15. It was then observed that the settlement could have been determined on the above ground following the procedure laid down in aforesaid clause 12 but the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 did not act in terms of the said clause. Without expressing any opinion on the disputed facts as to whether Proddyut Kumar Bose had at all exchanged the disputed property with the appellants and executed the power of attorney in their favour as alleged, etc., the learned Judges went on to observe that the Government could not avoid a valid settlement of any vested property without following the procedure for determination of the lease provided for in the deed of settlement itself.

16. Having already and clearly found that the procedure in the instant case was not followed in terms of the said clause 12, one expected that the impugned order would be struck down on that ground. But the learned Judges went on to consider whether the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Dhaka, had the authority to grant the settlement on 9.10.79 on the assumption that the disputed property was a vested property at the time of settlement. The learned Judges, upon referring to the up-to-date legal position as to vested property and the various circulars issued by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms from time to time, took the view that the ADC (Rev.) has not been given by Memo No. 5177(18) VP 497 dated 29.11.77 (Annexure F) the power to transfer or dispose of the exchange properties (now vested in the Government) without prior clearance from the Government which is now the requirement of section 3(1)(a) of the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act 1974 (Act XLV of 1974) read with clause 4(1) of the Circular No. 1A-1/77/156 RL dated 23.5.77. Accordingly, it was held that the settlement made by the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka, on 9.10.79 in favour of the appellants was without Jurisdiction and void ab initio. Upon such view of the matter the learned Judges found no reason to interfere with the impugned Order and the Rule was accordingly discharged.

17. Leave was granted to consider whether the aforesaid view taken by the High Court Division was legally correct or not.

18. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Counsel for the appellants, submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court Division fell into an error in not keeping in view the historical background that the disputed property was not an usual vested property simpliciter but it was subject to an agreement for exchange which took place long before the property became enemy or vested property under the law and that the Government, since 1968, have been dealing with these cases by issuing necessary instructions for regularising such cases of exchange of migrants' immovable property with bonafide Muslim refugees/expellees from India. The learned Counsel has referred to various circulars on the subject beginning from No. 1578 Gnl. dated 15.11.68 till date which are to be found in Chapter IX under the heading "Exchange Case" of the Land Administration Manual, published by Land Administration Board (Ministry of Land) on 1st. December, 1987. Relying upon the said circulars particularly the one dated 29.11.77 (Annexure-F), in terms of which the deed of settlement was executed, Mr. Huq submitted that the ADC was perfectly competent to transfer the property and execute the necessary document on behalf of the Government. Mr. Huq also submitted that even if prior approval of the Government was necessary, as held by the High Court Division, the same must be presumed in the present case inasmuch as it was the Government to whom the appellants had applied and the Government sent the case to the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka, for taking necessary action in the matter by its Memo dated 13.8.73 (Annexure E). The learned Counsel further submitted that the deed of settlement having been executed by a competent officer of the Government under its authority and the same having been acted upon by acceptance of rent and mutation of the appellants' name in the revenue record, the Government could no longer take the plea that its officer had acted without its authority. In support of his submission, he cited 1984 All England Law Reports (Vol. II) 767; 27 DLR 315 and PLD 1969 (SC) 407.

19. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for respondents Nos. 1, 2 and 3 supported the view taken by the High Court Division. The learned Counsel for respondents 4 and 5 while supporting the impugned Government order and the decision of the High Court Division, contended that the alleged deed of exchange and power of attorney were all false and fraudulent documents as Proddyut Kumar Bose had all along been living in the then East Pakistan and then in Bangladesh and continuing as the owner of the disputed property.

20. It may be observed that from the position taken by respondent Nos. 4 and 5 before the authorities and in this proceeding it follows that the property in question did not vest in the Governor at any time either as enemy or vested propert because Proddyut Kumar Bose, according to them, had been living in this country all along. The question whether the property is a vested property or not has not been an issue in this proceeding and we must proceed on the assumption that the property is a vested property (and claimed by the appellants as exchange property) as will appear from the impugned order of the Government itself (Anncxure M). Respondent Nos. 4 and 5, it is significant, have not raised any objection to this order nor do they object to the findings made by the High Court Division.

21. From the facts of the case as disclosed in the affidavits and annexures of the parties filed before the High Court Division, it appears apparently that Proddyut Kumar Bose, respondent No. 5, is a double-dealer, sometimes sailing with the appellants and sometimes with respondent No. 4 according to his own convenience. We shall see and say something more later on, but we should not be understood to have made any comment with regard to the genuineness or otherwise of the documents of the appellants or as to the claims made by the contending parties other than the Government. The High Court Division rightly refrained from making any findings of fact on contentious matters and proceeded to enquire only the legality of the order impugned.

22. The respondents have not disputed before us the findings made by the High Court Division that the Government without following the procedure as laid down in clause 12 of the deed of settlement had cancelled the same which it could not do. The High Court Division, however, refused to interfere with the impugned order holding that the deed of settlement was itself unauthorised because the ADC (Rev.) had not taken prior approval of the Government before executing the deed. We shall confine ourselves to the examination of this proposition upon which the High Court Division refused to interfere in the matter.

23. The exposition of the law relating to enemy and then vested property as given in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is correct and no exception can be taken to the same. The Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act 1974 (Act XLV of 1974)on being amended by the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) (Amendment) Ordinance 1976 (Ordinance No. XCIII of 1976) by the relevant clause of section 3 provides that all enemy property vested in the custodian of enemy property appointed under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules and continued in force by the Ordinance (1 of 1969) shall vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of by transfer or otherwise by the government or by such officer or authority as the Government may direct. Circular dated 23rd May, 1977 (Page 554 of the Manual), of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms Division containing instruction for administration, management and disposal of vested property by clause 4(1), provides that the ADC(Rev.) may, with the previous approval of the Government transfer or otherwise dispose of any vested property either by himself or through the Sub-divisional Officer in whose jurisdiction the property is situated. These are the provisions upon which the High Court Division put reliance.

24. It will be seea that from long time before, the problem of regularisation of genuine exchanges of immovable properties made by the refugees/ expellees from India with those of Hindu migrants from the then East Pakistan engaged the attention of the Government and instructions were being given from time to time to subordinate agencies in that behalf with the change of legal position due to supervening circumstances affecting such property.

25. In the present case the Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964, was in force when the alleged exchange took place between the appellants and respondent No. 5 The appellants applied to the Relief Commissioner under section 6 of the said ordinance for permission to execute the necessary document of title in respect of the property. But before anything was done, following outbreak of war between India and Pakistan, the character of the property changed and it became enemy property upon promulgation of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules. The then Government of East Pakistan by its memo dated 15 November, 1968 (page 610 of the Manual), considered the question of regularising the possession of the Muslim refugees and expellees from India on the immovable properties of Hindu migrants taken in exchange for their Indian properties without proper or legally enforceable documents of title. It provided that only the case of exchange prior to 6th. September, 1965, should be considered for regularisation. All cases of exchange made before that date were to be divided into two categories. The appellants case falls in the first category and was to be dealt with by the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Land and Buildings). The Deputy Custodian was to give effect to the exchange by executing necessary deed of transfer in favour of the refugees/expellees concerned on behalf of the migrant if he found the case of exchange to be genuine. Government Memo dated 29.11.73 (page 617 of the Manual) referred to the instructions contained in the Memo dated 15th November, 1968 and 23.12.69 and went on to say that in both the categories the Deputy Commissioner was to receive application for regularisation of exchanges. In the first category of cases (in which the appellants' case falls) when the Deputy Commissioner was satisfied about the genuineness of the exchange, he would furnish a certificate to that effect and the Assistant Custodian (L & B) would, on the basis of such certificate of genuineness, give effect to the exchange by execution of necessary deed of transfer in favour of the refugee/expellee concerned on behalf of the migrant. It provided that in either case no consideration money other than annual land revenue should be charged for such transfer or settlement. A power of review wits also given to the Deputy Commissioner which is not relevant for our present purpose. Another Memo dated 30.7.87 (at page 625 of the Manual) shows that the Government once decided that the regularisation of exchange cases should be referred to the Civil Court but by the said Memo again entrusted the power of registration to the Deputy Commissioners and Additional Deputy Commissioners (Rev.). In the same line another Memo dated 29.11.77 (Annexure-F) was issued which is very important for the present purpose and on the basis of which the deed of settlement was executed by the ADC(Rev.). It will be seen that while issuing the said Memo the government was well aware of Act XLV of 1974 and the earlier instructions issued by the Government in respect of exchange cases of which the property subsequently became vested in the Government. It provided that all cases of exchange made before 6.9.65 would now form a single category and since the properties have already vested in the government, there is also no question of execution and registration of a sale deed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner on behalf of the migrant Hindu. Such deed should be executed and registered on behalf of the Government by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.).

26. Reading all these circulars together and keeping in view the Government policy in respect of regularisation of the exchange cases taking place prior to the war of 1965, it is found that these cases formed a class by themselves and the property involved in such cases could not be equated with any other ordinary vested property. The instructions of the Government in respect of such property were always specific and indeed they have been separately treated and put in Chapter IX of the Land Administration Manual under the heading "Exchange Cases". The Memo dated 23rd May, 1977, upon which the High Court Division relied will be found in Chapter VIII of the Manual under the heading 'management of the vested property'. In determining the validity of the deed of settlement in the present case, therefore, all the circulars beginning from 15.11.68 relating to Exchange cases are relevant and it could not be said in view of Annexure F in particular that the ADC (Rev.) in the absence of prior approval as required under circular dated 23rd May, 1977, had no authority to execute the document in question on behalf of the Government.

27. On a reference to the impugned order dated 28.2.85 (Annexure M) which set aside the settlement made by the ADC on 10.9.79, the following grounds are found in support of the order:

"i) The property was not exchanged by the real and recorded owner.

ii) DC or ADC had no authority to entertain any prayer for regularisation of exchange case after 30.9.70 vide GO No. 879(19) Genl. dated 1.7.70.

iii) No reason or ground was given by the exchanger Mozaffar Ali and others as to why they applied to ADC on 1.4.78 i.e. after 18 years, when they had claimed that their property in India was exchanged and given by registered deed to Ajit Kumar Bose on 13.2.64.

iv) GO No. 5177 (18) 7/497/77 dated 29.11.77 did not give the ADC (Rev.) any authority to register any property on the basis exchange deed as the said property had, by that time, vested in the Government as vested property."

28. The High Court Division in its judgment by its finding as to failure of the Government to follow clause 12 of the deed of settlement impliedly negatived ground Nos. 1 and III above. As to ground No. II, the High Court Division observed that it was absolutely preposterous to claim that by circular dated 1.7.70. the Deputy Commissioners or the Additional Deputy Commissioners ceased to have any authority to entertain any prayer for regularisation of exchange cases after 30.9.70 and this was a sheer misreading of the circular dated 1.7.70 on the part of the Government respondents. It has already been pointed out that the respondents have not objected to the said findings. As to ground No. IV, we need only point out that the Memo dated 29.11.77 was not properly perceived by the authority which passed the impugned order dated 28.2.85. In the said Memo nowhere it has been said that the ADC will not have any authority to register any property because it became vested in the Government. On the other hand, the said memo shows that the Government being quite cognizant of the fact that the relevant properties have become vested in the Government under the Vested Property Laws, authorised the ADC's to execute and register the necessary document on behalf of the Government. Therefore, it is clear that none of the grounds enumerated in the impugned order of the Government is capable of sustaining the said order.

<u>29. Upon a close scrutiny of the matter it is found that the alleged absence of prior approval of the Government cannot be pressed into service for invalidating the order of settlement. The Government itself does not say, it is pertinent to observe, that the settlement was bad because the ADC did not take its prior approval. The High Court Division, therefore, was not justified in supplying a ground which never occurred to the Government. It has been noticed that under the provisions of section 3 of Act XLV of 1974, a vested property can be transferred by the Government or by such officer or authority as the Government may direct. In the present case it is clear from Annexure E that it is the Government which directed the ADC (Rev.) to take necessary action in the matter. The Memo dated 13.8.73 read with Annexure F along with all other circulars on this subject leave no room for doubt that the ADC (Rev.) was properly and duly authorised under the law by the Government to execute and register the deed of settlement on behalf of the Government. Therefore, the alleged absence of prior approval of the Government seems to be absent in the present case in any case.</u>

30. It falls to be observed that in cases of dispute over execution of document in Exchange cases the Government in its memo dated 29.11.73 provided that if anybody was aggrieved by any order of the Deputy Commissioner, he could go to the Civil Court for redress. The memo dated 23.11.85 (page 623) also says that there is no bar for going to the Civil Court for declaration and establishment of title on the basis of exchange, agreement or other claim. It is pertinent to observe that Proddyut Kumar Bose admittedly filed an application before the ADC (Rev.) for cancellation of the document on 7.4.80.
