He in his affidavit-in- opposition said that he entered into an agreement for sale of the property in question to Bulbul Academy of Fine Arts on 31.1.75 for consideration and had received Tk. 3,85,000/- more out of the fixed price after the bainapatra was executed. It is interesting, however, that he gave his address as resident of Nandalal Dutta Lane, Dhaka, at present of 7, Wiseghat, Dhaka. Be that as it may, the order sheet of the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka, in Exchange Case No. 21/77-78 (Annexure T to the affidavit-in-reply by the appellants at page 286) shows that respondent No. 4 Bulbul Lalit Kala Academy also raised objection to the deed of settlement besides respondent No. 5. From the last order dated 28.3.83 it appears that several adjournments were taken by respondent No. 5 and yet he did not finally appear at the hearing. The ADC rejected the objection petition observing that the aggrieved party may Lake shelter in the competent Civil Court, if they so desire. It does not appear that either respondent No. 4 or respondent No. 5 went to the Civil Court which would have been in consonance with the aforesaid order and the Government policy. Instead the respondent No. 4 trying to make a short circuit approached the President & CMLA consequent upon which the impugned order was passed. Respondent No. 5 seemed to have gone into hibernation since 1983 only to surface again during the proceedings in writ in 1987. Our attention has been drawn to an affidavit sworn by Pronob Kumar Bose, son of Proddyut Kumar Bose of Jorogram, Midnapur, filed by the appellants (Annexure-S at page 281-283), in which he stated that the deed of exchange was properly and legally executed by his father at Howrah in 1964, that the objection petition dated 7.4.80 was filed by his father under pressure, threat and duress and for the safety of his life and that he and his father permanently reside in India. The affidavit of Proddyut himself admitting the exchange (Annexure p, page 207-210) has already been noticed. Thus the facts disclosed in this case arc highly disputed and in the fitness of things, the parties should have been directed to the Civil Court instead of the Government taking upon itself the onerous task of resolving a complicated civil dispute after execution of the document of settlement in favour of the appellants in terms of its own policy and instructions given to its subordinate officers.

31. In view of the discussion above, it is found that the view taken by the High Court Division that the ADC could not make the transfer in question without the prior approval of the Government and as such the settlement made by him on 9.10.79 in favour of the appellants was void and without jurisdiction cannot be sustained and that it ought to have declared that the impugned Government order was passed without lawful authority.

32. In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed without any order as to cost and it is hereby declared that the order dated 28.2.85 (Annexure M) has been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 835 of 1991.
lawyer:
Md. Matiar Rahman with Md. Zakir Hossain and Quazi Aulad Hossain, Advocates ----- For the Plaintiff-Appellant. 
Md. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For Defendant-Respondent No. 2
parties:
Hosne Ara Begum   ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Government of Peoples Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and another ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque, J.: This First Appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed in Money Suit No. 9 of 1985 by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka, dismissing the suit.

2. Plaintiff is the appellant before this Court. Plaintiff claims right and title over the suit property by purchase. We need not go into the detailed discussions in respect of right and title of the plaintiff in view of the fact that the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 222 of 1976 and in that title suit she got a decree and it was declared that the suit property cannot be treated and declared as an enemy property, It is also on record that in the year 1969 the property in question was treated as enemy/vested property by the Vested Property Authority who leased out the same to different lessees. Ultimately the matter came before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court where the defendants, namely, the Government and the Vested Property Authority lost the case and the decree obtained by the plaintiff in the Title Suit was maintained. This matter has also been discussed by the trial Court in this suit and the trial Court found that it was not required for it to consider the question of title, since the matter went up to the highest Court of the country which settled it once and for all.

3. This is a suit for realisation of money on account of damage, compensation and mesne profits. In paragraph 16 of the plaint it is asserted by the plaintiff that out of 65 rooms of the two two-storied buildings total monthly rent will come to Tk. 20,000.00 per month. For compensation and mesne profits it will come to Tk. 21,60,000.00 from 2.3.77 to 2.3.85. The compensation and mesne profits for the vacant portion of the suit land measuring about 1 bigha and I katha will come to Tk. 42.00,000.00 @ Tk. 2 lakh per katha since the land had been trespassed and occupied after the same was taken over by the Government treating the same as enemy/vested property.

After giving calculation in the aforesaid paragraph the plaintiff prayed for a decree for a sum of Tk. 83,61,000.00 with a prayer that till the property is not released in her favour she will be entitled to monthly rent at rate of Tk. 20,000.00.

4. The defendant appeared and contested the suit by filing written statements contending inter alia that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the claims made in the plaint are absolutely incorrect and absurd and the plaintiff is not entitled to such damages as prayed for. It is their further case that assessments of compensation, damage and mesne profits as shown in the plaint are all imaginary and there is no basis at all for such claims inasmuch as no inquiry was made no survey was held and there is no evidence as to the damage and compensation as claimed by the plaintiff. The plaintiff examined one witness whereas the defendants examined two witnesses. The plaintiff also submitted some documents and papers which have been duly marked as exhibits in the suit. On the aforesaid pleadings of the parties the trial Court framed four issues which were heard and disposed of together. After considering the matter the learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiff failed to prove her own case as to the damage and compensation and as such the suit was dismissed by the impugned judgment. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment, the appellant preferred this appeal before this court.

5. The plaintiff examined herself as sole PW in this case. In her deposition she has stated the entire plaint case. She stated that in the disputed property there are 65 rooms the rent of which will be Tk. 20,000.00 per month at least her own house is situated near the suit property. Her house and her father's house are also there. Comparing with those houses she stated that since there are 65 rooms in the two buildings the minimum rent shall be Tk. 20,000.00 per month. Regarding other damages' and compensation for mesne profits of the vacant land no other documents have been produced excepting the statement made in the plaint. There was cross-examination of PW 1 which in our view is not necessary at all for our consideration.

6. The defendants examined one Madan Mohan Shah as DW 1. He stated that since 1960 he was there as tenant of the previous owner and in the year 1969 by virtue of VP Case No. 9 of 1969 the property was entitled and was enlisted and taken over as enemy/vested property and since then he was there as lesseee of the Vested Property Authority and had been paying rent to the Government. He has stated in his evidence that he is one of the previous tenants and afterward he became the tenant of the Vested Property Authority and it was taken over as vested property in 1969.

7. One Syed Fazlul Hoque who was Assistant Superintendent of Vested Property Authority office deposed as PW 2. He also stated that this property was taken over by the Government as vested property by VP Case No. 9 of 1969 and the Government gave possession to the lease holders and Government was realising rent from the lessees. This evidence is also with regard to the fact that the property was taken over in 1969 as enemy/vested property.

8. As regards documentary evidence it appears that the plaintiff submitted so many documents in order to prove her case. Exts 1 (Ka) are the two registered kabalas in favor of the plaintiff Exts 2 to 4 (jha) are all the certified copies of different orders of different courts including High Court Division and Appellate Division which show that this matter went up to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court with regard La the declaration of enemy property and ultimately the highest court of the country upheld the judgment and decree to the effect that this is not an enemy property. Ext. 5 is a letter dated 14.11.83 issued from the office of the Chief Martial Law Administrator by which the Martial Law Authority directed the Deputy Commissioner to take appropriate legal action in this matter in view of the fact that the plaintiff acquired title through the court upon the suit property Exts. 6 to 6(g) are the SA parcha of the suit property in which the name of the plaintiff was recorded. Ext. 7 is a letter issued from the Dhaka Pourashava. Ext. 8 is the letter vide office Memo No. 1106 (En.) VP. Ext. 8 (Ka) to 8 (cha) all are the letters to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka. From the side of the defendants some papers were filed before the Court which were marked as exhibits. Ext. A is the certified copy of the deed of gift executed by Sree Kallasha Chandra Shaha in favour of Sree Shontasha Kumar Shaha and another. Ext. B is the certified copy of the decree in Title Suit No. 32 of 1959 in the court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. Ext. C is the allotment letter of Memo No. 3005(11) E.P. dated 3.10.69. These are more or less-oral as well as documentary evidence as adduced by the parties.

9. We have stated above that the present suit has been filed claiming some damage, compensation and mesne profits over the suit property, It is the case of the plaintiff that she got a decree on 7.3.77 and filed that present suit on 6.3.85 So, at the rate of Tk. 20,000.00 per month she is claiming the compensation in the form of rent amounting to Tk. 21,60,000.00. In paragraph 16 of plaint it is asserted that for 65 rooms in the two suits buildings minimum monthly rent will come to Taka 20,000.00. That means the plaintiff is claiming compensation in the form of monthly rent of the 65 rooms of the two buildings. Now let us see what evidence the plaintiff has led before the Court in support of such claim. This assertion is made in paragraph 16 of the plaint. The plaintiff examined hereself as PW 1. In her deposition she also stated that monthly rent for the 65 rooms will be at least Tk. 20,000.00 and comparing the other neighboring buildings she made an assessment of rent of the disputed buildings. It is admitted position that the Government took over the suit property in the year 1969 as enemy/vested property and the Government leased out the same to the different lessees who paid rent to the Government from 1969. Mr. Shahidul Alam Chowdhury the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant respondent No. 2, very fairly submits that the defendant-respondent cannot challenge the right and title of the suit property in view of the fact that the matter went upto the Appellate Division and it was finally decided. So, in this Money Suit it is difficult for the defendant-respondents to challenge the right over the suit property. Further, it appears from the record that the plaintiff obtained decree in the year 1977 and the defendant-respondents went upto the Appellate Division but were unsuccessful. But they did not issue any release order of the suit property from the list of enemy/vested property list in favour of the plaintiff, though the plaintiff’s right and title had been accepted upto the highest court of the country. The learned Advocate further submits that he could not produce any paper to show before this court that the defendant-respondent had issued any order or letter releasing or dropping the suit property from the list of enemy/vested property which means till today the defendant-respondents have been possessing the suit property. Since the decree was obtained by the plaintiff in 1977 and since the defendant-respondents were unsuccessful even in the highest court of the country they ought to have issued a release order in favour of the plaintiff. So, we are of the view that the plaintiff is entitled to get compensation in the form of rent on the disputed property.

10. It is in the plaint that the two suit buildings are very old and dilapidated. It is totally unfit for human habitation. Plaintiff also got a plan passed from DIT for demolishing the two buildings and for reconstruction of new buildings there, Since it was admitted by the plaintiff that the suit properties are old and dilapidated and it was unfit for human habitation and for that reason she required to demolish it, we may consider the quantum of rent of the 65 rooms at this stage. In pursuance of the assertions and evidence as adduced by the plaintiffs in this suit, there are 65 rooms and they claimed rent of Tk. 20,000.00 per month which means on average the rent will come to Tk. 307.00 per room. Relying upon the assertion of the plaintiff to the effect that the buildings are very old and really unfit for human habitation we are of the view that the rent at best can be assessed at Tk. 100 per mom per month and in that way the monthly rent would come to Tk. 6,500.00 and yearly rent would come to Tk. 78,000.00. So we hold that the plaintiff is entitled to have compensation in the form of rent in the above way from the defendant-respondents for three years prior to filing of the suit. Three years rent in the form of above assessment would come to Tk. 2,34.000.00 which the plaintiff is entitled to in this "suit from the defendants. As the defendant-respondents have not yet released the property in favour of the plaintiffs the plaintiff will be entitled to get the compensation in the above manner from the defendant-respondents till the property is released in favour of the plaintiff.

<u>11. In this connection a question may arise as to whether in such a suit it is necessary to claim recovery of possession Mr. Matiar Rahman the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the defendant-respondents are not trespassers; rather by operation of law they treated the property as enemy/vested property. Now the Court declared that it is not enemy/vested property and as a result the defendant-respondents ought to have released the property in favour of the plaintiff deleting it from the list of enemy/vested property long ago. In a case like this a prayer for recovery of possession is not necessary. In support of his contention Mr. Matiar Rahman has referred to the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Basharatullah, 40 DLR 554. We are also of the view that since the defendant-respondents are not trespassers and since it was taken over as enemy/vested property under certain law and since the Court found right and title in favour of the plaintiff, it was required for the defendant-respondents to deliver possession of the suit property to the plaintiff in pursuance of the judgment of the Court. As the defendant-respondents failed to deliver possession of the suit property to the plaintiff, the plaintiff is entitled to the rent as we have stated above till the delivery of the property to the plaintiff by the defendant-respondents.</u>

12. The plaintiff also claimed Tk. 42 lakh for the vacant land measuring about 21 kathas @ Tk. 2 lakh per katha. It is her case that after the property was taken over as enemy property some tresspassers occupied the vacant portion of the premises measuring about 21 kathas and since it is not possible for the plaintiff to recover that portion o. the premises from lands of the trespassers and since it was due to the negligence of the defendant-respondents, she is entitled to claim such compensation. It is difficult to accept such contentions of the learned Advocate for the appellant. Such a claim, as we find from the record, is without any basis and material evidence on record. There is nothing on record to show that whether the tresspassers took forcible possession after it was taken over as enemy property or before it was treated as enemy property, During trial the plaintiff did not pray before the Court for a survey report by a Pleader Commissioner upon such an assertion. Had there been any pleader Commissioner and if any of the assertions of the plaintiff were examined and if any report came in favour of the plaintiff, then some argument could be advanced on the basis of that report. The plaintiff failed to get the matter surveyed or inquired through Court, rather it is an omnibus statement before the Court in one paragraph of the plaint and in such a situation it is difficult to accept such an assertion of the plaintiff for compensation at a sum of Tk. 42 lakhs with respect to the vacant place of the premises. We are of the view that the plaintiff has failed to establish such a claim for compensation for the vacant land of the premises at a sum of Tk. 42 lakhs. For the damages also the plaintiff claimed a sum of Tk. 20 lakhs in the plaint. But, unfortunately, that was also not inquired into or assessed in any manner whatsoever before or during pendency of the suit. On the self-same ground as we refused the prayer for compensation for the vacant land of the premises, we also cannot entertain such a claim of Tk. 20 lakhs in view of the fact that there is no evidence on record to show that during the period from taking the suit property as enemy/vested property till the filing of the suit the defendant- respondents caused willful damage to the property for a sum of Tk. 20 lakhs. We are not at all satisfied with the evidence as adduced in this case with respect to the above claim of the 20 lakhs made by the plaintiff.

13. Before parting with the case we may observe that since the plaintiffs right and title have been settled by the highest Court of the country and since the defendant-respondents being responsible officers of the Government have been managing and possessing the suit property since 1969 and since the decree was obtained by the plaintiff in the year 1977, it is desirable that the officers of the Government should take proper steps for releasing the property in favour of the plaintiff immediately inasmuch as it is no more an enemy property in the eye of law and the defendant-respondents have no lawful authority to keep possession of the suit property anymore. In this connection we may refer to Ext. 5 which has been produced by the plaintiff. In the year 1983 the plaintiff made a representation to the Chief Martial Law Administrator for releasing the suit property stating the entire fact of getting a decree from the Court over the suit property. In pursuance of such representation the office of the Chief Martial Law Administrator wrote to the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, by a letter dated 14.11.83 to the effect that after perusal of the certified copy of the court's judgment it appears that the applicant, namely, the plaintiff had been declared as absolute owner of the property and the premises in question are not enemy property. So, the Deputy Commissioner was requested to look into the matter and make necessary order as per law immediately under intimation to the Secretary of the Chief Martial Law Administrator. Though this letter was issued on 14th November, 1983, it appears that the Deputy Commissioner did not take any step whatsoever for taking further steps in view of the fact that it is not an enemy property which was accepted even by the Chief Martial Law Administrator's office at the relevant time. We may observe that the order from the office of the Chief Martial Law Administrator was binding upon all the authorities subordinate to the Chief Martial Law Administrator. Be that as it may, we express our view that since the highest Court of the country accepted the decree to the effect that the suit property is not an enemy/vested property, the authorities concerned must release the same in favour of the plaintiff who has been declared as legal owner by the court. Considering the above facts and circumstances and the material evidence on record, we are of the view that the plaintiff in this suit is entitled to a part decree only.

14. In the result, this appeal is allowed in part and the suit is decreed in part for an amount of Tk. 2,34,000.00 (two lakh thirty four thousand) in pursuance of our findings above with regard to the rent of the premises in question and in the similar way thereafter at the rate of Tk. 6500.00 per month upto the delivery of the possession of the suit property to the plaintiff. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we pass no order as to costs.

Send down the LC records immediately.

End.

lawyer:
MI Farooqui with M Saleemullah, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
Mashuque Hossain Ahmed, AAG ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Bakth Bibi ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani, J.: This application under Article 102 of the Constitution is directed against the judgment and order dated 7.3.89 passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 1022 of 1987. The case was filed by the petitioner Bakht Bibi for the release of a three storied building at 93 Chatteswary Road, Chittagong, from the list of the abandoned property declared abandoned and taken possession by the Government under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. By the impugned judgment and order the Court of Settlement dismissed the case.

2. Facts as found from the evidence given in the Court of Settlement are as follows:

In 1955 the petitioner came to Chittagong with her father from Afghanistan without passport. In 1961 she was married to Abdul Khaleq another national of Afghanistan residing at Chittagong and in time out of this wed-lock she gave birth to five children—two sons and three daughters. The said house property is known as Kabliwala Building which was constructed by her husband on the land purchased partly in the name of her husband and partly in her name by two registered sale deeds respectively dated 19.12.58 and 1.6.67. During the war of liberation her husband died. Thereafter she left this country for Afghanistan with her daughters leaving at Chittagong her two minor sons in the house of her maternal uncle Chunnu Mia a Peon in the local Custom Office. Subsequently in 1981 she came back to Chittagong with Afghanistani passport and made representations to the authority concerned for the release of her said house property; but in vain. Ultimately she filed the aforesaid case before the Court of Settlement stating that she being a national of Afghanistan, her said property did not come under the category of the abandoned property as defined in President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

3. The Government contested the case alleging that the petitioner was an imposter and not the widow of late Abdul Khaleqe. Both Abdul Khaleq and the petitioner were nationals of Pakistan. As the house property in question was left uncared for and the whereabouts of Abdul Khaleq was unknown to the Government, the same was rightly declared as abandoned property and was taken under the control and management of the Government.

4. Heard the learned advocates and perused the impugned judgment and order. It appears that the Court of Settlement dismissed the case on various grounds. We now propose to discuss and consider those grounds.

5. First ground, in the language of the Court of Settlement "It cannot be believed at all that the petitioner No. 1 Mrs. Bakth Bibi would leave for Afghanistan via India during the liberation war in 1971 leaving her sons, when according to her evidence, her two sons Md. Nadir and Md. Amanullah were minors" is not sustainable as being based on surmises and conjectures and also has been passed in ignorance of the evidence on record. It is not denied that before the war of liberation the petitioner had been living in Chittagong. From the passport issued to her by the Government of Afghanistan, photo copy whereof marked as annexure "E" we find that she was definitely at Kabul on 11.3.81 when the passport was granted to her at Kabul and thereafter, it is not denied, she came to Bangladesh in 1981.

6. The second ground, in the language of the Court of Settlement, "the case holding cannot be identified at all with reference to the alleged purchase deeds of Abdul Khaleq and Bakth Bibi noted above, showing their right and interest in the case holding" is also not sustainable. This ground, a third case, was invented by the Court of Settlement. The Government did neither challenge the indentity of the property in question vis-a-vis the sale deeds—nor the title of Abdul Khaleq or Bakht Bibi to the property in question. The case of the Government is that the petitioner was not the wife of Abdul Khaleq and as such she did not inherit the same. The Government, however, failed to challenge the claim of the petitioner that a portion of the land was purchased in her name and the Court of Settlement equally failed to notice this unchallenged fact.

7. Third ground, also in the language of the Court of Settlement, "the photo copy of passport was issued on 18.12.85 from the Embassy of Afghanistan in Dhaka valid upto 17.12.87 and there is nothing on record to show that she came in this country before that time" is an amazing and unfortunate finding. This finding is absolutely based on misreading of the evidence namely, the photo copy of the passport produced by the petitioner. We find from it that the passport was issued at Kabul in favour of the petitioner on 11.3.81, that the Indian as well as the Pakistani Embassy at Kabul granted transit visa to the petitioner on 4.5.81 and 11.5.81 respectively and that the Embassy of Bangladesh at Kabul granted entry visa to the petitioner on 7.5.81 and that subsequently the Embassy of Afghanistan at Dhaka on 10.3.82 extended the validity of the passport till 10.3.85. It is, thus, obvious that the Court of Settlement took this date though wrongly as the date of issuance of the passport.

8. Fourth ground, to quote from the impugned judgment, "it is very curious that petitioner claims the case holding by way of alleged purchase as per sale deed dated 6.5.67 noted above and at the same breath she has made her two sons Md. Nadir and Md. Amanullah petitioners in this case holding claiming interest in the case holding, but it is contradictory as two sons has no locus standi so long as the petitioner No. 1 is alive"-is also not sustainable. As already stated the land on which the building in question stands was purchased by two sale deeds, one in the name of the petitioner and the other in the name of Abdul Khaleque and as such petitioner's two sons also inherited a portion of the said property after the death of their father Abdul Khaleque.

9. The fifth ground, to quote, "It cannot be held that Abdul Khaleque is now dead. It is all the more curious that the petitioner in her petition dated 13.4.85 addressed to DC Chittagong, does not assert as to the death of her alleged husband Abdul Khaleque in 1971" is not sustainable. While deposing before the Court of Settlement the petitioner stated in her cross-examination that she had filed the death certificate of her father and husband but she was not further cross-examine challenging the genuineness of these certificates. The fifth ground that the petitioner is a Pakistan national according to her own showing in her alleged Kabala dated 5.6.67 is a queer finding of the Court of Settlement. In 1967 if the petitioner described herself as a Pakistani that does not mean that she remained a Pakistani for all time to come. Such a causal description of the citizenship of the purchaser in the sale deed written by a deed-writer cannot be basis for determining the citizenship of the purchaser. Moreover, the conduct of her husband indicates otherwise. We find from the record that as early as in 1963 her husband Abdul Khaleque applied for the citizenship of Pakistan but his prayer was rejected holding that he was still an Afghan national. Apart from that, the petitioner is a national of Afghanistan in view of the passport issued by the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan and this fact was not denied by the respondent Government.

10. The next ground is that the petitioner was not legally married to late Abdul Khaleque. This finding is also contrary to the unchallenged evidence on record. The petitioner appeared before the Court of Settlement and deposed that she was married to Abdul Khaleque in June, 1961, that the original Kabinnama was burnt and that she had filed the certified copy of the Kabinnama.

11. Last ground is that since admittedly the petitioner left Bangladesh before the war of liberation, leaving the property uncared for and her where about was unknown, the property was rightly declared as abandoned property. This finding is also erroneous. According to Article 2(1) of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 for the purpose of this Writ Petition, abandoned property means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, "including" any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh, but does not include" any property the owner of which is residing outside of Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh".

12. We hold that the petitioner is not a citizen of Pakistan but is a citizen of Afghanistan which was not at war with Bangladesh and as such her property cannot come under the category of "including" and her property comes under the category of "does not include" as the Government does not say that the purpose of her residing outside Bangladesh was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh.

13. Thus we come to the conclusion that none of the grounds upon which the Court of Settlement dismissed the petitioner's case is sustainable.

14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. It is declared that the judgment and order dated 7.3.89 being annexure 'J' to this writ petition passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 1022 of 1987 are declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and be of no legal effect. It is ordered that the house property at 93 Chatteswari, Chittagong, be excluded from the list of abandoned property and its vacant possession be given to the petitioner within three months from date.

There will be no order as to costs.

Naimuddin Ahmed, J.: I agree with the findings of my learned brother Mohammad Gholam Rabbani, J. to the effect that the disputed house in question originally belonged to Abdul Khaleque Khan and that Abdul Khaleque Khan died during the disturbances that took place in 1971 leaving the petitioner as his heir; that the petitioner left Bangladesh sometime after 25th day of March, 1971 and went away to Afghanistan; that the petitioner is a national of Afghanistan and that she came to this country after obtaining a passport from the Government of Afghanistan and also other travel documents from the Government of Bangladesh, for the reasons stated by my learned brother in his judgment.

17. It is an undisputed fact that after coming into force of President's Order No. 16 of 1972  i.e. the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 the Government treated this property as abandoned property as defined in Article of the said President's Order and took over possession of the property by applying section 7 of the said President’s Order No. 16 of 1972. It is also undisputed that this property was listed as abandoned property in the 'Ka' list by Notification in the Official Gazette on September 23, 1986 (Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary) at page No. 9762 (102) against Serial No. 84 under the provisions of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and it is also undisputed that in order to release the said property from the list of abandoned property as published vide the aforesaid notification in the gazette the petitioner filed an application in the Court of the Settlement which was registered as Case No. 1022 of 1987 and that the Court of Settlement dismissed the petition vide judgment and order dated 7.3.89 and affirmed the decision of the Government to treat this property as abandoned properly. As against the aforesaid decision of the Government to treat; the disputed house as abandoned property and the decision of the Court of Settlement affirming the aforesaid decision of the Government that the petitioner filed this Writ Petition before this court in its writ jurisdiction and obtained the present Rule. In order to ascertain whether the disputed house in question was "abandoned property" it is necessary to refer to Article 2 of the Presidents Order No. 16 of 1972, Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 which runs as follows:

"2. In this order, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context,

(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property  including.

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972), but does not include-

(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;

(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.

Explanation: "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(2) "Company" includes a banking company and insurance company;

(3) "Government" means the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(4) "Prescribed" means prescribed by the rule, order or direction made or given in pursuance of any of the provisions of this Order.

(5) "Property" means property of any kind, movable or immovable and includes any right or interest in such property and any debt or actionable claim, any security or negotiable instrument, any right under a contract and any industrial or commercial undertaking;

Explanation-"Security" includes share, scrip, stock, bond, debenture, debenture stock or other marketable security of a like nature in or of anybody corporate and any Government security."

<u>18. The definition of abandoned property appearing in Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was dealt with in a number of cases by the Appellate Division of this Court and also High Court Division of this Court The earliest of these cases relied upon by Mr. Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner; is M/s ATJ Industries Limited and others Vs. The Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR page 27. The meaning of "abandoned property" appearing in Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 has been elaborately dealt with and interpreted in this case. 'In subsequent cases also the meaning of "abandoned property" came up for consideration and in this connection, Mr. Farooqui placed reliance on 28 DLR (AD) 120 which arose out of the same case decided by the High Court Division and reported in 28 DLR 27. The last of the cases relied upon by Mr. Farooqui is Government of Bangladesh Vs. MS Ispahani reported in 40 DLR 116 in which Mr. Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. as his Lordship was then, traced the history of the gradual development of interpretation of "abandoned property" appearing in Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. The principle that has been settled in these cases culminating in Ispahani's case is that clause of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 has two inclusion sub-clauses being sub-clauses (i) and (ii) and also two exclusion, sub-clauses appearing as sub-clauses (a) and (b) thereof. It was laid down in this case that inclusion clauses (i) and (ii) are independent of the main clause (1) and it was also held in this case that exclusion clauses (a) and (b) qualify the main clause (1). We are however, not concerned with the exclusion sub-clause (b) as it is nobody's case that the disputed house was controlled and possessed by the Government under any law for the time being in force. We are mainly concerned with the exclusion sub-clause sub-clause (a). It is an undisputed fact that the disputed house was treated as abandoned property not by operation of inclusion sub-clause (i) or inclusion sub-clause (ii) but by operation of the main clause (1) which provided that a property would be deemed to be abandoned property if the person owning the said property was not present in Bangladesh or if his whereabouts were not known or if he had ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property. The Government appears to have applied this main clause (1) in treating the disputed house as abandoned property on the ground that the owner of the disputed house was not present in Bangladesh and that his whereabouts were not known and that he had ceased to occupy supervise or manage in person said property. The Government could have treated this property as abandoned property if the condition in only anyone of the three sub-clauses of clause (1) of Article 2 was present as all these three sub-clauses were held to be disjunctive and not conjunctive. It was also held in this case that while applying the exclusion clause (a) what was to be seen in the case of a person residing outside Bangladesh was whether he was residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh, before treating his property as abandoned property and if the answer was in the affirmative the property was to be deemed to be abandoned property. The crux of the principle was that the Government has to form an opinion as to whether the residence of the person outside of Bangladesh was a purpose prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh or not. It was not, however, argued in this case whether this exclusion clause (a) qualifies the entire main clause (1) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 and Mr. Farooqui advanced considerable argument on this point contending that the exclusion clause (a) qualifies the main clause (1) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. We have carefully perused the main clause (1) along with the exclusion (a) of Article 2 of the above President's Order and it appears to us that the main clause (1) has three parts consisting of the following:</u>

<u>(1) "who is not present in Bangladesh", or,</u>

<u>(2) "whose whereabouts are not known" or</u>

<u>(3) "who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property".</u>

<u>It appears that there three parts together constituted the entire sentence appearing in clause (1). The exclusion clause (a) does not specifically mention that it qualified only one of the above parts appearing in the main clause (1). So, it appears to us that exclusion (a) qualifies the entire paragraph consisting of the three above parts appearing in clause (1).</u>

<u>19. Since, we have held that exclusion clause (a) is an exception to the entire main paragraph appearing in clause (1) of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972, it has now to be decided whether the petitioner was entitled to get when the petitioner was out of the territory of Bangladesh when PO 16 of 1972 came into force on 28th February, 1972. There is nothing on record to show either before this court or before the Court of Settlement that the residence of the petitioner outside Bangladesh was for a purpose prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh and, as such, following the principles laid down in the aforesaid cases culminating in Government of Bangladesh Vs. M/s. Ispahani reported in 40 DLR 116 we are of opinion that without forming an opinion that the petitioner stayed outside Bangladesh for a purpose which was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh the Government could not treat the disputed house as abandoned property. Since the stay of the petitioner outside the territory of Bangladesh prior to on or after the date of promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 had not been proved to be prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh she ought to have been excluded from the operation of clause (4) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 and as such, her property i.e. the disputed house was not at all abandoned property within the definition of clause (1) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. In the above view of the matter, we are of the opinion that the treatment of the property and listing of the said property as abandoned property in the 'Ka' list in Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary at page No. 8762 (102) against Serial No. 84 dated September 23, 1985 and the decision of the Court of Settlement dated 7.3.89 in 1022 of 1987 affirming the above action of the Government are without authority and of no legal effect. I, therefore, agree with the order proposed to be passed by my learned brother.</u>

End.

lawyer:
MI Farooqui, with Md Salimullah, Advocates -----For the Appellant.
M Nurullah, with Md Ayenuddin and AQM Shafiullah, Advocates -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Yousuf (Md)------Appellant
Vs.
Hajee Abdul Wahab being dead his heirs Hajee Shahida Khatun and ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Karim J: This appeal at the instance of defendant No. 1 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23-4-1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka decreeing the suit for specific performance of contract being Title Suit No. 268 of 1981.

The appeal arises out of the suit filed by plaintiff Hajee Abdul Wahab (since deceased) which is a residential house in Dhanmondi residential area (Road 15A) in the city of Dhaka, belonged to defendant No. 1 Md Yousuf, who, being in urgent need of money, proposed to sell the property to the plaintiff for a sum of Taka 12,00,000.00 and accordingly, an agreement was executed by the defendant on 30-7-79 on receipt of taka one lac as earnest money with the stipulation that the balance amount (amounting to Taka 11,00,000.00) would be paid at the time of execution and registration of the sale deed by the defendant after, obtaining income tax clearance certificate and other necessary papers. It is further stated in the plaint that the defendant delivered possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of a further amount of Taka 5,00,000.00 through pay order No. 012702 dated 12-2-80. Thereafter the plaintiff repeatedly approached the defendant for getting the sale deed executed and registered, but the latter delayed the matter on the plea of his illness whereupon the suit was filed by the plaintiff for specific performance of contract.

2. Thy suit was contested by defendant No.1 by filing a written statement admitting that he was the owner of the suit property with possession in the same and that he executed an agreement for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 12,00,000.00 out of which he received taka one lac as earnest money on the day of execution of the agreement dated 30-7-79. The case of the defendant is that, he had been a reputed businessman of Dhaka and decided to sell the, suit property in order to raise fund, for enlarging his business and, with this end in view, he entered into a written agreement with the plaintiff to sell the suit property, the consideration being fixed at Taka 12,00,000.00 and the agreement was executed on 30-7-79 when taka one lac was paid as earnest money and it was decided to complete the sale transaction on or before 31st December, 1979, but the defendant having suffered a stroke on 2-11-79 was taken to Mitford Hospital for treatment and was subsequently shifted to PG Hospital, Dhaka, where he received treatment from 30-11-79 to 11-12-1979 and was under treatment of Professor Rashiduddin Ahmed, Neuro Surgeon. The defendant also received treatment in New Delhi under Professor Tandon, Neuron Surgeon, to whom he was referred by Professor Rashiduddin Ahmed, It is further stated that defendant did not recover from his illness and also received treatment in Pakistan under Dr. Jumma, Neuro Surgeon, and Professor Abdur Rob. In the meantime the plaintiff persuaded, Mrs Nasrin Sultana, wife of defendant No.1, to receive taka five lac and she handed over possession of the suit property without permission of her husband; It is further stated in the written statement that the result of the stroke was loss of speech and consciousness, impairment of power to express himself by speech or writing, which is an effect of brain damage, and now the defendant has to move with the help of his wife, Nasrin Sultana, and his business partner, Syed Masud Ali, who look after his business, because he is not physically or mentally capable of managing his business independently, without help from others and has been advised by his doctor to curtail his business activities and reside in a peaceful area to avoid tension. In May/June, 1981, defendant No. 1 personally met the plaintiff along with Syed Masud Ali and requested him to take back taka one lac paid to him and Taka five lac paid to his wife along with reasonable compensation because of change of situation in the life of the defendant. Though plaintiff agreed to consider the matter, unfortunately, he filed the suit against the defendant. It is further averred in the written statement that the Government, a necessary party in the suit for specific performance of contract, was not made a party within the period of limitation and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed because of the bar of limitation. The other point is that, specific performance of contract being an equitable relief should be refused in this case because of hardship the contract would cause to the defendant, who, because of the present state of his health, is not in a position to enlarge his business for which the contract was entered into.

3. In the trial Court the plaintiff examined four witnesses as against eight witnesses by the defendant. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit for specific performance of contract with the finding that the plaintiff was able to prove the contract between the parties and was entitled to get a decree for specific performance of contract. Against this judgment and decree, defendant No. 1 has preferred this appeal,

4. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Advocate for defendant No. 1 appellant, has submitted that the Court below erred in law in not holding that the suit was not properly constituted because the Government, though a necessary party, was not impleaded at the time of institution of the suit, and at a later stage when the government was added as a party (Pro-defendant No. 2), the suit became barred by limitation. Mr. MI Farooqui further submits that specific performance of contract is an equitable relief, and though it may be lawful to grant it, the Court may refuse to grant this relief in a proper case. The Court below should have considered the hardship of the defendant from his illness that occurred soon after the contract and its effect on his speech and free movement of his body and, in that view of the matter, the trial Court committed an error of law in not refusing the equitable relief of specific performance of contract Mr. Farooqui has, in this connection, referred to the decision in the case of Md Latifur Rahman vs Golam Ahmed Shah, 39 DLR (AD) 242, where specific performance was refused because of hardship it would have caused to the defendant and solatitium was granted to the plaintiff.

<u>5. Mr. Nurullah, learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent, has submitted that the suit is within time because the cause of action arose on 8-2-81 on refusal of the defendant to plaintiffs request for execution and registration of the sale deed and the suit was filed on 6-7-81. He submits that the plaintiff filed an application before the trial Court on 31-1-84 for adding the government as a pro-forma defendant in the suit and this application being in time, the suit cannot come within the mischief of limitation. He submits that the application dated 31-1-84 was allowed by the trial Court on 29-3-84 and filing of the application within the period of limitation saved the suit from the mischief of limitation. Mr. Nurullah further submits that the trial Court considered all aspects of the matter for decreeing the suit, because the question of hardship must be judged on the date of the contract and not in the light of the subsequent events and that physical disability of the defendant, if any, which was subsequent to the contract, cannot be argued as a ground of hardship to defeat the suit for specific performance of contract. In support of his contention Mr.Nurullah has referred to the decision in the case of Sankara Lings vs Ratnaswami, AIR 1952 Madras 389 and Qazi Din Mohammad vs Al-Haj Arzan Ali and another, 47 DLR (AD) 48. Nurullah submits that the case of Latifur Rahman and others vs Golam Ahmed Shah 39 DLR (AD) 242, is distinguishable from the facts of the present case and that the ground for solatitium does not apply to the facts and circumstances of the present case.</u>

6. It has been strenuously argued by Mr. Farooqui that the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is a necessary party in the suit for specific performance of contract and that the government having not being impleaded in time, the suit was barred by limitation and liable to be dismissed as such.

Article 6 of President's Order No. 142 of 1972 reads as follows:

"No person shall, without joining the government which shall be a necessary party, file or proceed with any suit-

(a) for the specific performance of any contract relating to the transfer of any immovable property or for declaration of title to, or assertion of ownership of, any such property;

(b) for enforcement of mortgage security in relation to any immovable property except where the mortgage is the movement or a local authority or a schedule Bank or a statutory Corporation or a Co-operative Society; or

(c) for partition of immovable property where the total area of the property involved exceeds one hundred standard bighas."

<u>7. Mr. Farooqui has referred to the case of Muzaffar Ali Chowdhury and others vs Abu Musa Chowdhury, 1 BCR ( 1981) 407 wherein a Division Bench of this Court held that in a suit for specific performance of contract, the Government was not a proper, but a necessary party. In that case there being no material on record to indicate service of summons on the government of Bangladesh, the Division Bench remanded the suit to the trial Court to proceed with the case after service of summons on defendant No. 3, namely, People's Republic of Bangladesh. Mr. Farooqui has also referred to the case of Asadunnessa and others vs Qumarazzaman and others, 26 DLR 363, wherein the Division Bench observed that President's Order 142 of 1972 applies to a suit for specific performance of any contract relating to transfer of immovable property and not of any suit for declaration of title to, or assertion of ownership of, any (sic).</u>

8. There is no doubt that the government is a necessary party in a suit for specific performance of contract relating to transfer of immovable property, which is the case before us.

<u>9. Mr Farooqui has further referred to the case of Sobharadri vs Parthasarathi reported in AIR 1932 Madras 583 where a suit was filed for recovery of compensation for fraudulent representation of the defendant at the time of the contract. The plaintiffs’ case is that the defendants sold to the plaintiff and his brother by a conveyance dated 17th February, 1917, certain villages including Penjendra, the suit village. The price of the village in question was fixed at 29 times the net income. The plaintiff claims that subsequently in a partition between him and his brother, that suit villages fell to his share (share of the plaintiff). The case of action in the suit arose on 1-4-1919 when the fraud was discovered and the suit was filed on 14th February, 1920. The plaintiff filed an application on 19th July, 1923, for adding his brother as pro-forma defendant. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court on the ground that the plaintiff is not competent to maintain the action in the absence of his brother, who was necessary party, and that when, on this defect having been pointed out, he applied for his brother being impleaded, the suit was barred by limitation. The appeal was dismissed by the Division Bench of Madras High Court on the ground when necessary parties were not joined within the period of limitation, the suit must be dismissed. The Division Bench further observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Section 22, the Limitation Act, provides, inter alia, that when a new party is added as plaintiff, the date of his being added is to be considered as regards him as the date of institution of the suit."</u>

10. We may quote section 22 of the Limitation Act, which reads as follows:

Section 22(1) Where, after the institution of a suit, a new plaintiff or defendant is substituted or added; the suit shall, as regards him, be deemed to have been instituted when he was so made a party.

(2) Nothing in sub-section (1) shall apply where a party is added or substituted owing to an assignment or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suit or where a plaintiff is made a defendant or a defendant is made a plaintiff."

11. Under Order 1, rule 10(5) of the CPC the proceedings against any person added as defendant shall be deemed to have begun only on the service of summons.

12. In the instant case the agreement was entered into on 30-7-1979 and the suit was filed on 26-7-81. According to the plaint, plaintiffs request for execution and registration of the sale deed was refused by the defendant on 8-2-1981 and the plaintiff submitted as application before the trial Court on 31-1-1984 for making the government a defendant (Pro-defendant No. 2 in the suit). The order sheet of the trial Court shows that this application was filed on 31-1-1984 and was allowed by the Court on 29-3-84. So, it is clear that the application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed before the expiry of the period of limitation (3 years under Article 113 of the Limitation Act) on 7-2-84. It is therefore, clear that the suit for filing of the application under Order 1 rule 10 of the CPC cannot come within the mischief of limitation for failure of the trial Court to dispose of the matter in time. In this view of the matter, the trial Court rightly found that the suit was properly constituted and not barred by limitation.

13. Mr. Farooqui has argued that specific performance of contract is an equitable relief, which is discretionary and should not be granted merely because it is lawful to grant and should be refused when its performance would involve some hardship on the defendant, which he did not' foresee, without involving any hardship on the plaintiff.

14. Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act reads as follows:

"The jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and the Court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so; but the discretion of the Court is not arbitrary but sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction by a Court of appeal.

The following are cases in which the Court may properly exercise a discretion not to decree specific performance:

(i) Where the circumstances under which the contract is made are such as to give the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendant, though there may be no fraud or misrepresentation on the plaintiffs’ part.

(ii) Where the performance of the contract would involve some hardship on the defendant which he did not foresee, whereas its nonperformance would involve no such hardship on the plaintiff."

15. The learned Advocate for the ,defendant appellant submits that the purpose, of the agreement for sale of the suit property was enlarging the business of the defendant under the agreement dated 30-7-79, but sudden stroke on 2-11-79 rendered the defendant physically incapable of looking after or enlarging his business with the result that specific performance of the contract was bound to cause hardship on the defendant which he did not foresee whereas its nonperformance would (cause) no such hardship on the plaintiff.

16. In this case we may examine the evidence adduced on the point of physical and mental incapacity of the defendant occurring after the contract. DW 3 Nasrin Sultana, wife of defendant No. 1, states that her husband entered into an agreement on 30-7-79 when he was in sound health and received taka one lac as earnest money; he did not deliver possession of the suit property to the plaintiff, Suddenly he fell ill on 2-11-79 when he was taken to Mitford Hospital and thereafter he was hospitalized in PG Hospital, Dhaka, for eleven days. The defendant also received treatment in New Delhi under Dr. Sharma, DW 3 further states that on 12-2-80 the plaintiff gave her taka five lac through pay order, which she received and that her, husband did not receive it. She further states that she did not receive the pay order with the consent of her husband and delivered possession of the suit property to the plaintiff. It was their residential house and the sale was for enlargement of the business of the defendant. She further states that in total they received Taka 6 lac from the plaintiff. She further states that the defendant cannot speak. She further states that after receipt oftaka six lacthey did not invest the amount in business but are winding up the business and that her husband is still undergoing treatment and went to India a few months ago for treatment.

17. DW 1 Dr. Rashiduddin Ahmed, professor of Neuro Surgery of PG Hospital, states that defendant No.1 was under his treatment and was in PG Hospital from 30-11-79 to 11-12-1979 and his condition was diagnosed as aphasis meaning complete loss of speech from an attack of CVA (cerebrovascular accident). It is the disturbance of blood supply to brain owing to blockage of an artery or bleeding in the brain. It causes brain damage, loss of speech and consciousness and may be fatal Theevidence of DW 1 further shows that the defendant developed paralysis of the right side two days after the attack. DW 1 referred the patient to Dr. Tandon, Department of Neuro Surgery, All India Medical Institute, New Delhi. In his letter Ext. B(1) Dr. Tandon opined that the patient needed conservative treatment and physiotherapy. The letter, Ext.A, dated 23-2-1980 from Professor Rashiduddin Ahmed to Dr. Tandon shows that defendant No. 1 had been a known diabetic for about 10 years before the stroke and became aphasic from a sudden onset of right hemiplegia, which occurred on 2nd November 1979. The letter (Ext, A) mentioned the condition of the patient as follows:

"As he was improving and progressing daily, I did not do an angio straightaway. He later came to my unit 4 weeks later (30-11-79). By that time he had recovered from his Rt hemiplegia quite well, although speech improvement was less satisfactory."

18. In his cross-examination Dr. Rashiduddin Ahmed (DW,1) states as follows:

"His condition has improved, hopefully. He is now sitting in my presence here and he is looking normal position."

It is clear from the evidence on record that defendant No. 1 had been a known diabetic for 91/2 years before the agreement dated 30-7-79 and the treatment shows improvement in his condition. It may be noted that now the defendant is not in sound physical and mental condition to manage his business as he used to do before his stroke on 2-11-79.

<u>19. We have seriously considered the question of hardship raised on behalf of the defendant appellant. In this connection we may refer to the decision, in the case of Sankarlinga vs Ratnaswami reported in AIR 1952 Mad 389 where the Division Bench observed that the question of hardship must be judged as on the date of the transaction and not in the light of subsequent events. Mr. Nurullah has referred to the decision in the case of Quazi Din Mohammad vs Al-Haj Arzan Ali, 47 DLR (AD) 48 wherein their Lordships observed that hardship is to be considered against the circumstances existing at the time of the contract. In that case the defendant had an alternative house at Fatullah which was sold two years after the contract for sale of the suit house at Kalabagan in Dhaka. So, their Lordships refused to maintain the plea of hardship put forward by the defendant.</u>

20. Mr. Nurullah has submitted that the defendant has an alternative house at Patlakhan Lane in the city of Dhaka where he has been living with his family for a long time and so the question of hardship does not deserve any consideration as was decided in the case of AIR 1952 Mad 389 and in the case of 47 DLR (AD) 48. DW 2 Syed Masud Ali, a business partner of defendant Md Yousuf since 1971, says that the defendant has been living in his house at Patlakhan Lane, Dhaka, since 1949. DW 3 Nasrin Sultana, wife of the defendant, says that she lives with her husband in their house at Patlakhan Lane.

<u>21. In this connection we may refer to the case of Latifur Rahman and others vs Golam Ahmed Shah and others, 39 DLR (AD) 242 where Maimur Sultan entered into a contract with the plaintiff to sell his residential house at a consideration of Taka 25,000.00 on 5-8-70. In pursuance of the contract Taka 6000.00.was advanced and subsequently another amount of Taka 2,500.00 was paid to the defendant. DW 1 Safurunnessa (widow of Maimur Sultan, who died during pendency of the suit) admitted that her husband entered into the agreement for raising fund for the purpose of marriage expenses of their two daughters, who were married on the same date. Her husband was a petty contractor and since they needed money for the purpose of the marriage, the housewas given as security for the loan and that they had no other house or shelter. She has no other source of income. Their Lordships held that in this case item No. 2 of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act came into play and the defendant appellant was directed to pay Taka one lac to the plaintiff in addition" to the amount of Taka 8,500.00 paid by way of advance. The facts of this case are clearly distinguishable from those of the instant case before us. In the present case hardship is absent for several reasons, one being that the defendant has been living with his family in an alternative house for a long time.</u>

22. In the written statement it is mentioned that in May/June, 1981, the defendant along with his business partner, Syed Masood Ali, went to the plaintiff and requested him to take back taka one lac paid to him as earnest money and taka five lac paid to his wife together with reasonable compensation in view of changed circumstances. It appears that remaining amount of taka six lac out of total consideration of Taka 12 lac is in deposit in Court to the credit of defendant No. 1. In the circumstances, the plaintiff having proved his case for specific performance about the execution of the agreement, the trial Court rightly decreed the suit for specific performance of contract and we find no ground to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the Court below. We find no merit in the appeal, which is liable to be dismissed.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is upheld.

Send down the record at once.

End.

Mr. T. H. Khan, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, (Mr. M. A. Wahab Miah, Advocate, Supreme Court, with him), instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hassain, Advocate¬on-Record ------ For the Appellants.
Mr. M.A. Jalil, Advocate-on-Record, Supreme Court ------ For Respondents Nos. 1, 4-8.
