full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-  Plaintiffs are the appellants, and this appeal has been brought by special. leave to consider a question of considerable public importance. It is whether a co-sharer in ejmali property, when he has been in exclusive possession of a specific and separate share thereof, well demarcated by boundaries, is entitled to retain his possession till legal partition, by an order of injunction against another who threatens him with dispossession. Both the trial Court and the appellate Court, on a concurrent finding, answered the question in the affirmative; but the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in revision answered in the negative.

2. This arises from O.C. Suit No. 175 of 1978 in the First Court of Munsif, Bajitpur. The suit land was held in jote right by Haidar alias Haider Sheikh and on his death his only son, Hossain Ali, inherited and possessed it. On the death of Hossain Ali his four sons and one daughter inherited it. The sons were Eksad Ali (Plaintiff No.2), Safar Ali (prodefendant No.2), pasand Ali (father of defendant No.1, Madhu) and Ahad Ali, while the daughter was Aptarunnessa (pro-defendant No.3). Ahad Ali died without any issue but before his death he had given 96½ decimals of his share to plaintiff No.1, Maharram Ali, who is son of plaintiff No. 2 Eksad Ali, by a Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 28 January 1966; at the same time Ahad Ali gave his remaining share, 65½ decimals, to defendant No.1 Madhu and his stepbrother sadhu alias Sadaruddin. Then Safar Ali gifted his entire share to plaintiff No.1 alone by a Hobabil-Ewaz dated 10 November 1977, and it is this Heba, which according to plaintiffs, enraged defendant No. 1 and triggered the trouble Case of the plaintiffs is that by an amicable partition the co-sharers have been in exclusive possession of their respective shares for about 20 years. Plaintiffs share has been separated from shares of other co-shares by specific boundaries and it is the plaintiffs who have been paying rent all along. After the Heba-bil-Ewaz in favour of plaintiff No.1 on 10-11-77, defendant No.1 gave out for the first time that Aidhar Sk. alias Haider Sk. had died leaving not only one son, Hossain Ali, but also one daughter named “Umar Ma” and that from the heirs of Umar Ma including Mohammad Ali and Abdul Ali defendant No.1 purchased their shares by three registered kabalas Exts. A and A(1) dated 13 March 1978 and kabala Ext. A(4) dated 28 April 1978. These kabalas, according to plaintiffs, are false and collusive documents executed by fictitious persons as Aider Sk. had no daughter like Umar Ma'. On the strength of these kabalas defendant No.1 threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession from their specific shares whereupon they filed the suit for permanent injunction to restrain the defendants from disturbing their possession.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No.1 alone denying the material allegations of the plaintiffs. His case, as already referred to, is that Haider Sk. left a daughter named 'Umar Ma' whose heirs transferred her share by the kabalas Ext s. A, A(1) and A(4) in 1978. He denied the amicable partition or exclusive possession of the plaintiffs in any specific share of the property which, he claimed, remained ejmali and as such no injunction can issue against him. The trial Court on consideration of evidence adduced by both the parties found the plaintiffs to be in exclusive possession of separate and well demarcated shares, and on that basis, decreed the suit by a judgment dated 30 June 1979. This judgment was confirmed in appeal by the Additional District Judge by judgment dated 31 January 1981 with an additional finding that Aidhar Sk. had no daughter named Umar Ma, but 'Umar Ma' the ostensible executant of the disputed kabalas, was a fictitious person invented by defendant No.1 who could not bring any witness is support of his claim excepting himself. The learned Single Judge, however, held by the impugned judgment dated 27 May 1986, in Civil Revision No.1484 of 1981, that since the parties were co-sharers in respect of the suit land one co-sharer could not be prevented by injunction from claiming and exercising his right over any part of the property.

4. It may be mentioned here that after filing the suit the plaintiffs got a temporary injunction restraining defendant No.1 from disturbing their possession in their specific areas of the suit land. But the order of injunction was violated by defendant No.1 on two occasions in respect of two plots of the suit land, Thereupon the plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Cases Nos. 144 of 1978 and 35 of 1979 under Order XXXIX, rule 7 Civil P.C. for punishment of defendant No.1. Both the Miscellaneous cases were allowed and defendant No.1 was held guilty and convicted and sentenced to civil imprisonment. Against this order of conviction in each case, defendant No.1 preferred two appeals which were heard along with the appeal against the decree in the suit but both the appeals were dismissed by the learned Additional District Judge. Thereupon the order of conviction was challenged in Civil Revision Cases Nos.1483 and 1485 of 1981; which were heard by the learned Single Judge, along with Civil Revision No. 1484 of 1981, that is, in the instant case. The learned Single Judge allowed all these Revision Cases and set aside the order of conviction and sentence. Leave to appeal was also sought against the order setting aside the conviction in each case, but it was refused and consequently leave was granted only in respect of the (High Court Division's order made in Civil Revision No.1484 of 1981 dismissing the plaintiffs O.C Suit No.175 of 1978.

5. Mr. T.H. Khan, learned Counsel for the appellants, has referred to all the three judgments in this suit, namely, that of the trial Court, appellate Court and the revisional Court. He has pointed out that the concurrent finding of the trial Court and the appellate Court that the plaintiffs have been in exclusive possession of their separate and specific shares, which are clearly demarcated "by ails", has not been disturbed or even referred to, by the learned Single Judge. The learned Counsel has also referred to the evidence of P. W s. 1, 2 and 3 as well as of D.W. 1, who is defendant No.1 himself, to the effect that the plaintiffs have been in exclusive possession of their separate shares which have been demarcated by boundary lines or ails and which have been shown in the Sketch Map drawn in the plaint. D.W.l, though he denied, in examination-in-chief, the plaintiffs claim of separate and exclusive possession, has admitted in cross-examination that the plaintiffs have been in possession of their shares which are demarcated by boundaries. Furthermore, the learned Counsel has pointed out, the finding of the appellate Court that Aidhar  Sk. left no daughter like 'Umar Ma' and that the claim of defendant No.1 that he purchased the shares of Umar Ma's heirs is false has also not been disturbed by the learned Single Judge. The learned Single Judge is found to have proceeded on the assumption that whether the plaintiffs exclusively possessed any specific shares of the suit-land, or not, if they arc co-sharers in the joint land, remedy by way of injunction would not be available to one co-sharer against another. The learned Single Judge observed:

"It appears from the facts as stated in the plaint that the defendant No.1 got some portion from Ahad Ali, one of the sons of Hossain Ali through Heba-bil-Ewaz and plaintiff also claimed certain portion of land in the same jute It apparently appears that the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 are co-sharers."

Thus upon this finding that the parties are co-sharers, the learned Single Judge held that the principle laid down in the case of Robert Watson & Co. V, Ram Chana Dutta and others, 18 ILR, CaI.10 is applicable to the present case and as such no injunction can be issued against the defendants as prayed for by the plaintiffs.

6. Mr. T.H. Khan has contended that the facts of "Robert Watson & Co. v. Ram Chand Dutta" are quite distinguishable from that of the instant case and that the principle laid down in that case has been misconceived by the learned Single Judge. The learned Counsel has contended that the principle of law as explained in the case of Robert Watson rather supports the appellant's case. He has also relied upon the following cases, Abdul Gani Talukder v. Rushan and others, 12 DLR 40; Sefatulla Sheikh v, Mst. Abjannessa Bibi,.5 DLR 39; Kumudini v Rashik, 11 CWN 517; Kameswari Dasya v. Sishuram Deka, AIR 1924 Cal. 792 and Ram Ray Singh v. Rajendra Singh, AIR 1943 All. 247. In all these cases the principle followed is that when a co-sharer of a joint property is in exclusive possession of a specific and well defined portion, he cannot be disturbed by another co-sharer who might have right over the entire property, but his remedy lies in partition. I need not refer to all these cases but I shall consider the cases of the Dacca High Court.

7. In the case of Sefatullah, a learned Single Judge of the then Dacca High Court held that "a person is not entitled to oust his co-sharer from a plot of land in exclusive possession of the latter on the plea that he has got title to every inch of the joint property and that if he feels that his co-sharer is in possession of some lands in excess of his share, his remedy lies in a suit for partition. In the case of Abdul Ganiv Rushan, Imam Hossain Chowdhury, J, as he was then, held:

"It is no doubt true that every co-sharer has equal right of enjoyment in every part and parcel of a joint land. If one co-sharer is in possession of a specific part of a joint land, the other co-sharers cannot dispossess him without a suit for partition."

The learned Judge then referred to the Principle of law as to partition as elucidated in "Freeman on Co-tenancy and Partition" and also relied upon the decision of the Privy Council in "Robert Watson & Co. v. Ram Chand Dutta and others" on which the learned Single Judge has also relied in the instant case.

8. This case of Robert Watson & Co. has been also reported in 17 Indian Appeals, 110. It is a decision of the Privy Council upon an appeal from the decision or the Calcutta High Court and the Board's judgment was delivered by Sir Barnes Peacock. This case arose from a suit filed in the Court of District Judge, Midnapor, by the plaintiff- respondent Ram Chand Dutta against his co-sharer Robert Watson & Co.- a body of indigo-planters praying for joint possession of the ejmali land or injunction. Plaintiffs share in the joint property was to the extent of two-third of fourteen annas- a fact not denied by the defendants who were engaged in profitable indigo cultivation of the entire ejmali land treating it as if it were their "own and exclusive" property. The principal question of law raised in that case was as to the right of tenants-in-common, inter se, to cultivate or to restrain the cultivation of the land. Both the trial Court and the appellate Court, namely the High Court, on a finding that the acts of the defendants amounted to actual ouster of the plaintiff, decreed the suit allowing the plaintiffs prayer for joint possession with the defendants in the alternative granting injunction to restrain the defendants from cultivating indigo or anybody else from doing so. But their Lordships of the Privy Council took the view that the judgment and decree of the courts in India were erroneous and held as follows:

"It seems to their Lordships that if there be two or more tenants in common, and one (A) be in actual occupation of part of the estate and is engaged in cultivating that part in a proper course of cultivation as if it were his separate property and another tenant in common (B) attempts to come upon' the said part for the purpose of carrying on operations there inconsistent with the course of cultivation in which A is engaged and the profitable use by him of the said part, and A, resists and prevents such entry, not in denial of B's title, but simply with the object of protecting himself in the profitable enjoyment of the land; such conduct on the part of A, would not entitle B, to a decree for joint possession. Their Lordships are further of opinion that the decree of the District Judge, so far as it orders an injunction to be issued ought to be reversed. It appears to their Lordships that, in a case like the present an injunction is not the proper remedy."

9. It appears clearly that the facts of the Privy Council case are distinguishable from that of the instant case. In that case the co-sharer in exclusive possession of the joint land was sought to be prevented by injunction from carrying on with the indigo cultivation, by a co-sharer out of possession intending to grow some other crops: in the instant case, the co-sharers in exclusive possession of their separate shares are seeking protection from court to maintain their exclusive possession from the onslaught of the other co-sharer who got no possession in the particular share which 'is in plaintiffs exclusive possession. The principle of law as enunciated in the Robert Watson's case is not applicable to the instant case and it is found to have been misapplied by the learned Single Judge.

<u>10. In the instant case the concurrent finding of the trial Court and the appellate Court is that the plaintiffs have been in exclusive possession over the suit land comprising separate and specifically demarcated shares by boundaries The finding is based upon the evidence of P,Ws. 1, 2 and 3 considered along with the evidence of D.W.1, the only witness examined defendant No.1. We find; no reason to disturb the finding Mr. Abdul jalil learned Counsel for the defendant-respondent does not dispute the principle of law as propounded in the cases referred to above but he argues that though defendant No.1 (D.W.1) admitted exclusive possession of the plaintiffs, he did not say that the exclusive possession covers the entire suit land claimed by the plaintiffs The learned Counsel has tried to show us that the plaintiffs exclusive possession-covers about 9 kanis of land which is about three and half acres whereas according to the plaint the plaintiffs claim a larger area measuring 4.46 acres. This is for the first time that this question as to the exact area under exclusive possession of the plaintiffs has been raised before us. It was not an issue before any of the courts below including the High Court Division, and as such it cannot be entertained here. Moreover, this point is sought to be raised when the main ground on which the suit was contested all through has fallen to the ground. The only question of law agitated in the suit all through was whether an injunction could issue at the instance of a co-sharer in exclusive possession of a separate and well defined share, against another co-sharer who threatens the former with dispossession. This question was rightly answered by the trial Court and the appellate Court but the learned Single Judge on an erroneous view of law reversed their decision.</u>

11. In the result; the appeal is allowed; the order of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the trial Court and the appellate Court is restored. The respondent will bear the cost of the appeal

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker J: This Rule Nisi was issued upon an application under Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh filed by the elder brother of the detenu calling upon the respondents to show cause why the detenu Mr. Moudud Ahmed, the former Vice-President of Bangladesh, now detained in his own house should not be brought before this Court so that it may certify itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner.

2. This Rule was issued on 2.1.91 and in the meantime the detenu was shifted to the Dhaka Central Jail on 29.1.91 from his 159, Gulshan Avenue residence where he is now being detained.

3. It is stated in the application that the detenu had actively participated is the student politics and democratic movements during his student-life; that he obtained his MA degree from the University of Dhaka and was called to the Bar as a Barrister-at-Law in the year 1966 and was enrolled as an Advocate of this Court in 1966, that he wrote a few books of which "Bangladesh : Constitutional quest for Autonomy" and "Bangladesh : Era of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman" are prominent; that he was elected as a Member of Parliament in 1979 and also twice thereafter; that he was appointed Adviser of the President in 1977 and elevated to the post of Minister in 1978 and thereafter he became Deputy Prime Minister, then Prime Minister and ultimately he was appointed Vice-President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh on 12.6.89; that he remained the Vice-President of the country till he voluntarily resigned on December 6, 1990, in whose place the Chief Justice of Bangladesh was appointed as Vice-President and who is now acting as President of Bangladesh as head of the Caretaker Government; that an order of detention under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 (hereinafter referred to as the said Act) was passed by the respondent No. 2 on 11.12.90, directing to detain the detenu in his house at Gulshan for 120 days for public safety and maintenance of public order; that the said order of detention has been annexed with the application and marked as Annexure-A, that the subsequent arrest and detention of the detenu under section 3(1)(a) of the said Act is not only unlawful and illegal but it is malafide and it has been made purely for co-lateral purposes to creates hurdle on the part of the detenu to contest the ensuing election of the Parliament, that the ground of detention of the detenu in the present context of facts has become totally non-existent and there is no reasons to pass such an order of detention which is malafide, illegal and unlawful; that the reason for detention as stated in the impugned order does not come within the scope of prejudicial activities and there was no material before the Government to pass such an order of detention; that on 24.12.90 the grounds for detention under section 3 of the said Act have been served upon the detenu, the copy of which is annexed with the application and marked as Annexure 'B'. That the grounds communicated to the detenu do not constitute any prejudicial act on the part of the detention; that the grounds are vague, indefinite, illusory and non-existent; that the ground No. 1 does not and cannot constitute any prejudicial act within the meaning of the said act; that as to ground No. 2 with regard to Press interview the detenu did not violate any law nor had he anything to do with the incident which occurred on 10th December, 1990. That ground Nos. 3 and 4 are not only vague and indefinite but also baseless and motivated and that the detenu voluntarily resigned from the post of Vice-President to enable to form the present Caretaker Government and that the whole purpose of this order of detention is to prevent the detenu from contesting the ensuing Parliamentary election.

4. That an affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the respondents, affirmed by a Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, has been filed by the respondents contending, inter alia, that the detenu had a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to the Jatiya Party and the earlier regime in the administration in order to destabilise the present situation and thereby to endanger public safety and public order and as such the detention of the detenu has become necessary with a view to preserve and protect the public safety and public order for having free and fair election in the country; that the detenu was removed on the 2nd January, 1986 from the post of Minister and he was tried before a Special Martial Law Court under Martial Law Regulation 11 and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 10 years and also to pay a fine of Tk. 3 (three) lakhs, in default to suffer imprisonment for three years more and subsequently this was reviewed by the erstwhile Chief Martial Law Administrator and on review he was released from jail; that on being released from jail the detenu was actively associated with BNP leader Begum Khaleda Zia but thereafter joined the Cabinet of former President Ershad and subsequently elevated to the post of Vice-President; that on analysis of the background of the detenu it shows that the detenu assumed different colors at different times with the change of political situation for acquiring power and in doing so he was widely reputed as a corrupt man which has created a strong political agitation against him; that it was not correct that the detenu resigned voluntarily on 6.12.90 and the chronology of political movement would show that the detenu had to resign due to political agitation launched by the people, restoration of democratic rights and for holding a and free election under the neutral Government; that during the tenure of his office the detenu had acquired the reputation as a corrupt man, that he was alleged to have adopted corrupt practice and favouritism, that in support of the allegation of corrupt practice by the detenu certain weekly magazine has been annexed with the affidavit which have been marked as Annexures X and Y series; that the detenu was detained for his prejudicial activities against public safety and maintenance of public order; that the detenu has a powerful background to destabilise the present situation and thereby he is quite capable to endanger public safety and public order; that there are sufficient materials before the detaining authority necessitating to pass the order of detention for preventing him from acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety and public order; that the detenu has been detained under one ground alone i.e. for maintenance of public safety and public order; that the detenu while staying in his own house after his resignation made a statement in the 'Morning Sun' on 8.12.90 which was published on 9.12.90 which shows that the detenu was maintaining a close liason with the former President as a result of which a section of the public was agitated and attacked his house on 10.12.90 by throwing cocktail showing public agitation against the detenu and thereby endangered public safety and public order; that the paper cuttings of the statement of the dam have been annexed with the affidavit and marked as Annexures Z and Z(1); that the dam was so long absconding and he was arrested on 20.12.90 from House No. 5, Road No. 7, Baridhara, Gulshan which, belonged to one Shamim Rahman Ansari who is connected with Beximco Company and the said. Beximco Company was widely reputed for having close association with the former President for which Beximco Office at Road No. 2 Dhanmondi was attacked by the picketers during the public agitation on 27.10. 90; that after making the statement to the Morning Sun the detenu was not found in his Gulshan residence and he was found hiding at Baridhara wherefrom he was arrested; that during the period of hiding the detenu seemed to have made several telephone calls, local as well as international, calling on sensitive officers of the Ministry and foreign embassies and this could be constituted overt acts on the part of the detenu to destabilise the present Caretaker Government by mobilising the erstwhile regime; that the statement of the detenu in the Morning Sun was placed before the former President and the former President has given a telephonic interviews to the correspondent of British Broadcasting Corporation and the said interview led to the public agitation and that the detenu was trying to mobilise support of sensitive persons to destabilise the Caretaker Government and thereby acted prejudicially to endanger public safety and maintenance of public order.

5. The petitioner filed an affidavit-in-reply to the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondents wherein it has been stated that the alleged materials mentioned in the affidavit-in-opposition are all of subsequent dates after the order of detention was passed; that the alleged background of political capability cannot be a ground for detention of the detenu under the Act; that the different paper cuttings are all extraneous matter of subsequent dates and as such these have no bearing on the order of detention and that the detenu was detained for co-lateral purpose and not for preventing him from doing any prejudicial act; that the petitioner reiterated his statement made in the application and further stated that the policy of the neutral Government is to allow every citizen to participate in the ensuing parliamentary election irrespective of his party affiliation and the detenu is contesting from two constituencies from the district of Noakhali. By a supplementary affidavit filed by the respondents it. has been stated that from the statement issued by the Acting President of the Jatiya Party it is clear that the leaders of Jatiya Party and its associates are making desperate efforts to destabilise the present Central Government which provides a bonafide impression that the detenu is likely to endanger maintenance of public order and public safety. In support of the statement extracts of the weekly magazine 'Purbabhash' dated 22.1.91 and Daily Hongkong Standard dated 28.1.91 have been annexed with the affidavit as Annexures z-5 and z-6. In reply to this the petitioner by an affidavit-in-reply stated that what was stated by the Acting President of the Jatiya Party or what has been published in the papers those have no relevancy for the disposal of the case and all these go to show that the detenu has been detained without any material available on the date of the order of detention and that to justify the illegal detention the respondents are trying to introduce all irrelevant and extraneous matters.

6. By a subsequent supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the respondents it has been stated that the detenu had never voluntarily resigned from the post of Vice-President, rather he was opposed to the installation of the present Caretaker Government which is evident from his interview with the correspondent of British Broadcasting Corporation on 2.12.90 and 3.12.90 and the relevant documents as mentioned by Radio Bangladesh and the relevant document are annexed therewith and marked as Annexures Z-7 and Z-8.

7. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, has contested that the order of detention of the detenu is illegal, malafide and it was made for collateral purpose inasmuch as there was no materials before the detaining authority to pass the impugned order on 11.12.90. The learned Advocate has contended that the grounds for detention furnished to the detenu are neither prejudicial acts within the scope of section 2 (I) of the Special Powers Act nor is there anything to show that the detenu was detained in order to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act intended and likely to endanger public safety or maintenance of public order. It has further been contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that there is no basis for the grounds nor the subsequent materials mentioned in the affidavit-in-opposition can be regarded as the basis for the passing of the impugned order of detention and as such the order of detention was passed malafide, for collateral purpose in order to prevent the detenu from effectively participating in the ensuing Parliamentary election.

8. The learned Attorney-General Mr. Aminul Huq, on the other hand, has contended that having regard to the antecedent history of political capability of the detenu the effect of his interview to the reporters of the Morning Sun and the fact of the abscondment of the detenu coupled with the overall prevailing situation in the country furnishes sufficient materials for the detaining authority to pass the impugned order to prevent the detenu from endangering public safety and the maintenance of public order.

9. Article 102(2)(b)(i), which confers jurisdiction upon this court, is in the following terms:"(2) The High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law-(b) On the application of any person, make an order (i) directing that a person in custody be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner."

10. Thus it is for the High Court Division to satisfy itself that the detenu is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner. The theory of subjective satisfaction as propounded by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Liversidge Vs. Sir John Anderson and another (1942 AC 206) is being followed in the Indian Jurisdiction so long; but since 1962 there was a radical change by Article 98(2)(b)(i) of the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan in a language substantially similar to the provision of Article 102 (2)(b)(i) of our Constitution and the Supreme Court of Pakistan in a series of decisions namely in the case of Golam Mani Vs. Government of West Pakistan (19 DLR (SC) 403), Mir Abdul Baqi Baluch Vs. Government of Pakistan (20 DLR (SC) 294) Government of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Agha Abdul Karim Shorish Kashmiri (21 DLR 1) held that the constitution has cast a heavy duty upon the court to satisfy itself that there is a competent law authorising the detention and the officers issuing an order have been lawfully vested with the power, that the action of the detaining authority is not malafide and that the action has not been taken upon extraneous or irrelevant considerations and without proper application of mind.

11. Our Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others (31 DLR (AD) 1) interpreted the provision of Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh along with the provision of section 3 of the Special Powers Act under which the detaining authority passed an order of detention; and held that the High Court Division is to be satisfied that the person in detention is not so held either without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner and interpreted the phases stating that the expression "without lawful authority" comprehends all questions of the competency or the vires of an enactment, that is, there must be a competent law empowering an authority to detain a person, and empowered authority acting under the conferred powers must be vested with that power by law and the expression "in an unlawful manner" comprehends the circumstances of the detention as to whether the action is malafide or colorable exercise of statutory powers or the action taken upon extraneous or irrelevant considerations and whether action is taken upon with the application of mind of the detaining authority. Considering the provision of section 3 of the Special Powers Act it has been held by their Lordships that section 3 standing by itself emphasises of the detaining authority to act in purely subjective manner but the Constitution has given a mandate to the High Court Division to satisfy itself, as a judicial authority that the detention is a lawful detention; and giving a harmonious interpretation it has been held that "the detaining authority's satisfaction is to a great extent subjective, but the order of detaining authority must be based on some materials which will satisfy a reasonable person that a conclusion could be so drawn on such materials," As to the adequacy or the sufficiency of the materials it must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division further pointed out that although the satisfaction of the detaining authority has got an objective basis, it has got a subjective feature as to the adequacy or sufficiency of the grounds which are beyond the purview of judicial review and the court cannot substitute its own satisfaction or opinion in place of that of the detaining authority.

12. The same view has been reiterated by our Appellate Division in the case of Mrs. Sajeda Parvin Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 40 DLR (AD) 178. In this case their Lordships of the Appellate Division have pointed out that the language of Article 102 of our Constitution and that of Article 98 of 1962 Constitution of Pakistan is radically different from Article 176 of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan and Article 226 of the Indian Constitution and held that "the court is to satisfy itself that the person is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner, the court is enjoined to consider the materials. What the court is concerned with, is to see that the executive or administrative authority had before it sufficient materials upon which a reasonable person could have come to the conclusion that the requirements of law were satisfied."

13. The above mentioned legal position as laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan and as well as by our Appellate Division are well sealed and has not been disputed by either side.

14. Now turning to the impugned order of detention, the impugned order is in the following terms:

“যেহেতু সরকার এই মর্মে সন্তুষ্ট হইয়াছেন যে জনাব মওদুদ আহমেদ (সাবেক উপরাষ্ট্রপতি) ১৫৯, গুলশান এভেনিউ, ঢাকাকে জন নিরাপত্তা ও জনশৃংখলা রক্ষার জন্য আটক রাখা প্রয়োজন।

এক্ষনে যেহেতু, সরকার The Special Powers Act, 1974 (Act 14 of 1974) Section 3 (I)(a) ধারায় বর্ণিত ক্ষমতা বলে উপরোক্ত জনাব মওদুদ আহমদকে এতদউদ্দেশ্যে এই আদেশ জারির দিন হইতে ১২০ (একশত বিশ) দিনের জন্য নিজগৃহে বন্দী রাখার আদেশ প্রদান করিলেন।”

15. It appears that the detaining authority passed the order under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act 1974 being satisfied that it was necessary for the maintenance of public safety and public order that the detenu should be detained. The grounds for detention which was communicated to the detenu on 24.12.90 Annexure 'B' reads as follows:

“১৯৭৪ সালের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইন (১৯৭৪ সালের ১৪ নং আইন) এর ৮নং ধারা মোতাবেক অন্তরীন করার কারণ অবগত করন।

১৯৭৪ সালের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ৮নং ধারা মোতাবেক সাবেক উপ-রাষ্ট্রপতি জনাব মওদুদ আহমদ, পিতা-মরহুম মওলানা মমতাজ উদ্দিন আহমদ, ১৫৯, গুলশান এভিনিউ, ঢাকাকে জানানো যাইতেছে যে নিম্নবর্ণিত কারণ সমূহের জন্য উপরোক্ত আইনের Section 3 (I)(a)ধারায় আপনারে অন্তরীন করার আদেশ প্রয়োজনীয় বলিয়া মনে করা হইয়াছেঃ

১।একজন দুর্নীতি পরায়ন ও ক্ষমতার অপব্যবহারকারী ব্যক্তি হিসাবে জনসাধারণের মনে আপনার বিরুদ্ধে ক্ষোভ রহিয়াছে এবং সাবেক রাষ্ট্রপতি ৪ঠা ডিসেম্বর, ১৯৯০ তারিখে রেডিও বাংলাদেশে এবং টেলিভিশনে পদত্যাগের ঘোষণা প্রচারের পর পরই বিপুল সংখ্যক জনসাধারণ রাজপথে নামিয়া আসে এবং বিভিন্ন স্থানে পূর্বেকার সরকারের সহিত সম্পর্কিত ব্যক্তিদের এবং প্রতিষ্ঠানের উপর স্বতঃস্ফূর্তভাবে জনসাধারণের পক্ষ হইতে হামলা পরিচালিত হয় যাহা এতকালের পুঞ্জীভুত ক্ষোভেরই বহিঃপ্রকাশ এবং ১নং অনুচ্ছেদে বর্ণিত পরিস্থিতির কারণে আপনার জীবরেন উপর জনসাধারণের পক্ষ হইতে হামলা পরিচালনের সমূহ সম্ভাবনা ছিল, এবং

২। আপনি গত ৮-১২-৯০ ইং তারিখে দৈনিক ‘মর্নিং সান’ পত্রিকার সাংবাদিকদের সহিত আপনার বাসভবনে একান্ত সাক্ষাৎকারে জাতীয় পার্টি ও আপনার নিজের ভবিষ্যৎ রাজনীতি সম্বন্ধে বিভিন্ন উষ্কানিম��লক বক্তব্য পেশ করেন যাহা ৯-১২-৯০ ইং তারিখের ‘দি মর্নিং সান’ পত্রিকায় প্রকাশিত হয়। ইহার ফলশ্রুতিতে জনগণের একটি অংশ উত্তেজিত হইয়া গত ১০-১২-৯০ ইংরেজী তারিখে আপনার বাসভবনে ককটেল বিস্ফোরণ ঘটাইয়া ভাংচুর করে। এর পর আপনি আপনার উপরোক্ত স্বীয় বাসভবনে হামলা চলাকালীন সময়ে উপস্থিত আপনার জীবনের নিরাপত্তা বিঘ্নিত হইত বলিয়া প্রতীয়মান হইতেছে, এবং

৩। আপনার আত্মগোপন করার ফলে জনমনে অসন্তোষ এবং ঘৃনার উদ্রেক হয় যাহার ফলে জন নিরাপত্তা (public safety)এবং জনশৃংখলা (public order) মারাত্মকভাবে বিঘ্নিত হইবার সম্ভাবনা দেখা দেয়, এবং

৪। উপরোক্ত অনুচ্ছেদসমূহে বর্ণিত অবস্থা এবং দেশে বিরাজমান পরিস্থিতির সামত্রিক বিবেচনায় সরকারের নিকট সন্সোষজনকভাবে প্রতীয়মান হইয়াছে যে জন নিরাপত্থা ‘public safety) এবং জন শৃখংলা(Public order)এর স্বার্থে ১৯৭৪ সালের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের 3(I)(a)ধারার বিধান অনুসারে আপনাকে অন্তরীন রাখা প্রয়োজন।

(২) উপরে প্রদত্ত ঘটনা ও তথ্যাবলী ছাড়া অন্য ঘটনা বা তথ্য বর্ণনা করা জনস্বার্থ বিরোধী হইবে বলিয়া তাহা প্রদান করা হইল না।

(৩) জ্ঞাতব্য যে এই অন্তরীন আটকাদেশের বিরুদ্ধে আপনি সরকারের নিকট নিবেদন করার অধিকার সংরক্ষণ করেন।
