16. It has been contended by Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, that the Court must be satisfied that there are materials on the basis of which the detaining authority passed the order of detention and that the ground must be related to the purpose of the statute and there must be a nexus between the order of detention and the ground furnished by the detaining authority. According to Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, there are three grounds as mentioned in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of Annexure B. The first of which is vague and indefinite and referred to the likelihood of an attacked on the life of the detenu; the second one is with regard to the statement given to the reporter of Daily Morning Sun by the detenu on 8.12.90 and an incident that occurred on 10.12.90 in the residence of the detenu for which the safety of the life of the detenu would have been affected had house been present at his house at the time of the occurrence; the 3rd ground mentioned therein is that the detenu went into hiding and this may be for the safety and security of his life. According to Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, these are three independent grounds which led to the conclusion mentioned in paragraph 4 i.e. for maintenance of public safety and public order. But, according to the learned Advocate, those are merely disturbance of law and order leading to disorder which is not necessarily for prejudicial activities. He has referred to the case of Ranabir Das Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs (28 DLR 48) in support of his contention wherein it has been held that contravention of law always affects the order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or public at large; mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is not necessarily sufficient for taking notion for prejudicial activities. In this connection he has also referred to the case of Pushker Mukharjee and others vs. The Slate of West Bengal (AIR 1970 (SC) 852) wherein it has been held that a mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is not necessarily sufficient for action under the preventive detention but a disturbance which will affect public order comes within the ambit of public order. According to Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq, the first ground cannot constitute any prejudicial act on the part of the detenu within the meaning of section 2(i) of the Special Powers Act and the order of detention was passed only to protect the detenu which is the duty of every Government to preserve the life and property of every citizen. According to the learned Advocate, the mere giving of an interview with the reporters of newspapers cannot be treated as a prejudicial act as it does not violate any law; and the incident that occurred on 10.12.90 at the residence of the detenu was an act of a handful of persons politically opposed to the detenu and the damage of the house of the detenu by a few miscreants cannot be regarded as endangering public safety and public order but it would be a matter of law and order only. Further, the mere absconding or hiding on the part of the detenu cannot be regarded as a valid ground for detention.

17. The learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, has contended that the reading of Annexure it would appear that there is only one ground for detention of the detenu which is for preventing the detenu from endangering public safety or the maintenance of public order. According to the learned Attorney-General, paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of Annex\i, 'B' are pieces of evidence or materials which led to the conclusion of the detaining authority as mentioned in paragraph 4. The learned Attorney-General further submitted that paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 4 were expressed in disjunctive manner but they constitute a single ground. In support of his contention the learned Attorney-General has referred to the case of The. State of Bombay Vs. Atma Ram Shridhar Veidya (AIR 1951 (SC) 157) wherein it has been pointed out that the grounds have formed the basis of satisfaction when formulated, are bound to contain certain facts but mostly they are deduction from facts. Ordinarily the ground in the sense is conclusion drawn by the authorities which indicate the kind of prejudicial act the detenu is suspected of being engaged in and that will be sufficient to enable him to make representation. According to the learned Attorney- General, Annexure B contained only one conclusion drawn from the facts stated in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3. It is submitted by the learned Attorney-General that it would appear from the ground there is a public resentment against the detenu for his alleged corrupt practice and abuse of power, that there was continuous agitation by the public at large immediately after the announcement of resignation of the former President on 4.12.90 for which there was probability of disturbance of public order even leading to attack on the life of the detenu; that as a matter of fact in view of his statement in the Morning Sun a section of public became excited and attacked his residence by exploding cocktail and damaging the house, and had the detenu been present at his house at that time there was likelihood of danger to his life and that there was a public resentment and hatred for his going into hiding as a result of which there is likelihood of serious disturbance to public safety and public order. According to the learned Attorney-General, paragraph 1 of Annexure B has a reference to the antecedent past history and past conduct of the detenu and this background of the detenu can be the basis of his detention. In support of his contention the .learned Attorney-General has referred to the case of Nurunnahar Begum Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others (29 DLR 372) wherein it has been held that preventive detention is called for only when certain prejudicial activities create impression in the mind of the detaining authority, that if the subject is allowed to remain free when he is likely to act prejudicially endangering public safety and these apprehensions can be formed, on the basis of antecedent history of the detenu. He has also referred to the case of Keshave Nilkanth Joglekar Vs. The Commissioner of Police, Greater Bombay and others (AIR 1957 (SC) 28) wherein it has been held that past activities of a person can be a ground for detention because what a person is likely to do in future can only be a matter of inference from various circumstances, and his past record will be valuable and often the only record on which it could be made. He has also referred to the case of Nagen Murmu Vs. The State of West Bengal (AIR 1973 (SC) 844) wherein it has been held that the past conduct antecedent history of a person can appropriately be taken into account in making a detention order. The learned Attorney-General, therefore, submitted that having regard to the antecedent past history of the detenu, his statement in the daily Morning Sun and his absconding along with the overall prevailing situation in the country justified the notion of the detaining authority in passing the impugned order of detention for the maintenance of public safety and public order. I find force in this contention of the learned Attorney-General. It is an isolated act which might lead to law and order situation, but the several facts stated in the ground of detention in the background of the overall prevailing situation of the country is to be considered as the basis for passing the impugned order of detention.

<u>18. It has been contended that the materials mentioned in the affidavit-in-opposition are of subsequent dates and thus cannot be the basis for the order of detention when it was passed on 11.12.90. It is true that the materials mentioned in the affidavit-in-opposition are of subsequent dates but these referred to the past activities of the detenu. An individual act, for example when A stabs B is purely a law and order matter but when during a communal riot a person of one community stabs a person of another community this cannot be regarded as a stray act because it would effect the whole ( community at large leading to endangering the public safety and public order. To my mind reading the ground as mentioned in Annexure B the detaining ) authority had before it the antecedent history of the I detenu, the recent outburst of a section of the people 3 for his statement in the Morning Sun, his n absconding along with the overall prevailing circumstances in the country justifying the passing of the impugned order of detention. The ground is obviously as mentioned in Annexures A and B for the maintenance of public safety and public order. An action by way of preventive detention must be passed on suspicion and the Court is not the tribunal to investigate whether circumstance exist warranting the restraint of the person. Having considered the materials on record I am of the view that the detaining authority had sufficient materials for passing the order of detention under section 3 of the Act for the purpose of preventive detention of the detenu for preventing him from endangering public safety and public order which is a prejudicial act within the meaning of section 2(f)(iii) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. In that view of the matter I am inclined to hold that the impugned order of detention is not liable to be struck down by this Court. The Rule is, therefore, discharged.</u>

Md. Badruzzaman J: I regret my inability to subscribe to the view of my learned brother Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker, J., that the detention of Mr. Moudud Ahmed is lawful. The facts of the case and the decisions of superior Courts including those of Pakistan Supreme Court and our Appellate Division relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule have been quite elaborately dealt with by him and it is needless for me to repeat the same except the important aspects of the case with which I respectfully differ with him.

20. Where the order of detention is challenged under Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution, the High Court Division is to be satisfied that the person in custody is not so held without lawful authority or in any unlawful manner. It is now a settled position of law that the constitutional obligation imposed upon this Court by Article 102 (2)(b)(i) is clearly to make an objective assessment of the materials on which the necessary satisfaction of the detaining authority had been based and to be satisfied that an average prudent man could reasonably be so satisfied. In this connection reference may be made to the decision in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD) 1 in which their Lordships of the Appellate Division held as under:

"The order of detention for its validity is to be tested on the basis, whether the detaining authority had before it materials which gave a rational probative value to the order and not extraneous to the purpose of the Act, and beyond which, the order of detention is immune from challenge, except on ground of malafides"

The Government, in exercise of its powers under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act 1974 ordered detention of Mr. Moudud Ahmed, former Vice-President of the Republic for 120 days "for public safety and maintenance of public order" without recording its satisfaction in express words that the detenu was required to be detained for preventing him from doing any prejudicial act. Section 3(1)(a) of the Act reads thus:

"3(1) The Government may, if satisfied with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order-

(a) directing that such person be detained;

"Prejudicial act", as defined in section 2(f) of the Act, reads thus: "Prejudicial act" means any act which is intended or likely-

(i) to prejudice the sovereignty or defence of Bangladesh.

(ii) to prejudice the maintenance of friendly relations of Bangladesh with foreign states;

(iii) to prejudice the security of Bangladesh or t9 endanger public safety or the maintenance of public order;

(iv) to create or excite feeling of enmity or hatred between different communities, classes or sections of people;

(v) to interfere with or encourage or incite interference with the administration of law or the maintenance of law and order;

(vi) to prejudice the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community;

(vii) to cause fear or alarm to the public or to any section of the public;

(viii) to prejudice the economic or financial interest of the State;"

Here we are concerned with a part of section 2 (f)(iii) which states that "prejudicial act" means any act which is intended or likely to endanger public safety or maintenance of public order. The act of the detenu unless intended or likely to endanger public safety or maintenance of public order cannot be the basis for an order under section 3(i)(a). If in any situation the maintenance of public order or public safety is endangered or disturbed by the acts of person of persons other than the detenu, the latter cannot be detained under that section. Since the impugned order of detention does not expressly record the satisfaction of the Government to the effect that the detention of the detenu is necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act or any act which is intended or likely to endanger public safety or maintenance or public order, the detention of the detenu is ex facie illegal and without lawful authority.

21. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that there is no basis for the 3 grounds on which the order of detention has been Made and that these grounds are vague, indefinite, irrelevant and extraneous. Mr. Aminul Huq, the learned Attorney General, on the other hand, has contended that the detenu had been detained under one ground alone and that paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of the Annexure-'B' constitute different pieces of evidence by which the Authority making the order came to the conclusion that the detenu was acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety and maintenance of public order. To substantiate his contention as to only one ground, he has referred to the words "এবং" (and) appearing at the end of the paragraphs 1-3 which show that the evidence stated therein constituted only one ground as stated in paragraph 4 that the detention of the detenu was necessary in the interest of public safety and public order. I am unable to accept this contention of the learned Attorney General as the expressions ১। “নিম্নলিখিত কারণসমূহের”

"in the preamble and ২। “১নং অনুচ্ছেদে বর্ণিত পরিস্থিতির কারণে”

in paragraph-1 of Annexure "B" and its reading in totality show that as many as three grounds as stated in paragraphs 1-3 were communicated to the detenu and the order of detention has been based on those grounds coupled with the prevailing condition in the country. It is also a settled position of law that if one of the grounds is vague or unsustainable, (though other grounds are not) the detention will be illegal as it is not possible to gauge in such cases in what manner or to what extent the vague or unsustainable ground operated on the mind of the detaining authority and contributed to the creation of his satisfaction as required under section 3 of the Act.

22. The first ground relates to the alleged corruption and abuse of power by the detenu which generated public anger against him and that his detention was necessary for his own safety which was likely to be jeopardised by the spontaneous attack of the people on the supporters of the former regime. If the detenu had practiced corruption or committed criminal misconduct by abusing his position while in office, the law would take its own course. The use of the extraordinary power of preventive detention contained in the Special Powers Act for purposes for which ordinary law is sufficient is a glaring proof of abuse of statutory powers by the detaining authority. Moreover the alleged corruption by itself would not come within the definition of prejudicial act as defined in section 2(f). The alleged corruption and abuse of power having been already committed, there would arise no necessity for detention of the detenu to prevent him from prejudicing the economic or financial interest of the state. From the perusal of this ground it is evident that impugned order of detention was passed to protect or save the detenu from attack by the people and for the safety of his life but it was not intended to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act. No person can be kept in protective custody for his own safety and such ground falls outside the ambit of the Special Powers Act.

23. As regards the 2nd ground it may be stated that the press interview given by the detenu on 8.12.90 which was published on the following day in the English Daily "Morning Sun" (Annexure '2' on the affidavit-in-opposition) does not contain anything which violated any law, nor it contained my provocative statement to endanger public safety or maintenance of public order. In that interview the detenu only emphasised that the caretaker Government should maintain neutrality and ensure the participation of all political parties including Jatiya Party in the coming election. The attack and damage caused to the house of the detenu on 10.12.90 allegedly by a section of the public cannot be the result or consequence of the said press interview as the same was very innocent. The Government, in all fairness, should have taken action according to law against persons who were responsible for the said incident and such undesirable incident should not have-been made an excuse for passing of the order of detention. Such a press interview by a political person like the detenu who till recently held the office of the Vice President of the Republic cannot be construed to be a prejudicial act when the Jatiya Party, to which the detenu belongs, or its members had not been debarred from participating in the parliamentary poll scheduled to be held on the 27th of this month. The detenu, in my view, has got legal right to make statement as reported in the 'Morning Sun' when the freedom of press and freedom of speech are guaranteed under Article 39 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. This ground also shows that the detention of the detenu was necessitated for the safely of his life and not to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act and thus this also falls outside the ambit of the Special Powers Act.

24. The 3rd ground relates to the hiding of the detenu which resulted in public dissatisfaction and hatred against him and which was likely to endanger public safety and public order. The order of detention was passed on 11.12.90 and the detenu was arrested on 20.12.90. If the detaining authority had reason to believe that the detenu had absconded or was concealing himself so that the order of detention could not be executed, the Government could take action in accordance with the provision of section 7 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 which reads thus :

"7. If the Government or a District Magistrate or an Additional District Magistrate mentioned in section 2(3), as the case may be, has reason to believe that a person in respect of whom a detention order has been made has absconded or is concealing himself so that the order cannot be executed, it or he may—

(a) make a report in writing of the fact to a Magistrate of the first class having jurisdiction in the place where the said person ordinarily resides; and there-upon the provisions of sections 87, 88 and 89 of the Code shall apply in respect of the said person and his property as if the order directing that he be detained were a warrant issued by the Magistrate;

(b) by order notified in the official Gazette direct the said person to appear before such officer, at such place, and within such period as may be specified in the order; and if the said person fails to comply with such direction he shall, unless he proves that it was not possible for him to comply therewith and that he had, within the period specified in the order, informed the officer of the reason which rendered compliance therewith impossible and of his whereabouts, be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both."

<u>25. The Government, it is evident, did not take any action in the light of section 7 till the arrest of the detenu. The hiding of the dctenu does not by itself constitute a prejudicial act. The act of absconding it no doubt a relevant piece of evidence under section 8 of the Evidence Act, but its value would always depend on the circumstances of such case. Mere absconding or hiding does not necessarily lead to a firm conclusion of guilty mind of the detenu. Even an innocent person may feel panicky or try to evade arrest when unjustifiably suspected of grave offence or of indulging in prejudicial act. The hiding of the detenu in a house at Baridhara might have been prompted by his instinct of self preservation.</u>

26. The facts stated in paragraph No. 4 of the Annexure-'B' cannot also be a valid ground for detention when the detenu, after he resigned from the office of the Vice-President, had not committed any overt act which could affect public order of affect the community at large. The prevailing situation in the country as referred to in paragraph 4 cannot be made an excuse to detain the detenu when he had not done any act to endanger public safety or public order. In this connection reference may be made to the case of Liversidge reported in 1942 AC 206 in which Lord Atkin laid down the famous dicta as under: "Amidst the clash of arms, the laws are not silent; they may be changed, but they speak the same language in war as in peace" respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition mentioned about reports published in several weekly papers after the date of the impugned order of detention in which allegations of corruption and abuse of power were made against the detenu. These publications being o subsequent dates, were not evidently before the detaining authority for its satisfaction when the order of detention was passed.

27. It has been contended by the learned Attorney General that the past conduct or antecedent history of a person can be taken into account in making an order of detention under the Special Powers Act. Without disputing the correctness of the contention, it may be said that such conduct or antecedent should ordinarily proximate in point of time and should have rational connection with the conclusion that the detention of the person is necessary. It has been repeatedly stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the detenu had a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to Jatiya Party and earlier regime in the administration and other areas to destabilise the present situation or the present caretaker Government and that in such situation the detention of the detenu was necessary to preserve and protect the public safety and public f order for holding free and fair election in the country. No such ground finds place in the grounds communicated to the detenu and such ground was not before the detaining authority at the time of passing of the impugned order of detention. This has been introduced in the affidavit- in-opposition to show that the detenu was indulging in activities which could come within the definition of prejudicial acts. This appears to be an after thought and a fiction of imagination. The order of detention, it is evident, has been passed in colourable exercise of authority and it has been vitiated by irrelevant grounds. This court cannot go beyond the grounds embodied in annexure-B on which the satisfaction of the detaining authority was based.

28. The object of enactment of the Special Powers Act, 1974 was to provide for special measures for the prevention of certain prejudicial invitees, for more speedy trial and effective punishment of certain grave offences and for matter connected therewith. Since the order of detention has been made without recording the satisfaction of the detaining authority that the detenu was required to be detained with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act, the order of detention must be held to be malafide as it was made contrary to the object and purposes of the Act. The grounds of detention show that the detaining authority was influenced by irrelevant grounds and extraneous consideration and there was no sufficient material before it to come to the conclusion that the detention of the detenu was necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any act which is intended or likely to endanger a public safety or maintenance of public order. The impugned order of detention was passed without any valid ground and without application of the mind of the detaining authority.

29. Having considered the facts and circumstances as detailed above, I am of the opinion that there is no material before this Court on the basis of which a prudent man may be satisfied as to the necessity of detaining the detenu for the purpose of preventing him from acting prejudicially to public safety or public order. I thus find that the order of detention of the detenu is illegal and that he is being held in custody without lawful authority and also in unlawful manner.

30. In the result, I would make the Rule absolute and direct that the detenu Mr. Moudud Ahmed be set at liberty forthwith, if he is not wanted in any other connection.

In view of the difference of opinion let the matter be placed before the learned Acting Chief Justice for necessary order.

End.

HIGH COURT DIVISION

(Special Original Jurisdiction)

Bimalendu Bikash Roy Choudhury J.

Writ Petition No. 12 of 1991.

M Mahmood ------ Petitioner

Vs.

Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and anr. ------Respondents

Judgment: March 4, 1991.

Rafiq-Ul-Huq with Shorful Islam Khan, Md. Azizul Huq and Anjuman Ara Shelly Advocates -------- For the Petitioner.

Aminul Huq, Attorney-General with Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General, Shahabuddin Ahmad, Deputy Attorney-General and Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, Assistant Attorney-General ------- For the Respondents.

Judgment

This Writ Petition has been preferred by one Mr. M Mahmood, son of late Moulana Momtazuddin Ahmed of House No. 11, Road No. 29, Sector 7, Uttara Model Town, PS Uttara, Dhaka challenging the legality of the detention of his younger brother Mr. Moudud Ahmed, erstwhile Vice-President of Bangladesh.

32. The matter was heard by a Division Bench of this court comprising IU Sarkar and B Zaman, JJ. After hearing the learned counsels for the parties my brother IU Sarkar, I took the view "that the detaining authority had sufficient materials for passing the order of detention under section 3 of the Act for the purpose of preventive detention of the &term for preventing him from endangering public safety and public order which is a prejudicial act within the meaning of section 3(0(111) of the Special Powers, Act, 1974", while my brother B Zaman, J opined that the order of detention is ex facie illegal as the impugned order does not expressly record the satisfaction of the Government to the affect that the detention of the detenu is necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any act prejudicial to public safety and public order. He was also of the view that the detaining authority failed to produce any material on the basis of which a prudent man could be satisfied as to the necessity of detaining the detcnu for the purpose of preventing him from acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety or public order and that the grounds of detention had no rational connection with the object of detention. There being thus a difference of opinion as to the validity of the detention, the learned Chief Justice by an order dated 16.2.1991, referred the matter to me for hearing and disposal.

33. The facts of the case have been fully set out in the judgment of my brother IU Sarkar, J. It is, therefore, needless to repeat the same. I, however propose to paint the back-drop with broad brush projecting the points raised before me.

34. On 11th December, 1990 the Government, in exercise of the power under section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act, passed an order directing that the detenu be detained for a period of 120 days from the date of the service of the order as it appeared to the satisfaction of the Government that his detention was necessary for the maintenance of public safety and public order. In pursuance of the said order the detenu was apprehended on 20th December 1990 and on the 24th December, 1990 the grounds for his detention were supplied to him. The English rendering of the grounds conveyed to the detenu runs thus:

a) That the public at large have a resentment in their minds against you as one indulging in corruption and misuse of power and with the announcement of the erstwhile President on the 4th of December, 1990 of his resignation a large number of people got down on the streets and made inroads upon the persons and institutions connected with the previous Government and spontaneous attack was conducted by the people upon the institution which is the expression of their pent up wrath and on account of the situation described in this first paragraph there was apprehension of attempt on your life, and

b) That on 8th December, 1990 last in your private interview with the journalist of "Morning Sun" in your house you had made various inciting statements about the future of Jatiya Party and yourself and also about your politics which has been published in the "Morning Sun". As a result a section of the public became incited and damaged your house by cocktail burst on 10.12.1990. Had you been present in the house after that, it appears, your life would have been jeopardized and.

c) That your abscondment has created dissatisfaction and hatred in the public mind as a result of which there is apprehension of serious disruption of public safety and public order, and

d) That on over-all consideration of the circumstances stated in the above paragraphs and the situation obtaining in the country it appears to the satisfaction of the Government that your detention under section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act. 1974 is necessary in the interest of public safety and the maintenance of public order.

e) Furnishing of any more facts and particulars than those given above would be against public interest.

f) You are further informed that you have a right to make a representation to the Government against the order of detention made against you."

35. The petitioner thereupon presented this petition. He alleged that the grounds have no rational nexus with the object mentioned in section 3(1) of the said Act. He also alleged that the particulars suffered from insufficient communication crippling the constitutional right of representation of the detenu. He alleged further that the preventive action was taken purely for ulterior purpose to create a hurdle for the detenu to contest in the next election.

36. In response to the Rule Nisi issued by this Court Major (Retd) Chowdhury Montajuddin Ahmed, Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairi of the Government filed affidavit-in-opposition, in para 4 of which it is averred that "the detenu had a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to Jatiya Party and earlier regime in the administration and other areas to destabilise the present situation and thereby it can endanger public safety and public order and as such for the time being his detention has become necessary with a view to preserve and protect the public safety and public order for having free and fair election in the country by the present caretaker Government."

37. The gravamen of the petitioner's grievance is that the impugned preventive action of the Government is beyond the purview of the said Act and hence violative of Article 32 of the Constitution which inhibits blanket and arbitrary deprivation of a person's liberty by authority.

38. The Special Powers Act was promulgated on 9th February, 1974 with one of its objects as gated in the preamble "to provide for special measures for the prevention of certain prejudicial activities". Section 2(f) defines prejudicial act to mean an act which is intended or is likely—

(i) to prejudice the sovereignty or defence of Bangladesh;

(ii) to prejudice the maintenance of friendly relations of Bangladesh with foreign states:

(iii) to prejudice the security of Bangladesh or to endanger public safety or the maintenance of public order:

(iv) to create or excite feelings of enmity or hatred between different communities, classes or section of people:

(v) to interfere with or encourage or incite interference with the administration of law or the maintenance of law and order:

(vi) to prejudice the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community;

(vii) to cause fear or alarm to the public or to any section of the public.

(viii) to prejudice the economic or financial interest of the State.

Section 3(1) (a) then lays down that the Government, may if satisfied with respect to any person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order directing that such person be detained".

<u>39. The said provision manifestly requires that before the Government can pass an order of detention it must be satisfied with respect to the individual person that his activities are directed against the object mentioned in the section and that it is necessary to prevent him from acting in such a manner. While empowering the Government to pass a preventive order the section thus appears to have expressly made it a part of its duty to satisfy itself about the existence of what the lawmakers regard as condition precedent to the exercise of that power. An order being indicative of the state of the mind of the authority making it, the concerned order of detention must expressly state that the Government is satisfied that it is necessary to make the order to prevent the individual from doing any prejudicial act. If the order is silent in that respect the detention will undoubtedly be not in terms of the section.</u>

40. The question then immediately arises whether the Government complied with the requirements of the section in passing the impugned order of detention. The first ground of attack against the validity of the order is that the detaining authority failed to record its satisfaction that it was considered necessary to make the order of detention with a view to preventing the detenu from doing any prejudicial act. The order of detention reads thus:

আদেশ

যেহেতু সরকার এই মর্মে সন্তুষ্ট হইয়াছেন যে জনাব মওদুদ আহমদ সাবেক উপ-রাষ্ট্রপতি ১৫৯, গুলশান এভিনিউ, ঢাকাকে জন নিরাপত্তার ও জন শৃংখলা রক্ষার জন্য আটক রাখা প্রয়োজন।

এক্ষনে সেহেতু সরকার The Special Powers Act, 1974 (Act XIV of 74) Sec. 3 (I)(a) ধারা অর্পিত ক্ষমতা বলে উপরোক্ত জনাব মওদুদ আহমদকে এতউদ্দেশ্যে এই আদেশ জারীর দিন হইতে ১২০ (এক শত বিশ) দিনের জন্য নিজ গৃহে বন্দী রাখার আদেশ প্রদান করিলেন।

ভারপ্রাপ্ত রাষ্ট্রপতির আদেশক্রমে

স্বাক্ষরঃ অস্পষ্ট

সিনিয়র সহকারী সচিব (নিরাপত্তা)

<u>41. Obviously, there is nothing in the order to even suggest that the Government was satisfied that it was necessary to make the order of detention with a view to preventing the detenu from doing any prejudicial act which is the sine qua non for exercise of the power under section 3(1) of the said Act. This omission undoubtedly constitutes a serious infirmity which has inevitably taken the order of detention out of the ambit of the section. Another ground of challenge urged on behalf of the petitioner is that the order of detention ex facie shows that the detenu was detained simply in the interest of public safety and the maintenance of public order. Section 3(1) read with section 2(f) of the Act clearly prescribes certain specific grounds on which alone a person may be detained without trial. If a person is detained on any ground other than those prescribed in the section, the preventive action will obviously be not in accordance with the law. The order of detention is plainly, on the face of it, purported to be made in the interest of public safety and the maintenance of public order. The Act nowhere sets out the same as a specific ground for preventive detention. I am, therefore, of the opinion that on its very face the impugned order of detention does not fall within the scope and ambit of section 3(1) of the Act.</u>

42. The view I have taken finds support from the decision in the case of Mrs. Tahera Chowdhury Vs. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh, 40 DLR 193. In that case an order of detention under section 3(1)(a) of the Act as in the instant case simply stated that it was made in the interest of public safety without mentioning that the detention of the detenu was considered necessary with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act. A question arose whether such an order was legal. A Division Bench of this Court answered it in the following terms:

"Section 3 of the Special Powers Act provides very expressly that the Government may, if satisfied with respect to any person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order directing that such person be detained. Thus it is absolutely clear that section 3 of the Special Powers Act only empowers the Government to direct detention of a person only if it is satisfied that with a view to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary to make his detention. Annexure 'A' the detention order nowhere mentions that the detention of the detenu was considered necessary to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act. Thus on the face of the order itself it is found to be without any legal authority in view of the provision of section 3 of the Special Powers Act.

It was further observed;

"the said order of detention gives the only ground for detention saying that detention order is considered necessary in the interest of public safety. There is no provision for making a detention order merely, in the interest of public safety throughout the Special Powers Act."

43. I now tuna to the grounds of detention in order to objectively analyse whether those have any rational connection with the object mentioned in section 3(1) of the Act. Paragraph 1 of the grounds alleged that the people had pent-up wrath against the detenu for his corruption and misuse of power and so when the erstwhile President made an announcement of his resignation or 4th December, 1990 a large number of people came out in streets and attacked the persons and the institutions connected with the previous Government for which there was apprehension for the security of the life of the detenu. Paragraph 2 alleged that the detenu in his private interview with the journalist of "Morning Sun" on 8th December, 1990 made certain statement about the future of Jatiya Party and about his politics and when the said statement was published a section of the public became incited and being so enraged they damaged the house of the detenu by cocktail burst on 10th December, 1990 and had he been present in the house his life would have been at stake. Paragraph 3 alleged that as the detenu went underground there was dissatisfaction and hatred in the minds of the public as a result of which there was apprehension of serious disruption of public safety and public order. The last paragraph alleged that on consideration of the said circumstances and the situation prevailing in the country it appeared to the satisfaction of the Government that the detention of the detenu was necessary in the interest of the public safety and the maintenance of public order.

<u>44. In none of the said paragraphs it is alleged that the detenu indulged himself in any activity endangering public safety and the maintenance of public order. The grounds, read as a whole, on the other hand, indicate that it was a section of the public which having had resentment in its mind against the detenu for his corruption and abuse of power was out to attack him and his property resulting in the breach of law and order for which it was necessary to give him protection from such attack. Section 3(1) of the Act confers on the Government the power to detain an individual for the purpose of preventing him from doing one or other of the 8 prejudicial acts mentioned in section 2(f)(1) to (viii) of the Act and for no other purpose. To keep a particular individual in detention for the purpose of protecting him from the onslaught of others is not contemplated within the four corners of the said provision.</u>

<u>45. In the affidavit-in-opposition it is, however, averred that the detenu has a strong background of political capability and such capability is sufficient enough to utilise entrenched support available to the Jatiya Party and the earlier regime in the administration and other areas to destabilise the present situation and thereby it can endanger public safety and public order for which detention was considered necessary with a view to preserving and protecting the public safety and public order. No such ground appears to have been stated in the document communicated to the detenu under section 8 of the Special Powers Act and the detenu had also no opportunity to make any representation in respect thereof. So the Government cannot now fall upon the same to defend its preventive action. Apart from that, the detenu might have a capability to create problems to public safety and public order, but that by itself cannot be the basis for passing an order of detention so long as he does not indulge himself in any prejudicial act endangering public safety and public order and the members of the public are not affected by his activities.</u>

46. In that view of the matter I find that the object of the detention does not fall within the scope of section 3(1) of the Act. There is also no other provision of law which authorises the Government to make an order for preventive detention of a particular individual. Article 32 of the Constitution enjoins that no person shall be deprived of personal liberty save in accordance with law. As the order of detention is found to be not covered by any law, the impugned action must be held to be violative of the said constitutional mandate.

47. In the view I have taken it is not necessary for me to go into the question whether there is any material basis for the impugned order of detention or not.

48. For all these reasons I am satisfied that the detenu is being detained without any lawful authority. I thus concur with the view expressed in the Judgment of my brother B Zaman, J.

The Rule is, accordingly, made absolute and I direct that the detenu Mr. Moudud Ahmed, son of late Moulana Momtajuddin Ahmed of 159, Gulshan Avenue, PS Gulshan, Dhaka now detained in Dhaka Central Jail be at once released from custody if not wanted in connection with any other case.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 107 of 1987.
lawyer:
MI Farooqui with M Saleemullah, Advocates ----- For the Appellant.
Kaiseruddin Ahmed, DAG ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Hashem (Md) ----- Appellant
Vs.
Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Jalil J : This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against a judgment and decree dated 30.6.87 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 353 of 1984 dismissing the suit.

2. The appellant as plaintiff filed the said suit for declaration that he is a citizen of Bangladesh and that the suit property is not an abandoned property.

3. The case of the plaintiff is, that he is a citizen of Bangladesh and a permanent resident of Dhaka since 1948. The Government leased out the suit property to the plaintiff on 5.6.1961 for 99 years commencing from 1.1.1961 with the building standing thereon at a consideration of Tk. 2,700/- and the possession of the same was delivered to him on 20.7.1961. The plaintiff was compelled to leave the suit property for the time being, for his personal safety just after the liberation of Bangladesh being a non-local and took shelter at 70, Water Works Road, Dhaka. Thereafter some persons took illegal possession of the property and later on it was listed as an abandoned property on 28.4.72. The suit property is not an abandoned property under any circumstances and it was listed as abandoned property due to misconception of President's Order 16 of 1972 and that the plaintiff made several representations to different authorities to release the suit property and restore possession to him but without any result and so he had to file the suit.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant namely, Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others by filing a written statement denying the material allegations and contending that the suit is not maintainable and that the suit property was taken over as an abandoned property and it has been under the control, management and supervision of the defendants and it has been allotted to one Begum Roushan Ara from 1972, as the whereabouts of the plaintiff was not known.

5. The plaintiff examined himself as PW 1 and defendant examined one witness as DW 1.

6. .The plaintiff substantiated his case as ma out in the plaint. DW 1 in his deposition stated that as the plaintiff was not available after liberation of Bangladesh the suit property was taken over as abandoned property and has been leased out to one Begum Roushanara.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing dismissed the suit on the grounds that a simple declaration without a prayer for consequential relief is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and thereby he held that the suit is not maintainable.

8. Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant, submitted that the learned Trial Court erred in dismissing the suit without considering that the property is in possession of the government and no prayer for recovery of possession is required.

9. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government, submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly dismissed the suit as the property is in possession of a third party as a lessee under the Government.

<u>10. The learned Subordinate Judge came to the finding that the plaintiff filed many papers which amply proved his right, title and interest in the suit property. The plaintiff asserted that he was granted lease for 99 years by the Government and he was in that house till the liberation of Bangladesh and also filed various papers and documents to show his title and those were not denied by the government. The defendant government also does not dispute the title of the plaintiff. So we find that the plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession of the suit land till 16.12.71. The Government defendant in its written statement asserted that during the liberation movement and afterwards the whereabouts of the plaintiff were not known and so the defendants rightly treated the suit property as abandoned property. Hence the Government is holding the property treating the same to be of the plaintiff. If it is declared by the Court that it is not an abandoned property the Government will have no reason to possess the same and will be under obligation to restore possession to the plaintiff and no prayer for recovery of possession as a consequential relief is necessary. Hence the suit is quite maintainable and it is not barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. It is the case of the defendant that the suit property has been leased out to one Begum Roushan Ara. The Government simply is in the management of the property which is to be done under Rule 10 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Building in the Urban Area) Rules, 1972, which runs as follows :</u>

<u>"10. The management and disposal of the building shall be done in the following manner</u>

<u>(a) lease on monthly basis.</u>

<u>(b) disposal on higher purchase system, and</u>

<u>(c) disposal by outright auction."</u>

<u>11. So the lease, if any, granted is a monthly lease. The defendant, however, did not file any paper relating to the alleged lease. Be that as it may, the lessee has no independent interest but her right depends on the Government's right and so she is neither a necessary party to the suit nor any prayer for her eviction is necessary, as the Government may evict her as monthly lessee if the property is declared as not abandoned property.</u>

12. The moot question is whether the suit property is an abandoned property.

13. The abandoned property has been defined in Article 2 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 as follows :

(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise, or manage in person his property, including—

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh."

14. It is in evidence that the suit property was taken over as abandoned property on 28.4.72 and soon thereafter the plaintiff approached the defendant for release of the property by the middle of June, 1972 and he also swore in an affidavit before a Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka on 5.6.1972 owing allegiance to Bangladesh which are not denied by the defendants.

15. It is in evidence that the plaintiff was all along in Bangladesh and made claim from time to time to the defendants for release of the property starting from 30.6.1972 to 18.7.84 and had filed copies of about 2 dozens letters which are marked exhibits without objection, but no action was taken. Only on 2.1.84 a letter was issued by the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar, Dhaka (Exhibit) to appear with his papers in support of his claim. The plaintiff alleged that he produced all his papers but no order was passed. However the claim of the plaintiff was never denied. Hence there is no question of limitation.

<u>16. There is no allegations that the plaintiff acquired citizenship of any other country. Plaintiff being admittedly a Pakistani national before liberation and a resident of Dhaka city and the suit property was leased out to him and after liberation of Bangladesh he continued to live in Dhaka and did not acquire citizenship of any other country, there is no reason to hold that he ceased to be a Bangladeshi national or lost his citizenship. It may be mentioned that just after the liberation he took shelter elsewhere at Dhaka but when he appeared and claimed his property his whereabouts were very much known and so there is no reason to treat the suit property as abandoned property.</u>

17. In this view of the matter we are of the opinion that the plaintiff is entitled to the decree prayed for and we also find that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in dismissing the suit holding that it is not maintainable.

18. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is decreed on contest and it is declared that the plaintiff is a citizen of Bangladesh and the suit property is not an abandoned property.

In the facts and circumstances of the case, we direct both parties to bear their respective costs althrough.

End.

lawyer:
MI Farooqui with M Salem Ullah, Advocates -----For the Petitioner.
MH  Khondker with AJ Mohammad Ali, Advocates -----For Respondent Nos. 1 & 2. 
Md. Faizul Kabir with Md. Omar Faruque, Advocates -----For Respondent Nos. 5-12 & 14-19
parties:
Rana Awan (Mrs) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Works, and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed J: By this application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution of an order passed by the Respondent No. 1 through the Respondent No. 2, the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh on 17.4.85 refusing to release certain properties from the list of abandoned properties which has been earlier declared as abandoned property under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972, has been called in question with a further prayer for directing the respondents to release the said property and deliver possession thereof to the petitioner.

2. The subject-matter of the writ petition is a commercial building situated on CS Plot No. 32 of CS Khatian No. 45 of Mouza Kaoran, JL No. 263 within PS Tejgaon, in the District of Dhaka, and bearing Touzi No. 9859 described in detail in the schedule to the application.

3. It is alleged by the petitioner that the land on which this building stands originally belonged to some persons named Dengu Purification, Dominic Purification, Alfred Purification, Bengu Purification and Maria Cruze and they sold this land to Alhaj Sheikh Mohammad Noor who was the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioner and others by executing and registering a deed of conveyance in the year 1961. Al-haj Sheikh Mohammad Noor then transferred this land to the petitioner and her four brothers, one sister and her mother by executing a deed of conveyance in the year 1969. The petitioner having paid Rs. 18,750/- out of the total consideration of Rs. 35,000/- was entitled to 12 annas share in this property and acknowledging this, she along with her co-sharers executed a declaration in the year 1966 before a Notary Public in Karachi. Accordingly, the petitioner is alleged to have acquired 12 annas share and her 12 annas share was duly recorded in the SA record of right. Thereafter, she and her co-sharers constructed a commercial building on this land she having spent 12 annas share of the total expenditure of the construction of this building and her co-sharers having spent 4 annas share of the said expenditure. She was a national of Bangladesh along with her husband and children. Some time in 1971 she went to Karachi with her children for attending a social function there and before her return from Karachi Bangladesh became independent on 16th December, 1971. In view of the law and order situation then prevailing in Bangladesh and the then Pakistan she could not immediately come back to Bangladesh and was repatriated to Bangladesh from Pakistan along with her children at the instance of her husband who also happens to be a permanent national and resident of Bangladesh. The Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh, also acknowledged her as a Bangladesh national and a permanent citizen of Bangladesh. The petitioner also alleged that she was all along a national of Bangladesh and never failed to manage or otherwise look after the property in question. Despite this fact the entire property including her 12 annans share therein was declared and treated abandoned property by the respondent No. 1. After her return from Pakistan in 1975 she tried to get. this property released by approaching various authorities but failed. She then filed an application to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar South. Dhaka under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 claiming that the said property was not at all abandoned property to the extent of her 12 annas share and also praying for releasing her share. After hearing her and considering all her papers the Sub-Divisional Officer, who was the prescribed authority dealing with such application, allowed her prayer, declared the property to the extent of her 12 annas share as not to be abandoned property and directed to release her share. The Sub-divisional Officer, Sadar South, then forwarded a copy of this order to the respondent No. 2 but in spite of this order the property was not released despite various representations made by her. Ultimately, on 17.4.85 by issuing the impugned letter under Memo. No. Sec.5/Dhaka-4/79 (part)/235 the respondent No. 1 informed her that the property had been correctly treated as abandoned property and, as such, her prayer was rejected.

4. The aforesaid order, it is alleged by the petitioner, is absolutely illegal and without lawful authority and, as such, the petitioner moved this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule in which the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 entered appearance and resisted the application by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending that the writ petition was not maintainable inasmuch as disputed questions of title are involved. The further contention of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 is that the Sub-divisional Officer, Sadar South, was not the proper authority to deal with an application under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and, as such, on the basis of the order of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar South, the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the impugned order to get any relief in this writ petition. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 have also challenged the alleged title of the petitioner to the extent of 12 annas share in the disputed property acknowledging, however, that the petitioner may have 2 annas share in the said property.

5. The respondent Nos. 5-12 and 14-19 also entered appearance and contested the writ petition by filing a joint affidavit-in-opposition almost on the same ground as has been taken by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. Their further contentions appear to be that the petitioner cannot claim 12 annas share in the property in question and that they are permanent lessees in different rooms of the building in question having taken lease from Syed Anwar Noor who happens to be one of the co-sharers of the Petitioner and was also Administrator of the estate called Noor Estate to which the disputed building in question formed a part.

6. Mr. M I Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, has first of all, argued that since the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar South, Dhaka, who was the prescribed authority, acting under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972, having passed a final order on an application under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and the Government having failed to prefer any appeal against the said order for setting aside order and also having to set aside the said order by way of revision, the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 had no alternative but to comply with and implement the said order of the prescribed authority and, in support of this submission, Mr. Farooqui has relied on two unreported decisions of this Court in Writ Petition. No. 149 of 1976 and Writ Petition No. 13 of 1977. In elaborating his argument Mr. Farooqui has submitted that since the legislature created a forum for a remedy against treatment of properties as abandoned properties by enacting Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and all concerned authorities were bound to comply with the order passed by the prescribed authority under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

7. Mr. MH Khondker, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents 1 and 2, had, on the other hand, contended that since the question as to the extent of title of the petitioner in the disputed property is involved, the said question cannot be decided within the ambit of this writ petition and in support of his contention he has relied upon the decisions reported in 16 DLR (SC) 453, 17 DLR (SC) 457, 14 CWN 31 and 87 CLJ 217. Mr. Khondker has also contended that the order of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar South, Dhaka for treating this property as not being abandoned property is absolutely without jurisdiction as he was not the prescribed authority under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

8. Mr. Md. Faizul Kabir, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of Mr. Md. Omar Faruque, the learned Advocate for the respondents 12 and 14-19, adopted the contentions of Mr. MH Khondker, the learned Advocate for the respondents 1 and 2.

9. Let us first of all, take up the maintainability of this writ petition. There cannot be any dispute as to the principle of law formulated by Mr. MH Khondker that when disputed questions of title involve disputed questions of fact such questions cannot be decided within the ambit of the extraordinary jurisdiction with which this Court is vested under Article 102 of the Constitution. In this writ petition, however, the petitioner has not at all agitated the question of her title and has not sought for any declaration as to the extent of her title in the disputed property. What she has prayed for in this writ petition is a declaration, in the face of the order on her application under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972, to the effect that the impugned order passed by the respondent No. 2 is without lawful authority and for a further direction for compliance with the order of the prescribed authority passed under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

10. We have carefully perused the averments made in the writ petition as well as the averments made in the affidavits-in-opposition and we are of the opinion that in order to dispose of this writ petition it is not at all necessary to determine the question of the extent of title of the petitioner and her co-sharers in the disputed property. In this writ petition the petitioner having claimed for a declaration that certain actions. of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Secretary, Ministry of .Public Works respectively, is illegal and without lawful authority and a further direction for implementation of the order passed by the prescribed authority passed under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972, we are of opinion that this writ petition in its present form is maintainable.

11. In this writ petition the petitioner has alleged that she acquired interest in the disputed property by way of transfer from her father Al-haj Sk. Mohammad Noor and that she was all along a national and citizen of Bangladesh. It has been further averred by her in the writ petition that during her temporary absence from the country in Pakistan this property was illegally declared as abandoned property to the extent of her 12 annas share and as such, she filed an application under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 before the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar South, Dhaka who was the prescribed authority constituted under the said Article and that the said prescribed authority declared her property to the extent of 12 annas share as not abandoned property and directed the concerned authorities to release the said share of the petitioner in her favour but in spite of this order the respondent No. 2 most illegally treated her share of the property as abandoned property by issuing the impugned order.

12. Mr. M H Khondker, the learned Advocate for the respondents 1 and 2, has tried to assail this stand of the petitioner by contending. that the Sub-divisional Officer, Sadar South, Dhaka was not the prescribed authority to dispose of an application filed under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. In this connection, Rules 4 and 5 of Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Buildings in the Urban Areas), Rules 1972 which were framed in pursuance of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 is a complete answer to the contentions of Mr. M H Khondker. Rule 4 of these Rules provides that an application under clause (1) of Article 15 shall be made to the Deputy Commissioner or to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. Rule 5 of this Rule also provided that an appeal under clause (1) of Article 16 shall be to the Deputy Commissioner when the order is passed by the Sub-divisional Magistrate. Consequently, there is no doubt that by Rule 4 of the aforesaid Rules that Sub-Divisional Officer was appointed as prescribed authority to dispose of an application under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

13. Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 provides as follows: 15. (1) Any person claiming any right or interest in any property treated by Government as abandoned property may make an application to the prescribed authority on the ground that.

(a) the property is not abandoned property or (b) his interest in the property has not been affected by the provision of this order:

(2) An application under clause (1) shall be made within three months of the date of the commencement of this order.

(3). On receiving an application under clause (2) the authority to which the application is made shall hold a summary inquiry in the prescribed manner and, after taking such evidence as may be produced, shall pass an order, stating the reasons thereof for rejecting the application or allowing it, wholly or in part, on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit to impose."

It, the &lore, appears that under clause (1) of Article 15 a prescribed authority is to find out whether the property is not abandoned property or whether the petitioner's interest in the property has not been affected by the provisions of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and in order to do so, the prescribed authority may, in view of clause (3) of Article 15. hold a summary inquiry in the prescribed manner and after taking such evidence as maybe produced, shall pass an order stating the reasons thereof either rejecting the application or allowing it wholly or in part. It, therefore, appears from the above provisions that the prescribed authority is empowered to give a finding whether a certain property declared as abandoned property is actually abandoned property or not and the prescribed authority can pass necessary orders directing release of such property from the list of abandoned property and directing the concerned  authority to deliver possession of the same to the petitioner as has been done in the instant case. The order of the prescribed authority in the case before us is Annexure-H. It appears that while considering the application of the petitioner filed under Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the prescribed authority considered all the documentary evidence produced by the petitioner before him including her nationality certificate issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs, and her title deed, etc. and came to the following findings:

"From the documents and papers, it is evident that the petitioner's father Al-haj Sheikh Mohammad Noor purchased the land of the property in question from Dengu Purification & 7 others under a registered Deed of Conveyance being No. 3557 dated 16.9.61, Thereafter, the said Al-haj Sheikh Mohammad Noor, transferred conveyed the land to his sons, daughters and wife under registered deed of conveyance bearing No. 9187 dated 18.9.65 for a total consideration of Rs. 25,000/00. The petitioner's name appeared as one of the purchasers but it is not clear the extent of the share of each purchaser from the said document, But the purchasers had made a Deed of acknowledgement/declaration in which the purchasers had made it clear that Mrs. Rana Awan (the petitioner) is the shareholder to the extent of 12/- annas inasmuch as she has invested Rs.18,750 out of the total consideration money Rs. 25,000/00. This deed also shows that the petitioner was to invest to the extent of her -/12/- annas share in the construction of the proposed commercial building. It is, therefore, clear that the petitioner is the owner of the said property to the extent of her -/12/- annas share which is not abandoned property in view of the facts that she is a national of Bangladesh confirmed by the Ministry of Home Affairs. It also transpires that she was stranded in Karachi, Pakistan and she was allowed to be repatriated along with her two children to Bangladesh by the Ministry of Home Affairs under their memo. No. 61-IMN/lII dated 17.1.75 and she reached Dhaka in the month of March, 1975 as contended by her. After reaching Dhaka she applied for the release of the said property on 20.12.77.

Under the above facts and circumstance, the share of the petitioner to the extent of 12/- annas is found not to be an abandoned property under the law and she is entitled to the restoration thereof. So far 4/- annas share is concerned, it remains abandoned vested in the Government."

<u>14. From the above, it appears that the prescribed authority was satisfied that the disputed property was not abandoned property to the extent of 12 annas share thereof and after finding this the prescribed authority directed release of -/12/- annas share of the property in favour of the petitioner. It is undisputed that as against this order no appeal was preferred to the Deputy Commissioner under Article 16 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 by any person whatsoever. It is also undisputed that by exercising its power under clause (2) of Article 16 the Government also did not at any time revise the order of the prescribed authority. So, it appears to us that the order of the prescribed authority constituted under a statute i.e. Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 read with Rule 4 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Buildings in Urban Areas) Rules, 1972 still holds good.</u>

<u>15. By enacting Article 15 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the legislature created a forum for giving relief to certain persons whose properties are declared or treated as abandoned property and that forum was vested with certain powers which included the power to declare certain property not to be abandoned property and also to give direction to release such property and to deliver possession of such property to the persons entitled. to such possession. It appears to us that in exercise of such statutory power the prescribed authority passed an order declaring -/12/- annas share of the disputed property as not being abandoned property and also directing release of the -/12/- annas share in favour of the petitioner and to deliver possession thereof to the petitioner. We have already found that this order still holds good and has not been set aside or revised by any appellate authority or by the revising authority. Consequently, it is not now open to the Government or to any other agency of the Government to ignore the order passed by the prescribed authority and to treat the property involving the said order as abandoned property and to refuse to comply with the observations and direction in such order passed by a statutory authority in exercise of its statutory power. In two unreported decisions in Writ Petition No. 13 of 1977 and in Writ Petition No. 149 of 1976 this view was reiterated.</u>

16. In Writ Petition No. 13 of 1979 the Government refused to comply with an order passed by the prescribed authority and on a writ petition by the affected person it was held that it was not open to the Government to do so. To use the exact words of his lordship Ruhul Islam, J., it is quoted as under:

"From Article 15 it appears that a forum has been created for the purpose of determining the claim of any person having right or interest in any property treated by the government as abandoned property. On receiving the application the authority is required to hold a summary enquiry in the prescribed manner and, after taking such evidence as may be produced, shall pass an order, stating the reasons thereof for rejecting the application or allowing it, wholly or in part, on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit to impose.

When an application is allowed, the order Passed by the prescribed authority is a final order unless it is revised by the Government as provided in clause (2) of Article 16 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Normally the decision given by the Prescribed Authority should be implemented unless there are very good and strong reasons for revising the name by the government.

Neither from the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 nor from the Rules made thereunder it appears that the Prescribed Authority when allowing an application under Article 15 is required to forward the records for releasing the property from the list of abandoned property but we have noticed that the Prescribed Authority instead of passing the release order sent the records to the Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development (Abandoned Property section) for releasing the property. We are given to understand that this is done on the basis of some instruction given by the Ministry although this is not contemplated under the statute. In this connection we observe that on account of this procedure adopted by the Prescribed Authority and the Ministry concerned purpose of creating the special forum under Article 15 is being defeated."

Similarly in Writ Petition No. 149 of 1976 it was held:

"In this view of the matter the opinion is. this order is illegal and since the respondent No. 3 had already found the right, title and interest of the petitioner in the said premises this property should have been released in favour of the petitioners. This is a petition for mandamus for a direction to do what they are required by law. The law says that on receiving any application the authority to which application is made shall hold a summary enquiry in the prescribed manner and after taking such evidence as may be adduced would pass an order stating the reason thereof. Here respondent No. 3 already found right title and interest in favour of the petitioners but unfortunately without releasing the property the procedure that has been adopted has practically deprived the petitioners from the fruits of the litigation for which there is no authority in the law."

17. Respectfully agreeing with the above decisions we are of the opinion that the impugned order passed by the respondent No. 2 is illegal and without lawful authority and in this view of the matter the petitioner succeeds in this writ Petition.

18. The Rule is accordingly. made absolute.The impugned order passed by the respondent No. 2 vide Memo. No. Sec. 5/Dhaka-4/79/(Part)/235 dated 17.4.85 is hereby declared to be illegal and without lawful authority. It is further directed that the respondents do comply with the order passed by the prescribed authority on 14.11.83 as contained in Annexure-H to the writ petition within 30 days from date.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.
