full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J.: In the application filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh the petitioner has challenged the judgment and order dated 11.6.87 passed by the Court of Settlement whereupon a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order vide Annexure B passed by the Respondent No. 2 and the impugned Memorandum Annexure C passed/issued by Respondent No. 1 pursuant to Annexure B should not be held to have been passed without any jurisdiction and are of no legal effect or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. Pending the hearing of the Rule the operation of the impugned judgment and order dated 11.6.87 passed by the Respondent No. 2 and also the Memorandum passed/issued by the respondent No. 1 dated 10.9.87 was stayed.

3. The case of the petitioner is that the Holding No. 57 New Eskaton within PS Ramna, Dhaka belonged to one Solaiman Pasha who while owning the said property transferred the same in favour of the petitioner, his wife and his sons by a series of documents dated 17.4.85. The petitioner has been in possession of the property since the date of his purchase. The petitioner on receipt of the notice appeared before the Ministry with the documents on 26.1.86 and the matter was heard but no decision was arrived at. To his utter surprise the holding in question was included in the abandoned list (known as Kha list) and published in the Bangladesh Gazette in serial 35 page 9764(6). The inclusion of the property in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings prompted the petitioner to make an application to the respondent No. 2 for the exclusion of the property from the said list and the application was registered as Case No. 184 of 1987.

4. In the said petition filed before the respondent No. 2 it is stated, inter alia, that having purchased the property in question from Solaiman Pasha the petitioner has been possessing the same since his purchase. The petitioner received a notice from the respondent No. 1 as contained in Memo No. Sec 12/1-R/153/86/101 dated 19.1.86 addressed to the occupant of the said property. Pursuant to the said notice the petitioner appeared before the respondent No. 1 with all his documents on 26.1.86 and the matter was heard but no decision was taken. The notice was not addressed to the petitioner by name but it was addressed to the occupants in the property in question. The petitioner filed an application under section 7 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 with a prayer for the release of Holding No. 57, New Eskaton, Dhaka from the list of abandoned buildings published in the official Gazette dated 23.9.86. The petitioner also claimed title and possession therein from the date of his purchase.

5. The respondent No. 2 having heard the case of the petitioner by his judgment and order dated 11.6.87 dismissed the case of the petitioner on contest by respondent No. 1 and maintained the inclusion of the said property in the list of abandoned property.In pursuance to the impugned judgment and order the respondent No. 1 issued Memo No. Branch 13/1/R-153/86/150 dated 10.9.87 corresponding to 24.5.94 BS to the petitioner directing him to surrender possession of the said property within 7 days from the date of receipt of the notice with a direction to the Executive Engineer, Public Works, Maintenance Division, respondent No. 3, for taking necessary measures to take over possession of the said property. The petitioner in the application also challenged the judgment and order of the respondent No. 2 and obtained the Rule.

6. The respondent No. 1, Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Bangladesh Secretariat contested the writ petition by filing affidavit-in-opposition wherein they have denied all the material allegations made in the petition. It is submitted that during the war of liberation Solaiman Pasha, a non-local owner of the property in question, was not traceable and his whereabouts was also not known to anyone and the property in question was left uncared for and as such as per provisions of President's Order 16 of 1972 the property was vested absolutely in the Government as abandoned property. It was further stated that a sangstha named Bangla Motor Juba Sangha Samabaya Samity unauthorisedly occupied the premises just after the President's Order 16 of 1972 came into operation. Solaiman Pasha never executed and registered the sale deed in favour of the petitioner and his wife and sons. The petitioner in collusion with the attested witnesses floated the aforesaid deeds in question which has no basis. The sale deeds are void ab initio, null and void, inoperative, collusive, without consideration, sham paper transactions and also hit by Article 6 of President's Order 16 of 1972. The property in question has been treated as abandoned property from the date when President's Order 16 of 1972 came into operation. The survey report dated 30.8.83 shows that Bangla Motor Juba Sangha Samabaya Samity was in unauthorised occupation of the holding in question. Accordingly, a notice was issued upon the Samity on 28.11.85 asking the Samity to vacate the holding. It is also stated that the kabala alleged to have been executed by Solaiman Pasha in favour of the petitioner and his wife and sons are hit by the provisions of Article 6 of President's Order 16 of 1972. The kabalas were registered long after the property was treated as abandoned property and the petitioner has no locus standi to claim the property.

<u>7. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that having regard to the facts that the property in question was owned by Solaiman Pasha who being the real owner having transferred the same by executing registered sale deeds to the petitioner and others on receipt of valuable consideration, the inclusion of the property in the 'Kha' list of abandoned buildings under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 by the Government was illegal and in that view of the matter the order of the respondent No. 2 is without jurisdiction and is of no legal effect. It is argued that the purchase documents being valid documents the presumption of validity and authenticity of transfer is attached with the same, and therefore, the order of the respondent No. 2 dismissing the appeal without taking into consideration this aspect of the matter and the law involved therein is to be held to have been passed without jurisdiction and of no legal effect. Mr. Khan Saidur Rahman submits that the possession of the property by Sangstha, an unauthorised occupant, does not render the premises to be treated as abandoned property. It is also submitted that at the time while the transfer was made by registered document Solaiman Pasha was the owner of the property and the petitioner having acquired title by way of purchase from the person having valid title mere inclusion of the property in the 'Kha' list of the property does not render the sale invalid so as to bring the property within the mischief of abandoned property. The learned advocate submits that the inclusion of the property in the 'Kha' list of abandoned property without serving any notice to the petitioner in contravention of the provision of section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 is illegal and without jurisdiction. The learned Advocate also submits that mere non occupation of the property by the owner at the time of transfer will not render it as abandoned property. The learned Advocate further contends that a person being the owner of the property may remain temporarily away from the property living somewhere in the country but such temporary absence of the owner will not divest him of the title in the property and the right to transfer. The learned Advocate has cited the case of Sultanuddin Chowdhury Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 32 DLR 252 wherein it is held:</u>

<u>"A kabala executed and registered in Bangladesh in 1975 creates a presumption that the registration authority was satisfied that the executants was a valid citizen and national of Bangladesh since an Indian National as such could not transfer any property in Bangladesh by way of any registered deed."</u>

<u>It is further held:</u>

<u>"The authority in the Government could not question and annul the validity of such title by an executive order. If the Government wanted to claim the title in such property it could only do so by way of an appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the registered kabala as such."</u>

8. It is true that a registered kabala carries with it a prima facie presumption of title of the parties to the kabala but this presumption is rebuttable by evidence. In the instant case it has been found by the learned Court of Settlement from the evidence on record that the real owner was not in possession of the premises in the year 1983. There is nothing on record to show that Solaiman Pasha ever moved the appropriate authority for restoration of possession of the premises in his favour and from this the learned court has drawn inference that the whereabouts of Solaiman Pasha was unknown in November, 1985 while the sale deeds were alleged to have been executed. It was further found by the learned Court of Settlement that none of the witnesses have had any acquaintance with Solaiman Pasha prior to the execution and registration of the Kabalas. In such circumstances, doubt arises regarding the identity of Solaiman and for that matter it was further held that since the real owner did not file any application till 1985 it would be deemed that he was not within Bangladesh after the liberation.

9. The above are the finding of fact arrived at by the Court of Settlement on evidence and we have little scope to interfere with such finding in a writ application.

10. Mr. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General for the respondents, argued that the kabala alleged to have been executed by Solaiman Pasha in favour of the petitioner and his wife and sons are hit by section 6 of President's Order of 1972 since those were registered after the holding in question was treated as abandoned and vested in the Government. Article 6 of President's Order 16 of 1972 provides that "no person shall, except in accordance with the provisions of this Order or any rules made there under, transfer any abandoned property in any manner or create any charge or encumbrance on such property, and any transfer made or charge or encumbrance created in contravention of this Order shall be null and void." In the instant case the kabalas were alleged to have been executed and registered in the year 1985 after the holding in question was treated as abandoned property by operation of President's Order 16 of 1972 in favour of the petitioner and his relations in contravention of the provision laid down in Article 6 of President's Order 16 of 1972. During the long period from the date of promulgation of the Ordinance till before the 28th November, 1985 the date of execution and registration of the kabalas, admittedly the vendor Solaiman Pasha was not found in the holding and his where about was also not known. There is no iota of evidence, either documentary or otherwise, to show that he possessed the property in question and or he ever made any representation before the authority for the release of the property himself. There appears to be no evidence also as recorded in the Court of Settlement that before the date of execution and registration of kabala he was seen anywhere in the country. Under such facts and circumstances it cannot be denied that the holding in question was unauthorisedly occupied by the Bangla Motor Jubo Sangstha Samabaya Samity. Now the question is whether the property in question is abandoned or not. Article 2(1) of the President's Order 16 of 1972 provides that:

"2(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not 'known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include-

(a) ……………………………………………………………………..

…………………………………………………………………

(b) …………………………………under any law for the time being in force."

11. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman having cited the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Messrs. ATJ Industries Ltd. and others reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 and the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Mirza Shahab Ispahani reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116 submits that before treating a property as abandoned and including the same in the list the Government is to form an opinion as to the purpose of the absence of the owner and in the absence of such opinion the property of an owner cannot be regarded as abandoned property simply because of his temporary absence.

12. In the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Messrs ATJ Industries Ltd. and others reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 it was observed:

"On the first question, a reference to the language of Article 2(1) set out above indicates that the language is not free from ambiguity. It appears that the legislative authority has employed multiple system in the definition. It has first defined with denotation and connotation the words abandoned property and then has employed an inclusive definition, and then an exclusion clause. It has also added an explanation. Interpretation of the definition of clause no doubt creates some complexity. The best way to interpret it is to give a harmonious meaning to all the clauses of Article 2(1) so that each clause gets its own meaning and at the same time harmonises with the meaning of the whole. The defining part denotes property owned by a person who is either not present in Bangladesh, or whose whereabouts are not known, or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property. A question may arise whether the three sub-clauses are disjunctive or conjunctive. We think they have been used disjunctively and there is no need to construe them conjunctively.

Then comes the inclusive definition. In the inclusive definition is included two categories of property, first is the property owned by a person who is a citizen of a State which after 25th day of March, 1971 either is at war or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh; the second is the property taken over by the Government under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1971. So far as the inclusion clause is concerned both the categories of properties come within the meaning of the definition of abandoned property."

13. In the case of Mirza Shahab Ispahani reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116 applying the principle laid down in the case reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 and 30 DLR (SC) 101 found that the Govt. is to form opinion as to the purpose of absence of the absentee owner and in the absence of such opinion the property of an absentee owner cannot be regarded as abandoned property.

14. Mr. Abdul Mannan, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, submits that in the present case the real owner Solaiman Pasha appears to have not been in occupation and possession of the property in question and his whereabouts was not known and therefore the inclusion of the property under Article 2(1) of President's Order 16 of 1972 will come into operation and will be governed by the main part of the definition and not by the exclusion clause.

15. In reply to the contention raised by Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman that no notice was ever issued and served on the real owner Solaiman Pasha and thereafter to the petitioner, Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General submits that the property has been treated as abandoned property by operation of law and the real owner Solaiman Pasha was not in possession and his whereabouts being not known the question of serving notice to the petitioner under Article 7(3) of President's Order 16 of 1972 did not and could not arise. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has referred to the finding of the learned Court of Settlement in his judgment to the effect that the survey report dated 30.8.83 shows that Bangla Motor Juba Sangha Samabaya Samity was in unauthoriscd occupation of the holding in question and accordingly, a notice was issued upon the Samity on 28.11.85 asking them to vacate the holding. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman then submits that the petitioner being the owner of the property in question by way of transfer from the real owner by registered sale deed, mere inclusion of the property in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned property does not ipso facto render the same to be treated as abandoned property. The learned Advocate submits that before including the property in the 'Kha' list no notice was served on the petitioner and thus the provision of law relating to the issuance and service of the notice under Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 has been violated. With regard to the submission of the learned Advocate it is found that the real owner and the petitioner were not in possession of the holding in question at the relevant time and the learned Court of Settlement found that the notice was issued upon the Juba Samity on 28.11.85 and the Samity having been found in occupation of the said holding was asked to vacate holding in question. Furthermore the Govt. by invoking the aid of Ordinance No LIV of 1985 included the disputed holding in the "Kha" list of the Abandoned Buildings by Notification of Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 28.11.1985 and Article 5(2) provides as follows:

"The lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such."

16. So by operation of section 5(2) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 the inclusion of the property in question in the 'Kha' list as abandoned property and publication of the same in the official Gazette is conclusive evidence of the fact that the property is abandoned and has vested in the Government. The presumption arising out of sub-section 2 of section 5 of the Ordinance No LIV of 1985 that the Gazette is conclusive evidence of the fact that the building in question in abandoned and has vested in the Government has not been rebutted by the petitioner.

17. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman has then challenged the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement contending that the Court of Settlement has arrived at a finding that the notice was issued in respect of the property in question and that the whereabouts of Solaiman Pasha was unknown till November, 1985 and that he was not in Bangladesh after the liberation are made on surmises and not based on any materials on record.

<u>18. We have gone through the impugned judgment and order of the Court of Settlement who after consideration of the facts and circumstances rightly found that the kabalas executed and registered in favour of the petitioner and his relations are hit by section 6 of President's Order 16 of 1972, the same having been registered after the holding in question was treated as abandoned property. There being no apparent illegality of impropriety in the order of the Court of Settlement we find no reason to disturb the decision arrived at by the Court of Settlement and hence the petitioner is not entitled to any relief in the form of declaration that the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement and consequently the impugned order issued by respondent No.1 pursuant to the order of respondent No. 2 are passed/made without jurisdiction and as such is of no legal effect.</u>

The Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs. The stay granted by this court earlier is hereby vacated. Send down the records at once.

End.

full_judgment: Md. Mozammel Hoque J : This First Appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 553 of 1981 (formerly Title Suit No. 888 of 1979). decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff. 2. Respondent No. 1 being plaintiff instituted the aforesaid Title Suit for declaration of title and also for a declaration that the treating of the suit property as vested and nonresident property is illegal and without jurisdiction. It is the case of the plaintiff that the suit property originally belonged to Kailash Chandra Das, Nitta Nanda Das and Radhakanta Das and their names were duly recorded in CS Khatian. By amicable partition the present suit property fell in the share of Nitta Nanda Das and this Nitta Nanda Das subsequently transferred the suit property to one Ram Chandra Paul by an amalnama in the year 1953 BS (1947 AD). The SA record was prepared in the name of Ram Chandra Paul. By an agreement dated 5.5.69 this Ram Chandra Paul sold his property to the present plaintiff and delivered possession of the suit property to the plaintiff on receipt of an earnest money amounting to Taka 50,000.00 out of total consideration money at Taka 80,000.00. After few months this Ram Chandra Paul died without executing and registering the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff. However, Gour Gopal Paul, the only son of Ram Chandra Paul, after receiving the balance consideration of Taka 30,000.00 executed and registered two sale deeds on 4.12.79 in favour of the plaintiff and thereby the plaintiff acquired right, title and possession in the suit property. The defendant had no right, title and interest in the suit property. It came to the knowledge of the plaintiff that the suit property was recorded in the name of the defendant No. 2 the Assistant Custodian, Vested and Non-Resident Property, in RS Khatian. This created some doubt about the title and possession of the plaintiff and that is why he filed the present suit for declaration that treating the suit property as vested and non resident property is illegal and without jurisdiction. 3. The defendant No. 2 namely, the Assistant Custodian, Vested and Non-Resident Property contested the suit by filing written statement denying the allegations of the plaintiff and stating 'inter alia' that the suit is not maintainable and the plaintiff has no cause of action. It is their case that this Ram Chandra Paul, the vendor of the plaintiff, was the owner, no doubt, but he left this country in 1953. Thereafter, one Abdul Kader, a non local, had been residing in the holding with his family and also inducted some other persons in the suit holding as his tenants without any lawful authority. That the said unauthorised occupant Abdur Kader recently demolished the shed in the suit holding ousting the tenants and brought one Mr. Mojibur Rahman and amongst the occupants some had filed application for lease of the suit holding. Since the owner Ram Chandra Paul left this county long ago and was permanently residing in India, the Government took over that property as vested and non-resident property. The plaintiff created forged documents in order to grab the suit property. 4. On the aforesaid pleadings of the parties four issues were framed by the trial Court which were considered and disposed of together. The plaintiff examined three witnesses including himself and the contesting defendant No. 2 examined one witness. The plaintiff submitted so many papers and documents which have been marked as exhibits. After considering the evidence on record the learned Subordinate Judge passed the judgment and decree in the aforesaid suit decreeing in favour of the plaintiff. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court dated 25.1.86 passed in Title Suit No. 553 of 1981 (formerly Title Suit No. 888 of 1979), the defendant No. 2 preferred this appeal. The plaintiff examined himself as PW 1. He reiterated his case as he stated in the plaint. He also proved the papers and documents, namely, Exts.-1 to 8(c). He categorically denied that his vendor Ram Chandra Paul did not leave this country in 1953. He stated that he purchased the suit property by two documents, Exts. 4 and 4(a) on payment of the balance consideration Taka 30,000.00. He further stated that it was wrongly recorded in RS Khatian in the name of defendant No. 2. Against this wrong recording, the plaintiff preferred appeal which was allowed and thereafter the name of the plaintiff was recorded instead of the defendant No. 2. 5. PW 2 is one Amir Ali. He knew Ram Chandra Paul and the suit property. He stated that there was an agreement for sale in between Ram Chandra Paul and the plaintiff at a sum of Taka 80,000.00. Out of that Taka 50,000.00 was paid. After the death of Ram Chandra, his son Gour Chandra Paul executed the sale deed on receipt of balance consideration of Taka 30,000.00. He was witness of the agreement as well as the two kabalas. In fact, he corroborated with the evidence of PW 1 in material particulars. He also denied that Ram Chandra went to India and thereafter the property was taken over as vested and non-residence property. 6. PW 3 is one Shantalal Shah. He knew the plaintiff and the suit property. He also corroborated with the evidence of PW 1 in respect of the agreement as well as the sale of the property to the plaintiff. He also stated that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit property. After the death of Ram Chandra Paul his son Gour Chandra Paul executed the two sale deeds in favour of the plaintiff. He further stated that he was witness in the agreement dated 5.5.69 and after the death of Ram Chandra Paul his son Gour Chandra Paul executed and registered the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff, Nothing can be brought out in favour of the defendant on cross-examining PW 3. He stated that towards the end of 1969 Ram Chandra Paul died leaving behind only one son, namely, Gour Chandra Paul. He knew Ram Chandra Paul and Gour Chandra Paul. 7. On behalf of the contesting defendant one Md. Abdul Hamid deposed as DW 1. He stated that he is serving as Assistant in the office of the Vested and Non-Resident Property. He stated that in CS record the suit property was recorded in the name of three persons. Now, the suit property is vested property and it was leased out to several lessees. The lessees paid the rent upto 1984. Since the owner left this country and went to India, it was taken as vested and non-resident property. In VP Case No. 11 of 1979 the property was leased out to the lessees. He stated that he did not know as to whether the plaintiff is living in the suit property with his family members. He could not say whether the property was enlisted in the cause list of vested and non-resident property. He stated that the Ext. B is the death certificate of Ram Chandra Paul. He was not present at the time of hearing of the proceeding of correction of record of rights. RS record stood in the name of the plaintiff. The plaintiff also paid the municipal taxes and rents to the Government. He could not say where Ram Chandra Paul died. No notice was served upon the plaintiff in the VP Case. He failed to produce any papers to show that any notice was served upon Ram Chandra Paul. 8. Ext-1 is the copy of CS parcha which was prepared in the name of three brothers who were the original owners of the suit property. Ext. 2 is the SA parcha prepared in the name of Ram Chandra Paul. Ext.-3 is the death certificate of Ram Chandra Paul which shows that Ram Chandra Paul died on 18.11.69 at 53, Piary Das Road, Dhaka. This certificate was obtained on 23.12.81 from the Dhaka Municipal Corporation. Exts. 4 and 4 (a) are the two registered documents executed and registered in favour of the plaintiff by Gour Chandra Paul, son of Ram Chandra Paul. Ext.-5 is the SA parcha prepared in the name of Ram Chandra Paul. Ext-6 is the copy of the Khatian prepared in the name of the present plaintiff. Ext. 7 is the certified copy of order-sheet of Case No. 605 of 1984 which was case for correction of record of rights in the name of the plaintiff and it appears that after considering the materials on record the name of the plaintiff was recorded in the record of rights after making necessary correction. Ext-8 is a rent receipt issued in the name of Ram Chandra Paul. Ext-8 (a) is another rent receipt in the name of Ram Chandra Paul, but rent was paid through the present plaintiff. Ext-8 (b) is a certificate of Mutation Officer which shows in the municipal corporation the name of the present plaintiff was mutated in respect of the suit property. Ext-8 (c) is another rent receipt in favour of the present plaintiff given by Dhaka Municipal Corporation. These are more or less the oral as well as documentary evidence of the parties. 9. At the outset it may be mentioned that the defendant No. 2, the present appellant, only examined one witness who is an Assistant of the Vested and Non-Resident Property Office, but no papers and documents have been filed in support of the case of the defendant No. 2. It is their case that since in 1953 the owner Ram Chandra Paul left this country and went to India, this property was treated as vested and non-resident property in VP Case No. 11 of 1979. 10. Mr. Moksudur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the property in question is a vested and non-resident property and it is vested in the Government by the omnibus notification issued in the month of December, 1965. Since the owner left this country before 1965, the property was rightly treated as vested and non-resident property. He further submits that since the property in question acquired the character of enemy property after 1965, it was not illegal even if the Vested Property Case was started in the year 1979. 11. It is admitted by both the parties that Ram Chandra Paul was the real owner of the suit property. It is the categorical statements made before the Court by three PWs to the effect that on 5.5.69 the plaintiff entered into an agreement also with Ram Chandra Paul for purchasing the property at a consideration of Taka 80,000.00 and out of which Taka 50,000.00 was paid to Ram Chandra Paul. The three witnesses proved the execution of the agreement dated 5.5.69 and the payment of advance consideration money of Taka 50,000.00 in their evidence and the three witnesses stated that a few months after that agreement Ram Chandra Paul died in this country. In the SA record it appears that it was prepared in the name of Ram Chandra Paul in respect of suit property. Considering this record of right as well as the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 it clearly shows that Ram Chandra Paul died in this country in the year 1969 leaving behind his only son Gour Chandra Paul. On the basis of the above evidence it is held that the property in question can never be treated as enemy property inasmuch as the owner of the property lived in this country till 1969 and died leaving behind his only son Gour Chandra Paul. This Gour Chandra Paul sold this suit property by two registered documents in favour of the plaintiff in the year 1979 on receipt of the balance consideration money of Taka 30,000.00. So, it is proved beyond any doubt that in the year 1969 the owner Ram Chandra Paul entered into an agreement with the plaintiff to sell the suit property and after his death his only son Gour Chandra Paul executed and registered two sale deeds in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property. From the evidence of the PWs as well as from the record of rights and rent receipts which have been marked exhibits in this case it appears that the plaintiff is in possession in the suit property since the agreement in the year 1969 and had been living there with his family members. There are some tenants in the suit property who after it was treated as vested and non-resident property used to pay rent to the Government and in this way they are treated as lessees of the Government. 12. The defendant simply stated that the original owner Ram Chandra Paul left this country in 1953. In support of that contesting defendant failed to produce any evidence whatsoever. Further, excepting this DW 1 and the case record of VP Case No. 11 of 1979 no other papers have been produced before the Court in support of the claim of defendant No. 2 that the suit property is vested and non-resident property. The defendant No.1 admitted that Ram Chandra Paul was the original owner who died in this country on 18.11.69 as per death certificate given by the Dhaka Municipal Corporation. The plaintiffs have filed the copies of CS, RS and SA record of rights and also produced rent receipts and the municipal tax receipts which have been marked as exhibits as stated above. Considering these aspects and the depositions of the PWs as well as the deposition of DW it is clearly proved that the plaintiff is in possession in the suit property since 1969 after the execution of the agreement. Since Gour Chandra Paul, son of Ram Chandra Paul, executed and registered two sale deeds and thereby transferred the suit property in favour of the plaintiffs, we hold that the plaintiff has been able to prove his right, title and possession in the suit property. 13. Mr. SS Haldar, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 1, submits that by no stretch of imagination the property in question can be treated as vested and non-resident property in pursuance of VP Case No. 11 of 1979 in view of fact that the relevant enemy property law has been repealed in the year 1976. During Indo-Pak war in 1965 the Emergency Ordinance as well as Emergency Rules came into force. After the withdrawal of emergency the Enemy Property Ordinance (Emergency Provision), 1969 came into force in which several provisions of the Emergency Powers Rules were kept alive. In 1974, under Emergency Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (repealed) Ordinance, 1974 was promulgated which was subsequently made Act No. XLV of 1974. Then Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Ordinance, 1974 came into force vide Ordinance No. V of 1974 which was subsequently converted into Act No XL VI of 1974. Under the provisions of the aforesaid Ordinance the vested and non-resident properties were being administered. Then by Ordinance No. 92 of 1976 namely, Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) (repealed) Ordinance 1974 was promulgated and in that Ordinance the previous Act XL VI of 1974 was repealed but a saving clause was there which speaks that if any proceeding was taken or any list was prepared in respect of any property as vested and non-resident property, then that will continue. Excepting this saving clause the law is totally repealed. Relying upon the aforesaid provisions of law Mr. Haldar submits that question of treating the suit property as vested and non-resident property in the year 1979 by starting VP Case No. 11 of 1979 does not arise at all. We find substance in the above contentions of Mr. Haldar. In an unreported case of Civil Revision No. 3375 of 1991 (Dhaka) and 114 of 1968 (Barisal) a Single Bench of this Court took the view that after the repeal of Vested and Non-Resident Property Ordinance vide Ordinance No. 92 of 1976 there was no scope for starting any VP case under the provisions of the aforesaid law afresh and if any proceeding is started for treating a property as vested property, under law that will be absolutely without jurisdiction. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the evidence both oral and documentary on record and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the parties, we hold that the plaintiff has acquired right, title and possession in the suit property and treating the suit property as vested and non-resident property is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction. We have gone through the judgment of the trial Court It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has considered each and every aspect of the case and the material evidence on record and passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff. The findings of the learned Subordinate Judge are based on record and, as such, we do not find any reason to interfere with the findings of the trial Court in any manner whatsoever. 14. In the result, this appeal is dismissed with costs and the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court are hereby affirmed. Send down the LC records immediately to the trial Court. End.

case_source: From the Judgment and order dated 23-5-83 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in F.A. No. 44 of 1981.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J:- This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court Division in F. A. No. 42 of 1981.

2. The predecessor of the appellants filed Title Suit No. 31 of 1977 in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract stating, inter alia, that there was an agreement between S.M. Ismail on the one hand and Hemnalini Basu (the predecessor of respondents 1 and 2) on the other band. The Bainapatra is dated 13.4.63. The stipulation was that the property will be sold to S.M. Ismail at a consideration of Tk. 35,000/-. Hemnalini received Tk. 27,400/- as advance and executed a bainapatra and delivered possession of the property. It was stipulated that Hemnalini would execute a registered deed of sale within 4 years and give the possession of the rest of the property at that time. Hemnalini died on 12.6.64 leaving respondent Asim Kumar Basu as her heir. The plaintiffs case was that he approached Hemnalini during her life time for execution of the deed and after her death the plaintiff approached respondent No. 1 but his request was not complied with. Thereafter the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 was promulgated and the property had been vested to the Custodian of the Enemy Property. The plaintiff impleaded in this suit the Asstt. Custodian of Enemy Property as defendant No. 2 and S. M.Ismail filed the suit on 8.1.70 being T.S.No. 2 of 1970 and the Assistant Custodian. filed written statement on 29.4.70 and another additional written statement was filed on 10.7.72. Asim, respondent No. 1 also filed a written statement on 14.9.72.

3. The defence case was that there was no contract for sale between Hemnalini and S.M. Ismail and no bainapatra was executed by her and the Bainapatra was forged and fraudulent nor Ismail was given possession of the suit property though he trespassed in the suit property in August, 1970. The suit property became enemy property and the Custodian had leased out to several persons on monthly rent and they were in possession.

4. In the meantime on 12.7.72 one Sova Rani filed application stating that she is one of the two daughters of Hemnalini Basu as such she, as an heir, inherited the estate of late Hemnaiini. On court's order Sova Rani was added as the defendant in the suit as defendant No. 3 but she did not file any written statement.

5. In compliance with the provisions of P.O. 142 of 1972 Government of Bangladesh was added as. defendant No. 4 and it adopted written statement filed by the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property.

6. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Bainapaira was a genuine document and the appellants were in possession of the part of the suit property and the suit is maintainable inasmuch as heirs of Hemnalini and the Custodian were impleaded. Further the suit was not time-barred.

7. This decree was challenged in F.A. No. 44 of 1981 by Asim Kumar and Soya Rani. The Custodian, however, did not file any appeal and at the time of hearing the Assistant Custodian entered appearance and supported the appeal of the respondents 1 and 2.

8. The High Court Division considered that the question of possession was not material in this case and considered that the document in question namely Bainapatra was a genuine one. The High Court Division negatived the argument that the suit was time-barred and found the suit having been filed on 8.1.70, was within three years from the date of the Bainapatra and therefore the suit was not time-barred. The High Court Division repelled the contention as to the nature of the property whether it was stridhanor not inasmuch as there was no evidence as to when HemnaIini acquired the property. The learned Judges considered that prime question was that after vesting of the property in the custody of the Enemy Property, whether the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 could execute a kabala as heirs of Hemnalini.

9. The High Court Division further noticed that though assistant custodian did not challenge the decree by himself whether in view of the provision of Defence of Pakistan Rules and the General Notification No. 1199 dated 3.12.65 and paragraph 4 of the East Pakistan Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order the contract could be specifically performed and then answered the query by observing:

"All legal right and obligations that followed from the agreement in question were snapped."

Next the High Court Division considered "that such property could only be transferred with the approval of the Govt. but as the Government did not enter into any agreement with the plaintiff and the suit property being an enemy property vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property the Government cannot be compelled by a decree of the court to perform the contract which had become frustrated after the war broke out". In this view of the matter the appeal was allowed and the judgment and decree of the trial court were set aside.

10. The heirs of the plaintiff are the appellants before this Court. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed canvassed that the High Court Division having found that the contract was genuine and the suit was not time-barred ought to have upheld the decree specially when the Custodian of the Enemy Property did not challenge the decree but by reasoning which is not tenable in law, the High Court Division had reversed the judgment and order of the trial court and set aside the decree.

11. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed appearing for the respondent contended that in view of Defence of Pakistan Rules and the East Pakistan Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Disposal Order, 1966 such decree is in executable and the custodian cannot transfer any property. The High Court Division rightly set aside the decree inasmuch as the supervening impossibility had frustrated the contract.

12. We have heard able arguments of both sides and we shall presently consider the legal consequence from such contract the contract has been found genuine. Question of nature of the property whether Stridhan or not does not merit Consideration inasmuch as the issue was not raised before in the pleading and therefore the contention does not merit any consideration. The relevant provision of rule 182, as it stood on the promulgation on the 6th of September, 1965, was to the following effect;

182. collection of debt of enemy firms and custody of property-It) With a view to preventing the payment of money to an enemy firm, and preserving enemy property in contemplation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace, the Central Government may appoint a Custodian of Enemy Property for Pakistan and one or more Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property for such local areas as may be prescribed and may by order- (b) Vest or provide for vesting in the prescribed Custodian such enemy property as may be prescribed. This rule was amended on 2.11.65 wherein the word "management" in the sub-heading was substituted in place of the word "custody" and the expression ..preserving enemy property in contemplation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace" was replaced by an expression viz " to provide for the administration and disposal by way of transfer or otherwise of enemy property or . matters concerned therewith or incidental thereto."

Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed argued that notwithstanding the amendment the Legislature's intendment seems to be the preservation of enemy property till conclusion of peace and the right, title and interest of the enemy was not sought to be extinguished in any way. Reliance was placed on a decision Benoy Bhusan Bardhan Vs. The Sub-Divisional Officer, Brahmanbaria & another 30 DLR SC 139. Mr. Ahmed argued that Hemnalini might haw executed a bainapatra but the property having been vested in the custodian as enemy property the contract has become frustrated and the High Court Division rightly took the view in this factor.

13. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed traced the history of this Legislation and contended that though in 1974 the Legislature passed two Ordinances, namely Ordinance IV of 1974 and Ordinance No. V of 1974, subsequently the Government acquired the power for disposal by Acts 92 and 93 of 1976 and the evolution of law was not traced in the case of Benoy Bhusan 30 DLR (SC) 139 and as such the decision is not a good law.

<u>14. President's Order No. 29 of 1972 (dated 26th March, 1972) provided that all properties and assets which were vested in the Government of Pakistan or any officer appointed by such Government or were vested in or managed by any Board constituted by or under any law or in the former Government of East Pakistan shall be deemed to have been vested in the Government of Bangladesh on and from 26th day of March, 1971. The property thus vested in the Custodian, Enemy Properly under the Defence of Pakistan Rules had now vested by operation of law in the Government of Bangladesh.</u>

15. The suit was filed in 1970 and the plaintiff made the Custodian as defendant No. 2 and again made Government of Bangladesh also as defendant No.4 upon promulgation of P.O. 142 of 1972 which stipulated that no suit for specific performance of contract could be instituted without impleading the Govt. which is a necessary party.

16. The Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Ordinance 1974, Ordinance No. IV of 1974 was promulgated on 23.3.74 and it repealed the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision) Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 and the saving section 3 reads as follows:

"3. Saving- (1) Notwithstanding the repeal of said Ordinance and anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on such repeal-

(a) all enemy property vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules continued in force by the said Ordinance shall vest in the Government.

(b) All enemy firms the trade or business of which was being carried on by any person or Board authorised under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules continued in force by the said Ordinance shall vest in the Government.

Explanation (i) The terms "Enemy Property" and "Enemy firms" used in this section shall be deemed to have the same meaning as assigned to those terms in the Defence of Pakistan Rules continued. in force by the said Ordinance.

(ii) In this sub-section, "Custodian of Enemy Property" includes an Additional Custodian of Enemy Property, a Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property and an Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the Defence of Pakistan Rules continued in force by the said ordinance."

By this Ordinance, therefore, the property vested unmistakably in the Government. In passing it may be noticed that Ordinance No. I of 1969 purported to continue certain provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules and the Ordinance ceased to have effect.

<u>17. Rule 182 was also continued in force. This was repealed by Ordinance IV of 1974 as mentioned above. Therefore, the position emerges that the Enemy Property which previously vested in the Custodian or Assistant Custodian now vested by section 3 in the Government notwithstanding repeal of Ordinance I of 1969.</u>

18. On the same day i. e. on 22.3.74 another Ordinance was promulgated namely, the Vested and Non-Resident Property Administration Ordinance. 1974 being Ordinance V of 1974 and vested property was defined as "any property which has vested in the Government under section 3(1) of the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision) (Repeal) Ordinance.1974 (Ordinance IV of 1974). It provided in Part III "that the vested property shall be under the charge of a Committee and the Committee shall take such measures as may be necessary for the good management and protection of such property for the assertion of title thereto." It provided "that the Committee shall not be entitled to transfer except by monthly or annual lease any vested property." Similar provision was made in Part V insofar as non-resident property is concerned but in section 10 a non-resident has been given a right to dispose of such property by exchange or gift. subject to certain condition and upon disposition the property shall cease to vest in the Committee (Section 10. sub-section 3). Thus for the first time a legislative change has taken place and a non-resident had also been given a right as to its property to dispose of his property. This Ordinance No. V was converted into an Act being Act XLVI of 1974.

<u>19. Next on 27.11.76 the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration)(Repeal) Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance, No. 92 of 1976) was promulgated. It repealed the Vested and Non-Resident Property Administration Act, 1974 (Act XLVI of 1974).</u>

<u>20. On the same day the Enemy Property Continuance and Emergency Provision (Repeal) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1976 being Ordinance 93 of 1976 was promulgated with retrospective effect from 23rd March, 1974. It amended section 3 of the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act of 1974. Act XLV of 1974 which was previously Ordinance No. IV of 1974. It may be noted that enactment repealed the Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 and by section 3 vested the property in the Government which earlier vested in the Custodianand now by Ordinance 93 of 1976 it further amended section 3 of Act XLV of 1974 and coded:</u>

<u>"and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of by transfer or otherwise by the Government or any such officer or authority as the Government may direct"</u>

<u>By this amendment of section 3 of Act XLV of 1974 the entire complexion was changed and power was given for disposal or transfer to the Government vide section 2 of Ordinance 93 of 1976.</u>

<u>21. The legislative process now becomes clear that when initially the Defence of Pakistan Rules intended for the preservation of the property till conclusion of peace the Government changed the policy as early as on 2.11.65 and deleted the portion "Preserving Enemy Property in contemplation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace," and replaced it. by new provision "to provide for the administration and disposal by way of transfer connected therewith or incidentally thereto". Subsequently by P.O. 29 of 1972 such property was vested in the Govt. of Bangladesh and though under the Ordinance Nos. 4 & 5 of 1974 the property was kept in charge of the Committee and the non-resident could dispose of his property subject to the approval of the Committee, this process was done away with in 1976 when the Government took power for transfer and disposal of such property.</u>

<u>22. In this legal background, this is too late to say that the Government has no power of transfer and disposal of the Enemy Property in pursuance of direction of court. From the above analysis of the legal position it is clear that the property is now vested in the Government and the Assistant Custodian has no claim in respect of such property. The High Court Division had fallen into an error in its conclusion when it says:</u>

<u>"Custodian's power to transfer enemy property could only be exercised with the approval of the Government. As the Government had not entered into any agreement with the plaintiff and the suit property being an enemy property vested in the Custodian of enemy property the Government cannot be compelled by a decree of the Court to perform the contract which had become frustrated after the war broke out between the country where the property was situated and the enemy country where the owner or owners were permanently residing.</u>

<u>With respect, the reason is fallacious in the setting of legal position. The Custodian is no more in control and management of the property. It is the Government since 1976. Plaintiff made the Government a party to the suit. He is seeking to enforce the contract which he entered into with Hemnalini. She having died her sons and daughters being residents of enemy country, the property was taken over as enemy property by the Custodian. When the suit was filed in 1970 the property was vested in the Custodian no doubt but by the provision of P. O. No. 29 of 1972 this had vested in the Government.</u>

23. In 1974 the non-resident could dispose of his property with the permission of the Committee. The contractual power of non-resident was not taken away. The only condition was that has to be done subject to the approval of the Committee.

24. In 1976 this Committee had been done away with and it is only Govt. which appeared in the scene as a sole authority and got power of disposal and transfer by Ordinance 93 of 1976.

25. It is not correct to say that the agreement had been frustrated. The agreement was very much alive and power of transfer was available even with Custodian subject to certain condition and this power was vested in the Committee and the non-resident was given the right to transfer his property with the approval of the Committee and thereafter Government took up the power of control and management and disposal and transfer. When this power is available there is no reason to hold that the contract entered into by Hemnalini could not be specifically performed. If it had been the position that the contract should not be enforced in public interest the Government would have said so and specific power was available to the Government in Rules 176 and 178 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules cancelling such contract in public interest. That was not done nor such position was taken by the Government. In this view of the matter, therefore, the opinion of the High Court Division appears to be in error.

26. Now the question of Benoy Bhusan, it is submitted, that exposition of law that has been made in that decision was not strictly necessary for the disposal of that case. In that case a notice was served upon the appellant that he was in continuous occupation of certain property without any document which belonged to Indian nationals and to show cause why the said property should not be declared as enemy property. The appellant took the stand that a portion of property which stood in the name of Paresh Chandra Bardhan was acquired on the basis of valid document and a portion of the property standing in the name of Chittotosh Bardhan were debuttor property and the appellant being the elder member of the family managed the said property for the Sheba Puja etcand the remaining property were ejmali properties and he being a co-sharer was in lawful possession of such property.

27. The Sub-Divisional Officer, Brahinanbaria repelled the contention of the appellant and declared the property as enemy property and recommended the lease of the said land to other persons.

28. The appellant challenged the order before the High Court in writ jurisdiction and the learned Judges of the High Court Division disposed of by the judgment on 1.12.69 holding that the respondents were authorised to exercise necessary powers for taking possession of the disputed land upon partition which were enemy properties and directed the Custodian to look into the court's order properly and leave out the legitimate share of the appellant in the properties before taking possession of the shares of Indian nationals.

29. The appellant then obtained special leave which was granted by the Supreme Court of Pakistan to consider the question whether the Sub- Divisional Officer was competent to exercise the power of the Assistant Custodian and whether the Custodian could take possession of any ejmali land of which the appellant was in possession as a co- sharer without partition of the said land.

30. In this setting of facts the Appellate Division came to the conclusion that as a co-owner of an undivided share of the joint land has his right, title and interest" in every grain of soil constituting the joint land and cannot therefore be said to be in unlawful possession of such land, even if he is in exclusive possession thereof and it was further held that the Custodian of Enemy Property representing the share of enemy owner cannot go into possession of the joint land by dispossessing the co-sharer in possession of the said land without partitioning the same according to law. In this view of the matter the appeal was allowed and the impugned orders were declared to have been taken without lawful authority.

31. In passing, in the judgment considerable portion was devoted as to the nature of rule 182 and the legal consequences therefrom. The entire judgment was based upon a philosophy in paragraph 21 of the judgment which reads as follows:

"21. The predominant idea behind taking over and management of the enemy property under these Emergency Legislations seems to have been the prevention of certain acts which might be prejudicial to the war efforts of the Government of Pakistan and the preservation of the said properties during the continuance of the war. It seems to have been never in the contemplation of the Government of the country to acquire for itself any beneficial interest in the properties of an individual enemy owner under the said provisions. But to protect and manage the properties, so that the rightful owners could get back their properties on the conclusion of peace".

32. It was observed that right, title and interest was not sought to be extinguished in any way but were purported to be placed instead in temporary hibernation so to say during the continuance of the emergency (para 20). It was concluded that-

"subsisting interest of the enemy owner is high lighted by the provision of clause (iv) of paragraph 3 which authorised the Custodian concerned to incur expenditure for Ute maintenance of the individual enemy owner or his family (para 20).

With respect, this was the misreading of law itself. Paragraph (iv) of section 3 reads as under;

"(iv) The Custodian, where the enemy property belongs to an individual enemy subject or any individual resident in enemy territory may incur such expenditure out of the income of the property as he considers necessary or expedient for the maintenance of that individual Of of his family in Pakistan."

The Custodian will spend money for the maintenance of individuals or his family in Pakistan. He is not to spend money for the maintenance of individual enemy subject, who is resident of enemy country. The law was considered in a particular perspective and this is evident from another paragraph where it is said:

"The main object of the said rule does not appear to have been affected in any way by such amendment as the relevant provisions of the Enemy Property (Custody and Administration) Order, 1965 which declared and specified the rights of the Custodian in whom the properties of an enemy had vested did not undergo any alteration whatsoever."

The Defence of Pakistan Rules promulgated in pursuance of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance are in the nature of subordinate legislation. It is well settled that subordinate legislation cannot override the provision of the parent Legislation. The initial difference between subordinate legislation and the Statute lies in the fact that a subordinate law making object is bound by the terms and its delegated or derived authority and courts of law as a general rule will not give effect to the rules etc. thus made unless satisfied that all the conditions precedent to making of the rules have been fulfilled. Even in paragraph 3(1) it is stated that the Custodian shall have all the rights, powers, duties and liabilities of the owner of such property.

33. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed could not deny that the obligation of the owner Hemnalini had devolved upon the Custodian when her property was vested in him. There is no law which bars the Custodian for executing the document which the owner had she been alive would have to do so in uursuance of the decree of court.

34. Repeated emphasis was given in the judgment of Benoy Bhusan [30 DLR (SC) 139] that" these were essentially temporary measures for the management and protection of properties" (para 20) and notwithstanding the amendment of 2.11.65 which radically altered the law the judgment rests primarily on the expression "preserving Enemy Property in contemplation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of the peace."

35. This expression was borrowed from the English enactment. Section 7 of Trading with Enemy Act, 1939. That section so far as is relevant provides as under:

"With a view to preventing the payment of money to enemies and of preserving enemy property in contemplation of arrangements to be made at the conclusion of peace."

The argument of the defendant in the case of R.J. Reuter Co. Ltd. Vs. Ferd Mulhens 1953 All E.R. 1160 centred on. the opening word and it was contended 'that the section contemplated for preserving the Enemy, Property in contemplation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace, and the argument was that the purported transfer of shares and the selling of trade mark were not contemplated by the section. The question before the court was whether it conferred the power of sale or transfer.

<u>36. The Court of Appeal repelled the contention and concluded that the opening words of the section ought not to have treated as having restricted effect for which Counsel for the defendant contended. It was observed that the Trading with the Enemy (Amendment) Act, 1914 contained a preamble substantially in the same form as the opening words of section 7 of the Act of 1939. In Re Munster, Russel J. explained the expression and said (1920) Ch. 278:</u>

"In my judgment the Act of 1914 does not depart from these principles or involve confiscation. Under its provisions, the enemy is deprived of beneficial ownership during the war. And the Custodian, after the termination of the war, is bound to deal with it in such manner as his Majesty (keeping no doubt, in view the arrangements made at the conclusion of peace) may by Order in Council direct... The phraseology used in the preamble and in section 5 establishes in my judgment that, pending its disposition by Order in Council after the determination of the war, the property is removed from the control and from the beneficial ownership of the enemy. At the termination of the war fresh consideration will arise: and whether the enemy will rec9ver, and to what extent he will recover, the beneficial owners his will depend upon the arrangements made at the conclusion of peace ... and upon the terms of any Order in Council, made, I doubt not, with those arrangements in view under section 5".

Birkett L.J .observed in 1953 All E.R.(2) page 1182:

"when the transfer of the trade marks was made in June, 1951, it was made in the light of the provisions of the Act of 1949 and the statutory instrument, and the "arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace referred to in Section 7 of the Act of 1939 could never be such arrangements as would contemplate the handing back of the enemy property to German nationals,"

Romer L.J. observed at page 1184:

"Throughout the war and down to the date of the assignment the defendants possessed no legal rights in relation either to the registered trade marks or in relation to the good will of the business which they had formerly carried on here, All that the defendants did possess was the suspended beneficial interest to which I have already referred and if the Custodian had the power to sell the trade marks and good will, as in my judgment, he had even, this somewhat shadowy interest was automatically destroyed by the exercise of that power and nothing survived to the defendants."

That was the law in England on the phraseology that "the arrangement would be made at the conclusion of peace." But in our law Rule 182 was amended on 2.11.65 and the expression "preserving the enemy property in contemplation of arrangement to be made at the conclusion of pence" "was replaced by new expression" and to provide for the Administration and disposal by way of transfer or otherwise of enemy Dtoperty or matter concerned therewith or incidental thereto.

<u>37. With this amendment the entire complexion was changed. The emphasis was no more for preservation of enemy property but it was for disposal by way of transfer. In the words of Romer LJ. whatever shadowy interest the defendant had that was automatically destroyed by the exercise of the powers by the Custodian and nothing survived to the defendants. The decision in Benoy Bhusan's case unfortunately having noticed the amendment in rule 182 observed - "the main object of the said rule does not appear to have been affected in any way by such amendment as the relevant provision of the Enemy Property (Custody and Administration) Order, 1965 which declared and specified right of the Custodian in whom the properties of any enemy had vested did not undergo any alteration whatsoever", to say the least, with respect, is misreading of the law itself. A case is an authority for the principle laid down in the facts and circumstances of that case and in Benoy Bhusan's case the question was whether the Custodian could take possession of the share of the enemy in a property without effecting partition. While in this judgment no opinion is expressed on the decision in Benoy Bhusan (30 DLR(S.C) 139) on its facts of that case the exposition of law detailed from paragraphs 11 to 21 do not commend to us as correct exposition of law namely Defence of Pakistan Rules read with paragraph 4(7) of the Enemy Property (Custody and Registration) Order, 1965 and Act Nos. 45, 46 of 1974 and Ordinance Nos. 92 and 93 of 1976.</u>

38. Even in England it was held that whatever shadowy interest left for the defendant was automatically destroyed by the exercise of that power conferred by section 7 and nothing survived to the defendants. How an argument could be built up in view of the amendment dated 2.11.65 to say "that it seems to have been never in contemplation of the Government of the country to acquire for itself any beneficial interest of the property of an individual enemy owner under the said provision, but to protect and manage the property so that original owners get back their properties at the conclusion of peace" appears to be unfounded in law inasmuch as there was no contemplation of any arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace whereas by amendment it provided for the administration, disposal and by way of transfer or otherwise the enemy property.

39. In this view of the matter the argument of the respondent that the Custodian could not execute the kabala in question in pursuance of the decree of specific performance of the contract does not hold good. The High Court Division unfortunately had fallen into this very error and took the view that neither could the Custodian execute the document nor could the Government do so inasmuch as the Government was not party to the contract.

40. The contract was made by Hemnalini and she died within a year of the agreement. Plaintiff was asking for the kabala and since the property became enemy property the defendants, the heirs of Hemnalini could not execute lcabala. It was only the Custodian who could do it inasmuch as he stepped into the shoes of the owner itself with the power of transfer available to him on and from 2.1.65 which was conferred by amendment itself.

41. The subsequent legislations were not noticed in the case of Benoy Bhusan in 30 DLR at page 139. Neither Ordinance 1 of 1969 was noticed which continued rule 182 nor P.O. 29 of 1972 was noticed which vested such property in the Government. Further the Ordinance IV of 1974 and V of 1974 which were repealed and re-enacted- being Act Nos. 45 and 46 of 1974 when a non-resident could dispose of his property with the approval of the Committee nor Ord. Nos. 92 and 93 of 1976 which repealed Act 45 and 46 of 1974 were considered in Benoy Bhusan.

42. In Act 93 of 1976 power was given to the Government to dispose of the property and nothing was left for making the settlement that such property was to be preserved till conclusion of peace. As has been noticed in R.J. Reuter Co. Ltd. versus Ferd Mulhens, Ali England Report, 1953 Volume II page 1160 that even such expression that arrangement to be made at the conclusion of peace, it could never be "such arrangement as to the contemplating giving back of this enemy property to German national". It is for the legislature to decide as to what is to be done with such property at the conclusion of peace but not for the court.

<u>43. To opine that such legislation intended "to protect and manage the property so that the original owners could get back their properties at the conclusion of peace" is to read something in law which is not there and especially in view of the amendment dated 2.11.65. The opinion is that such conclusion is not warranted by law.</u>

<u>44. In view of the above analysis of the legal position there is no hesitation in saying that since the Government did not cancel the contract by declaring it against the public interest the contract is alive and the machinery has been provided by the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance namely, the preservation of jurisdiction of Civil Court (section 16). The Civil Court had exercised its jurisdiction and passed the decree and the Custodian who stepped into the shoes of the original owner e.g. Hemnalini has power to transfer this property by way of executing kabala. Whatever little right that was left for the non-resident the subsequent legislation clarified the point that the Government had power to transfer or disposal of such properly vide Act 93 of 1976. If the Government had power of transfer, as provided by the Act, the next question is what prevents the Government to execute the document in pursuance of a decree of specific performance of contract Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed could not lay his hand on any such law.</u>

45. In the result, therefore, appeal is allowed. Judgment and order of the High Court Division are set aside and those of the trial court restored, and the plaintiff gets the Kabala in pursuance of the decree of the trial court There will be no order as to costs.

End.
