18. From the above agreements, it appears that the agreement dated 15.7.85 shall be treated and considered as a part of the agreement dated 8.3.85. It is stipulated that as per agreement dated 8.3.85 the respondent No. 1 was unable to get the mortgaged property released and take back the documents and papers from the Pubali Bank and the respondent No. 1 was unable to perform his part of the agreement as made earlier. Considering the circumstances they felt it necessary to enter into this further agreement which is part and parcel of the previous agreement. In paragraph 1 of the subsequent agreement it is stipulated that the respondent No. 1 has given an undertaking to the effect that by 31st March, 1986 from the date of execution of this agreement i.e. 15.7.85 the respondent No.1 shall get the mortgaged properties situated at 109 Hrishikesh Das Road with three storied building and the Printing Press namely, Jatiya Mudran and other machineries and connected features, released in favour of the petitioner No. 1 and the respondent No. 1 will hand over all the documents which were also with the Pubali Bank as collateral security. On such undertaking given by the respondent No.1 the petitioner had transferred all their rights and interests namely, their shares in the aforesaid company in favour of the respondent No. 1 and they waived all their rights as they had at the relevant time in the M/s Corn Flour Ltd, M/s Monospool Paper Products Ltd. and the properties of the company situated at Kamarkhali. In the previous agreement the sons and wife of the petitioner No. 1 were witnesses and in subsequent agreement their names have been specifically mentioned that they had transferred their shares in favour of the respondent No.1 as per terms of the agreement.

19. In the second part of Paragraph 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85 it is stipulated that if for any reason the respondent No.1 does not fulfill the undertaking he had taken or as per his undertaking if he does not hand over the mortgaged properties after releasing it from the said Pubali Bank within the specified time, or if he fails to fulfill his commitment, then the subsequent agreement dated 15.7.85 along with the agreement dated 8.3.85 would be considered as cancelled and according to the claim of the petitioner No. 1, respondent No. 1 will be liable for all compensation for damages. It is also stipulated in the last sentence of the agreement that in such a situation the petitioners will naturally be considered to be restored to their original right and title in the company. As regards this last sentence the respondent No.1 had taken objection to the effect that this is a subsequent alteration and addition and this is a forgery for which the entire agreement is void. I will consider this objection separately with regard to this last sentence later on.

20. Let me see first whether the petitioners have been able to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreements, or the respondent No. 1 had failed to perform his part of the agreements. The petitioners have categorically stated in their application that in pursuance of the aforesaid two agreements, though in the eye of law one agreement, the petitioners have fulfilled all the terms and conditions and they transferred all their shares in the company in favour of the respondent No. 1 and they had withdrawn the two money suits against the respondents. There was no monetary consideration for transferring these shares to respondent No. 1, rather only consideration was the terms and conditions of the agreement on which the petitioners transferred their shares to the respondent No. 1. In the affidavit-in-opposition, this statement of the petitioners has not been at all denied. Their assertion that they have waived all their rights and title in other properties as mentioned in the agreement has also not been denied by the respondents. So, from the application and affidavit-in-opposition and other papers filed by both the parties, it appears that the petitioners have fulfilled all the terms of the agreements as they were required to do.

21. Let me now consider how far the respondent No. 1 has been able to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreements which he was required to perform. It was stipulated in the agreement dated 8.3.85 that by 31st March, 1985 the respondent No. 1 would pay Tk. 5 lacs to the petitioner No. 1 and second installment of Tk.2,50,000.00 would be paid to the petitioner No.1 by 30th March, 1986 and last installment of Tk. 2,50,000.00 will be paid to the petitioner No. 1 by 30th July, 1986. Out of the total amount of Tk.10 lacs, it appears that the respondent No.1 had paid on different dates a sum of Tk. 6,10,000.00 which the petitioner No.1 also admitted. It is the case of the respondent No. 1 that he offered the money to the petitioner through one Rabindra Nath Chakraborty, but the petitioner No. 1 refused. From Annexure 40 to the affidavit in-opposition, it appears that on 8th of October, 1986 in the morning this RN Chakraborty went to the residence of petitioner No. 1 but he was not available. Then he approached his wife to tell Mr. Mohiuddin to contact him (RN Chakraborty). As Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed did not contact him, he went to the residence of Mohiuddin Ahmed on 13.10.86 and offered the money, but he said that he would not take this money. He further stated that probably in the third week of July, 1986 a sum of Tk. 25,000.00 was also given to Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed but he could not collect any money receipt for the same. In this connection, I may refer to the agreement that the last instalment was to be paid to the petitioner No. 1 by the respondent No. 1 by 30th July, 1986. From Annexure-39 to the affidavit-in-opposition, it appears that Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed on 15.5.86 received Tk. 10,000.00 and before that he took several amounts on different dates. After 15.5.86 there was no offer of money to the petitioner No. 1. Then only on 8th October, 1986 it is alleged that one R.N. Chakraborty went to the residence of Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed to give him Tk. 25,000.00, but the fact remains that 30th July, 1986 was the last and final date for the payment of last installment. So, from the document of the respondents and their statements it appears that the respondent No. 1 failed to pay Tk. 10,00,000.00 in total on or before 30th July, 1986 as per agreement made between himself and the petitioner No. 1. The respondent could not produce and evidence before this Court to show that respondent No. 1 had fulfilled the terms of the agreement as regards payment of Tk. 10 lacs within the stipulated time rather his own paper which has been annexed with the affidavit-in-opposition shows that he is a defaulter as he failed to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreement as regards the payment of Tk. 10 lacs to the petitioner No. 1 within the time fixed.

Let me now consider the second condition as regards releasing the properties of the petitioner No. 1 which were mortgaged to the Pubali Bank for taking loan for the respondent No. 2 company. It is stipulated in paragraph 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85 that by 31st March, 1986 from the date of the agreement the respondent No. 1 shall get the mortgaged properties released in favour of petitioner No. 1. The first sentence of paragraph No. 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85 runs in the following:

“ অত্র চুক্তিপত্র সাক্ষরের দিন হইতে আগামী ৩১ শে মার্চ, ১৯৮৬ তারিখের মধ্যেই ২য় পক্ষ ১ম পক্ষের উক্ত ১০৯, হৃশিকেশ দাস রোডস্থ তিনতলা পাকাবাড়ী......   ”

22. In this sentence the word “মধ্যেই” is very relevant and significant for the purpose of the present case. It appears that the respondent No.1 had given such an undertaking or taken such a responsibility that he must get the mortgaged house and press released from the Pubali Bank in favour of the petitioner No.1 by 31.3.86. There is no proviso or any other clause in the agreement by which or for which a lenient or different interpretation can be given to this undertaking which the respondent No.1 had taken and given. Now I am to consider whether the respondent No.1 acted in accordance with the terms of the contract and whether he had ever fulfilled the terms of his undertaking given in the agreement. In the affidavit-in-opposition, Annexure-41 is dated 22nd January, 1985. This IS a letter from the Deputy General Manager of the Head Office of Pubali Bank to the Assistant General Manager, Local Office of the Pubali Bank. This relates to the release of collateral securities of the properties mortgaged by Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed in favour of M/s. Paper Converting and Packaging Ltd. It is not very relevant as it was a correspondence made prior to the date of agreement. Annexure-42 to the affidavit-in-opposition is the Bank Guarantee of Tk. 25 lacs given by the National Bank Ltd. in favour of the company which was given to the Pubali Bank. It is also dated 2nd March, 1985 whereas the agreement was made on 8.3.85. So, this Bank Guarantee was also given before the date of agreement. Annexure-43 of the affidavit-in-opposition is dated 14th January, 1987. This is the letter written by the Managing Director, Pubali Bank Ltd., Head Office, Dhaka. The respondent No.1 stated that since he had purchased all shares of Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed and his sons and wife, he had undertaken all- the liabilities of Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed including those relating to Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, ICB, Pubali Bank, Ltd. which also included Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed's personal security which was offered and given in the interest of the company. In the event of any fresh undertaking if needed to cover the liabilities of Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed, Mr. Lutfur Rahman (respondent No. 1) agreed to do so. In view of the above, it is so cited that Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed may please be relieved from all his liabilities including his personal security offered in the interest of the bank. This letter was written on January 14, 1987, whereas a deadline of releasing the mortgaged property from Pubali Bank expired on 31st March, 1986. Obviously, it appears from the record that respondent No.1 failed to fulfill the second term of the agreement by not getting the house and the press released in favour of Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed by 31st March, 1986.

23. In the background of all the documents and papers submitted before the Court, Mr. M Nurullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that there was no violation of the terms of the aforesaid agreements by the petitioners and there was no allegation to that effect also. He further submits that the time is the essence of the contract and since the documents and papers produced before the Court have unmistakably shown that the respondent No.1 had failed to pay Tk. 10 lacs to the petitioner No.1 and also failed to get the mortgaged properties of the petitioner No.1 released from Pubali Bank within the stipulated time according to the terms of the agreements, the agreements stood cancelled by operation of the terms of the agreement and the petitioners reverted back to their original position as on 8.3.85.

24. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, on the other hand, submits that as regards payment of Tk.10 lacs, since the petitioner No.1 refused to take the money the respondent No.1 was unable to pay it. This submission of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed has not been substantiated by any paper on record. Rather the paper namely, the letter of Mr. RN Chakraborty, the Chief Accountant, dated 14.10.86 clearly shows that Tk.25,000.00 was offered after the last date of payment of installment as the last date was 30.7.86. Petitioner No. 1. and respondent No.1 are full brothers. Money was to be paid by the respondent No.1 to the Petitioner No.1 as per terms of the agreement. It is difficult to understand why Mr. RN Chakraborty was dragged in this matter of payment of money to the petitioner No.1. Respondent No.1 could have issued a cheque or bank draft in favour of the petitioner No.1 and sent it by registered post. If it was refused, then such a contention could be given some weight. Further, it could not be shown that by the last date i.e. 30.7.86 the respondent No.1 offered the remaining amount of Tk. 10 lacs to the petitioner No.1, because the alleged offer of Tk. 25,000.00 does not fulfill the terms of the agreement. Since the respondent No.1 failed to fulfill his own obligation as per terms of the agreement, he is not entitled to get any benefit out of it.

25. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed next submits that from the very beginning the respondent No.1 was trying hard to get the mortgaged properties released from Bank and to take back the documents and for that reasons respondent No.1 had to give Bank Guarantee of Tk. 25,00,000.00 of the National Bank on mortgaging his own property, but a third party namely the Pubali Bank had intervened in the matter in the meantime. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that as per agreement the respondent No.1 tried to get the mortgaged properties of the petitioner No.1 released from Pubali Bank and as such the respondent No.1 had not violated any terms of the agreement. It is difficult to accept the contention of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed. As per agreements the respondent No.1 was bound to get the properties released by 31st March, 1986. If he failed to do so the agreement would be considered to be cancelled because the specific condition to that effect was made in the agreement itself. Whether the respondent No.1 tried to get the properties released or not is immaterial, but it is to be considered whether he in fact got the properties released in favour of the petitioner No.1 within the fixed period in accordance with the terms of the agreement. I have found above that the respondent No.1 had failed to fulfill the terms of the agreement by not getting the mortgaged property released from Pubali Bank by 31st March, 1986. Mere endeavour to get the property released is not the condition, even the letter of the respondent No.1 vide Annexure 43 dated 14th January, 1987 shows that he was soliciting that Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed might be relieved of all his liabilities including his personal securities offered in the interest of the company. Annexure-44, a letter of Pubali Bank dated 5.2.87 shows that the properties would not be released unless the full repayment of the settled amount of the liabilities of the company was made. That means upto 5.2.87 the liabilities of the Pubali Bank had not been met up by the respondent No. 1. Even the letters of the respondent No.1 vide Annexure 48 and 49 of supplementary affidavit show that the respondent No.1 could not settle the liabilities of the Public Bank before 12th  March, 1990. In the certificate given vide Annexure-50 it appears that there was no statement of the Pubali Bank that since the liabilities are satisfied, the properties of petitioner No.1 are released. On the last day of argument Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed has produced a photo copy of a letter dated 12th May, 1990 of the Pubali Bank and submitted that the liabilities of the Pubali Bank as regards the respondent No. 2 has been liquidated but as regards other collateral securities against loan which do not belong to M/s. Paper Converting and Packaging Ltd. shall be taken up with the owner of the property Mr. Mohiuddin Ahmed in due course. All these are subsequent facts inasmuch as the due date expired on 31st March, 1986. Even the last letter of Pubali Bank dated 12.5.90 shows that the mortgaged properties of the petitioner No. 1 were not released.

26. Mr. M Nurullah, the learned Advocate, submits that the petitioner No.1 had not mortgaged his aforesaid property to Pubali Bank on taking any other personal loan. He further submits that though the two money suits were pending in the Court against the petitioner No.1 filed by Pubali Bank, in those two suits no order of attachment of the personal properties of the petitioner No.1 has been passed. So, these letters have been procured by the respondent No. 1 in collusion with the Pubali Bank and these letters cannot in any way affect the rights of the petitioners in their properties which had been mortgaged to the Pubali Bank. The said letters could not also prove that the respondent No. 1 fulfilled the terms within the stipulated time. I find force in the above contention of Mr. M Nurullah. Since the respondent No.1 totally failed to fulfill the terms of the agreements on two counts as discussed above, I hold that both the agreements stood cancelled in pursuance of the terms of the agreement itself.

27. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that the present application under section 38 of the Companies Act is not maintainable inasmuch as in the agreement the company was not a party and the petitioner Nos. 2-5 were not the signatories of the agreements and as such the petitioners are incompetent to invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 38 of the Companies Act. It is not disputed that the petitioner No.1 and respondent No.1 are two brothers. Petitioner No.1 was the Chairman of the Board of Directors and the respondent No.1 was the Managing Director. It is also not disputed that properties of the petitioner No.1 were mortgaged to the Pubali Bank for the aforesaid company respondent No. 2. Since misunderstanding cropped up between the two brothers, one brother and his sons and wife transferred their shares to the respondent No.1 on the terms and conditions as laid down in the two agreements. Petitioners were the real share-holders like the respondent No.1 in the company. This was some sort of package deal in between the members of the same family. Petitioner No.1 and respondent No.1 signed the agreements as parties and the sons and wife of the petitioner No.1 were the witnesses. In pursuance of the terms and conditions of the agreement petitioners sold their all shares to the respondent No.1 without any other monetary consideration excepting the terms and conditions laid down in the agreement. Since it was held above that the agreement stood cancelled for non-fulfillment of the terms and conditions of the agreements by the respondent No.1, petitioners are entitled to revert back to their original position and to have their shares back in the company as they had on 8.3.85. Originally the petitioners were the registered share-holders and now they are praying before this Court for restoring themselves to original position in the company. Section 38 of the Companies Act runs as follows:

"If-(a) the name of any person is fraudulently or without sufficient cause entered in or omitted from the register of members of a company; or

(b) default is made or unnecessary delay takes place in entering on the register the fact of any person having ceased to be a member the person aggrieved, or any member of the company, or the company, may apply to the court for rectification of the register.

<u>28. The petitioner Nos. 2-5 in the present case are parties on the basis of the agreement in which they were witnesses and the petitioner No.1 was the signatory. They transferred their shares to the respondent No.1 as per terms of the agreements without having any other consideration. Even in the second agreement, the names of the petitioner Nos. 2-5 have found place in paragraph No.1. For the reasons discussed above and in view of the provisions of section 38, I am of the view that the petitioners are competent to invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 38 of the Companies Act, although the company was not a party in the agreements. In the case of Sirish Chandra Das Vs. Sri Sri Cnhatteswari Debi Bigraha, 38 DLR (AD) 283, it is held that the consenting parties have got right to challenge the document if it is otherwise illegal. In the present case since the petitioner Nos. 2-5 are consenting parties and since they have been aggrieved for non-fulfillment of the terms of the agreements by the respondent No.1 they are also considered as aggrieved persons to come before this Court under section 38 of the Companies Act.</u>

29. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed further submits that since there are disputed questions of facts involving in the present case which cannot be resolved on filing affidavits, the petitioners are not entitled to invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 38 of the Act inasmuch as it is merely a summary proceeding. In every case the facts will be disputed as one party will allege and the other party will deny. But from the materials available on record and on the basis of the facts which in fact cannot be disputed, this Court can decide the matter under section 38 of the Act. No doubt it is a summary proceeding under section 38 of the Act but it is a discretion of the Court to see whether the point at issue can be disposed of and resolved on the basis of the materials available on record. If the case is complicated and very doubtful and if it appears that without resorting to some other procedure a case cannot be disposed of, this Court should not interfere with such a matter. But if it is apparent on the face of the records that legal rights of the parties are clear and the same can be settled on the basis of the materials on record, then this Court can interfere with the matter under section 38 of the Act In the present case it appears to me that the documents and papers filed by the parties are so clear that the rights of the parties can be settled on the basis of those papers and the case can be disposed of accordingly.

30. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed further submits that the shares were duly transferred to the respondent No.1 by the petitioners under section 34 of the Companies Act. So, it is a transaction passed and closed and it cannot be reopened. I am unable to accept the above submission of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed inasmuch as the above transfer of shares by the petitioners was subject to the terms and conditions of the agreements.

31. Mr. M Nurullah has referred to the case of AR Shaw Vs. The Diamond Rock Boring Company Ltd. 1877 QB Division (Vol. II), 463 and submits that their Lordships observed as follows:

Regarding jurisdiction of this Court:

"The Chief Baron read the later part of section 35. I cannot imagine any language better adopted for conferring a jurisdiction to decide disputes between two alleged members of a company in respect of the title to shares therein. I think, therefore, that the jurisdiction exists."

It is further held that:

"But the Joint Stock Companies Act 1857 section 9, greatly increased the effect of the earlier enactment, for it expressly gave power to decide questions of title arising between two or more alleged holders of shares.

It is further observed as follows:

"Looking at all the words of section 35 and giving them a reasonable construction, I think that the legislature intended to give the Court jurisdiction to make an order so as to decide questions of title, trusting to the discretion of the Court not to decide in this summary manner any intricate or difficult question of title; but that, if the Court thinks fit, they have jurisdiction to make the order in all cases."

32. In the case of United Planters and Traders Ltd. Vs. Md. Mosharraf Hossain Khan, 34 DLR 343, the learned Company Judge of this Court held that the provisions of section 38 are very wide and the Court has ample scope and power to grant relief and save the parties from being harassed and unnecessarily relegated to protracted litigation in a simple case.

<u>33. In the case of M/s Anath Bandhu Guha & Sons Ltd. 7 PLR (Dac) 159, their Lordships held as follows:</u>

<u>"We have set out the relevant provisions of law and the cases at length as not only this case was argued at some length, but also because we have not got many decisions of Pakistani Courts on this point though there is a large number of decisions of other countries, and we have no doubt that the provisions of section 38 of the Companies Act are very wide, and in appropriate cases give a Judge dealing with Company matters a very wide discretion in granting speedy relief to the holder of shares, as it has been held in Ex Parte AR Shaw's case, and also in a number of cases. It is not necessary for the Court to find that there has been actual default on the part of the Company, and even in cases other than that of default of the Company under section 38 the Court has ample scope and power to grant relief, and save the parties from being harassed, and unnecessarily relegated to protracted litigation in a simple case. It has even held that the jurisdiction given to the Court under section 38 of the Companies Act, is not limited to the cases mentioned in this section (section 35 of English Companies Act) vide Burns Vs. Siemens Bros. Buckley on the Companies Acts, 12th Edition, at page 261 says: "When there is no dispute as to a person being, or having ceased to be, a member, the summary jurisdiction under this section to compel the Company to perform the ministerial duty of entering the fact on the register is clear As between alleged share-holders and the Company, there are numerous cases in which this section has been used for determining the equities, although, if the case be one of difficulty and complication, the Court may refuse the motion without prejudice to an action being brought. As between the applicant and the Company, the Court will enforce the ministerial duty if the application shows a clear right; and will not readily refuse to proceed and leave an action to be brought."</u>

34. In my opinion the principle laid down in the aforesaid decisions is very much applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case and as such I find that there are no intricate and complicated questions of fact which will preclude this Court from deciding this case on merit and as such I find little substance in the contention of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed.

35. Let me now consider the objection raised by Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed as regards the last portion of paragraph 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85. According to Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the meaning and interpretation is that if the respondent No. 1 fails to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreements, the petitioner No.1 will be at liberty to go to the Court and pray for compensation for the alleged damages. Neither the petitioners can come under section 38 of the Companies Act before this Court nor even they are entitled to file a suit for specific performance of contract under the Specific Relief Act. It is difficult to accept the contention of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, because this is not the correct interpretation of the concluding portion of paragraph 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85. It has clearly prescribed that if within the stipulated time the respondent No. 1 fails to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreement, the agreement dated 15.7.85 along with agreement dated 8.3.85 shall stand cancelled and I have already held that for non-fulfillment of the terms and conditions by the respondent No.1 these two agreements stood cancelled and the petitioners reverted back to their original position as share-holders of the company. Not only that, the petitioners would get their rights and interests back as they had previously in the said company and in other properties as covered by those agreements.

36. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed lastly submits that the last sentence as contained in the agreement dated 15.7.85 was nothing but a forgery. He submits that in the draft agreement vetted by the Legal Adviser of the company there was no such sentence. The sentence runs as follows:

“ঐরুপ অবস্থায় কোম্পানীর প্রথম পক্ষ স্বাভাবিক ভাবেই পূর্বাস্থায় পূনঃ প্রতিষ্ঠিত হইয়াছেন বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে।”

37. The learned Advocate submits that this sentence was added by a separate typewriter subsequently and, on the face of it, it appears to be inserted later on with malafide intention. He submits that the last sentence has brought material alteration which has affected and changed the very intention and spirit of the agreement. Not only that, it has also completely changed the character of the agreement. Since it is done subsequently with mala fide intention and since it affected the very character of the agreement itself the entire agreement is void. So, the premium already obtained by the respondent No.1 out of the agreements will not be affected because of the fact that this forgery has been committed by the petitioners.

38. From Annexure-45 of the affidavit- in-opposition (alleged vetted draft agreement) it appears that at the bottom of page 1 it is written as "seen" and then some signature is put which is allegedly the signature of the Legal Adviser and then date was put as 10.8.85. From page No. 2 at bottom it appears that the word "seen" is there and below it the alleged signature of the Legal Adviser and then date was put as 15.8.85. This Annexure-45 is allegedly a draft agreement settled and vetted by the Legal Adviser on 10.8.85 but the second agreement between the two brothers was executed on 15.7.85. It is difficult to understand as to how this draft agreement was vetted by the Legal Adviser at a later dated on 10.8.85 whereas the final agreement was executed at an earlier date on 15.7.85. This is absolutely a concocted and frivolous document which the respondent No.1 has filed before this Court in order to mislead the Court. If the draft agreement allegedly vetted by the Legal Adviser is a concocted and frivolous one, the final agreement dated 15.7.85 stands valid and it cannot be challenged in any manner whatsoever. This alleged draft agreement was the only weapon relying upon which the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 is challenging the agreement dated 15.7.85 as being forged. Since the draft agreement has no legal basis, the final agreement dated 15.7.85 cannot be called a forged document. Moreover, the alleged draft agreement shows two different dates of vetting at two different pages.

39. In this connection it may be mentioned that in paragraph 11 of the affidavit-in-opposition the respondent No.1 has tried to make out a story of inserting the last sentence in the agreement dated 15.7.85 at a subsequent date. It is alleged that the petitioner No.1 got both the original and duplicate copies of the agreement dated 15.7.85 signed by the respondent No.1, but with malafide intention the petitioner No.1 did not hand over the duplicate copy of the agreement to the respondent No.1. Such allegations have been totally denied by the petitioners in paragraph 9 of their affidavit-in-reply slating that such allegations are totally false, concocted and motivated. It is difficult to believe this story as the respondent No.1 has tried to make out in paragraph 11 of the affidavit-in-opposition. Both the petitioner No.1 and the respondent No.1 had put their signatures and their eldest brother Shahabuddin Ahmed put his signature as witness in the agreement dated 15.7.85. Petitioner No.1 has stated that the duplicate copy of the agreement was given to the respondent No.1. After the agreement was executed the respondent NO.1 had done so many things and made so many correspondences in this matter.

Moreover, he took all the shares of the petitioners and got the same registered in the register of the company as per terms of the above agreement. He never raised any objection as regards the last sentence. For the first time before this Court he is now trying to make out a 3rd case which was nobody's case at any point of time. For the reasons stated above it is difficult to believe that the respondent No. 1 came to know about the addition of last sentence only after getting a copy of the application along with a copy of the agreement dated 15.7.85.

40. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that the first word of the last sentence starts from below after the last word of the previous sentence. Merely because the first word  “ঐরুপ” of the last sentence is typed a bit below the straight line of the previous sentence, it cannot be conclusively proved that this is a forgery. Rather, it appears that on 15.7.85 both the brothers namely, Mohiuddin Ahmed and Lutfur Rahman had put their signatures on the document itself and their eldest brother Shahabuddin Ahmed is one 'of the attesting witnesses. So, I find that the respondents have failed to produce any evidence before this Court to show prima facie that the last sentence was subsequently inserted and as such it is a forged document, rather the alleged draft agreement Annexure-45 allegedly vetted by the Legal Adviser appears to be a forged one.

<u>41. Mr. M Nurullah, the learned Advocate, submits that even if it is presumed, though not admitted, that the last sentence was added subsequently, it will not affect the merit of the agreement at all because it has not made any material alteration in the true intention and character of the agreement itself. He submits that if this sentence is deleted even then the agreement will remain as it is and it will not bring any different meaning to the terms of the agreement. I find substance in the above contention of Mr. Nurullah. If an alternation changes the character of a document and alters the rights, liabilities and legal position of the parties, in that case only it can be said that such an alteration is a material alteration which amounts to forgery and for such forgery the document may be treated as void. In this connection Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed has referred to the case of Nathu Lal and others Vs. Mt. Comti Kuar and others reported in AIR 1940 (PC) 160. In the aforesaid decision it is held by their Lordships of the Privy Council as follows :</u>

<u>"If an alteration (by erasure interlineations or otherwise) is made in a material part of a deed after its execution, by or with the consent of any party thereto or person entitled thereunder, but without the consent of the party of parties liable thereunder, the deed is thereby made void. The avoidance however is not ab initio or so as to nullify any conveyancing effect which the deed has already had; but only operates as from the time of such alteration and so as to prevent the person who has made or authorised the alteration and those claiming under him, from putting the deed in suit to enforce, against any party bound thereby who did not consent to the alteration, any obligation, covenant or promise thereby undertaken or made.</u>

<u>A material alteration is one which varies the rights, liabilities, or legal position of the parties ascertained by the deed in its original state or otherwise varies the legal effect of the instrument as originally expressed, or reduces to certainty some provision which was originally unascertained and as such void, or may otherwise prejudice the party bound by the deed as originally executed.</u>

<u>The effect of making such alteration without the consent of the party bound is exactly the same as that of cancelling the deed. The avoidance of the deed is not retrospective and does not revest or reconvey any estate or interest in property which passed under it. And the deed may be put in evidence to prove that such estate or interest so passed or for any other purpose than to maintain an action to enforce some agreement therein contained."</u>

<u>42. In this decision the principle has been laid down as to how far an alteration in a document can be treated as forgery. It appears from the above decision that if the alteration varies the rights and liabilities of the parties and changes the legal character of a document, it may be treated as forgery. But the above decision is not of any assistance to Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed inasmuch as the principle laid down there is not applicable in the present case. The alleged alteration is by way of addition of the last sentence in the agreement. In my view, such addition cannot be called a material alteration inasmuch as it does not alter the rights and liabilities of the parties and change the true and legal character of the document viz, the agreement dated 15.7.85. Further if the alleged addition is deleted, in my view, the true intent and character of the document will not be changed, because the actual consequence for non-fulfilment of the terms of the agreement is very much there i.e. if the respondent No.1 fails to fulfil the terms of the agreement, then the two agreements together will stand cancelled. In fact both the agreements stood cancelled on and from 31.7.86 for the default of the respondent No.1. Without the alleged last sentence the agreement dated 15.7.85, in my opinion, stands as a full-fledged and self-contained document. So, the contention of forgery as raised by Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed has no substance.</u>

43. Mr. M Nurullah further submits that the respondent No. 1 has in fact committed fraud upon his own full brother, because by giving false assurance and baseless hope he made his brother and other family members transfer their all shares of company to him knowing full well that it would not be possible for him to fulfil his commitment within the fixed time. During pendency of the case only on 12.5.90 respondent No.1 made full payment towards the liabilities of Pubali Bank which he ought to have done on or before 30.7.86 as per terms of agreements. Mr. Nurullah further submits that the fraudulent motive of the respondent No.1 in fact put the petitioners on the street. Is find force in the above contention of Mr. Nurullah.

44. From the materials on record, it appears to me that this is merely an allegation that the last sentence was an outcome of forgery but the respondent No.1 has failed to make out a case of forgery. I have given my anxious consideration on this last sentence as well as on the other parts of the agreement and it appear to me that it is very much consistent with the other parts, and the element of forgery is totally absent. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record I am of the view that the petitioners have been able to make out their case and as such they are entitled to have the relief as prayed for in the application.

45. Before conclusion, I cannot but make certain observations. It has already been seen that as per agreement the petitioners had already parted with their shares in favour of respondent No. 1 and withdrawn the pending suits. They fulfilled all their obligations. After performing their part of the contract, they have been running from door to door for getting their properties back. On the other hand, the respondent No.1 has been merrily enjoying the shares of the petitioners in the company for last 5 (five) years at' Managing Director and leisurely defending the cases. Such a person shall not be allowed to enjoy the premium of the agreement which has already stood cancelled because of non-fulfillment of the terms by the respondent No. 1 himself. In fact, taking advantage of sincerity and simplicity of his own elder brother (Mohiuddin) the respondent No. 1 has brought him and his family members on the street because, on the one hand, the petitioners were made to transfer all their shares infavour of the respondent No.1 and, on the other hand, their residential house and the source of income viz, the printing press are still under mortgage with Pubali Bank. Now the respondent No.1 has come up before this Court with a new case that the petitioners, as per agreement, may sue for compensation only and nothing else. It does not look nice to hear it at least from the mouth of the respondent No.1. Such a person does not deserve to have discretionary relief from the Court.

In the result, this application is allowed with costs and the respondents are directed to rectify the share-register of the company by inserting the names of the petitioners in place of the name of respondent No.1 in respect of the shares which the petitioners had held on 8.3.85 in the above company.

End.

case_source: The eviction of the petitioner and his family from his property at 53, Aga Mashi Lane, Dhaka, by the respondents on 15.3.86 by deploying a contingent of Police Force vide Memo. No. IX/AP-SUK 10/82/413 dated 15.3.86 of the Ministry of Works.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J. :- This Rule Nisi obtained under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calls upon the respondents to show cause as to why the enlistment of the petitioner's property situated at 53, Aga Mashi Lane, Dhaka as an abandoned property and the petitioner's eviction therefrom on 15.3.83 by use of force shall not be declared to be without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect, being mala fide, illegal, without jurisdiction, colourable exercise of power and violative of tile principles of natural justice.

<u>2. The petitioner claims to have purchased the property in question from one Musammat Nek Khatun Begum by registered sale deed No. 4134 dated 19.6.80, a photocopy of which is Annexure L. After the said purchase, the petitioner mutated his name in the Government's revenue record, municipal record, WASA and electricity authorities and paid ground rent, municipal taxes, WASA and electricity bills regularly and was in peaceful possession thereof. Photocopies of the records of right, rent receipt, municipal tax receipt, WASA and electric bills are Annexures M, N, O, P and Q respectively. The petitioner alleges that while possessing the property partly in person and partly through tenants. the petitioner developed litigation with his tenants and also with next-door neighbour Mr. Khondker Mushtaq Ahmed, a former President of Bangladesh. The petitioner alleges that Mr. Khondker Mushtaq Ahmed constructed a building on the boundary wall of the petitioner and that is the cause of dispute with him. The petitioner also asserted that from the date of promulgation of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972, (P.O. No. 16 of 1972) upto 15.3.36 the petitioner's predecessor-in-interest Musammat Nek Khatun Begum and thereafter the petitioner were in continuous and peaceful possession of the said property as its true and lawful owner. It was never declared as an abandoned property.</u>

3. On 15.3.86 at about 10/10-30 a.m. a contingent of about 100 police force led by the Officer-in-Charge of the Kotwali Police Station, Dhaka. the respondent No. 3 Mr. Kamrul Hassan, Authorised Officer & Section Officer, Ministry of Works and the respondent No. 4 Mr. Dewan Shah Alam, Sub-Divisional Engineer, P.W.D., Maintenance Division (A.P.) surrounded the petitioner's property and asked the petitioner to vacate the same forthwith. Upon the petitioner's queries the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 gave him a copy of a letter being Memo. No. Sec-X/AP-SUK-10/82/413 dated 15.3.86 (Annexure R) purportedly written to the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka Metropolitan Police by the Deputy Secretary, Abandoned Property Section of the Ministry of Works, requesting him to provide a contingent of police force consisting of 100 police personnel on 17.3.86 at about 10-00 a.m. to evict the unauthorised occupants from the abandoned house at 53, Aga Mashi Lane, Dhaka. From the said Annexure R, the petitioner came to know for the first time that he was an unauthorised occupant in his own house which he purchased lawfully from its true and lawful owner 6 years ago. The petitioner requested the respondent Nos 3 and 4 without success to allow him some time to make representations to the higher authorities. They made a list of the articles in the house and asked the police personnel to throw them out on the street, which they did, causing colossal damage to the petitioner. The respondent Nos. 3 and 4 along with the police personnel violated the privacy of the petitioner's family who are religious and who observe strict pardah. They threw out the petitioner, his family members and their belongings on the street and the respondents took over possession of the petitioner's property by use of sheer force.

3A. The respondent Nos.3 and 4 and the police officer present noted down the eviction of the petitioner and taking over of the petitioner's property on a sheet of paper and all of them signed the same. The petitioner managed to obtain a photocopy thereof which is Annexure F. It is the contention of the petitioner that from 26.2.1972 upto 15.3.86 neither the petitioner nor his predecessor-in-interest was ever informed that the petitioner's property was an abandoned property. The Government never exercised any act of possession or management or treatment of the said property as an abandoned property. No opportunity was given to the petitioner to show cause as to why he shall not be evicted from his own property. The property cannot under any stretch of imagination be declared as an abandoned property. The petitioner went to the Ministry of Works on 16.3.86 and inquired as to the reason of his eviction, but he received no satisfactory answer. The officers of the Ministry failed to show any paper to the petitioner to the effect that the property was ever declared as an abandoned property. The petitioner alleges that there cannot be a more grave instance of executive high-handedness and abuse and misuse of public authority than the present one.

Having failed in his attempt to obtain restoration of his property the petitioner obtained the present Rule.

The petitioner has traced the history of ownership of the property in question for about a century to which we shall revert later on.

4. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1, it has been stated that the property in question became abandoned on the promulgation of P.O. No. 16 of 1972. It specifically came to the knowledge of the respondent No. 1, the Secretary, Ministry of Works on a survey report dated 15.8.83 made by a Special Survey Team. Accordingly, Notice in Form II was issued against the petitioner vide Memo. No. Sec-X/Suk-10/82/429 dated 30.5.85 directing the petitioner to surrender possession of the property to the respondents within 7(seven) days of the service of the notice or to show cause against surrender within the said period. The notice was duly served upon the petitioner but he he did rot respond to the same. At the time of survey the petitioner could not produce non-option certificate of the owner Musammat Nek Khatun Begum. Nor he could show any clearance certificate regarding sale or the Nationality Certificate of Musammat Nek Khatun Begum. It has been asserted in the affidavit-in-opposition that Musammat Khatun Begum was a non-local and she left Bangladesh during liberation movement deserting the house and never came back. The petitioner was given chance on several occasions to vacate the house and to surrender vacant possession of the same to the respondents who have not violated any law and rules nor the privacy of the petitioner's family. Regarding the document of purchase of the petitioner (Annexure L) it has been asserted that this is a false sale deed and at the time of its execution Musammat Nek Khutun Begum was not present in Bangladesh.

5. By filing an affidavit-in-reply, the petitioner has controverted the averments made in the affidavit-in-opposition. It has been stated that Musammat Nek Khatum Begum was enlisted as a voter as is evident from the Voters List printed and published by the Election Commission on 7.12.76. A photocopy of the said Voters List is Annexure T. Musammat Nek Khatun Begum was present in Bangladesh in 1980 when she sold the property to the petitioner and as further evidence thereof the petitioner enclosed photocopy of an assessment order dated 20.2.80 in respect of the assessee Musammat Nek Khatun passed by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Dhaka, Circle-T, Dhaka (Annexure V).

6. In the Writ Petition, the petitioner has traced the devolution of the property in question for about a hundred years. The property originally belonged to one Siddheswari Debi of Kayettully, Dhaka. She sold the said property to one Sonatan Nielsen by registered sale deed No. 3859 for the year 1895. Sonatan Maisan sold the property to Du lat Maisani by registered sale deed No. 2372 for the year 1898. After her death, her successors-in-interest sold the property to Kali Mohan Das by registered sale deed No. 3446 for the bear 1906. Kali Mohan Das sold it to Sreemati Sukhada Sundary Shome by registered sale deed No. 1387 dated 15.3.1914 (photocopy is Annexure A). The said property was marked as plot No. 146 under khatian No. 15837 in Mouza Shahar Dhaka. After the preparation of C.S. Khatian Sreemati Sukhada Sundary Shome was recorded as owner thereof. Photocopies of the C.S. map and C.S. Khatian are Annexures B and C respectively. The successive heirs of Sreemati Sukhada Sundary Shome exchanged the said property with the properties of the petitioner's predecessor-in-interest Musammat Nek Khatun Begum situated at 13 Mominpur, Alipore, District 24 Parganas, West Bengal, India by registered deed of exchange No. 1162 dated 10.2.59 (photocopy of the deed of exchange is Annexure D). Musammat Nek Khatun Begurn mutated her name in the Government's revenue records and paid rents upto 1930. Photocopies of S.A. Khatian and rent receipts are Annexures E and F respectively. Musammat Nek Khatun Begum also mutated her name in the municipal records, WASA and Electricity authority and paid Municipal taxes, WASA and electric bills since the day of acquisition of her title in the said property upto 1980. The municipal and other records are Annexures G, H, I and J. Musammat Nek Khatun Begum not only possessed the said property personally but also let out a part thereof under a written lease deed, photocopy of which is Annexure K. At the time of hearing Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner produced before us the original copies of all the Annexures A-V for our inspection and satisfaction.

<u>7. As against this impressive array of century-old documents of title all that the respondent No. 1 has asserted in the affidavit-in-opposition is that the aforesaid facts of devolution of property are not known to the said respondent and that the said respondent has no comment to make upon the said story of the petitioner. The respondent No. 1 has only asserted that the petitioner has created a false deed only to grab the property.</u>

<u>8. In view of the succinct nature of the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 1, we asked Mr. Md. Delwar Hossain learned Assistant Attorney General to place before us the relevant file of the Ministry of Works for our inspection. We regret to say that it makes a dismal reading.</u>

<u>9. There was a house to house survey conducted by a Survey Team which submitted a report on 15.12.83. In the remarks column it has been stated that the present occupant (i.e., the petitioner) purchased the land along with the two-storied building from the original owner (i.e., Musammat Nek Khatun Begum) under a deed mentioned in column 8. (This is the same deed as Annexure L). It has been further stated that the original owner was a "non local and Urdu speaker" whose whereabouts are not known to the occupant. "Probably she left the country for good". The occupant could not produce the following :-1) Non-option Certificate. 2) Clearance Certificate and 3) Nationality Certificate. Finally, in the remarks column there is a remark that the house seems to be abandoned within the meaning of PO No. 16 of 1972.</u>

<u>10. In the Government file, we also find a copy of a notice allegedly issued to the petitioner by the respondent No. 3 vide Memo No. Sec-X/Suk-10/82/829 dated 305.85 directing the petitioner to surrender possession of the property to the respondents within 7 (seven) days of the service of the notice, stating that the property is an abandoned property. There is an endorsement that the notice was served, but by whom, when and how has not been noted down. There is no signature of the petitioner on the body of the copy of the notice. The assertion of the respondent No.1 that the petitioner received a copy of the notice has not been substantiated. What is more, there is absolutely no order from any authority whatsoever on perusal of the report date 15.12.83 of the survey team that the Government is satisfied that the property is an abandoned property. The Survey team merely performed the investigative functions of the Government, but the team has no authority to declare any property as an abandoned property.</u>

<u>11. It appears that some lower level officers, without referring the file to the higher officers, were deciding between themselves as to what property was to be pounced upon as an abandoned property. Between themselves they were usurping the functions of the Government as the satisfying authority. The decision to declare the property as an abandoned property, was not taken by any higher officer of the Government. No responsibility for this decision was taken by any officer of the Government. In the affidavit-in-opposition and in the file, too, there is total absence of any decision in this regard.</u>

<u>12. Next we find on the record a photocopy of an application dated 11.2.86 addressed to the Inspector General of Police signed by 50 persons alleging, inter alia, that the petitioner had obtained possession of the property in question by fake and forged documents and that he was a smuggler. He had indulged in litigation and was creating disturbances in the locality and so the property in question should be taken over by the Government and the petitioner should be punished after seizure of his passport. Among the signatories to this application is one Khandker Mushtaq Ahmed of 54, Aga Mashi Lane, Dhaka, the next-door neighbour of the petitioner who has alleged enmity with his said neighbour.</u>

13. Next we find a slip pad of the Minister, Ministry of Works, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh where the following comments are written in hand without any initial or signature:-

"Minister

Ministry of Works

Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh

Noor Hossain

53, Aga Mashi Lane, Dhaka is an abandoned property. This individual should (sic) by evicted immediately and the house should be allotted to Democratic League."

<u>14. It appears that martialling of a huge contingent of police force for summary eviction of the petitioner from his own property is a sequel to these extra-legal developments.</u>

<u>15. There seems to be absolutely no material whatsoever that any serious effort was made to ascertain as to whether NIusammat Nek Khatun Begum left the country before, after or on the promulgation of P.O. No.16 of 1972 or whether the petitioner is an unauthorized occupant thereof. There is also no material that the petitioners’ document, of title (Annexure L) is a fake and forged document. No authorised person of the Government took the burden of satisfying himself that the property is an abandoned property. Nobody cared to inquire from the petitioner as to on what authority he was enjoying the property. He was never given an opportunity to show his documents of title to any authority. The property was never declared as an abandoned property. In such circumstances the sudden and surreptitious taking over of possession is a blatant interference with the right of quiet and peaceful enjoyment of a citizen's property. This is executive high handedness at its worst.</u>

<u>16. The public authorities have allowed themselves to be used or abused to further the private interests of others. They have not acted in the public interest. They have misused their powers in a most reprehensible manner arbitrarily and male fide. It is action such as this which leaves a bitter taste in the mind and brings the actions of constituted authorities into disrepute and disaffection. We only hope that the Government machinery will purge itself of these overzealous functionaries, high and low, and restore a minimum modicum of decency, fair play and propriety in discharging the affairs of the Republic. If occurrences such as this arc frequent and rampant then it will soon be an uninhabitable society. No citizen's property will be safe from covetous eyes.</u>

<u>17. We have no manner of doubt that in the absence of any contradiction the petitioner has succeeded in establishing in this Court that he has prima facie and unassailable ownership and enjoyment of the property in question. Their is absolutely no material that Musammat Nek Khatun Begum left Bangladesh at any time prior to the sale of the property to the petitioner. Her name was included in the Voters List in 1976 and in 1980, she was an income tax assessee. There is nothing to show that the petitioner created a forged document of title. On the face of these uncontroverted facts the law of abandoned property can have no manner of application to the property in question and there cannot be any earthly reason to disturb the petitioner in the peaceful enjoyment of his property. A manifest injustice and a severe wrong have been done to the petitioner by the impugned action which needs to be disapproved of in the strongest possible terms and in the interest of justice the petitioner should be restored to possession forthwith.</u>

<u>18. Mr. Mr. Delwar Hossain, learned Assistant Attorney General submits that under section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 the petitioner has an alternative remedy to make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the property from the list of abandoned property. The submission is simply untenable because (section 7 applies to the list of buildings which have been published in the Official Gazette.) Admittedly, 53, Aga Mashi Lane, Dhaka is not a listed property under Section 5 of the said Ordinance.</u>

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with costs which we assess at Tk. 2,000 (Taka two thousand) only. It is declared that the enlistment of the petitioner's property situated at 53, Aga Mashi Lane, Dhaka as an abandoned property and the petitioner's eviction therefrom on 15.3.86 by use of force have been made without lawful authority and are of no legal effect, being malafide, illegal, without jurisdiction, colourable exercise of power, violative of the principles of natural justice, void and inoperative.

We further direct the respondents to restore the petitioner to vacant possession of his said property within 7(seven) days from the service of a copy of this judgment to the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, who represents Bangladesh in the petition.

A.K M. Sadeque, J.—I agree.

End.

parties:
Sheikh Ahmed & ors ----- Petitioners 
Vs. 
Abdul Alim ----- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman, J: This Rule at the instance of the defendants-petitioners Nos. 1 to 3 is directed against the judgment and decree passed by Mr. Alauddin Sardar, Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 231 of 1980 reversing those of Mr. Md. Ali Khan, Munsif-in-Charge, 4th Court, Patiya in Other Suit No. 85 of 1978.

2. The facts relevant are these: The plaintiff Abdul Alim filed a suit for permanent injunction against the petitioners one Kamaluddin and his vendor. The plaintiffs case was that he purchased 26 sataks of land described in the schedule to the plaint from the defendant Kamaluddin by registered kabala dated 22.3.72 and has been in possession thereof since then and he also mutated his name in the recent settlement record and has been paying rents to the government. His further case was that defendant Nos. 1 to 3, the present petitioners, without having right title and interest threatened the plaintiff to dispossess from the land in dispute.

3. The petitioners who are the defendants filed written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to their father Md. Ishaque and on his death the disputed land devolved upon them and his step-brother Kamaluddin the vendor of the plaintiff. Their case was also that Kamaluddin was insane and his where about was unknown and the kabala was a forged document. The land in dispute belonged to the four sons of Md. Ishaque and Kamaluddin had no right to transfer more than his share in disputed land.

4. The learned Munsif on contest dismissed the suit. The plaintiffs appeal against that decree was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge.

5. Mr. M Fazlul Karim, in support of the Rule, submitted that the defendants-petitioners were in exclusive possession of the land in suit which was adjacent to their homestead where they grew different crops and as such the Court of appeal below was wrong in decreeing the suit reversing the judgment of the trial Court as in the DP Khatian Ext. A series the land was recorded in the name of the defendants-petitioners. It was also contended by him that Kamaluddin was a minor at the time of the purchase of the disputed land and he was a benamdar and had no right to transfer the entire land in favour of opposite party and no title has accrued to the opposite party under the kabala dated 22.3.72 in question Ext. A(1). He submitted that as the petitioners were in possession of the disputed land which is recorded in DP Khatian in their name and as Kamaluddin was only a co-sharer in the disputed land the lower appellate Court illegally decreed the suit as a whole. The learned Advocate for the petitioners further submitted that the land being ejmali property and other co-sharers being in possession jointly with the plaintiff-opposite party the decree for permanent injunction for the entire land is not sustainable in law as because a co-sharer cannot deprive other co-sharers from enjoyment of the property and the plaintiff-opposite party at best is entitled to a decree to the extent of his share of the land in dispute.

6. Mr. AKM Abdul Hakim, the learned Advocate appearing in opposition to the Rule, submitted that the Court of appeal below on a proper consideration of the exhibits namely Kabala Ext. A(1) dated 22.3.72, Ext. 3 series the rent receipts and Ext. A series, the PWs and BS Khatians and also considering oral evidence of the PWs and the DWs came to a finding that the plaintiff proved his case of exclusive possession in the disputed land. This finding as to possession being based on evidence on record can not be set aside, he submitted. It was further argued by him that it is not correct that a co-sharer in exclusive possession of a property is not entitled to get a decree for permanent injunction against the defendants until institution of a partition suit. He further submitted that even if transferee from a co-sharer is found in exclusive possession of the entire land which has been transferred to him in which others are also cosharers the purchaser is entitled to get a decree for permanent injunction against the other co-sharers without bringing a suit for partition. Mr. Hakim in support of his contention cited the case of Ahmed Miaji and others Vs. Eakub Ali and others, 12 DLR 708 and Muhammad Muzaffar Khan Vs. Muhammad Yusuf Khan, 11 DLR (SC) 78. I shall presently consider the decisions.

7. The instant suit is a suit for permanent injunction. In a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is required to prove his possession in the land in suit. For the purpose of determination of possession in such a suit the Court is required to arrive at a finding as to possession of the parties in the disputed land. No doubt it can look into the question of title incidentally. In this case the plaintiff sought permanent injunction in respect of 13 sataks of land appertaining to RS plot No. 457 and 13 sataks of land appertaining to RS plot No. 456. The plaintiff's claim is based on Kabala Ext. 1(a) dated 22.3.1972. In support of his case the plaintiff filed the kabala Ext. 1(a), the rent receipts Ext. 3 series showing payment of rent in respect of the land in suit and also examined witnesses including himself as PW1, PW2 is one Abul Faiz, the scribe of the kabala, PW3 is Rustam Ali Khan and PW4 is Siddique Ahmed. While defendants in support of their case filed certain documents namely Ext.A series, the PS and the BS Khatians and also examined witnesses. Defendant No. 1 was examined as DW 1 while DW 2 was one Mokbul Ali.

8. From a careful examination of the judgment of the lower appellate Court it appears that if first found that Md. Ishaque, father of the defendants Nos. 1 to 4 purchased the suit land from RS recorded owners in the benami of his eldest son Kamaluddin, the vendor of the present opposite party Abdul Alim. Secondly, he found that there was no evidence on record to support the case of the defendants that Kamaluddin was insane. He also found that the kabala Ext. 1(a) executed by Kamaluddin in favour of the present opposite party Abdul Alim was not a forged document and the lower appellate Court also found that Kamaluddin did not challenge the kabala executed by him in favour of Abdul Alim. But the lower appellate Court held that Kamaluddin was a benamdar of his father Ishaque and he was entitled to inherit to the extent of 6-1/2 sataks of land out of the disputed land.

<u>9. Now, let us pass on to the question of possession. It appears that the lower appellate Court, on consideration of both oral and documentary evidence, came to the finding that the defendants could not prove their possession by examining one Obaidul Hoque and one Serajul Hoque through whom defendants were in possession of the suit land. The lower Court did not place any reliance upon the uncorroborated evidence of defendant No.1 to the effect that the defendants were in possession of the disputed land through Obaidul Huq and Serajul Haque as the defendants failed to examine those persons in support of their possession in the disputed land. The lower appellate Court with regard to the statement of DW 2 Mokbul Ali observed that in cross-examination the DW2 admitted that he could not say the name of the cultivators of the suit land. In view of the evidence on record as to possession the lower appellate Court came to the finding that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land. It seems to me that the aforesaid finding is based on solid foundation and I do not find any error of law in reaching such a finding by the lower appellate Court. As from evidence it is found by the lower appellate Court that the opposite party recorded his name in the recent records of right and has been paying rents and are is possession in the entire disputed land. I have no occasion to hold that this finding on possession by the lower appellate Court is not a proper finding of reversal. Although the lower appellate Court found that the opposite party is entitled to the extent of .06 1/2 acres of land out of the entire disputed land but for that matter it cannot be said that the defendants were in ejmali possession of the disputed land with the plaintiff in view of the finding that the plaintiff is in exclusive possession of the disputed land. Therefore the contention of Mr. Karim that plaintiff and the defendants were in ejmali possession and the plaintiff can only retain his possession to the extent of his share i.e. to say in 0.06-1/2 acres of land, can hardly be accepted. The contention must fail. Now let me consider the question as to whether a plaintiff who is a co-sharer in respect of a plot of land and is found in exclusive possession of the entire land can maintain a suit for permanent injunction against the other co-sharers. The paramount consideration which falls for consideration in a suit for permanent injunction is whether the plaintiff has been successful in proving his case of exclusive possession. No doubt the question of title may be looked into incidentally but decision on title in a suit for permanent injunction is not guiding principle for holding that the suit is not maintainable without partition suit. Where a plain-tiff purchases the disputed land from his vendor of which his vendor is a co-sharer only and there are others also co-sharers of the sold land to the plaintiff and where on evidence in suit of permanent injunction it is found that the plaintiff is in exclusive possession of the entire land, I am of the opinion that the suit for permanent injunction is quite maintainable without instituting a suit for partition. It is unfortunate that in this case the lower appellate Court while deciding the suit for permanent injunction entered into the question of title although prima facie on the face of the kabala itself the plaintiff has proved his title, more so when the lower appellate Court itself has observed that the vendor of plaintiff did not challenge the kabala. In this suit the finding regarding title of plaintiff to the extent of 6-1a sataks is irrelevant. However, if the defendants are aggrieved by the transfer in question they have a remedy for redress of their grievance in law in a properly constituted suit for relief or reliefs and to establish their title in the disputed land. In the instant case it has been found by the lower appellate Court that plaintiffs vendor Kamaluddin had 1/4th share in the disputed land but also the lower appellate Court on evidence on record found that the plaintiff was in exclusive possession of the disputed land. Unless and until a suit for partition is instituted, on the face of the finding on possession of the plaintiff arrived at by the lower appellate Court, I hold that the plaintiff can not be evicted from possession of the disputed land to the extent of the share of other co-sharers. Now let me consider in this context the case of Ahmed Miaji and others Vs. Eakub Ali Munshi and others, 12 DLR 708 referred to by Mr. Hakim. In that case it had been held by the learned Chief Justice:</u>

<u>"It is no doubt true that the finding of both the Courts below is that there was no partition by metes and bounds amongst the cosharers in exclusive possession of specific plot of land should be dispossessed by another co-sharer. If any such co-sharer is dispossessed from his specific land certainly he has got the right to recover possession of the land he was dispossessed. If anybody is aggrieved by such exclusive possession of a portion of joint land let him go to the  partition suit for his remedy but so long that is  not done then the possession of the co-sharer of the specific land must be respected, subject to the determination of their question of title."</u>

<u>In Muhammad Muzaffar Khan's case 11 DLR (SC) 78 it was held by SA Rahman, J. that alienation of specific plots transferred to the vendee would only entitle the latter to retain possession of them till such time as an actual partition by metes and bounds takes place between the co-sharers. I am fortified in my view by the aforesaid judicial pronouncements of both the Supreme Court of Pakistan and the High Court of East Pakistan in holding that the present suit for permanent injunction simpliciter is maintainable without a suit for partition and the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land on the finding of the lower appellate Court is to be retained.</u>

10. I do not find any reason whatsoever to interfere with the judgment and decree impugned before me. I affirm the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court.

The result is the Rule is discharged. No order as to costs.

End.
